t: Over 63% of MFS patients exhibit scoliosis exceeding 10 degrees, often with associated thoracic lordosis, lumbar kyphosis, spondylolisthesis, dural ectasia, and pedicle dystrophy.
Young MFS patients show lower than average bone mineral density at the lumbar spine and femur, which tends to decrease further over time.
Muscle mass measured by DXA is decreased in children with MFS and worsens from childhood to adulthood compared to healthy age-matched controls.
The incidence of fractures is higher in children with MFS than in the general population of the same age and location, attributed to low bone mineral density.
Intracranial aneurysm and intracranial dissection prevalence rates in MFS were found to be 14% and 3%, respectively.
Patients with MFS are more likely to experience significant stress, anxiety, and depression, with a decreased existential level of satisfaction impacting quality of life and social relationships.

FBN1 mutations are classified into haploinsufficiency (HI) mutations (about one-third), causing reduced fibrillin-1 protein, and dominant-negative (DN) mutations (two-thirds), which produce abnormal fibrillin-1 that impairs ECM function.
FBN1 mutations located within the middle region of the gene (exons 24-32) correlate with earlier disease onset and a more severe MFS phenotype.
Expression levels of the extracellular matrix metalloproteinase inducer (EMMPRIN) significantly correlate with the severity of thoracic aortic disease in MFS.

A clinical randomized trial showed losartan decreased the average rate of aortic root dilation in adult MFS patients, independent of age, sex, blood pressure, aortic root size, FBN1 mutation status, or concurrent beta-blocker use.

A mid-1990s randomized trial demonstrated that prophylactic beta-blockade with propranolol slowed the rate of aortic dilatation and onset of aortic complications in MFS, establishing beta-blockers as standard preventive treatment.
A recent meta-analysis found no evidence of clinical benefit from long-term beta-blockade in people with MFS.
Compared to beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors do not significantly attenuate aortic growth velocity, though they demonstrated superiority in improving aortic distensibility and stiffness.
The risk of aortic dissection (type A or B) is eight times increased in pregnant MFS women compared to never-pregnant MFS women.
More than 90% of patients with classic-type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome harbor a heterozygous mutation in genes encoding type V collagen, COL5A1 and COL5A2.

Specific heterozygous arginine-to-cysteine substitution mutations in COL5A1 (c.934C>T/p.Arg312Cys, c.1720C>T/p.Arg574Cys, c.3277C>T/p.Arg1093Cys) confer high vascular fragility and rupture risk, mimicking the vascular type of EDS.

Vascular type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in COL3A1, characterized by arterial rupture/dissection under age 40, sigmoid colon rupture, and tissue friability with high surgical risk.

Screening of 765 patients with adult-onset thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection (TAAD) for copy number variants identified a recurrent 16p13.1 duplication in 1% of TAAD cases compared with 0.09% of controls, indicating incomplete-penetrance risk for thoracic aortic disease.
Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) can share skeletal habitus, low muscle mass, and mitral valve prolapse with MFS, with MVP reported in up to 55% of Klinefelter cases.

Connective tissue disorders including Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, and familial thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection syndrome are listed as recognized risk factors for acute aortic dissection.

A 40-year-old male with hypertension and polysubstance abuse (cocaine, methamphetamine, alcohol) but no Marfan syndrome, connective tissue disorder, or family history presented with an atypical painless acute thoracic aortic dissection extending from the aortic root to the diaphragmatic hiatus, manifesting only as dyspnea and cough rather than the classic tearing chest/back pain.
Laboratory workup in this patient with painless AAD showed markedly elevated NT-proBNP, elevated CRP, and rising leukocytosis, alongside normal troponin, despite the absence of chest pain.
In a prior international registry of over 7,300 AAD cases, cocaine use was implicated in 1.8% of patients.
A cited prior study reported a statistically significant association between amphetamine abuse and acute aortic dissection.

Most previously reported cases of painless aortic dissection occurred in elderly patients (>65 years) with comorbidities such as hypertension and diabetes, or in patients with predisposing genetic conditions such as Marfan syndrome, contrasting with this younger patient without such typical risk factors.
Loss-of-function defects in the TNXB gene cause Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
CAH-X syndrome, a contiguous gene deletion of TNXB and CYP21A2 causing hypermobile EDS, is estimated to occur in 7%-15% of patients with 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
Tnx-knockout mice show reduced collagen content and altered connective tissue architecture, indicating TNX regulates collagen deposition in connective tissue.
Patients with CAH-X syndrome commonly present with skin laxity and musculoskeletal features such as joint hypermobility and subluxation.
Chronic arthralgia is reported to be more prominent in adult CAH-X patients compared with children.
Cardiac abnormalities including septal defects, chamber enlargement, or great vessel enlargement occur in about 25% of CAH-X syndrome patients.
Patients with CAH-X syndrome frequently have gastrointestinal abnormalities such as gastroesophageal reflux, hernia, and rectal prolapse.
Patients with biallelic deletion of TNXB have more severe clinical manifestations of CAH-X syndrome than those with a monoallelic deletion, indicating a gene-dosage effect.

Combined p.P31L and four promoter SNPs reduce CYP21A2 transcriptional activity 5-fold and residual enzyme activity to less than 6%, producing a more severe phenotype than the P31L genotype alone would predict.
Severe CYP21A2 genotype groups (0 and A) correlate strongly with the salt-wasting phenotype (91%-97%), whereas intermediate groups (B and C) show a weaker correlation (45%-57%).
Microconversion of sequence variants from the CYP21A1P pseudogene into CYP21A2 accounts for nonfunctional protein synthesis in 70%-75% of 21-OHD cases.
Large gene rearrangements from unequal crossover during meiosis, producing deletions, duplications, or chimeric genes, account for the remaining 25%-30% of 21-OHD cases.
CYP21A2 and its pseudogene CYP21A1P share 98% sequence identity in coding regions and 96% in intronic regions, complicating molecular diagnosis.
The p.V282L CYP21A2 mutation is common among Ashkenazi Jews with 21-OHD but rarely observed in Asian populations, reflecting ethnic variation in mutation prevalence.
The p.Q319* nonsense mutation is the most common CYP21A2 variant in the Tunisian population.
In Korean patients with 21-OHD, large deletions are the most common CYP21A2 mutation, followed by the I2G splicing mutation and p.I173N.
The worldwide incidence of classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, based on neonatal screening, ranges from 1:14,000 to 1:18,000 births.
Deficiency of complement C4 correlates strongly with autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus.
In Caucasians, RCCX module copy-number alleles occur as monomodular (~17%), bimodular (~69%), or trimodular (~14%) structures.
Combined PCR-based Sanger sequencing and MLPA analysis can achieve up to 98% accuracy in genetic testing for 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
Because molecular detection of TNXA/TNXB chimeras is laborious and not routinely performed, diagnosis of CAH-X syndrome relies primarily on clinical assessment using the Beighton 9-point scale.
Whole exome sequencing identified TAAD gene variants in 10 of 37 (27.0%) early-onset isolated Stanford type B aortic dissection patients.
Multivariate Cox regression identified carrying a TAAD gene variant as the only independent risk factor for aortic-related adverse events (ARAEs) after TEVAR, conferring a 4-fold increased risk.
Kaplan-Meier analysis showed patients carrying TAAD gene variants had a significantly lower event-free survival rate from ARAEs compared to non-carriers.
Hypertension was significantly less prevalent among patients carrying TAAD gene variants compared to non-carriers.
Other vascular abnormalities, including branch artery aneurysm and dissection, were significantly more common in patients carrying TAAD gene variants.
All-cause mortality was significantly higher in patients with TAAD gene variants compared to those without.
Aortic-related mortality trended higher in patients with TAAD gene variants but did not reach statistical significance.
A novel pathogenic TGFBR1 nonsense variant (p.W458X) was identified in an early-onset isolated TBAD patient.
A novel likely pathogenic COL3A1 missense variant (p.G660V), classically associated with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, was found in a patient with isolated (non-syndromic) early-onset TBAD.

The FBN1 p.N1893S variant, previously reported in patients with Marfan syndrome, was detected in two isolated AD patients from the same family who had no ectopia lentis or skeletal deformity, suggesting incomplete phenotypic penetrance.

A copy number variant duplication in MYH11 was identified as a candidate causal variant using the DECoN CNV-detection pipeline, consistent with prior reports of recurrent MYH11 duplications in aortic dissection with congenital heart malformation.
A copy number variant deletion in LOX was identified as a candidate causal variant in an early-onset isolated TBAD patient.
Age of onset did not differ significantly between patients with and without TAAD gene variants.
Maximum ascending and descending aortic diameters were slightly larger in patients with TAAD gene variants but did not reach statistical significance.
SIBO prevalence was reported as 100% among fibromyalgia patients compared with 20% of controls, with somatic pain severity correlating significantly with breath hydrogen level.

A meta-analysis of 37 studies found SIBO prevalence of 36.7% in IBS patients; glucose breath test and jejunal culture (but not lactulose breath test) showed significantly higher SIBO detection in IBS versus controls.
Patients with diarrhea-predominant IBS (IBS-D) were more likely to have SIBO than patients with other IBS subtypes.

A separate meta-analysis of 25 studies found SIBO prevalence significantly higher in IBS patients than controls overall, with a much stronger association when compared with healthy controls than with non-IBS disease controls.
Among IBS patients, female sex, older age, and the IBS-D subtype were each independently associated with increased odds of SIBO.
Methane-type SIBO was more prevalent in constipation-predominant IBS (IBS-C) than in diarrhea-predominant IBS (IBS-D), the opposite pattern to that seen for hydrogen SIBO.
Serum IL-1β (and IL-1α in another study) were higher in SIBO-positive IBS patients than SIBO-negative IBS patients, while serum IL-10 was lower in the SIBO-positive group.
IL-10 levels were reduced in IBS patients with SIBO compared with those without in a separate study, with no significant differences in TNF-α, IL-6, or IL-8.

SIBO prevalence was markedly higher in children with IBS than in control children, with bloating being the only abdominal symptom that significantly differed between SIBO-positive and negative groups.

IBS-D patients with SIBO had significantly lower BMI but higher abdominal pain scores than IBS-D patients without SIBO, and dietary fat proportion was higher in SIBO-positive IBS patients, positively correlating with breath methane peak.

The presence of SIBO did not affect overall IBS symptom severity or associated psychological disorders in two separate studies, although orocecal transit time was significantly increased in SIBO-positive IBS patients.
Children with autism had a significantly higher SIBO incidence than controls, and autistic children with SIBO had higher Autism Treatment Evaluation Checklist scores than those without SIBO.
SIBO was detected significantly more often in patients with post-COVID-19 IBS than in patients with typical (non-COVID) IBS.

Patients with autonomic neuropathy in type 1 diabetes had a higher prevalence of SIBO, associated with higher daily insulin requirements, consistent with autonomic dysfunction impairing intestinal motility as a driver of bacterial overgrowth.
CKBA reduced serum IgE levels and alleviated skin inflammation in a calcipotriol (MC903)-induced mouse model of atopic dermatitis.
CKBA restrained mast cell degranulation both in vitro and in vivo.
RNA-seq analysis of anti-DNP/DNP-HSA-activated bone marrow-derived mast cells showed that CKBA downregulated ERK signaling.
Using an ERK activator (t-butyl hydroquinone) and inhibitor (selumetinib/AZD6244), the authors demonstrated that CKBA suppresses mast cell activation via the ERK signaling pathway.
The title proposes famotidine as a potential agent to reduce mast cell activation implicated in post-COVID-19 cognitive impairment.
MRGPRX2 expression in skin mast cells is increased in patients with chronic urticaria compared to unaffected states.
Circulating levels of substance P (SP) in skin mast cells are increased in chronic urticaria patients.
Fisetin prevented urticaria-like symptoms in OVA/SP co-stimulated and SP-stimulated murine models of chronic urticaria.
Fisetin inhibited mast cell activation, including calcium mobilization and degranulation of cytokines and chemokines, by binding to MRGPRX2 in MRGPRX2/HEK293 and LAD2 mast cell models.
Bioinformatics analysis suggested that fisetin has a potential interaction relationship with Akt in the context of chronic urticaria.
Western blotting showed fisetin downregulated the phosphorylation levels of Akt, P38, NF-κB, and PLCγ in C48/80-activated LAD2 mast cells.
The patient had persistently elevated serum tryptase levels (13.3 and 13.6 ng/mL) while consuming multiple bananas daily and experiencing chest pain.
Following discontinuation of banana consumption, the patient's tryptase levels normalized (8.4 and 8.1 ng/mL) and her chest pain resolved.
The patient tested positive for banana-specific IgE at 1.31 kU/L, along with positive IgE to birch (3.02 kU/L) and latex (0.43 kU/L).
The paper reports what is described as the first case of Type I Kounis syndrome (allergic coronary vasospasm without underlying CAD) caused by banana allergy.
Prior literature cited describes three variants of Kounis syndrome occurring at different frequencies: Type I in 72.6% of patients, Type II in 22.3%, and Type III in 5.1%.
Mus a 1, a banana profilin/actin-binding protein, is described as the most notable mediator of IgE cross-reactivity between birch pollen and banana, underlying oral allergy syndrome.
Latex allergy and banana allergy show cross-reactivity, with nearly 20-50% of people with natural rubber latex allergy showing hypersensitivity after eating banana.
Banana fruit allergy is an uncommon cause of allergy in the general population, affecting around 0.6% of people, though it is more common among atopic individuals.
CSK positively regulates FcεRI-induced production of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines in mast cells through the LYN/SHP-1/STAT5 signaling axis.
CSK negatively regulates calcium response and degranulation in mast cells via the CSK-LYN-SYK-LAT-PLCγ axis or a complementary FYN-dependent pathway.
CSK negatively regulates mast cell chemotaxis via a CSK-integrin signaling axis.
Studies in PAG knockout mast cells suggest that CSK-binding proteins other than PAG-1 exist, implying additional adaptor mechanisms recruit CSK to regulate SFK signaling in mast cells.
A splice-donor variant in GCSAML (rs56043070[A]) was the most significant and largest-effect variant associated with increased risk of urticaria across four populations.
A predicted splice-donor variant in NFKB1 was associated with a modest increase in urticaria risk.
An intergenic FCER1A variant (rs6703348[G]) was associated with decreased urticaria risk and correlates with increased FCER1A expression, decreased serum IgE, and decreased asthma risk.
An upstream C4A variant was associated with reduced urticaria risk, implicating complement innate immunity in urticaria pathogenesis.
An intronic eQTL variant at CBLB was associated with decreased urticaria risk, implicating this gene in type 2 immune response/mast cell physiology.
An upstream ZFPM1 variant was associated with decreased urticaria risk.
An intronic sQTL variant at TBL1XR1 was associated with increased urticaria risk.
An upstream TPSD1 variant was associated with increased urticaria risk and correlates with increased plasma TPSAB1 (tryptase) levels and higher TPSD1/TPSB2 RNA expression at the tryptase locus.
An intronic STAT6 sQTL variant was associated with decreased urticaria risk and also with protection against asthma, allergic rhinitis, and atopic dermatitis.
The GCSAML urticaria risk variant is associated with decreased basophil percentage of white blood cells, driven mainly by homozygous carriers.
The GCSAML urticaria risk variant is also associated with decreased platelet count under the additive model.
The GCSAML urticaria-risk variant is associated with greater plasma levels of tryptase alpha/beta-1 (TPSAB1), independent of disease status.
The GCSAML urticaria-risk variant is associated with greater plasma levels of tryptase beta-2 (TPSB2), independent of disease status.
The GCSAML urticaria-risk variant is associated with increased plasma KIT (mast/stem cell factor receptor) levels in heterozygotes, though this trans-pQTL deviated from additive model expectations.
The GCSAML urticaria-associated variant showed significant trans-pQTL associations with increased plasma levels of P-selectin (SELP) and SIGLEC6, both linked to mast cell activation.

The GCSAML splice-donor variant disrupts the canonical splice-donor site, causing heterozygotes to have 43% lower expression of the primary transcript and homozygotes to express none of the primary transcript, with a compensatory increase in a novel exon-2-skipping transcript.
A positive genetic correlation was found between urticaria and asthma diagnoses.
The STAT6 urticaria-associated variant is the top trans-pQTL for plasma IL5RA levels, a receptor implicated in eosinophil/IgE regulation and asthma.

GCSAML was previously identified as a mast cell-specific gene, expressed up to 20 times more highly in human mast cells than in basophils (the cell type with second-highest expression), based on the FANTOM5 transcriptome dataset.
Selenium nanoparticles (LET-SeNPs) activate the Nrf2-Keap1 signaling pathway to enhance expression of antioxidative selenoproteins at mRNA and protein levels.
LET-SeNPs inhibit mast cell activation, contributing to antiallergic activity.
LET-SeNPs are metabolized to seleno-amino acids promoting selenoprotein biosynthesis, which suppresses ROS-induced COX-2 and MAPK activation.
The selenoprotein-mediated suppression of COX-2/MAPK signaling reduces the release of histamine and inflammatory cytokines from mast cells.

In an allergic mouse model, LET-SeNPs increased selenium content and selenoprotein expression in the skin, decreased mast cell activation and inflammatory cell infiltration, and produced high therapeutic effects on allergic dermatitis.

In a non-human primate (Macaca fascicularis) model, LET-SeNPs similarly increased skin selenium content and selenoprotein expression, decreased mast cell activation and inflammatory infiltration, and showed high therapeutic effect on allergic dermatitis.
Based on Class I evidence, IVIG is not recommended for idiopathic small fiber neuropathy or SFN associated with trisulfated heparin disaccharide or FGFR-3 autoantibodies.
The consensus panel found insufficient evidence to make a recommendation on IVIG use for autonomic neuropathy.
AT1R expression rises rapidly during the early proliferation phase of wound healing, then declines with a small resurgence during remodeling.
AT2R becomes dominant in the later remodeling phase of wound healing, with dramatic up-regulation relative to AT1R.
Topical angiotensin II and angiotensin(1-7) improved wound repair and increased keratinocyte/epidermal stem cell proliferation and epithelialization across four wound models.
AT1R signaling stimulation accelerates keratinocyte migration, whereas AT1R blockade or AT2R activation reduces migration speed in rat wounds and cultured keratinocytes.
Oral losartan administered for 14 days sped up epidermal repair in a streptozotocin-induced diabetic wound mouse model.

Topical 1% valsartan gel markedly accelerated wound healing in diabetic mice and aging pigs, acting via AT2R since the effect was lost in AT2R-null mice, and outperformed topical losartan in healing rate.
Topical application of 5% captopril gel delayed wound healing rate.
AT1R and angiotensin II concentrations were found to be higher in keloid and hypertrophic scar tissue than in normal human skin.

In a clinical trial of 30 participants (20 losartan, 10 placebo), topical 5% losartan ointment applied twice daily for three months significantly improved Vancouver Scar Scale scores including vascularity, pigmentation, pliability, and height.
Both valsartan (ARB) and enalapril (ACEI) prevented pathological scar formation in a rabbit ear wound model, with valsartan more effective at reducing fibroblast cell count and epithelial thickness.
AT2 receptor stimulation with agonist C21 reduced TNF-α-induced IL-6 expression in human skin fibroblasts.
Ang II increased collagen content and TIMP-1 expression in mouse skin fibroblasts, an effect inhibited by valsartan (AT1R blockade) and augmented by AT2R inhibition.
AT1R is highly expressed in squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) but poorly expressed in basal cell carcinoma (BCC).
A randomized clinical trial in a population at high risk of skin cancer found that ACEI or ARB users had a lower incidence of basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma.
In renal transplant recipients, ACEI or ARB consumption was associated with a drop in the incidence of BCC and SCC.
AT1R blockade with TCV-116 decreased melanoma growth and angiogenesis in wild-type mice, while AT1R-deficient mice showed reduced angiogenesis compared to wild-type.

Down-regulation of AT1R-encoding AGTR1 via miR-410 suppressed melanoma tumor growth and migration, but ectopic AGTR1 expression in melanoma cell lines lacking endogenous AT1R also suppressed tumor growth, an apparently contradictory oncogenic-vs-suppressor role.
ACE I/D gene polymorphism is reported in psoriatic patients and may contribute to elevated serum ACE levels observed in psoriasis.
In an imiquimod-induced psoriatic inflammation mouse model, topical 1% losartan significantly decreased the PASI score along with reduced IL-17a, angiotensin II, and AT1R expression.

In the MRL-lpr mouse model of systemic lupus erythematosus, RAS-modifying therapies (losartan, lisinopril, angiotensin(1-7), Nor-Leu-3 angiotensin(1-7)) significantly reduced the onset and severity of skin rashes.
A case report described therapeutic effect of losartan on epidermolysis bullosa in a 6-year-old patient.

Losartan ameliorated dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa in RDEB mice by reducing TGF-β signaling and halting fibrosis, with proteomics showing decreased levels of multiple tissue inflammation-related proteins.
Losartan has shown beneficial effects in treating Myhre syndrome, a connective tissue disorder characterized by skin thickening.
HGD and HFD feeding reduced fecal pellet counts and fecal size compared with NFD controls, indicating diabetic constipation.
Both total GI transit time and colonic transit time were significantly prolonged in HGD- and HFD-fed mice compared to NFD controls, indicating colonic dysmotility.
Colonic tissue histomorphology showed no obvious lesions or necrosis in HGD or HFD groups, indicating dysmotility occurs without structural colonic damage.
HGD feeding significantly decreased colonic autonomic (rhythmic) contraction frequency compared with NFD controls.
Electrical field stimulation (EFS, 2-32 Hz)-induced colonic neuromuscular contractions were decreased in both HGD and HFD groups relative to NFD controls.

Carbachol-induced cholinergic colonic contractions were attenuated in HFD-fed mice but showed no significant change in HGD-fed mice versus NFD, indicating divergent cholinergic phenotypes between the two diets.
KCl (120 mM)-induced colonic muscular contraction did not differ among NFD, HFD, and HGD groups, indicating no structural muscular damage.
EFS (4-32 Hz)-induced colonic neuromuscular relaxation was distinctly increased in HGD and HFD groups compared with NFD.
Pre-incubation with the nNOS inhibitor l-NAME significantly decreased EFS-stimulated colonic relaxation in NFD, HFD, and HGD groups, confirming a nitrergic mechanism of relaxation across diets.
Colonic nNOS protein expression was significantly upregulated in HGD-fed mice compared with NFD and HFD groups, despite unchanged mRNA levels.
Overall gut microbiota composition (beta diversity) in the NFD group differed significantly from that in the HGD and HFD groups.
Family-level Clostridiales abundance was increased in HFD-fed mice compared with other groups.
Family-level Rhodospirillaceae abundance was increased in HGD-fed mice compared with other groups.
Genus-level Insolitispirillum abundance was increased in HGD-fed mice.
Genus-level Turicibacter abundance was decreased in HGD-fed mice and positively correlated with fecal area, suggesting a role in colonic motility/constipation.
Species-level Insolitispirillum_sp. and Clostridium_sp._A9 abundance increased in HGD-fed mice, while Turicibacter_unclassified abundance declined in HFD-fed mice.
Turicibacter abundance correlated positively with fecal area, whereas Clostridiales abundance correlated negatively with fecal area, linking these taxa to stool output/constipation severity.
No significant correlation was found between Insolitispirillum abundance and fecal area, despite its increased abundance in HGD mice.
Hyperinsulinemia was observed only in the HFD group, while plasma insulin was only marginally increased by HGD feeding, indicating a distinct metabolic phenotype between diets.
Hypertriglyceridemia was observed only in the HGD group, not the HFD group, indicating diet-specific dyslipidemia patterns.
Insulin sensitivity (via insulin tolerance test) was impaired by both HGD and HFD feeding compared with NFD controls.
A meta-analysis found a 58.5% success rate for sacral nerve stimulation (SNS) in patients with overactive bladder who had failed botulinum toxin A therapy.
A systematic review reported an 80% success rate for medium- to long-term SNS therapy in patients with fecal incontinence.

The anti-inflammatory effect of SNS on intestinal inflammation was largely abolished by bilateral vagotomy, indicating mediation via a spinal afferent-vagal efferent pathway rather than direct sacral innervation.

In a placebo-controlled study of 53 patients, a 3-week course of SNS with conventional parameters (14 Hz, 300 μs) was ineffective in treating slow transit constipation, confirmed by long-term follow-up.

In an open-label study of 6 patients with diarrhea-predominant IBS, 2 weeks of temporary SNS reduced IBS total symptom scores by 42%, improved quality of life by 40%, and reduced abdominal pain by 44%.

In a randomized, controlled, crossover trial of 26 patients with IBS-D or IBS-M, SNS-on periods produced significant improvement in IBS symptom score and IBS-related quality of life compared with SNS-off periods.
In a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled crossover study of 21 patients with IBS-D or IBS-M, SNS improved IBS symptoms, pain, and daily bowel movement frequency compared to SNS-off.

In a rodent model of colonic hypersensitivity induced by neonatal acetic acid, optimized SNS parameters (14 Hz, 330 μs, 40% motor threshold) substantially improved visceromotor reflex responses to colorectal distention via autonomic and opioid mechanisms.

In a pig model of TNBS-induced increased intestinal permeability, acute SNS enhanced mucosal repair by suppressing ZO-1 expression/redistribution while increasing pFAK/FAK and the cytokines IL-1β and IL-4.

In a rodent IBD model, intermittent SNS at 5 Hz/500 μs was significantly more effective at reducing disease activity index and inflammatory cytokines than continuous 14 Hz/210 μs stimulation used for fecal incontinence.
In TNBS-treated rats, 1-hour daily SNS was significantly more potent than 0.5-hour daily SNS at reducing colonic myeloperoxidase activity, and comparable to 3-hour daily SNS.
TNF-α tissue levels were doubled in TNBS-treated rats compared to normal controls, and this elevation was normalized by SNS with optimized (but not fecal-incontinence) stimulation parameters.
The anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 was substantially suppressed in TNBS-treated rats but normalized by optimized SNS.
Pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-13 and IL-5 were suppressed by SNS treatment in the rodent TNBS colitis model.

SNS activated neurons in the nucleus tractus solitarius (assessed by c-Fos expression) and increased vagal efferent activity as measured by heart rate variability spectral analysis, supporting a spinal afferent-brainstem-vagal efferent pathway.
SNS increased colonic tight junction protein expression (Zonula Occludens-1, Occludin, Claudin-1, and Junctional adhesion molecule-A) and reduced colonic permeability in TNBS-treated rats.

SNS reversed TNBS-induced reduction in choline acetyltransferase-positive enteric neurons and reduced TNBS-induced elevation of nitric oxide synthase-positive neurons, while also reducing colonic Th1 cells and increasing Treg cells.
In 5 patients with fecal incontinence and Crohn's disease-related anoperineal lesions, temporary and chronic SNS (up to 3 years) improved continence but did not change Crohn's disease symptom scores.

In a single case of refractory ulcerative proctitis with fecal incontinence, 3 weeks of SNS decreased both fecal incontinence score and ulcerative colitis disease activity score, with sustained improvement and improved rectal barrier permeability at 18 months.
Acute SNS reduced gastric fundic tone and increased gastric accommodation in rats via a vagal efferent, nitric-oxide-dependent mechanism, as the effect was blocked by the NOS inhibitor L-NAME.
SNS normalized glucagon-induced abnormal gastric and small intestinal slow waves, restoring the percentage of normal slow waves in rats.
In rats, SNS with parameters derived from rectal tone effects enhanced vagal activity, released acetylcholine, accelerated colon transit, and substantially improved opioid-induced constipation.
All three RCTs in irritable bowel syndrome patients showed significantly greater improvement in interoception for the interoception-based intervention (IBI) compared to control conditions.
Two of three RCTs in irritable bowel syndrome demonstrated significantly greater reduction in mental/gut symptom severity for the IBI compared to controls.
Two of three RCTs in substance use disorder showed significantly greater improvement in interoception for the IBI versus control.
Fibromyalgia RCTs showed indicative evidence for IBI superiority in improving interoception (two of three trials positive), but this was not accompanied by symptom improvement.

In PTSD, three of five RCTs showed IBIs superior to control for improving interoception while two showed inferior effects, and the largest PTSD trial (n=338) found no significant between-group effect.
Despite indicative evidence that IBIs improve interoception in fibromyalgia and PTSD, this improvement did not correspond to significant improvements in disease symptom severity in either disorder.
Eating disorder RCTs showed indicative evidence of IBI superiority for reducing symptom severity, with both available RCTs positive.
Across all 31 included RCTs, most interoception-based interventions were significantly more effective than control conditions at improving interoception overall.
Across all 31 RCTs, IBIs were significantly better than controls at reducing mental health symptoms in only about half of trials, with a similar number showing no difference.

IBIs targeting both attention to bodily signals and metacognitive appraisal of those signals more often produced significant symptom improvement than IBIs targeting signal awareness alone, though no such difference was found for improving interoception itself.

Among the six adequately powered RCTs (n≥50 per arm), only 50% found significant IBI superiority for interoception and only 16.7% found significant superiority for symptom improvement, both lower than rates seen across all studies.
Preliminary evidence (single positive RCT) supported IBIs improving interoception in autism spectrum disorder.
Preliminary evidence (single positive RCT) supported IBIs improving interoception in patients with sleep disturbance.
Evidence for IBIs improving interoception was inconclusive in chronic pain, depression, and eating disorders, with mixed results across the available RCTs.
Of the 16 RCTs reporting follow-up data, half showed a significant prolonged improvement in interoception in favor of the IBI, while only 37.5% showed sustained symptom improvement.
Rats subjected to chronic unpredictable stress (CUS) showed depressive behavior along with elevated serum corticosterone and proinflammatory cytokines compared to non-stressed controls.
ECG and HRV analysis showed that chronically stressed rats had elevated heart rate, diminished vagal tone, and altered sinus rhythm compared to controls.
CUS rats developed cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis accompanied by increased myocardial caspase-3, iNOS, and TGF-beta1 expression relative to controls.
Serum cardiac troponin I (cTnI), a marker of myocardial injury, was increased in chronically stressed rats compared to controls.

Two weeks of alternate-day transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) after chronic unpredictable stress alleviated the stress-induced cardiac abnormalities (hypertrophy, fibrosis, and elevated apoptotic/fibrotic markers) in rats.
Chronic unpredictable stress increased serum corticosterone levels in rats.
Chronic unpredictable stress increased serum proinflammatory cytokine levels in rats.
Electrocardiogram and heart rate variability analysis showed that chronically stressed rats had altered sinus rhythm compared to controls.
Two weeks of alternate transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation therapy after chronic unpredictable stress helped alleviate the cardiac abnormalities induced by stress.
The authors developed and validated a rat model of chronic unpredictable stress by exposing rats to random stressors daily for 8 weeks.
Among 678 primary care patients attended during the second and third COVID-19 waves in Spain, panic disorder was diagnosed in 36 patients, a prevalence of 5.3%.
Panic disorder was diagnosed more frequently in women (23/36, 64%) than men in this primary care cohort.
Patients with panic disorder consumed significantly more daily cups of coffee/caffeine equivalent than patients without panic disorder.
Patients with panic disorder had significantly higher external life-stressor scores on the Holmes–Rahe scale than those without panic disorder.
A high stress score (>300) on the Holmes–Rahe scale was an independent predictor of panic disorder in multivariate logistic regression.

Financial difficulties in the family nucleus (unemployment, mortgage/rent payment difficulties, financial hardship in the last 6 months) were significantly more frequent among patients with panic disorder.
Having other personal financial difficulties in the past 6 months was an independent predictor of panic disorder in multivariate analysis.
Fibromyalgia was significantly more frequent among patients with panic disorder than among those without.
Chronic fatigue syndrome was significantly more frequent among patients with panic disorder than among those without.
Chronic fatigue syndrome was an independent predictor of panic disorder in multivariate logistic regression, with the strongest point estimate among covariates tested.
Irritable bowel syndrome was significantly more frequent among patients with panic disorder than among those without.
Irritable bowel syndrome was an independent predictor of panic disorder in multivariate logistic regression.
Chronic pain was significantly more frequent among patients with panic disorder than among those without.
The overall category of functional somatic syndrome (fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome, chronic pain, IBS combined) was significantly more frequent among patients with panic disorder.
Migraine was significantly more frequent among patients with panic disorder than among those without.
Dermatologic diseases as a whole were significantly more frequent among patients with panic disorder than among those without.
Nervous system diseases overall were significantly more frequent among patients with panic disorder than among those without.
Prior/concomitant COVID-19 infection was not significantly different between patients with and without panic disorder.
8.1% of participants with confirmed COVID-19 infection met the IOM diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS.
2.8% of participants were classified as having COVID-19-related ME/CFS.
4.6% of participants were determined to have disease-related fatigue distinct from full ME/CFS.
0.7% of participants showed ME/CFS that was not related to COVID-19.
3.7% of participants were considered to have long COVID-19.
Almost one-fourth of the study participants had a family history of ME/CFS.
NK cells from ME/CFS patients showed a significantly lower slope (rate of Ca2+ entry) of TRPM7-mediated calcium influx following naltriben stimulation compared with healthy controls.
Amplitude and half-time of maximum response (T1/2) of TRPM7-mediated calcium influx following naltriben stimulation did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.

Following TRPM7 channel-kinase desensitisation with NS8593, ME/CFS patients showed significantly higher amplitude and T1/2 values than healthy controls, indicating impaired desensitisation of TRPM7 in ME/CFS.
Slope of TRPM7 response following NS8593 inhibition/desensitisation did not differ significantly between ME/CFS and HC cohorts.
ME/CFS patients demonstrated significantly greater functional impairment across all WHODAS domains compared with healthy controls.
SF-36 quality-of-life scores were significantly reduced in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls in all domains except the wellbeing measure.
Full blood count parameters were within normal range and did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.

Prior research (cited within this paper) identified loss of TRPM3 ion channel function, reduced surface expression, and impaired Ca2+ mobilisation in the NK cells of ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Prior flow cytometric analyses (cited within this paper) showed elevated TRPM2 expression on NK cell membranes of ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.

A previous study (cited within this paper) found significantly higher co-localisation of TRPM7 with cortical actin after pharmacological inhibition than activation in ME/CFS patients (not seen in HCs), and greater TRPM7-PIP2 co-localisation after antagonist treatment in HCs than ME/CFS.
A cited retrospective study found that aripiprazole, suggested to act via TRPM7 to reduce microglial activation, was associated with significant symptom improvement in a majority of ME/CFS patients.

Two-sample Mendelian randomization using the IVW method found that genetically predicted higher abundance of genus Paraprevotella was causally associated with increased risk of ME/CFS, though MR-Egger did not support this association.

IVW and weighted median Mendelian randomization methods found that genetically predicted higher abundance of genus Ruminococcaceae_UCG_014 was causally associated with increased risk of ME/CFS, although MR-Egger did not support the association.

The study notes that ME/CFS patients frequently show gut microbiome dysbiosis and high comorbidity with irritable bowel syndrome, consistent with a gut-immune-brain axis role in disease pathogenesis, though prior microbiome studies show inconsistent taxonomic findings.
Plasma miR-142-5p was significantly increased in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Plasma miR-150-5p was significantly increased in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Plasma miR-448 was significantly increased in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls and is proposed as a novel ME/CFS biomarker.
Plasma miR-140-5p was significantly downmodulated in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, contrasting with prior reports of upregulation.
miR-127-3p was significantly increased in the severe ME/CFS subgroup compared with controls, suggesting utility as a severity marker.
miR-143-3p was increased in the severe ME/CFS subgroup compared with controls (reported p-value likely a typographical value of 0.05).
miR-448 was overexpressed across all ME/CFS severity subgroups compared with controls, with increasing levels correlating with greater disease severity.
Downmodulation of miR-140-5p correlated with symptom severity, reaching significance only in the moderate ME/CFS subgroup.
miR-124 and miR-142 showed a trend of increase with higher disease severity subgroups, but the differences from controls were not statistically significant for miR-124.
Plasma IL-17A was significantly decreased in ME/CFS moderate and mild subgroups compared with controls.
Plasma IL-2 was significantly decreased in ME/CFS moderate and mild subgroups compared with controls.
Plasma IL-21 was significantly decreased in ME/CFS moderate and mild subgroups compared with controls.
Plasma IL-23 was significantly decreased in ME/CFS moderate and mild subgroups compared with controls.
Plasma IL-6 was markedly reduced in the severe and moderate ME/CFS subgroups compared with controls.
Plasma TNF-α was significantly decreased in the moderate ME/CFS subgroup compared with controls.
HHV-6A/6B positivity was more than double in ME/CFS patients versus controls, but the difference was not statistically significant.
Mean HHV-6A/6B viral load in PBMCs was markedly higher in ME/CFS patients than controls but did not reach statistical significance.
miR-448 showed weak inverse correlations with most tested inflammatory cytokines (except IL-17A and TNF-α) across the study cohort.

Bioinformatic network analysis predicted that dysregulated ME/CFS miRNAs (miR-127, miR-140, miR-142, miR-143, miR-150, miR-448) preferentially target genes including ZNF426, MMP13/14, STAT1, SPIC, SMUG1, SMAD3, PRDM1, and PPIE.

Functional enrichment analysis (WikiPathways) of predicted miRNA targets implicated extracellular matrix remodeling, cytokine signaling (IL-6, Oncostatin M, IL-7, TGF-β), apoptosis, PI3K-mTOR cell cycle regulation, NOD-mediated microbial immune response, and senescence/autophagy pathways in ME/CFS.
Among ME/CFS patients, saliva anti-HAdV IgG was significantly higher in those with a systemic SARS-CoV-2 antibody response than in those seronegative for SARS-CoV-2.
ME/CFS patients with a local (saliva-only) SARS-CoV-2 antibody response also showed significantly elevated saliva anti-HAdV IgG compared to SARS-CoV-2-seronegative ME/CFS patients.
In healthy donors, saliva anti-HAdV IgG did not differ significantly between those with a systemic SARS-CoV-2 response and SARS-CoV-2-seronegative healthy donors.
In healthy donors, saliva anti-HAdV IgG did not differ significantly between those with a local SARS-CoV-2 response and SARS-CoV-2-seronegative healthy donors.
ME/CFS patients with a systemic SARS-CoV-2 response had significantly higher saliva anti-HAdV IgG than healthy donors with a systemic SARS-CoV-2 response.
Baseline saliva anti-HAdV IgG, independent of SARS-CoV-2 infection status (negative-ME vs. negative-HD), did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients and healthy donors.
Multiple regression analysis showed that gender, age, and history of mononucleosis were not confounding factors for saliva HAdV IgG levels.
Unlike saliva, plasma anti-HAdV IgG levels showed no significant differences between systemic, local, or negative SARS-CoV-2 response subgroups in either ME/CFS or healthy donors.
No correlation was found between anti-HAdV IgG in plasma and anti-HAdV IgG in saliva, suggesting the mucosal immune response is discrete from the systemic response.
In a longitudinal paired analysis of 18 individuals (5 ME/CFS, 13 healthy donors) sampled before and after documented SARS-CoV-2 infection, saliva HAdV IgG significantly increased after infection.
Citing their prior work, the authors note that elevated saliva anti-EBNA1 IgG after mild/asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection was found to be exclusive to ME/CFS patients, not healthy donors.
The authors propose that HAdV acts as a chronic mucosal irritant that facilitates frequent reactivation of EBV, potentially in synergy with HHV6, as a mechanism underlying ME/CFS pathology.

The authors note that a majority of ME/CFS patients report irritable bowel syndrome with gut symptoms (stomach cramps, bloating, diarrhea, constipation) years prior to ME/CFS onset, which they speculate may impair the antiviral response to EBV-induced mononucleosis.

The authors mention that brincidofovir, a lipid conjugate of cidofovir active against double-stranded DNA viruses including adenovirus, is used clinically in immunosuppressed transplant patients to control HAdV infections, and suggest this and immune therapies as potential strategies relevant to ME/CFS/long COVID.
The authors note that prior serology studies found no association between ME/CFS and human adenovirus using plasma antibody analysis.
Postural sway during a 30-second static stand test was worse (greater) in both long COVID and ME/CFS participants compared with healthy controls, but did not differ between the two patient groups.
Timed Up and Go test performance was worse in both long COVID and ME/CFS participants than in healthy controls, with no significant difference between the two patient groups.

5 Times Sit to Stand test performance was worse in both long COVID and ME/CFS participants than in healthy controls, with no significant difference between the two patient groups; 87% of long COVID participants exceeded the muscle weakness threshold on this test.
Long COVID and ME/CFS groups showed similarly impaired balance and physical capacity relative to each other, despite very different illness durations (~16 months vs ~16 years).
At 3 months post-symptom onset, 66.7% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients reported fatigue and 16.1% reported substantial fatigue.
By 6 months post-symptom onset, fatigue prevalence declined to 59.5% and substantial fatigue to 6.9%, representing a reduction from 3-month levels.
A greater number of pre-existing comorbidities at hospitalization was a significant predictor of fatigue at 3 months post-viral infection after adjusting for age, sex, and time.
Older age was associated with a subtle protective effect against developing fatigue at 3 months follow-up.
Number of pre-existing comorbidities at hospitalization was significantly associated with substantial fatigue at 3 months, adjusting for age.

Patients with fatigue versus those without showed statistically significant differences in depression severity (PHQ-9), quality of life (EQ-5D), shortness of breath, and overall health scores at 3- and 6-months.

In mixed-effects modeling adjusted for age and comorbidities, fatigue was correlated with nearly all patient-reported outcome measures at 3- and 6-months, except for the self-care dimension and follow-up time itself.
No patient who was free of fatigue or substantial fatigue at 3 months went on to develop new fatigue or substantial fatigue by 6 months follow-up.
Dyspnea (shortness of breath) was associated with fatigue at 3- and 6-months but only marginally associated with substantial fatigue, possibly due to small sample size.

Using the same cohort, a related analysis found dyspnea to be the most common and persistent COVID-19 recovery symptom, present in 42% of patients at 6 months, with unexplained dyspnea (not related to lung function/imaging abnormalities) in 14% and 19% at 3- and 6-months respectively.
General fatigue scores (MFI) changed significantly over time differently between the AIR and active control groups, with a medium effect size interaction.
The AIR group showed a very large within-group reduction in general fatigue over 3 months, more than four times the effect size seen in the active control group.
The active control (general health and wellness) group also showed a significant, medium-effect reduction in general fatigue over time, primarily between baseline and month 3.
At months 1 and 2, the AIR group had significantly lower general fatigue than the active control group, with a difference approaching significance by month 3, while no baseline difference existed.
By month 3, the AIR group's general fatigue mean score approached the standardized normal range reported for US adults on the MFI general fatigue subscale.
The interaction between group and time for the SF-36 energy subscale only approached statistical significance, with no significant between-group differences at any single timepoint.
The AIR group showed a large within-group increase in SF-36 energy scores over 3 months, double the effect size of the active control group.
The active control (general wellness) group also showed a significant, large-effect increase in energy over time, though smaller than that seen in the AIR group.
The absolute increase in energy scores from baseline to month 3 was almost twice as large for the AIR group compared to the active control group.
Retention through the full 3-month study was higher in the AIR group than the active control group.

Among first-degree relatives of probands with interstitial cystitis or related nociplastic/psychiatric disorders, 26 of 30 possible bidirectional disorder interrelationships showed significantly increased risk.
Among second-degree relatives of probands, 23 of 30 possible bidirectional disorder interrelationships between interstitial cystitis and the other nociplastic/psychiatric conditions were significant.
Among third-degree relatives, only 7 of 30 possible bidirectional disorder interrelationships remained significant, indicating attenuated but still detectable clustering at greater genetic distance.

The overall pattern of results supports a shared, heritable component underlying interstitial cystitis and its comorbid nociplastic pain and psychiatric conditions (fibromyalgia, IBS, ME/CFS, major depressive disorder, panic disorder).

Among the three fatigue dimensions assessed by parent report, 'sleepy and inactive/blunted responses/lacking in energy' was the most frequently observed, followed by 'difficulty concentrating' and then 'localized pain'.
Children who could fall asleep within 15 minutes showed a significantly lower degree of fatigue.
Children who slept through the night showed a significantly lower degree of fatigue.
Absence of nocturnal enuresis was significantly associated with a lower degree of fatigue.
Absence of sleepwalking was significantly associated with lower fatigue in children.
Sleeping 10–11 hours per night on weekdays was significantly associated with lower fatigue and was the strongest sleep-related association observed.
Sleeping 10–11 hours per night on weekends/holidays was significantly associated with lower fatigue.
Going to bed before 9 p.m. on weekdays was significantly associated with lower fatigue, one of the strongest associations found.
Going to bed before 9 p.m. on weekends/holidays was significantly associated with lower fatigue.
Waking up before 7 a.m. on weekdays was significantly associated with lower fatigue.
Waking up before 7 a.m. on weekends/holidays was significantly associated with lower fatigue.
A regular sleep schedule was significantly associated with lower fatigue in preschoolers.
No significant differences with degree of fatigue were found for 'no sleep talking' or 'no sleep terrors'.
Eating three meals of consistent quantity at a punctual time each day was significantly associated with lower fatigue.
Chewing slowly was significantly associated with lower fatigue.
Eating at least three servings of vegetables daily was significantly associated with lower fatigue.
Drinking at least 1500 mL of boiled water daily was significantly associated with lower fatigue.
Avoiding Western-style fast food (e.g., hamburgers, French fries) was significantly associated with lower fatigue.
Avoiding instant noodles/instant foods was significantly associated with lower fatigue.
Avoiding processed foods was significantly associated with lower fatigue.
Avoiding fried, creamy, or fat-rich foods was significantly associated with lower fatigue, the strongest dietary association observed.

No significant associations with degree of fatigue were found for eating breakfast daily, avoiding late-night snacks, not being a picky eater, eating from all six major food groups, eating at least two fruits daily, avoiding snacks, or avoiding sodas/sugar-sweetened beverages.
Using the extreme group approach, 28.38% of preschoolers were classified as high fatigue, 46.67% as middle fatigue, and 24.93% as low fatigue based on total fatigue scale scores.

Test–retest reliability of the parent-completed Assessment Scale for Symptoms of Fatigue in Children and the Children's Health-Related Habits Questionnaire was high and statistically significant over a 4-week interval.
The global prevalence of CFS is estimated to be substantially higher in females than in males.
Prior literature cited in the paper reports that males with CFS are less likely to report chronic pain and have fewer immunological symptoms than females with CFS.
A cited meta-analysis found that approximately 39-44% of GPs did not accept CFS as a genuine clinical condition.
Cited literature found that patients with longer diagnostic journeys to CFS diagnosis were less likely to experience spontaneous recovery.

Male participants in this study experienced prolonged diagnostic delays, with one participant taking approximately 8 years and another 4 years to receive a formal CFS diagnosis, exceeding NICE recommendations.
Two participants in the study were misdiagnosed with clinical depression and prescribed antidepressants before eventually receiving a CFS diagnosis.
Participants reported being referred to specialists for other conditions (chronic migraine, insomnia, irritable bowel syndrome) before their CFS symptoms were recognised.

Participants described healthcare providers dismissing or delegitimising their CFS symptoms as psychological or non-genuine, including one GP labelling the condition 'pseudo M.E' and another stating 'CFS doesn't exist'.
Adherence to hegemonic masculine norms (strength, self-reliance) led participants to delay seeking medical help and to conceal or 'battle through' their symptoms before diagnosis.

Participants reported that CFS diminished their ability to fulfil masculine social roles (breadwinner, physical work, social drinking), producing guilt, self-hatred, and strain on relationships and employment.

Participants experienced delegitimisation of their illness from family, friends, and employers, though support varied by individual (e.g., a supportive female supervisor vs. an unsupportive male supervisor).
Confiding in other males with CFS was reported by participants to positively contribute to illness acceptance, emotional comfort, and mental health.
Participants perceived existing CFS support groups (e.g., yoga classes) as female-dominated and not accessible or appealing to men, highlighting a lack of male-targeted support resources.

Patients with EDS-hypermobility type/JHS and craniocervical instability commonly experience myalgic encephalomyelitis, chronic fatigue, depression, extreme occipital-cervical pain, and severe widespread pain that is difficult to relieve with opioids.
The severe, opioid-resistant pain in EDS-HT/JHS patients with craniocervical instability is proposed to result from chronic neuroinflammation, opioid-induced hyperalgesia, and central sensitization.

The authors propose a paradigm shift from opioid-based anesthesia/analgesia to perioperative opioid-minimization strategies for EDS-HT/JHS patients with CCI undergoing occipito-cervical/thoracic fixation/fusion.
A postoperative combination of anti-hyperalgesic coadjuvants (lidocaine, ketamine, and dexmedetomidine) was used for its opioid-sparing effect in this patient population.

A subgroup of remitted RRMS patients (identified by cluster analysis) show activated immune-inflammatory response system (IRS) and compensatory immunoregulatory system (CIRS) profiles including M1, Th1, Th17, and T-cell growth factor activity.

MS patients with high immune activation (cluster analysis) had significantly increased M1, Th1, Th17, T-cell growth, and growth factor activity compared with low-IRS MS patients and healthy controls, with no difference between low-IRS patients and controls.
Patients in the high-IRS-activation MS subgroup showed increased composite neurotoxicity scores compared with low-IRS patients and controls.
Th2 and CIRS responses were increased in the low-immune-activation MS subgroup but not in the high-activation subgroup, suggesting compensatory upregulation only in some patients.
No significant differences in Th1/Th2 ratio were found between MS patients and controls, nor in any immune profile between RRMS and SPMS.

No significant effects of disease-modifying or immunosuppressive drug treatments (IFN-β/betaferon, natalizumab, fingolimod, hydrocortisone, methylprednisolone) on immune profile variables were found, and immune profiles did not differ between treatment groups.
There were no significant differences in RBC count, hematocrit, hemoglobin, or the PC_RBCs composite between MS patients and healthy controls.

Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) were significantly lower, while red cell distribution width (RDW) was significantly higher, in MS patients compared with healthy controls.
RBC counts, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and PC_RBCs were significantly lower in female participants than in male participants across the combined sample.
PC_RBCs (composite of RBC count, hematocrit, hemoglobin) showed significant inverse correlations with MS disability composite (PC_disabilities) and MSSS scores.
Combined Th1, CIRS, and Th17-axis cytokine activity explained 42.2% of the variance in MS disability composite scores (PC_disabilities) across the whole sample.

T-cell growth factor, CIRS, and Th1 profiles positively predicted 53.3% of the variance in MSSS (MS severity) scores across the whole sample; in patients only, Th1 and CIRS explained 17.8% of MSSS variance.
Th17-axis, white blood cell count, and CIRS (all positively) plus PC_RBCs (inversely) explained 50.6% of variance in the composite psychopathology score (PC_PP, depression/anxiety/fatigue).
Within MS patients only, white blood cell count (positively) and PC_RBCs (inversely) predicted 17.1% of the variance in the composite psychopathology score.
Pure physiosomatic symptom scores were best predicted (50.3% of variance) by Th17-axis, WBC count, CIRS (all positively) and sex.
Chronic fatigue symptom scores due to MS were predicted (41.7% of variance) by neurotoxicity composite score, sex, and CIRS.
Automatic linear modeling identified IFN-γ, IL-17, and sIL-1RA (all positively associated) as the best predictors of MS disability, jointly explaining 45.9% of the variance in PC_disabilities.
Automatic linear modeling showed WBCs, IL-10, and IL-6 (positively) and PC_RBCs (inversely) as best predictors, jointly explaining 47.4% of variance in the composite psychopathology (PC_PP) score.
All neuropsychiatric rating scale subdomain scores (depression, anxiety, fatigue, physiosomatic, autonomic, sleep) were significantly higher in remitted MS patients than in healthy controls.
MS disability composite scores were significantly associated with the composite psychopathology score (chronic fatigue, depression, anxiety) both in the combined sample and within patients alone.
In hEDS patients, higher depression scores correlated negatively with use of positive-emotion language when describing pain metaphors.
Depression scores correlated negatively with 'body care' language content in pain metaphors.
Depression scores correlated positively with use of anger-related language in pain metaphors.
Anxiety scores correlated negatively with 'friends' language content in pain metaphors.
Anxiety scores correlated negatively with 'humans' language content in pain metaphors, indicating more dehumanized narrative with greater anxiety.
Anxiety scores correlated negatively with 'body care' language content in pain metaphors.
Higher pain (McGill Pain Questionnaire) scores correlated negatively with 'friends' language content in pain metaphors.
Higher pain scores correlated negatively with 'humans' language content in pain metaphors.
Higher pain scores correlated strongly and negatively with 'body-care' language content in pain metaphors, the strongest correlation observed in the study.

hEDS patients with high pain perception (MGPQ ≥36) used significantly different linguistic/metaphorical measures compared to those with low pain perception (MGPQ ≤35) on independent-samples t-test across multiple LIWC categories.

hEDS patients with lower pain perception tended to metaphorize their pain as a tolerated companion or friend (e.g., 'a troublesome companion in life'), reflecting a more humanized, positive relationship with pain.

hEDS patients with higher pain perception metaphorized their pain as a dehumanized, external invader or enemy (e.g., 'a rodent eating viscera', 'a weight crushing me'), reflecting a struggle to expel pain from the self.
The high-pain hEDS group showed reduced use of future-tense language in pain metaphors compared to the low-pain group, associated with a perceived immobility and 'painful eternity'.

Switching to flecainide 100 mg twice daily combined with metoprolol succinate 25 mg once daily produced a dramatic reduction in PVC burden (to only 3 PVCs on Holter) and resolution of symptoms after 3 months.
Escalated propafenone (150 mg TID) plus metoprolol succinate failed to reduce PVC burden after 3 months of therapy in the case patient.
Verapamil 40 mg three times daily, after discontinuation of prior antiarrhythmics, produced no reduction in PVC count after three months.
Despite RVOT-morphology PVCs suggesting RF ablation candidacy, ablation was judged not appropriate for this EDS patient due to risk of vascular/cardiac structural perforation.
In a study of 28 patients with joint hypermobility syndrome/hEDS undergoing 24-hour Holter-ECG, various supraventricular arrhythmias were observed but no ventricular arrhythmias were found.
A cardiovascular autonomic functional-testing study of 35 patients with JHS/EDS-HT reported no cardiac arrhythmias in any patient.
Literature indicates that mitral valve prolapse in EDS patients is associated with a higher incidence of ventricular arrhythmias, though this was excluded as a mechanism in the presented case.
In this patient, MRI excluded mitral valve prolapse and mitral annulus disjunction, leading authors to conclude the ventricular arrhythmia was clinically independent of EDS-related valve pathology.

A Spanish national ablation registry reported 4 deaths among 7,840 catheter ablation procedures, including one aortic rupture 48 hours post-ablation in an EDS patient, illustrating elevated procedural risk.

A case report describes successful RF ablation of AVNRT in a type IV EDS patient using magnetic navigation with a non-traumatic floppy catheter, with no complications and arrhythmia-free at 6-month follow-up.

A case report describes successful RF ablation of ventricular tachycardia in an EDS patient using a transvenous transseptal approach (avoiding retrograde aortic access) with no complications and no VT recurrence per ICD follow-up.
Some cases of hypermobile EDS are thought to be caused by mutation in the tenascin-X (TNXB) gene.
Classic EDS is caused by mutations in COL5A1 and COL5A2, affecting type V collagen structure.
Vascular EDS is caused by mutation in COL3A1, affecting type III collagen, conferring risk of vascular rupture.
Autonomic disorders including thermoregulation, bowel/bladder dysfunction, and orthostatic intolerance affecting heart rate and blood pressure have been observed in hypermobile EDS.

Propafenone metabolism shows a clear gene-concentration relationship due to polymorphic CYP2D6-mediated 5-hydroxylation, causing nonlinear pharmacokinetics in extensive metabolizers, whereas flecainide response is minimally affected by CYP2D6 phenotype at steady state.

A homozygous single-base-pair insertion (frameshift) in exon 4 of ADAMTS2 was identified in an affected kitten and proposed as the causal variant for dermatosparaxis Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in this cat family.

A heterozygous missense variant in COL1A2 was also identified as a candidate variant in the affected kitten but was not pursued further as the causal variant, with ADAMTS2 favored based on cosegregation and functional plausibility.

A previously known feline COL5A1 classical EDS variant was excluded as causative in this family because it did not cosegregate with the phenotype, with 4 unaffected cats homozygous for the mutant allele.

Transmission electron microscopy of affected skin showed severely abnormal collagen fibrils with an 'empty-tube' hollow appearance and electron-dense ribbon-like structures up to 250 nm in diameter, consistent with dermatosparaxis.
Affected kittens showed significantly reduced growth compared with their unaffected littermates.

Beyond cutaneous fragility, the index kitten had additional internal complications including a diaphragmatic hernia, rectal prolapse, and colonic intussusception, potentially related to connective tissue fragility.
Unlike human and canine EDS, joint hypermobility was not observed in any of the ADAMTS2-affected cats, consistent with prior reports that this feature is largely absent in feline dEDS.

The human ClinVar database lists a comparable ADAMTS2 frameshift variant (c.691del) at an analogous position as pathogenic, supporting the plausibility of the feline c.698dup variant as disease-causing.

Applying ACMG/AMP consensus criteria, the authors classified the feline ADAMTS2:c.698dup variant as pathogenic based on PVS1 (null variant in a gene where loss of function is a known disease mechanism), PM2 (absent from 77 control genomes), and PP1 (cosegregation with disease in multiple affected family members).
The authors suggest inbreeding within the free-roaming farm cat population likely provoked the outbreak of this lethal autosomal recessive disease.
Compression garments reduced pain at the most painful joint from a mean VAS of 71.5 mm at baseline to 53.5 mm at 6 months and 45.7 mm at 2 years, a statistically significant improvement.
Pain at joints other than the most painful joint also improved from baseline to 2 years, though not all comparisons reached statistical significance.
Neuropathic pain, assessed by the painDETECT questionnaire, improved from baseline to the 2-year follow-up.
Functional independence improved over the 2-year period of compression garment use.
Proprioception and balance, measured with the Berg Balance Scale, improved over the 2-year period of compression garment use.
The incidence of sprains and dislocations/subluxations decreased over the 2-year period of compression garment use.

A novel likely pathogenic COL3A1 exon 27 deletion was identified in Patient 1 via targeted gene panel sequencing and confirmed by cDNA and genomic Sanger sequencing, having been undetected by prior conventional Sanger sequencing.

Whole-genome sequencing identified a novel heterozygous COL3A1 intron 16 variant (c.1149+6T>C) in Patient 2, not previously reported in literature or gnomAD, later confirmed by RNA studies to alter splicing.

RNAseq and cDNA Sanger sequencing in Patient 2's fibroblasts confirmed exon 16 skipping, producing an in-frame deletion of 33 amino acids in the collagen triple-helical domain, at approximately one-third the abundance of normal transcript.

Although SpliceAI predicted a low probability of splice alteration for c.1149+6T>C (Δ=0.13), other in-silico tools (TraP, dbscSNV ADA) predicted high deleteriousness and RNA studies confirmed a real splicing effect, illustrating discordance among prediction tools and limitations of SpliceAI alone.

Analysis of 721 HGMD-reported COL3A1 disease-causing variants showed SpliceAI Δ scores were highest for canonical splice-site variants, intermediate for noncanonical intronic variants, and lowest for exonic variants.
Among 160 intronic COL3A1 variants classified as disease-causing by HGMD, SpliceAI achieved 98.8% sensitivity (158/160) using a Δ score cutoff of 0.2.
COL3A1 RNA expression is markedly higher in cultured skin fibroblasts than in whole blood, supporting the use of fibroblast-derived RNA for splicing studies in suspected vEDS.

Three brothers of Patient 2, none suspected of having vEDS, were incidentally found to carry the TGFBI p.R124H variant, which is associated with Avellino corneal dystrophy, unrelated to the vEDS phenotype.

AlphaFold-based 3D structural modeling showed low per-residue confidence (pLDDT) in the triple-helical region for both variant collagen structures compared to the normal protein, with structural deviations (RMSD) of 0.6 Å in Patient 1 and 1.2 Å in Patient 2.

Patient 1 presented with a traumatic carotid-cavernous fistula and multiple arterial aneurysms/dissections consistent with vEDS, and ultimately died at age 39 from a ruptured left renal artery aneurysm despite biennial CT angiography surveillance.
Patient 2 had a comparatively later onset of vEDS complications (first major complication at age 42) and remains alive at age 57 on conservative outpatient follow-up without surgical intervention.

Both novel COL3A1 pathogenic variants (an exon 27 deletion and an intronic splice variant) were missed by initial conventional Sanger sequencing of coding exons, demonstrating a diagnostic gap that required targeted NGS panel/WGS combined with cDNA sequencing to resolve.

Right intrathoracic subclavian artery aneurysms are rare and pose specific anatomic challenges to surgical repair, occurring in patients with genetic arteriopathies such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
A patient with Marfan syndrome and a right intrathoracic subclavian artery aneurysm underwent open surgical repair.
A patient with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and a right intrathoracic subclavian artery aneurysm underwent endovascular repair.
A patient with unspecified Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and a right intrathoracic subclavian artery aneurysm underwent hybrid (combined open and endovascular) repair.
The authors conclude that operative approach for right intrathoracic SCAA repair should be individualized based on the patient's underlying genetic diagnosis.
In a Danish study of 499 patients diagnosed with IBS by general practitioners, 75% fulfilled the Rome-III criteria for IBS, implying 25% of clinically recognized IBS is excluded by Rome-III.
In a Canadian specialist-referral cohort, 69% of clinically diagnosed IBS patients (251/365) fulfilled Rome-III criteria after exclusion of organic disease.
Mutations in MCM6, particularly the LCT-13910 C/T SNP, regulate downregulation of lactase and can lead to lactase persistence into adulthood, explaining variable lactose tolerance.
Two European studies found lactose malabsorption (by oral tolerance test or hydrogen breath test) in 24-27% of patients with IBS.

Among IBS patients with lactose malabsorption, a lactose-free diet led to symptom relief in 39% in one study and a 69% decrease in symptoms in another, with 82% remaining symptom-free at 5-year follow-up.
Low-FODMAP diet studies using the IBS Severity Scoring System report response rates of 50-80% in patients with IBS.
Rare pathogenic variants in the sucrase-isomaltase gene, implying reduced ability to digest sucrose and starch, were found in 4% of patients with IBS.
In patients with sucrase-isomaltase gene variants, a diet reduced in carbohydrates, starch, and sucrose led to a ≥50-point decrease in IBS-SSS in 74% of patients.
A meta-analysis found the pooled prevalence of IgA antibodies to tissue transglutaminase in IBS patients was 5.7%, with an odds ratio of 4.5 for biopsy-proven celiac disease compared to controls.

A recent meta-analysis found the pooled prevalence of microscopic colitis among IBS patients was 7.4% in cross-sectional studies and 7.1% in case-control studies, slightly lower than the 10.9% prevalence found in non-IBS diarrhea patients.
A systematic review and meta-analysis found that 32.5% of patients with inflammatory bowel disease in remission had IBS-like symptoms.

It was proposed that patients with idiopathic bile acid malabsorption (bile acid diarrhea) have impaired secretion of the enterocyte hormone FGF19, which normally controls hepatic bile acid synthesis, leading to bile acid overproduction.
Several studies show that about 25% of patients with diarrhea-predominant IBS (IBS-D) have bile acid diarrhea.

Pimentel and colleagues initially reported that 78% of IBS patients had an abnormal lactulose hydrogen breath test suggesting small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, and 48% no longer met IBS criteria after antibiotic treatment.

A study using massive parallel sequencing of jejunal mucosa-associated bacteria found no difference in bacterial composition between IBS patients and healthy controls, and oro-cecal transit time (not true SIBO) was shown to explain abnormal LHBT results.
A recent meta-analysis of indirect SIBO tests found 31% of IBS patients had findings indicating SIBO compared to 21% of controls.

A UK study of 314 IBS-D patients found low fecal elastase-1 (<100 μg/g), indicating exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, in 6.1% of patients, with symptom response to enzyme supplementation in 18/19 of these.

Loss-of-function mutations in SCN5A, encoding the NaV1.5 sodium channel expressed in smooth muscle and interstitial cells of Cajal, were found in 2.2% of patients with IBS and were associated with IBS-like symptoms.

A genome-wide association study of 53,400 IBS cases and 433,201 controls identified six genetic susceptibility loci for IBS; four implicated genes (NCAM1, CADM2, PHF2/FAM120A, DOCK9) are linked to mood/anxiety disorders and nervous system expression, suggesting shared etiologic pathways between IBS and anxiety.

A meta-analysis of case-control studies found patients with IBS have increased Lactobacillaceae, Bacteroides, and Enterobacteriaceae, and decreased Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium compared to controls, though changes were subtle.
UK researchers reported that 49% of patients with unexplained gastrointestinal symptoms at a tertiary referral center had clinical evidence of joint hypermobility.
Joint hypermobility was reported in 33% of patients referred from primary care to GI clinics and 35.4% of those specifically fulfilling IBS symptom criteria.

A Mayo Clinic retrospective study found gastrointestinal symptoms in 56% of EDS patients overall, with IBS-like symptoms in 30.3% of hEDS, 18.6% of classical EDS, and 14.8% of vascular EDS patients; among those investigated, 22.3% had abnormal gastric emptying, 28.3% abnormal colonic transit, and 60% a rectal evacuation disorder.

A US case-control study of hospitalized patients found gastrointestinal conditions in 44% of EDS patients vs 14% of controls, with IBS (OR=7.44) and gastroparesis (OR=12.26) strongly associated with EDS, along with food allergy (OR=3.88) and autonomic dysfunction (OR=4.45).
Postural tachycardia syndrome (PoTS), neurocardiogenic syncope, and orthostatic hypotension are described as common autonomic manifestations in patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

In a large online-survey case-control study of persons with HSD/hEDS, 98% met Rome-IV criteria for functional gastrointestinal disorders and 90% met criteria for functional bowel disorders, compared to 40% of population controls.

The authors report clinical use of bedtime subcutaneous octreotide (25-50 μg) after an initial antibiotic course to prevent recurrent small intestinal bacterial overgrowth in patients with HSD/hEDS and enteric dysmotility, with some success.
A study of 107 adults with autism spectrum disorder found 86% had at least one gastrointestinal symptom, 54% had three or more symptoms, and 62% reported diarrhea.

Using Wisconsin Medicaid claims data on 143 adults with ASD aged 40-88, 50% had been diagnosed with a gastrointestinal disorder, with no difference between those with and without intellectual disability.
In a UK tertiary referral study, 49% of patients with unexplained gastrointestinal symptoms had clinical evidence of joint hypermobility assessed by a self-reported 5-point questionnaire.
A study of patients with rectal evacuatory dysfunction found joint hypermobility in 32% of them.
A study of patients referred from primary care to GI clinics found joint hypermobility in 33% of them.
In a separate analysis of the same primary-care-to-GI-clinic cohort, joint hypermobility was present in 35.4% of patients who fulfilled the symptom criteria for IBS.

A Mayo Clinic retrospective study found gastrointestinal symptoms in 56% of EDS patients overall, with IBS-like symptoms in 30.3% of hypermobile EDS, 18.6% of classical EDS, and 14.8% of vascular EDS patients.
In the same Mayo Clinic EDS cohort, physiological testing found abnormal gastric emptying in 22.3%, abnormal colonic transit in 28.3%, and a rectal evacuation disorder in 60% of those investigated.

A US case-control study of hospitalized patients found gastrointestinal conditions in 44% of EDS patients vs 14% of controls, with IBS (OR=7.44) and gastroparesis (OR=12.26) strongly associated with EDS.
The same US case-control study also found significant associations of food allergy (OR=3.88) and autonomic dysfunction (OR=4.45) with EDS.
Postural tachycardia syndrome (PoTS), neurocardiogenic syncope, and orthostatic hypotension are reported to be common comorbidities in patients with EDS.
An online case-control survey found that 98% of persons with HSD/hEDS met Rome-IV criteria for functional gastrointestinal disorders.
In the same online survey, 90% of HSD/hEDS patients fulfilled criteria for functional bowel disorders compared to 40% of population controls.

The authors report using bedtime subcutaneous octreotide injections (25-50 μg) after an initial antibiotic course to prevent recurrent small intestinal bacterial overgrowth in patients with HSD/hEDS and enteric dysmotility, with some clinical success.
The authors state that antihistamines and mast cell stabilizers may have a role in treating food hypersensitivity in HSD/hEDS patients, but note that randomized controlled trial data are lacking.
A study of 107 adults with autism spectrum disorder found that 86% had at least one gastrointestinal symptom, 54% had at least three symptoms, and 62% reported diarrhea.

Using Wisconsin Medicaid claims data on 143 adults with ASD aged 40-88 years, 50% had been diagnosed with gastrointestinal disorders, with no difference between those with and without intellectual disability.
