Atypical sensory processing is reported in 82-97% of children with autism, which the authors relate to the heightened conscious sensitivity to gut signals seen in functional gastrointestinal disorders.

The authors' own review of new referrals in 2022 found that 12% of patients with symptoms lacking an organic correlate had already been diagnosed with ASD in childhood, with clinical suspicion that unrecorded ASD may be even more prevalent.
Mutations in the human COL12A1 gene, which encodes collagen XII, cause an Ehlers-Danlos/myopathy overlap syndrome with skeletal abnormalities and muscle weakness.
Collagen XII is widely expressed across multiple connective tissues of the developing joint.
Lack of collagen XII in mice destabilizes tendons and the femoral trochlear groove, inducing patellar subluxation in the patellofemoral joint.
Collagen XII deficiency in mice is associated with an ECM damage response in tendon and secondary quadriceps muscle degeneration.
Patellar subluxation was identified as a clinical feature in human patients with collagen XII deficiency.
The findings provide an explanation for joint hyperlaxity in both mice and human patients with collagen XII deficiency.
EDS diagnosis was significantly more common among rural pediatric migraine patients than non-migraine patients, though prevalence was low overall.
A proposed mechanism links chronic joint hypermobility in EDS to migraine via stimulation of cervical afferents and activation of the trigeminal cervical complex.
Depression diagnosis was significantly more common among children/adolescents with migraine compared to those without migraine.
Anxiety diagnosis was significantly more common among children/adolescents with migraine compared to those without migraine.
Unhealthy weight (overweight/obese) showed only a marginally significant difference between migraineurs and non-migraineurs.
Elevated blood pressure was not significantly associated with migraine status in this rural pediatric sample.
OSAS diagnosis rates did not significantly differ between migraineurs and non-migraineurs.
Narcolepsy diagnosis did not significantly differ between migraineurs and non-migraineurs.
RLS diagnosis did not significantly differ between migraineurs and non-migraineurs, in contrast to prior studies.
Migraine diagnosis was significantly more common in females than males in this rural pediatric population.
Children and adolescents with migraine had a significantly higher mean number of comorbidities than those without migraine.
A significantly higher proportion of migraineurs had multiple (vs one) and medium (vs low) comorbidities compared to non-migraineurs.
Male sex was a protective factor against migraine diagnosis in both bivariate and multivariable logistic regression models.
Race categorized as 'Other' (vs White or Black) was significantly associated with increased odds of migraine diagnosis.
Depression was significantly associated with increased odds of migraine in both bivariate and adjusted multivariable models.
Anxiety was significantly associated with increased odds of migraine in both bivariate and adjusted multivariable models.
Unhealthy weight showed only a marginal, non-significant association with migraine in logistic regression models.
Among overweight/obese children, depression was significantly more prevalent in those with migraine than without.
Among overweight/obese children, anxiety was significantly more prevalent in those with migraine than without.
The review notes that autonomic nervous system manifestations in connective tissue dysplasia are predominantly sympathicotonic in nature.
The paper states there is evidence linking headaches and musculoskeletal pain with connective tissue dysplasia in both children and adults.
Thoracic spine self-mobilization significantly reduced the sum of lumbar rotation angles from L1 to S1 during trunk rotation compared with sham after 4 weeks.
No significant between-group difference was observed for individual segmental lumbar rotation angles (L1/2 through L5/S1), only the summed L1-S1 value differed significantly.
VAS pain scores after trunk backward bending were significantly lower in the thoracic spine self-mobilization group than in the sham group after 4 weeks.
There was no significant difference in Oswestry Disability Index scores between the thoracic spine self-mobilization and sham groups.
Thoracolumbar rotation ROM was significantly greater in the thoracic spine self-mobilization group than in the sham group after 4 weeks.
Erector spinae muscle stiffness measured by Myoton Pro showed no significant difference between the thoracic spine self-mobilization and sham groups.
The tennis ball self-mobilization device was easy to use and portable, resulting in a high compliance/implementation rate of 96%.
1H-MRS studies found significantly higher glutamate levels in FM patients than healthy controls in several pain-processing brain regions.
FM patients showed higher CSF glutamate levels than both chronic migraine patients and healthy controls, with levels correlating with neurotrophin production but not clinical pain.
Multiple studies found significantly higher CSF substance P levels in FM patients than healthy controls, though the relationship with clinical pain severity was absent or inverse.
Serum substance P findings in FM were inconsistent, with one study finding no difference from controls and two more recent studies finding elevated levels.

Serum substance P levels decreased significantly after massage therapy, acupuncture, or salmon milt extract supplementation, treatments that improved clinical pain, though a direct correlation with SP change was not established.
Both available studies measuring CSF NGF found significantly higher levels in FM patients compared to healthy controls, correlating with BDNF levels and chronic pain duration but not pain severity.
Peripheral NGF levels did not differ between FM patients and healthy controls in one study, contradicting a role for peripheral growth factor levels in FM pathophysiology.
One study found reduced peripheral NGF levels in FM patients compared to controls, with no relation to other serological biomarkers or clinical data.
Several studies found higher CSF, plasma, and serum BDNF levels in FM patients compared to healthy controls.
Other studies found no difference in plasma or serum BDNF levels between FM patients and controls, and one study found significantly lower serum BDNF in FM patients.

Serum BDNF levels decreased rapidly in FM patients after one month of duloxetine treatment, supporting BDNF's role in pain modulation, though levels did not differ from other chronic nociceptive pain disorders.
Mu opioid receptor availability is reduced in multiple pain-processing brain regions in FM patients and correlates significantly with the affective dimension of pain.
FM and osteoarthritis patients with moderate/severe pain showed a lower percentage of B cells and natural killer cells expressing MOR compared to controls, inversely related to pain intensity.
Endogenous enkephalin levels are higher in the CSF of FM patients, consistent with an overactive opioidergic system.
Systematic reviews/meta-analyses found FM patients have a distinct peripheral blood cytokine profile with increased TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8, and IL-10 compared to healthy controls.

CSF IL-8 levels in FM patients were higher than in healthy controls, rheumatoid arthritis patients, and even higher than peripheral blood IL-8 in the same FM patients, suggesting CNS (astrocyte/microglial) origin.

Skin biopsy cytokine gene expression findings in FM patients were conflicting, with one study detecting TNF, IL-1β, and IL-6 expression only in FM patients (not controls) and another finding no differences.
A 2015 clinical trial found that the mast cell stabilizer ketotifen failed to reduce pain sensitivity or improve clinical pain and symptom severity in FM patients.
FM women had higher plasma PTX-3 levels than healthy controls, with no difference between depressed and non-depressed FM patients.

Monocytes from FM women without depression released more PTX-3 than controls both constitutively and after LPS stimulation, while neutrophil PTX-3 release did not differ, suggesting monocytes as a peripheral PTX-3 source in FM.

Some studies found reduced plasma NPY levels in FM patients compared to controls, including low NPY after 30 minutes on a tilt table, suggesting hypofunction/hyporeactivity of the sympathetic stress axis.

Other studies found higher NPY plasma and serum levels in FM patients compared to controls, along with lower HRV and a significant relation between HRV and NPY, suggesting a maladaptive sympathetic-adrenal response.

A meta-analysis found FM patients have significantly lower vitamin D levels than healthy controls, and a second meta-analysis found low serum vitamin D positively associated with chronic widespread pain conditions including FM, though causality could not be inferred from observational data.

A third meta-analysis found no difference in circulating vitamin D concentration or deficiency prevalence between FM patients and healthy controls, attributed to poor-quality data and heterogeneity in underlying studies.

FM patients showed differences in gut microbiome composition compared to healthy controls, correlating with serum metabolite alterations, with differentially abundant species implicated in short-chain fatty acid and bile acid metabolism.

Choline, a marker of glial activation, was elevated in the anterior insula of FM patients compared to controls, with reduced anterior insula-putamen connectivity; both findings associated with worse pain interference.
Power spectrum analyses of HRV showed FM patients have reduced HRV, reflecting sympathetic hyperactivity and decreased parasympathetic tone.
FM patients show flattened diurnal cortisol variation and HPA axis hyporeactivity, including delayed/reduced ACTH response to stress stimuli such as IL-6 injection or hypoglycemia.

Small fiber neuropathy has been described in FM patients, supporting the hypothesis of small fiber damage as an early trigger of pain, though its causal/primary role remains debated with mixed replication.
COMT gene polymorphisms have been proposed as a predisposing factor for FM development, but reports across studies remain contradictory.
Fibromyalgia patients show increased numbers of mast cells in the papillary dermis compared to controls, suggesting a peripheral source of neurosensitizing mediators reaching the CNS.
A 2015 clinical trial found that mast cell stabilizer ketotifen did not reduce pain sensitivity or improve clinical pain and symptom severity in FM patients.
Skin biopsy gene expression studies found TNF, IL-1β and IL-6 expressed in FM patients' skin but undetectable in healthy controls.
A separate study found no differences in cytokine expression in skin samples of FM patients compared to healthy controls, contradicting an earlier report.
Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of peripheral blood samples found FM patients have elevated levels of TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8 and IL-10 compared to healthy controls.
A longitudinal study found a relation between chemokine levels, particularly IL-8 and MCP-1, and the severity of pain in FM patients.
During pain therapy, IL-8 levels decreased concordantly with pain intensity, but this relation was statistically significant only after six months of treatment.

IL-8 levels in the cerebrospinal fluid of FM patients were higher than in both healthy controls and rheumatoid arthritis patients, and higher than in peripheral blood in the same FM patients, suggesting a CNS (astrocyte/microglial) source.
It has been hypothesized that thalamic mast cells contribute to neuroinflammation and pain in FM by releasing neurosensitizing mediators that stimulate diencephalon microglial cells.
Plasma pentraxin-3 (PTX-3) levels were higher in women with FM compared to healthy controls, with no difference between FM patients with and without depression.
Monocytes from women with FM without depression released more PTX-3 than those from healthy controls, both constitutively and after LPS stimulation, while neutrophil PTX-3 release did not differ.
Some studies found reduced plasma NPY levels in FM patients compared to controls, along with low NPY after tilt-table testing, suggesting sympathetic axis hypofunction and hyporeactivity.

Conversely, other studies found higher plasma and serum NPY levels in FM patients versus controls, along with lower HRV and a significant NPY-HRV relationship, suggesting a maladaptive increase in sympathetic-adrenal activity.
None of the studies examining NPY plasma/serum levels found a significant relationship between NPY levels and clinical pain in FM, limiting its use as a pain biomarker.
A meta-analysis by Makrani et al. found significantly lower vitamin D levels in FM patients compared to healthy controls.

A second meta-analysis found a positive association between low serum vitamin D levels and chronic widespread pain conditions including FM, though no causal relationship could be inferred from observational data.

A third meta-analysis found no difference in circulating vitamin D concentration or deficiency rates between FM patients and healthy controls, attributed to poor-quality data and heterogeneity in prior studies.
Clos-Garcia et al. described differences in gut microbiome composition between FM patients and healthy controls, correlating with serum metabolite alterations.

A review highlighted that differentially abundant gut bacterial species in FM include short-chain-fatty-acid producers and bile-acid metabolizers, suggesting a possible correlation with clinical phenotype and symptom severity.
Personality traits such as neuroticism and extraversion have been reported to relate to pain duration and severity in fibromyalgia.
Coexisting clinical manifestations of fibromyalgia such as sleep disorders, anxiety, and intestinal irritability suggest underlying autonomic nervous system dysfunction.
Predisposing psychosocial factors including coping styles, anger, suicide risk, lack of physical activity, and lack of social support are reported to maintain persistent pain in fibromyalgia.
The authors propose that personality traits could serve as biomarkers in fibromyalgia diagnosis, potentially supported by artificial intelligence algorithms for diagnostic and prognostic purposes.
One included RCT of Tai-Chi found a significant correlation between changes in heart rate variability (autonomic modulation) and changes in pain intensity.
Five of six RCTs examining the relationship between hypothesized mechanisms (e.g. improved aerobic fitness) and pain outcomes found no significant relationship after exercise intervention.
A resistance exercise RCT found no significant change in plasma nerve growth factor and no significant relationship with pain outcomes.
The same resistance exercise RCT found no significant change in plasma brain-derived neurotrophic factor and no significant relationship with pain outcomes.

Twelve weeks of combined exercise significantly improved self-esteem and quality of life, with self-esteem positively correlated with the SF-36 mental health component, but self-esteem was not significantly correlated with pain scores.

Larsson et al. found that 15 weeks of resistance exercise improved pain acceptance and reduced fear avoidance, with a significant positive relationship between improvements in pain scores and global impression of change scores.

Aquatic environment properties (buoyancy, thermal effects, tactile/mechanoreceptor stimulation, relaxation) were the most frequently hypothesized physical mechanism for exercise-related pain relief, cited in 12 of 17 aquatic exercise trials.
Exercise-induced hypoalgesia (EIH), attributed to activation of the endogenous opioid system, was the most frequently hypothesized neurophysiological mechanism, cited in 15 of the 50 included RCTs.
Fibromyalgia is associated with sympathetic hyperactivity that may relate to its pathogenesis, and yoga/meditation were hypothesized to reduce this hyperactivity as a pain-relief mechanism.
Qigong was hypothesized to improve fibromyalgia symptoms via regulation of immune markers including C-reactive protein and interleukin-6.
Symptom improvement after exercise in fibromyalgia may be partly due to amelioration of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis dysfunction.
Muscle oxygenation improvement via strength or aerobic exercise was hypothesized to reduce peripheral and central sensitization and improve clinical pain in fibromyalgia.

Studies outside this review (not included) found that individuals with FM have impaired exercise-induced hypoalgesia and increased pain sensitivity following various types of exercise, contrasting with the healthy-individual-based EIH mechanism cited by most included studies.
Compared to healthy controls, individuals with fibromyalgia have autonomic dysfunction implicated as an important cause of symptoms.
A prior systematic review found preliminary evidence that aerobic exercise reduces autonomic dysfunction in fibromyalgia, but not resistance exercise.

Preliminary evidence cited in included studies showed that both single-session and long-term exercise increased growth hormone and serum cortisol levels (HPA function markers) in individuals with fibromyalgia.

A systematic review found that effects of single-session exercise (25-45 min) on pro- and anti-inflammatory biomarkers in fibromyalgia were unclear overall, though an overall anti-inflammatory effect of exercise was observed.
A case-control study demonstrated improved muscle oxygen kinetics after 8 weeks of aerobic exercise, supporting muscle oxygenation as a mechanism for pain reduction.

A systematic review reported positive effects of hyperbaric oxygen therapy on pain outcomes in fibromyalgia, proposed to work via improved tissue oxygenation, reduced glial cell activation/inflammation, and improved metabolic function.
The prevalence of fibromyalgia in the general population is estimated at 1-5%, varying by diagnostic criteria used.
FM diagnosis often takes more than 2 years and patients see an average of 3.7 different physicians before diagnosis.

Nociplastic pain, common in FM, is presumed to arise from decreased inhibition or amplification of pain signaling in the peripheral and central nervous systems, though the mechanism is not fully understood.
The 1990 ACR tender-point-based criteria were difficult for primary care physicians to apply and neglected key associated symptoms like fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and sleep disturbance.
The 2010/2011 ACR criteria (widespread pain index) can lead to misclassification because they do not account for the spatial distribution of pain locations or define generalized pain.
Among six diagnostic criteria sets compared, the 2016 revised ACR criteria showed the best diagnostic performance for FM.
The AAPT criteria performed worst among compared FM diagnostic criteria in sensitivity, specificity, and classification accuracy.
Multisite pain (used in AAPT criteria) was found to be a stricter criterion than the widespread pain index used in the ACR criteria.
Pregabalin improved pain and sleep disturbances across six randomized controlled trials in FM patients.
A meta-analysis found pregabalin improves pain, fatigue, sleep, and HRQoL but not depression in FM patients, with small effect sizes.

Duloxetine and milnacipran, serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors, decreased pain, improved clinical condition, reduced fatigue, improved mood, and enhanced HRQoL, though effect sizes were small to marginal.
Amitriptyline reportedly decreased pain and fatigue while improving sleep and HRQoL in FM patients, with small-to-moderate, unconfirmed efficacy due to methodological limitations.
A meta-analysis of five trials found cyclobenzaprine improved global functioning and elicited moderate improvements in pain and sleep quality in FM patients.
Tramadol combined with acetaminophen decreases pain and FIQ score and improves physical functioning in FM patients.
Adding milnacipran to pregabalin improved pain, overall condition, and symptoms in FM patients with incomplete response to pregabalin monotherapy, in a randomized trial.
Patients receiving combined pregabalin and duloxetine had better pain relief, physical function, and HRQoL outcomes than those receiving either drug alone.
The Spanish Society of Rheumatology guidelines do not recommend NSAIDs, opioids, or benzodiazepines for FM due to insufficient evidence of efficacy and risks of addiction or side effects.

Meta-analyses show that exercise (aerobic, aquatic, resistance, strengthening) improves pain, fatigue, sleep, depression, and FIQ scores in FM patients, with all exercise types considered equally effective.
Traditional and acceptance-based CBT are effective for reducing pain, negative mood, and disability, and for improving HRQoL in FM patients.
Internet-based CBT (ICBT) reduces negative mood and disability and improves HRQoL in FM patients, but has not demonstrated at least 50% pain reduction.
Recent meta-analyses show tDCS and rTMS are safe and effective for relieving pain and related symptoms in FM patients, contrasting with an earlier meta-analysis's findings.

A meta-analysis of nine RCTs found multicomponent therapy effective for reducing pain, fatigue, and depressed mood, and for improving self-efficacy and physical fitness in FM patients, though benefits were short-lived.

In a clinical sample of adults with alcohol use disorder (AUD), chronic pain and evidence of central sensitization, as measured by a validated fibromyalgia-survey-based surrogate, were highly prevalent.
Greater central sensitization scores were associated with worse health-related quality of life among participants with AUD.
Participants with higher central sensitization more strongly endorsed pain as a reason for AUD onset, maintenance, escalation, treatment delay, and relapse.
The paper reports that patients with mast cell activation syndrome experience a relapsing-remitting pattern of joint disease (arthropathy).
Adding sIgE to a mixture of 4 Ara h 2 peptides improved the diagnostic performance of Ara h 2-sIgE alone for peanut allergy, with AUC increasing from .89 to .92 (borderline significance).
The combination of Ara h 2-sIgE and peptide mix-sIgE achieved 85% sensitivity and 96% specificity for peanut allergy diagnosis.
sIgE to individual Ara h 2 peptides showed the highest specificity (91%-96%) but lowest sensitivity (10%-52%) among the tested measures.
Ara h 2-sIgE alone had 69% specificity and 87% sensitivity for peanut allergy diagnosis.
Peptide mix-sIgE alone had 82% specificity and 63% sensitivity for peanut allergy diagnosis.
Peptide 3 of Ara h 2 directly induced mast cell activation in the LAD2 mast cell line functional assay.
The Ara h 2 peptide mix inhibited Ara h 2-induced activation of mast cells sensitized with plasma from Ara h 2-positive peanut-allergic patients.
Large-cohort studies have shown that statins reduce the severity of asthma.
The authors previously found that statins inhibit IgE-induced mast cell function, though effects varied widely among mouse strains and human donors.
Upregulation of HMGCR, the statin target enzyme, likely underlies the variable statin resistance observed in mast cell inhibition experiments.
Statin inhibition of mast cell function appeared to be mediated by suppressing protein isoprenylation events using cholesterol pathway intermediates, rather than by cholesterol reduction itself.
Genetic depletion of the isoprenylation enzymes farnesyltransferase and geranylgeranyl transferase 1 significantly reduced FcεRI-mediated degranulation and cytokine production in mast cells.
Genetic depletion of K-Ras, the substrate of the isoprenylation enzymes, significantly reduced FcεRI-mediated degranulation and cytokine production.
Pharmacological inhibition with the dual farnesyltransferase/geranylgeranyl transferase 1 inhibitor FGTI-2734 similarly reduced FcεRI-mediated mast cell degranulation and cytokine production.
Both farnesyltransferase and geranylgeranyl transferase 1 must be inhibited together to reduce mast cell function, indicating a redundant requirement for both isoprenylation enzymes.
The dual farnesyltransferase/geranylgeranyltransferase-1 inhibitor FGTI-2734 suppressed mast cell-dependent anaphylaxis in vivo.
FGTI-2734 suppressed allergic pulmonary inflammation in vivo.
FGTI-2734 suppressed airway hyperresponsiveness in an allergic mouse model in vivo.
K-Ras is identified as a critical isoprenylation substrate whose modification is required for FcεRI-induced mast cell function, and thus a potential target for allergic disease.

Among 194 surgical procedures in patients with known mastocytosis, 91.8% involved chronic antimediator therapy and/or perioperative prophylactic medications, and only one case of intraoperative anaphylaxis occurred overall, in a patient who underwent surgery before mastocytosis diagnosis and thus received no prophylaxis.

Among procedures with prophylaxis, 10 were potentially complicated by mast cell activation as inferred from intraoperative administration of inhaled albuterol (n=3) or intravenous diphenhydramine (n=8).
Intraoperative anaphylaxis can be the first presenting sign of mastocytosis, as illustrated by a patient whose anaphylaxis occurred during a procedure preceding formal diagnosis and prophylaxis.

Con-, HF- and DTM-SCS all significantly reduced mechanical hypersensitivity (increased log10 PWT) compared to sham after 48 hours of continuous stimulation, with no significant differences between the three active paradigms.
None of the SCS paradigms (Con, HF, DTM) affected the motivational/operant aspect of pain, as measured by MCAS exit latency or crossing duration.
Con-SCS significantly increased spinal dorsal horn Tnf-α RNA expression after 48 hours compared to both Sham-SCS and DTM-SCS.
RNA expression of Il-1ß, Il-4 and Il-10 in the spinal dorsal horn was not significantly affected by any SCS paradigm (Con, HF, or DTM) compared to sham.

A composite index (pro- minus anti-inflammatory cytokine log2 expression) suggested Con-SCS shifts the spinal inflammatory balance toward a pro-inflammatory state, while HF- and DTM-SCS shift it toward an anti-inflammatory state, relative to sham; this was descriptive/indicative only, without formal statistics.
No significant differences were found in RNA expression of microglial marker Itgam, astrocyte marker Gfap, or T-cell marker Cd3d among Sham-, Con-, HF-, and DTM-SCS groups after 48 hours.
No significant differences in RNA expression of microglial proliferation markers Irf8 and Adgre1 were observed between SCS paradigms and sham.
No significant differences in RNA expression of P2x4, Mapk14, or Bdnf were found between any SCS paradigm and sham in the spinal dorsal horn.
Treatment with total alkaloids (TA) from Alstonia scholaris reduced pulmonary inflammation, MUC5AC mucus production, and airway hyperresponsiveness in OVA-induced asthmatic mice.
TA administration inhibited eotaxin production and reduced eosinophil recruitment in the lungs of OVA-induced asthmatic mice.
TA significantly decreased Th2 and Th17 cytokines while increasing Th1 cytokines, restoring the Th1/Th2/Th17 cytokine balance disrupted in asthma.
TA reduced ILC2 cell numbers, likely by inhibiting IL-33, IL-25, and TSLP levels in BALF and suppressing IL-33/ST2 signaling in lung tissue.
TA decreased total IgE (tIgE), OVA-specific IgE (OVA-IgE), and MCP-1 levels in serum/BALF of OVA-induced asthmatic mice.
By lowering IgE and MCP-1, TA inhibited mast cell activation and subsequent leukotriene (LTB4, LTC4, LTD4, LTE4) release in the asthma model.
TA treatment increased E-cadherin expression in lung tissue as assessed by immunohistochemistry, suggesting restoration of airway epithelial barrier integrity.
TA treatment decreased leukotriene (LTB4, LTC4, LTD4, LTE4) levels in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, consistent with inhibition of mast cell mediator release.
RT-qPCR showed TA treatment reduced gene expression levels of IL-33 and ST2 in lung tissue, corroborating protein-level findings of pathway inhibition.
Six patients with small fiber neuropathy were found to be seropositive for ANCA antibodies, suggesting a possible novel association between ANCA positivity and SFN.
MPO-specific ANCA antibodies were identified alone in 4 of the 6 SFN patients.
PR3-specific ANCA antibodies were identified alone in 1 of the 6 SFN patients, and combined with MPO in another.
Systemic ANCA-associated vasculitis was noted in 2 of the 6 patients with SFN and ANCA positivity, while the remainder had isolated SFN without systemic manifestations.
Five of the six patients with ANCA-associated SFN received immunosuppressive treatment, with 3 experiencing partial improvement and 3 showing symptom stabilization.
Stabilization of SFN symptoms after AAV treatment was accompanied by improvement in ANCA antibody titer, suggesting a possible causal association between ANCA and SFN, though this cannot be proven.
This ANCA-associated SFN presentation is distinct from the more typical ANCA-mediated peripheral neuropathy phenotypes of mononeuropathy multiplex or axonal sensorimotor neuropathy.
Across 34 participants using the PsyMate ESM smartphone diary, 1,058 of a possible 2,380 beep signals were completed, giving an overall response rate (compliance) of 44.5%.

The ESM response rate observed in this secondary chronic pain cohort (44.5%) was notably lower than the 71.1%-86% response rates reported in earlier ESM studies of psychiatric or primary chronic pain populations, though still above the 33% minimum threshold considered necessary for valid ESM analysis.
Individual missing-data rates for ESM beep signals varied widely across participants, ranging from 13% to 97% with a median missing rate of 54.1%.

A multilevel binary logistic regression found that age, gender, education level, work state, HADS anxiety/depression score, and substance abuse (tobacco, alcohol, drugs) did not predict low ESM response rates, and missingness appeared to be completely at random.
In the general evaluation questionnaire, most of the 19 respondents rated the ESM study week as a normal week and felt the answer options represented their experiences well.
Participants reported that using the PsyMate ESM diary did not meaningfully affect their social contacts, daily activities, or mood.
The average time participants took to complete each ESM beep signal was 87.48 ± 56.49 seconds, supporting low time burden of the tool.

The earliest and latest scheduled daily beep signals were completed less often than other beep signals (6.9% and 9.4% completion respectively), suggesting a mismatch between the beep schedule and participants' wake-sleep rhythm.

Seven of 34 participants experienced technical issues with the ESM smartphone application, mostly related to smartphone operating systems, and for five participants these issues could not be resolved during or after the study period.
No differences in ESM response rates were found between the three secondary chronic pain diagnostic groups (small fiber neuropathy, spinal cord injury, rheumatoid disorder).

The study cohort of 34 participants with chronic secondary pain-related disability comprised 19 with small fiber neuropathy, 11 with spinal cord injury, and 4 with rheumatoid disorder, recruited from a single rehabilitation outpatient clinic in the Netherlands.

On the hand (thenar), warm detection threshold (WDT) and cold detection threshold (CDT) measured with the method of limits (MLI) differed significantly among the three age groups, with the youngest group showing lower WDT and higher CDT than both older groups.
In the trigeminal (supraorbital) region, only CDT measured by MLI differed significantly by age, with the 18-39 group showing higher CDT values than both older groups.

On the foot dorsum, all five QST parameters (WDT-MLI, CDT-MLI, WDT-MLE, CDT-MLE, HPT) differed significantly among age groups, with older subjects generally showing reduced thermal sensory discrimination and higher pain thresholds.
Female subjects showed significantly lower WDT on the hand with the MLI method compared to males, indicating better warm-stimulus discrimination in women.
Female subjects showed significantly lower WDT on the foot with the MLE paradigm compared to males, indicating better warm-stimulus discrimination in women.
Female subjects showed higher CDT on the foot with the MLI paradigm compared to males, indicating better cold-stimulus discrimination in women.
Female subjects had lower heat pain thresholds (HPT) on the hand and trigeminal area compared to males, consistent with lower pain thresholds reported previously in women.

WDT values were significantly higher (worse discrimination) on the foot compared to both the hand and trigeminal area, with no difference between hand and trigeminal area, for both MLI and MLE methods.
CDT values were significantly lower on the foot compared to both the hand and trigeminal area, and lower on the hand compared to the trigeminal area, for both MLI and MLE methods.
Heat pain thresholds were higher on the foot than on the hand or trigeminal area, and higher on the hand than the trigeminal area.
WDT values obtained with the method of levels (MLE) were consistently lower than those obtained with the method of limits (MLI) across all body sites.
CDT values obtained with the MLE method were consistently higher than those obtained with the MLI method across all body sites.
Age correlated positively with WDT-MLI (worsening warm detection with age) at all three body sites, most strongly on the foot.
Age correlated negatively with CDT-MLI (worsening cold detection with age) at all three body sites.
Age correlated positively with WDT-MLE on the trigeminal area and the foot.
Age correlated positively with heat pain threshold (HPT), but only on the foot, suggesting age-related length-dependent loss of nociceptive small fiber sensitivity.

Some older subjects (predominantly men aged 60-80) were unable to perceive the cold stimulus on the foot with the MLI paradigm, and in two of these cases even with the MLE paradigm, indicating age-related loss of foot cold sensation in otherwise healthy individuals.

Reference threshold values in subjects older than 40 years could exceed the Q-Sense device's low temperature cut-off (20°C) on the foot, limiting the device's sensitivity for detecting cold hypoesthesia in this age group, consistent with a prior report but observed in both sexes here (more often in men).

The review reports that alterations in gut microbiome composition and function contribute to the pathogenesis of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), and that diet/nutrition can modulate this relationship.
The review states that biochemical pathways involving immune function, intestinal permeability, and mucosal inflammation are dysregulated in IBS.
A high-fiber diet was reported to increase short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production and improve symptoms in patients with IBS.
Probiotics and prebiotics were reported to modulate the gut microbiome and improve clinical outcomes in patients with IBS.
A low-FODMAP diet, which limits specific fermentable carbohydrates, was reported as potentially useful for easing fibromyalgia symptoms.
A diet high in anti-inflammatory foods (fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean protein) was reported as potentially beneficial for individuals with fibromyalgia.

Women with fibromyalgia who interacted with natural biotic/abiotic sensory stimuli for 30 minutes showed a significant reduction in clinical pain intensity compared with those exposed to synthetic imitations.
Cold pain thresholds, measured as cold-water immersion tolerance time, increased significantly more in the nature-stimulation group than in the placebo (synthetic imitation) group.

A significant group by time interaction was found for mechanical hyperalgesia (assessed via monofilament wind-up) between the nature-stimulation and placebo groups, though the abstract does not specify the direction of within-group change.
Pressure pain thresholds increased significantly more in women with fibromyalgia who received the nature-based multisensory stimulation than in those receiving synthetic imitations.
In the merged GSE45485/GSE76885 skin biopsy dataset, 86 genes were differentially expressed between SSc patients and healthy controls, with 58 upregulated and 28 downregulated.

GO and KEGG enrichment of SSc DEGs highlighted extracellular matrix organization, granulocyte/myeloid leukocyte migration, collagen-containing ECM, cytokine activity, and cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction pathways.
WGCNA identified the MEblue gene co-expression module as most strongly correlated with SSc disease trait.

Intersection of DEGs, top 30 highest-connectivity WGCNA genes, and top biologically important genes in the MEblue module yielded seven hub genes (THY1, SULF1, PRSS23, COL5A2, NNMT, SLCO2B1, TIMP1) implicated in SSc pathogenesis.

GSEA of the seven hub genes showed enrichment in autoimmune disease pathways, microbial infection pathways, inflammatory signaling (NF-kB, TNF, chemokine, AGE-RAGE), immune response pathways, and fibrosis-related pathways.
THY1 expression was significantly higher in SSc skin samples than healthy controls and showed high diagnostic accuracy (AUC 0.903) in the discovery cohort.
SULF1 expression was significantly higher in SSc skin samples than healthy controls and showed high diagnostic accuracy (AUC 0.903) in the discovery cohort, with combined THY1+SULF1 AUC of 0.922.
THY1 and SULF1 expression positively correlated with established SSc causative genes (TGFB1, CTGF, COL1A1, COL1A2, IL6, CCL2, VCAM1, THBS1) in the discovery cohort.
THY1 and SULF1 diagnostic performance was replicated across four independent validation GEO cohorts, with AUCs ranging from 0.756 to 1.000.
CMap analysis using the top 30 highest-connectivity WGCNA genes identified ten small-molecule compounds with predicted therapeutic potential against SSc.
Molecular docking showed BRL-50481 binds PDE4B, PDE4D, and PDE7A with favorable (negative) binding energies, supporting its predicted phosphodiesterase-inhibitor mechanism against SSc.
Molecular docking showed dipyridamole binds PDE2A, PDE5A, PDE10A, and SLC29A1 with favorable binding energies.
Molecular docking showed SB-525334, a TGF-β receptor/ALK5 inhibitor, binds TGFBR1 with favorable binding energy, and it can cross the blood-brain barrier per ADMET prediction.
Molecular docking showed GW-311616 binds ELANE with favorable binding energy, consistent with a predicted anti-SSc mechanism.
HRQoL score declined significantly during the acute SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to before infection.

Three months after infection, HRQoL score was slightly lower than before infection, but this decrease was smaller than the minimal detectable change and thus not considered clinically relevant at the population level.
Nearly half of the cohort (49%) had post COVID-19 condition, defined as reporting at least one symptom related to their SARS-CoV-2 infection three months afterwards.
Having post COVID-19 condition was strongly associated with a decrease in HRQoL over time following infection.
Women were more likely than men to experience a decrease over time in HRQoL following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
People with a lower educational level were more likely to experience a decline in HRQoL over time following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Having a pre-existing chronic disease was associated with a marked decrease over time in HRQoL following COVID-19 infection.
People with obesity (BMI≥30) were more likely to have a decline in HRQoL following SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to those with normal BMI.
People who were not vaccinated against COVID-19 at the time of infection were more likely to experience a decline in HRQoL compared to those with a complete primary vaccination schedule.
Being hospitalised following SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with a decline in HRQoL over time.
A greater number of acute COVID-19 symptoms at the time of infection was associated with a decline in HRQoL score.

The negative association between PCC and HRQoL was significantly stronger among participants who had been hospitalised due to COVID-19, indicating an interaction effect between PCC and hospitalisation.
HRQoL score at three months post-infection showed a gradual decrease with increasing number of PCC symptoms, from a mean of 0.95 with no symptoms to 0.65 with 10 or more symptoms.
The most frequently self-reported PCC symptoms in the cohort were fatigue/exhaustion, headache, memory problems, loss of smell and/or taste, shortness of breath, and sleeping problems.

Shortness of breath as a PCC symptom was associated with problems across all five dimensions of HRQoL (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) three months after infection.
Fatigue/exhaustion and memory problems were associated with problems in the mobility, usual activities, and anxiety/depression dimensions of HRQoL.
Muscle pain was associated with problems in mobility, usual activities, and pain/discomfort dimensions of HRQoL.
Sleeping problems, dizziness, and chest pain were each associated with problems in the usual activities dimension of HRQoL.
Headache, joint pain, dizziness, persistent cough, chest pain, and stomach pain were significantly associated with problems in the pain/discomfort dimension of HRQoL.

The pain/discomfort dimension had the highest proportion of people reporting problems three months after infection, and this was substantially higher in people with PCC than in people without persistent symptoms or the non-COVID matched control group.
The anxiety/depression dimension had the second-highest proportion of problems, higher in people with PCC than in those without symptoms or the matched non-COVID control group.
The self-care dimension had the lowest proportion of people reporting problems among those with PCC, only slightly higher than in people without symptoms or the matched non-COVID control group.

After FDR correction across 40 gray matter and 20 white matter ROIs, COVID-19 case status was not significantly associated with DBSI-RF (a putative marker of neuroinflammatory cellularity) in any brain region.

Nominally significant (uncorrected p<0.05) increases in DBSI-RF were observed in COVID-19 cases in the right caudate, amygdala, caudal and rostral anterior cingulate cortex, lateral orbitofrontal cortex, and fusiform gyrus, though none survived FDR correction.
Left caudal middle frontal gyrus, superior parietal lobule, and postcentral gyrus showed nominally significant reductions in DBSI-RF among COVID-19 cases relative to controls.
The temporal portion of the left superior longitudinal fasciculus showed a nominally significant increase in DBSI-RF among COVID-19 cases.

COVID-19 case status was significantly associated with increased DBSI-HF (a putative marker of vasogenic edema) in the left precentral and postcentral gyri and the caudal portion of the right middle frontal gyrus after FDR correction.

Additional cortical regions and white matter tracts, including bilateral superior frontal gyrus, bilateral pars triangularis, and the right cingulum bundle, showed nominally significant increases in DBSI-HF among COVID-19 cases.

In post-hoc analyses restricted to cases tested ≤60 or ≤90 days before imaging, no DBSI-RF or DBSI-HF group differences survived multiple testing correction, and the previously significant DBSI-HF effects seen in the full sample were no longer evident in these shorter time-window subgroups.
Whole-brain voxel-wise threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) analysis of delta DBSI-RF and DBSI-HF maps found no significant clusters distinguishing COVID-19 cases from controls.
Excluding the 13 hospitalized COVID-19 cases from the main analyses did not materially change the DBSI-RF or DBSI-HF results, suggesting symptom severity was not driving the observed associations.

Only 10% of health professionals had received formal teaching about ME/CFS during medical school, while 44% had received continuing medical education about it, totaling 49% with some prior teaching, which was not significantly different from the hypothesized 50% threshold.
Only 43% of health professionals reported knowing how to diagnose ME/CFS, significantly lower than the hypothesized 50% threshold, indicating a diagnostic confidence gap.
Health professionals' confidence in dealing with ME/CFS patients was slightly below the scale midpoint but only marginally significant, indicating tentatively low confidence.
Participation in a 120-minute ME/CFS webinar significantly increased health professionals' knowledge test scores from baseline to post-webinar.

In the waiting-list control condition, repeating the knowledge test without webinar participation did not significantly increase scores, indicating the knowledge gain in the intervention group was not due to practice effects.
In Study 2's intervention condition, knowledge test performance was significantly higher at T2 than T1, confirming the webinar's effect against the control comparison.
Baseline knowledge levels did not differ significantly between the control and intervention groups in Study 2, supporting equivalence prior to the intervention.

Despite the overall knowledge improvement, about one third of participants persistently failed to correctly distinguish chronic fatigue from the full clinical picture of ME/CFS even after the webinar.

Around one third of health professionals incorrectly believed psychological trauma can trigger ME/CFS, suggesting persistent subtle psychologization of the illness despite most correctly rejecting a psychosomatic framing.
Despite random assignment, control condition participants in Study 2 were on average six years younger than intervention condition participants, a baseline demographic imbalance.

Participants who completed both T1 and T2 questionnaires did not differ from those who dropped out after T1 on demographics, experience, confidence, or baseline knowledge, indicating no selective dropout.
Among the combined baseline sample of health professionals, only a small minority (11%) reported never having seen a patient with ME/CFS in clinic or practice.
Some ME/CFS patients show distinct EBV antibody profiles, defective EBV-specific immune responses, and higher anti-EBV-dUTPase antibodies/active infection relative to healthy controls.
Active HHV-6 infection, HHV-6 antibody levels, and HHV-6 transcripts in brain/spinal cord tissue are more prevalent in ME/CFS.

ME/CFS biopsies show increased enterovirus presence in muscle and stomach tissue plus higher serum antibodies compared to healthy controls, and infected stomach biopsy material could transmit disease to immunodeficient mice.
A six-month valacyclovir trial increased physical functional capacity and improved cardiac function in EBV+ ME/CFS patients.
A six-month valganciclovir trial produced similar positive responses in a separate ME/CFS cohort.
Isoprinosine increased NK cell activity and IL-12 production and improved clinical health measures in most participants in an ME/CFS cohort.
Multiple trials in adolescent and adult ME/CFS patients suggest IVIG is a promising treatment via immunomodulatory effects.

A genome-wide association study found no significant genetic relationship between COVID-19 severity/hospitalization and ME/CFS susceptibility, though shared immune dysregulation and inflammation were noted.
Hypercoagulability, microclot loads, and hyperactivated platelets are extensive in post-acute SARS-CoV-2 syndrome but observed less frequently in pre-2020 ME/CFS cases.

PBMC metabolic assays in ME/CFS show reduced glycolysis, decreased mitochondrial respiration, lower coupling efficiency, and altered pyruvate dehydrogenase/CoA metabolism, indicating insufficient ATP production and dysregulated FAO.
Two studies found decreased ATP production in ME/CFS PBMCs, with one also reporting reduced coenzyme Q10 levels.
No significant differences were found in PBMC mitochondrial complex activity in ME/CFS compared to healthy controls.
Studies conflict on PBMC mitochondrial mass in ME/CFS, with one reporting decreased mass and another finding no difference versus healthy controls.

A study on ME/CFS PBMCs found significantly increased non-mitochondrial ATP production and increased mitochondrial cristae condensation, with no differences in mitochondrial morphology or membrane potential.
Proteomic analyses of PBMCs and lymphoblasts in ME/CFS show increased expression of ketone body metabolism enzymes, acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, and fatty acid oxidation enzymes.
Isolated ME/CFS CD4+ and CD8+ T cells show reduced basal glycolysis at rest, with CD8+ cells also reduced after stimulation.
ME/CFS CD8+ T cells show decreased proton leak, reduced ATP production, and lower mitochondrial membrane potential both at rest and after activation compared to healthy controls.
Both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from ME/CFS patients show elevated fatty acid oxidation compared to healthy controls.
ME/CFS CD4+ T cells show increased expression of the inhibitory receptor PD-1, associated with a hypometabolic, FAO-favoring state.
ME/CFS CD8+ T cells show reduced cytotoxicity compared to healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients under 50 show an increased CD4+/CD8+ T cell ratio and increased CD8+ effector memory T cell frequency.
CCR6+ Th17 cells in ME/CFS produced less IL-17 than controls despite a higher frequency of these cells.
Treating ME/CFS CD8+ T cells with IL-2 and a CD3/CD28 activation cocktail did not rescue the metabolic differences seen in these cells, unlike the reversibility typically seen in classic anergy.
GLUT1 expression was not decreased at rest in either CD4+ or CD8+ ME/CFS T cells, and CD8+ T cells were able to upregulate GLUT1 to control levels after stimulation.
A study of ME/CFS serum found elevated levels of phosphorylated ATG13, a protein that restricts autophagy in active cells.

Flow cytometry of ME/CFS whole blood found significantly increased CD4+CD73+CD39- and regulatory T cell (Treg) populations compared to healthy controls, supporting an anergic feature in ME/CFS CD4+ T cells.
A gene expression study reported elevated expression of four NFAT-related genes in ME/CFS, consistent with features of anergy/exhaustion.
Transcription-factor binding site analysis in PBMCs showed upregulation of EGR2/3, but this finding was only associated with EBV-linked ME/CFS infection or reactivation.
Increases in microRNAs that regulate Sirt1 suggest that Sirt1 expression may be lower in ME/CFS PBMCs, contrary to the anergic transcriptional profile which typically shows upregulated Sirt1.
Increased plasma IL-10, which suppresses cytokine production in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, has been reported in ME/CFS, similar to levels seen in anergic and exhausted T cell states.
ME/CFS plasma cytokine analyses have not definitively shown decreased IL-2 production compared to healthy controls, as would be expected in a classic anergic state.

Flow cytometric analyses in ME/CFS have shown increased CD4+PD-1+ cells and an increased Th17 population, alongside decreased cytokine production in other T cell populations, all features consistent with an exhausted immune cell state.
A study in moderately severe ME/CFS patients found decreased CD8+KLRG1+ and CD4+KLRG1+ population frequencies compared to healthy controls.
A DNA methylation study of ME/CFS PBMCs revealed a hypo-methylated state in the IRF4 enhancer region, suggesting upregulation of this exhaustion-related transcription factor.

SASP-like pro-inflammatory cytokines including TNFα, TGFβ, IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-4, IL-6, and IFNγ positively correlate with ME/CFS disease severity, consistent with a senescence phenotype, though overall cytokine findings in ME/CFS show varying consistency.
In two studies, the frequency of senescence-associated CD4+CD28- and CD8+CD28- T cell populations was not increased in ME/CFS PBMC samples compared to healthy controls.
A third study found decreased proportions of terminally differentiated effector CD8+ T cells in ME/CFS compared to a healthy cohort.

A flow-cytometric analysis found significantly lower abundance of CD57, a common senescence marker, in ME/CFS CD3+ T cells, and slightly lower frequency of CD3+CD57+ cells compared to healthy controls.
In moderately severe ME/CFS patients, CD4+ T cells showed increased expression of KIR2DL5 (part of the KIR receptor family), an NK-like senescence marker.

A 2018 report on ME/CFS whole-blood DNA found significantly different telomere lengths compared to healthy controls, with female participants under 45 years old contributing substantially to this phenotype, suggesting shortened telomeres unrelated to general aging.
A DNA methylation gene ontology analysis in total PBMCs indicated that the p38 MAPK signaling pathway was upregulated in ME/CFS compared to controls.
Elevated NF-κB production has been detected in ME/CFS lymphocytes, which antagonizes p53 transcription — the opposite of what is typically seen in T cell senescence.

A longitudinal study measuring NK cell cytotoxicity and cytokine secretion in ME/CFS patients at 0, 6, and 12 months found inconsistent and sometimes opposing levels of TNFα, IFNγ, IL-10, IL-17A, and IL-2 within the same individuals over time.

Flow-cytometric analyses found lower frequencies of NKG2C+ (activating receptor) NK cell populations in ME/CFS, which could contribute to reduced NK cell function, while NKG2A+ and CD57+ senescence-related subsets showed no difference from healthy controls.
TSH levels, though within normal range, were significantly higher in SSc-CFS patients than in SSc-NCFS patients and healthy controls.
Arthralgia was more frequently present in SSc-CFS patients compared to SSc-NCFS patients.

Immunomodulatory therapy use was associated with higher rates of arthralgia, and vasodilator use (without immunomodulators) was associated with digital ulcers, likely reflecting treatment-by-indication bias rather than a causal effect on ME/CFS symptoms.
Severe fatigue, measured by MFI and FACIT, was significantly higher in SSc-CFS patients than in SSc-NCFS patients.
Two-thirds of SSc-CFS patients also met diagnostic criteria for comorbid fibromyalgia.
Widespread pain index scores were significantly higher in SSc-CFS patients than in SSc-NCFS patients and healthy controls.
Symptom severity score (fatigue, tiredness, cognitive impairment) was significantly higher in SSc-CFS patients than SSc-NCFS and healthy controls.
Quality of life, measured by SF-36 physical and mental component scores, was significantly lower in SSc-CFS patients compared to SSc-NCFS patients and healthy controls.
HADS depression scores were significantly higher in SSc-CFS patients than in SSc-NCFS patients and healthy controls, though overall depression rates were similar across groups.
Rates of anxiety and HADS anxiety scores were significantly higher in SSc-CFS patients compared to SSc-NCFS patients and healthy controls.
SSc-CFS patients had significantly higher Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores than SSc-NCFS patients, though rates of clinically defined sleep disturbance were similar.
Cognitive failure scores did not differ significantly between SSc-CFS, SSc-NCFS, and healthy control groups.
Use of immunomodulatory and vasodilator medications was not associated with ME/CFS-related symptoms in SSc patients.
Mitochondrially encoded ND4 expression showed a trend toward reduced expression in SSc-CFS patients compared to SSc-NCFS patients.
Mitochondrially encoded Cytochrome B expression was significantly lower in SSc-CFS patients compared to both healthy controls and SSc-NCFS patients.

Nuclear-encoded COX7C expression was significantly increased in SSc-CFS patients compared to SSc-NCFS patients, without corresponding changes in CoxIV protein, suggesting a possible compensatory role.
Mitochondrial D-loop expression, a marker of mtDNA transcription, was not significantly different between SSc-CFS, SSc-NCFS, and healthy control groups.
Protein levels of TFAM, a mitochondrial transcription factor controlling mtDNA copy number, were similar between SSc-CFS and SSc-NCFS patients.
Cell-free mtDNA integrity (ratio of mtDNA230 to mtDNA79 fragments) did not significantly differ between SSc-CFS, SSc-NCFS, and healthy controls, though SSc-CFS patients trended lower.
CyB expression correlated with fatigue severity as measured by the FACIT scale.
COX7C expression correlated inversely with fatigue severity as measured by the FACIT scale.
mtDNA integrity correlated inversely with fatigue severity as measured by the MFI scale.
CyB expression correlated with quality of life (reduced) as measured by SF36-Vitality.
mtDNA integrity correlated with reduced quality of life as measured by SF36-Vitality.
ND4 expression correlated with increased skin involvement (mRSS) and reduced lung diffusion capacity (DLCO SB), as well as FVC and FEV1, in SSc patients.
CyB expression correlated with increased skin involvement (mRSS) and reduced lung diffusion capacity (DLCO SB) in SSc patients.

A trend toward reduced presence of anticentromere antibodies (ACA) was observed in SSc-CFS patients compared to SSc-NCFS patients, potentially relevant given ACA's association with less fibrotic disease.
CyB and Cox7C gene expression correlated with fatigue severity as measured by the FACIT scale in SSc patients.
Cell-free mtDNA integrity correlated with fatigue severity as measured by the MFI in SSc patients.
CyB expression and mtDNA integrity both correlated with reduced quality of life as measured by the SF-36 Vitality subscale.
ND4 and CyB gene expression correlated with increased skin involvement (mRSS) and reduced lung diffusion capacity (DLCO SB) in SSc patients.
ND4 expression was significantly correlated with pulmonary function measures FVC and FEV1 in SSc patients.
A trend toward reduced presence of anticentromere antibodies (ACA) was observed in SSc-CFS patients compared to SSc-NCFS.

31P-MRS testing showed markedly prolonged phosphocreatine recovery (Tc=80s) in the tibialis anterior muscle of the fatigued patient S1, compared with 30s in her unaffected sibling S2 and 37-40s in healthy volunteers, and this was reproducible on repeat testing.
Patient S1 fibroblasts had lower oxygen consumption rate and decreased respiratory complex IV subunit proteins MTCO1 and MTCO2 compared with sibling control S2 fibroblasts.
WASF3 protein was increased ~40% in patient S1 fibroblasts compared to sibling control S2, coinciding with a ~34% decrease in MTCO1.

shRNA knockdown of WASF3 in patient S1 fibroblasts improved basal respiration and increased spare respiratory capacity to the level of control S2 cells, demonstrating a causal role for WASF3 in the patient's bioenergetic deficiency.
WASF3 knockdown decreased phosphorylation of p53 (Ser46) and p38 but not JNK in patient S1 cells, indicating these are downstream of WASF3-induced respiratory inhibition.
Overexpressing WASF3 in mouse C2C12 myoblasts with wild-type p53 induced p38 phosphorylation while decreasing respiration and complex IV subunits, without affecting other respiratory complexes.

WASF3 overexpression induced transcription of the mitochondrial biogenesis gene PGC1α and respiratory complex genes including MTCO1, suggesting a compensatory feedback response to WASF3-induced mitochondrial disruption.
Knocking down p38 in WASF3-overexpressing myoblasts worsened mitochondrial respiration and reduced PGC1α levels, supporting p38 activation as a compensatory response to WASF3-induced dysfunction.

In a human BAC transgenic mouse model, WASF3 was significantly increased in tibialis anterior, gastrocnemius, and soleus skeletal muscle, with associated decreases in complex IV subunits but not other respiratory complexes.
WASF3 Tg mouse soleus muscle showed a significantly lower OCR/ECAR ratio (reduced oxidative metabolism relative to glycolysis) and lower muscle glycogen content compared with wild-type mice.

WASF3 Tg mice showed higher resting blood lactate levels than wild-type mice, mirroring elevated resting blood lactate reported in ME/CFS patients that correlates with postexertional malaise severity.

WASF3 Tg mice showed ~50% reduction in maximal treadmill running capacity while four-paw grip strength was unchanged compared with wild-type littermates, despite normal body weight, morphology, and lifespan.

WASF3 was enriched in mitochondrial fractions of C2C12 myoblasts, and mitochondrial WASF3 migrated faster than the cytosolic form on SDS-PAGE; alkaline phosphatase treatment shifted the band, indicating mitochondrial WASF3 is post-translationally phosphorylated.

WASF3 overexpression in C2C12 myoblasts/myotubes and WASF3 Tg mouse skeletal muscle both showed ~50% reduction in respiratory supercomplex III2+IV (assessed by CIII FeS protein immunoblot and in-gel COX activity), while complex I activity was not reduced.

Preincubating mitochondrial lysates with WASF3 antibody selectively reduced the SC III2+IV band without affecting complex I activity, confirming that WASF3 physically associates with the supercomplex and that antibody binding interferes with its assembly.

Both full-length WASF3 (aa 1-499) and C-terminally truncated WASF3 (aa 1-332) inhibited mitochondrial respiration and decreased MTCO1, and proximity-biotinylation showed both constructs specifically labeled the Complex III subunits UQCRC1 and UQCRFS1, indicating the WASF3 N-terminal region mediates the interaction with CIII that blocks supercomplex assembly.
Skeletal muscle biopsies from a cohort of postinfectious ME/CFS patients showed significantly increased WASF3 protein and decreased Complex IV subunit proteins compared with healthy volunteers.
In ME/CFS muscle biopsy samples, Complex IV subunit levels (MTCO1, COX17) showed significant negative correlations with both WASF3 and PERK levels.
The ER stress marker PERK was significantly higher in ME/CFS patient muscle biopsy samples compared with healthy controls.

WASF3 protein levels were not appreciably increased in heart, brain, or liver of WASF3 transgenic mice compared with skeletal muscle, though mild complex IV subunit reductions were still observed in these tissues.

mRNA levels of mitochondrial genes ND1, MTCO1, and ATP6 were significantly increased in skeletal muscle and heart of WASF3 transgenic mice, likely reflecting a compensatory feedback response to WASF3-induced mitochondrial disruption.
WASF3 transgenic mouse soleus muscle showed a significantly lower OCR-to-ECAR ratio than wild-type, indicating a metabolic shift from oxidative phosphorylation toward glycolysis.

WASF3 transgenic mice had higher tail blood lactate levels than wild-type mice, mirroring elevated resting blood lactate reported in ME/CFS patients that correlates with postexertional malaise severity.
Gastrocnemius glycogen content was significantly lower in WASF3 transgenic mice than wild-type, attributed to increased glucose utilization secondary to mitochondrial disruption.
WASF3 transgenic mice showed a ~50% reduction in maximal treadmill running capacity compared with wild-type littermates, despite unchanged grip strength and normal appearance/lifespan.

Electron microscopy showed no significant difference in myofilament striation pattern, and α-actinin levels were unchanged between WASF3 transgenic and wild-type muscle, suggesting structural sarcomere integrity is preserved despite bioenergetic disruption.

Subcellular fractionation showed WASF3 is enriched in mitochondria, and the mitochondrial form migrates faster than cytosolic WASF3 on SDS-PAGE; alkaline phosphatase treatment shifted the band, indicating mitochondrial WASF3 is phosphorylated.

WASF3 overexpression in C2C12 myoblasts increased WASF3 immunoreactivity at the ~720-kDa respiratory supercomplex band while decreasing CIII (UQCRFS1) and CIV (COX) in-gel activity at that band, with CI activity unaffected, indicating WASF3 specifically disrupts supercomplex III2+IV.

Skeletal muscle mitochondria of WASF3 transgenic mice showed reduced supercomplex III2+IV levels (FeS protein, MTCO1, in-gel CIV activity), while CI activity and CV subunit ATP6 were unaffected, confirming the cell-culture findings in vivo.

Quantification showed ~50% reductions in supercomplex III2+IV in-gel COX activity in both WASF3 transgenic mouse muscle and WASF3-transfected cells, while CI activity was even higher than in respective controls.
Because heart WASF3 was not significantly increased in transgenic mice, there were no observable alterations in respiratory complex stoichiometry or overall mitochondrial activity in the heart.

Preincubating mitochondrial lysates with WASF3 antibody (versus nonimmune IgG) selectively reduced the 720-kDa supercomplex III2+IV band without affecting the CI band, providing direct evidence that WASF3 physically interacts with and disrupts the supercomplex.

Both full-length WASF3 (residues 1-499) and a C-terminal truncated form (residues 1-332) inhibited mitochondrial respiration and decreased MTCO1 levels when overexpressed, indicating the N-terminal mitochondrial-membrane-embedded region is sufficient for respiratory inhibition.

Proximity-dependent biotinylation (BioID) showed that both full-length and truncated WASF3 specifically increased biotinylation of complex III subunits UQCRC1 (Core I) and UQCRFS1 (Rieske FeS protein), indicating direct physical proximity of WASF3 to complex III components important for its assembly and dimer stability.

Only full-length WASF3 (not the C-terminal truncated form) promoted biotinylation of actin in the BioID assay, confirming the C-terminal domain mediates actin interaction as a specificity control distinct from the N-terminal mitochondrial interaction.

Skeletal muscle biopsies from a cohort of postinfectious ME/CFS patients showed significantly increased WASF3 with concomitant decreases in complex IV subunit proteins compared with healthy volunteers.
ME/CFS muscle samples showed significantly higher PERK but lower BiP compared with controls, a discordant pattern termed 'ER Stress Response Failure' implicated in metabolic disorders.
In ME/CFS patient muscle samples, complex IV subunit levels (MTCO1, COX17) showed significant negative correlations with both WASF3 and PERK levels.

Treating human myoblasts with the ER stress inducers thapsigargin or tunicamycin increased WASF3 protein (without increasing its mRNA) and decreased complex IV subunit MTCO1, demonstrating posttranslational induction of WASF3 by ER stress.

LPS injection in mice, a model of human chronic fatigue, posttranscriptionally increased WASF3 in skeletal muscle along with ER stress markers PERK and BiP, and WASF3 levels were inversely correlated with MTCO1.
Patient S1 fibroblasts showed a higher basal level of PERK than sibling S2, suggesting increased ER stress underlies aberrant WASF3 regulation in the patient.

Despite increased PERK, phosphorylation of eIF2α was paradoxically lower (i.e., activated) in patient S1 cells, indicating a failure of the normal ER stress response (ER Stress Response Failure) also seen in ME/CFS muscle biopsies.
Salubrinal, a PP1 inhibitor that prevents eIF2α dephosphorylation, decreased both PERK and WASF3 levels in patient S1 fibroblasts, more effectively than TUDCA.

Salubrinal treatment restored decreased supercomplex III2+IV levels in patient S1 fibroblasts while complex V levels remained unchanged, indicating targeted specificity of the ER stress-WASF3-supercomplex pathway.
MTCO1 protein levels showed a significant negative correlation with WASF3 protein levels across ME/CFS and control muscle samples.
COX17 protein levels negatively correlated with WASF3 protein levels in the combined ME/CFS and control muscle samples.

Self-reported sleep disorder decreased significantly from the first to the second visit (46.9% to 41.4%).

A relevant proportion of post-COVID patients had several ME/CFS-associated symptoms but did not fulfill full ME/CFS diagnostic criteria, most often because sleep disturbance was not reported.

The expert panel reached consensus that long COVID affects multiple organ systems and presents through a range of symptoms.
Experts agreed that individuals with symptoms consistent with ME/CFS and post-exertional malaise (PEM) should be carefully supported and monitored before engaging in physical activity.

The panel did not reach consensus that people with long COVID can resume regular physical activity simply because it does not currently provoke symptoms or post-exertional symptom exacerbation, and this statement was rejected.

The panel rejected the inclusion of low-level physical activities (e.g., walking causing moderate heart rate increases), muscle-use activities, and flexibility/functional movement training as generic long COVID support components, consistent with concern that exercise may be detrimental in long COVID/ME-CFS/PEM.
Consensus was reached that long COVID support should adopt a multidisciplinary approach involving physiotherapists, clinicians, rehabilitation specialists, and exercise scientists.
Consensus was reached that cognitive and physical pacing of activities (regulating energy use) should be included in long COVID rehabilitation and support.
Consensus highlighted that post-exertional malaise/post-exertional symptom exacerbation should be a key consideration in long COVID care, addressed through pacing and fatigue management strategies.
Consensus was reached that long COVID services should offer psychological well-being support for patients who require it.
Experts agreed that long COVID rehabilitation and support should focus on breathlessness, cognitive dysfunction, fatigue, respiratory function, restoring functional capacity, and sleep disturbance.

The panel agreed that pre-existing conditions with overlapping symptoms, specifically ME/CFS, should be considered in the design of long COVID rehabilitation, but did not extend this to chronic respiratory diseases such as COPD, asthma, or pneumonia, nor acute respiratory infections such as pneumonia.

The panel rejected the idea that support mechanism design for long COVID could draw lessons from other chronic respiratory diseases (e.g., asthma, COPD) or acute respiratory infections (e.g., pneumonia), reflecting a view that long COVID is mechanistically distinct.
Consensus was reached that people living with long COVID require detailed clinical assessments and functional screening assessments during diagnosis and treatment.

Consensus that respiratory function should be assessed to establish rehabilitation needs reached 81% overall agreement, but the healthcare professional subgroup only reached 69.1% agreement, below the 80% consensus threshold.
Consensus (88% overall) was reached that long COVID cannot be predicted by the severity of symptoms during the acute (first 2 weeks) phase of COVID-19 infection.
Consensus was reached that it remains unknown whether individuals living with long COVID will make a full recovery.
Consensus (87% overall) found there is a lack of clear referral pathways to support people living with long COVID across all healthcare settings, though the HCP subgroup only reached 69% agreement.

There is inadequate and inconsistent support amongst all healthcare services for individuals living with long COVID, and a lack of understanding among healthcare professionals about how to support these patients, according to expert consensus.

A 57-year-old woman with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome developed severe valgus ankle deformity as a donor-site complication after free vascularized fibular grafting (FVFG) used to revise an ulnar nonunion.

Generalized joint hypermobility due to ligamentous laxity is more prevalent in children than adults, explaining why valgus ankle deformity after FVFG is common in pediatric patients (up to 40% incidence) but rare in adults without connective tissue disease.
The overall prevalence of Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome in the general population is reported as one in 5000.

The authors hypothesize that in adults with EDS, weak syndesmotic ligaments cannot adequately support the ankle after fibular shaft removal, causing force to be dispersed to the distal fibular remnant and syndesmotic ligaments, leading to displacement and valgus deformity.

The authors recommend that adults with EDS undergoing FVFG may benefit from syndesmotic stabilization (screws or suture devices) or primary syndesmotic fusion to prevent valgus ankle deformity, or alternatively should have structural grafts harvested from an alternative donor site such as the iliac crest.

Angiotensin II type 1 receptor blockers such as losartan have shown a protective role against aneurysmal formation by preventing noncanonical ERK1/2 activation in TGF-β signaling.

Aortic walls of MFS patients show fragmentation and disorganization of elastic fibers in the media, calcification, thickening of all layers from collagen/amorphous matrix accumulation, and focal intimal thickening in all vessels.
Altered collagen structure in MFS produces degradation products that attract inflammatory cells, and the resulting inflammatory process aggravates disease severity.
