Patients with COL3A1 dominant-negative mutations (glycine missense and splice-site variants) have earlier, more severe disease and greater risk of aneurysms, dissections, and ruptures of medium-sized vessels such as the carotid arteries compared to the aorta.

vEDS diagnosis requires two of four clinical criteria (thin translucent skin; arterial, intestinal, or uterine rupture; easy bruising; characteristic facial appearance) together with confirmation of the responsible genetic mutation.

In a vEDS mouse model, progressive fragmentation of the intima and media was seen with sparing of the adventitia, leading to proliferation of smoothelin-positive medial vascular smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts forming a collagenous scar.
The FBN1 truncating mutation is associated with a higher probability of aortic events and earlier onset age compared to missense mutations.

ESC guidelines recommend surgery in MFS at aortic root diameter ≥50 mm, or 46-50 mm with family history of dissection, progressive dilation >2 mm/year, severe AR/MR, or desire for pregnancy; in LDS a more aggressive threshold of >42 mm is recommended due to tissue fragility, while no established cut-off exists for vEDS.
In a trial, the group of vEDS patients treated with celiprolol had a lower risk of cardiovascular events compared to the control group.
A long-term observational study with average follow-up of 5 years confirmed increased survival in vEDS patients treated with celiprolol, especially at a dosage of 400 mg/day.
No differences were found in rate of aortic dilatation or frequency of clinical events between losartan and beta-blocker groups, though losartan use is associated with a lower long-term risk.

In LDS, TGFBR2 mutation, female gender, aortic tortuosity, hypertelorism, and translucent skin are factors associated with worse prognosis and greater risk of aortic dissection, warranting more timely surgery.

GenTAC registry data show that aortic surgery in MFS patients is associated with excellent outcomes, while vEDS patients have higher cardiovascular mortality likely due to greater disease aggressiveness.

Endovascular treatment (TEVAR) is not first choice in syndromic aortic diseases due to significantly high endoleak risk and higher reoperation risk, but is preferred in emergency life-saving situations due to lower perioperative mortality than open surgery.

Gene panel testing identified a pathogenic de novo splice-site variant (c.1662+1G>A) in COL3A1, disrupting the donor site of intron 23 and causing exon 23 skipping, confirming the diagnosis of vascular EDS.

The patient's pathology revealed segmental absence of the intestinal muscularis propria (SAIM), an extremely rare finding whose coexistence with vEDS has only been reported once before, in a 16-year-old patient.
GI tract perforations account for 82% of all gastrointestinal complications in vEDS patients, with a mean age of onset of 24 years and mortality of up to 12%.

More than 50% of vascular complications in vEDS involve the thoracic or peritoneal cavity, with medium-sized vessels such as mesenteric, renal, or splenic arteries typically affected, due to aneurysm formation, spontaneous vessel wall rupture, or fistula formation.

In approximately 20% of vEDS patients, hernia formation is the initial disease manifestation, and vEDS patients are 2.5 times more likely to develop inguinal hernia than the general population, rising to about 10 times greater risk in young males up to 19 years old.

Rectal prolapse affects about 4% of EDS patients, typically occurring in children or newborns, without increased incidence specifically in vEDS, and is associated almost exclusively with digestive tract ruptures.
Approximately 4% of EDS patients are diagnosed with gastrointestinal diverticulosis on endoscopic examination.
While overall postoperative mortality in vEDS patients is low (~2%), mortality specifically related to GI perforation complications is 45% and to arterial complications is 41%.

About 68% of vEDS patients required surgery for complications such as arterial dissection or intestinal/hollow viscus perforation, compared with only 10% of all EDS patients requiring GI surgery and 33% specifically for vascular-type EDS.
Vascular EDS accounts for less than 4% of all EDS cases, has an estimated prevalence of 1:20,000 to 1:50,000, and carries a median life expectancy of approximately 50 years.

COL3A1 genotype predicts phenotype severity: null mutations are linked to delayed symptom onset (after age 20) limited to vascular events, in-frame exon-skipping splice variants and glycine substitutions are linked to reduced survival, while small residue glycine substitutions confer a milder phenotype.
The patient's high-output enterocutaneous fistula was managed conservatively with total parenteral nutrition, antibiotics, and octreotide, successfully reducing fistula output before discharge.

Surgical mesh placement for abdominal wall closure in this vEDS patient became infected twice, requiring removal both times, illustrating poor wound healing and tissue fragility characteristic of the syndrome.
Following diagnosis, combined enteral and high-calorie parenteral home nutrition via a port catheter for short bowel syndrome resulted in the patient gaining 6 kg over two months post-discharge.

Over roughly two years, the index patient underwent seven laparotomies for recurrent small bowel/colon perforations, ultimately developing short bowel syndrome, a persistent enterocutaneous fistula, wound dehiscence, and a postoperative abdominal hernia.

In a 20-year-old man with type II EDS undergoing scoliosis correction surgery, postoperative avulsion of branches of the left internal iliac artery caused retroperitoneal hemorrhage, hypovolemic shock, and retroperitoneal compartment syndrome.
The patient developed a deep vein thrombosis of the left common femoral, popliteal, and greater saphenous veins shortly after discharge, requiring readmission and therapeutic anticoagulation.

At 3-year follow-up, the patient's neurological deficits had substantially recovered, with 4/5 tibialis anterior strength, normalized gait without foot drop, and no need for assistive devices, though some dorsal foot sensory loss persisted.

A review of 19,360 general pediatric scoliosis correction cases found that only 0.5% of patients experienced a nonfatal hematological complication and 0.01% developed a deep vein thrombosis, indicating low baseline vascular complication rates in non-EDS populations.

In a cohort of 85 general scoliosis correction patients, 13 required ICU admission postoperatively, but only 1 was due to hematological instability, suggesting hematological complications are uncommon in non-EDS scoliosis surgery.
Among 260 pediatric and adult patients undergoing scoliosis correction (general, non-EDS), no major bleeding events occurred and only 1.5% had a minor bleeding event.

Vogel and Lubicky reported four EDS cases with neurological and vascular complications following scoliosis surgery, including segmental artery avulsion requiring aortic repair, two cases of paraplegia, and one case of foot/ankle weakness with transient neurogenic bladder.

Akpinar et al described five EDS patients who failed brace treatment and required surgery for severe curves (mean lumbar 69.7°, thoracic 46.4°), one of whom suffered a potentially fatal rupture of the common iliac artery and vein during blunt dissection.

Uehara et al reported large-volume blood loss in an EDS patient undergoing spinal surgery for kyphoscoliosis despite prophylactic intranasal vasopressin, indicating tissue fragility can overcome pharmacologic bleeding-control measures.

Pozdnikin and Ryzhakov reported no significant neurological or vascular injury in surgical correction of eight EDS patients with kyphoscoliosis, contrasting with other reports of high complication risk.
Jasiewicz et al reported that none of 11 EDS patients undergoing scoliosis correction suffered vascular or neurological complications.
A retrospective NSQIP database review of 21,490 pediatric spinal surgery patients (56 with EDS) found no significant difference in bleeding complication rates between patients with and without EDS.
Scoliosis is reported to account for up to 23.4% of musculoskeletal conditions in patients with EDS, contributing to increased susceptibility to spinal deformity in this population.

Risk factors that may alert surgeons to potential abdominal/retroperitoneal compartment syndrome after spine surgery include high-volume fluid resuscitation, organ failure, prone positioning, and hypotension.
Preoperative angiography is generally of little diagnostic benefit for predicting vascular injury risk in EDS patients because many do not have detectable structural vascular defects or occlusions.

Whole genome sequencing identified a novel heterozygous splice acceptor variant in COL5A1 (c.501-2A>C) at the exon 4 boundary, considered the likely causal variant for classical EDS in the affected cat.

A second heterozygous COL5A1 missense variant (p.Arg827Trp) was found in the case cat but is analogous to a human variant (p.Arg828Trp) classified in ClinVar as likely benign, suggesting it is not causal for EDS.
A heterozygous COL6A1 variant (p.Arg493Gln) was identified in the case cat but the analogous human variant is of uncertain or benign significance and not considered causal for the cat's phenotype.

A heterozygous COL17A1 variant (p.Gly1410Ser) was found in the case cat, absent from ClinVar and very rare in gnomAD, and considered unrelated to the cat's EDS phenotype since COL17A1 disorders present differently (junctional epidermolysis bullosa-type conditions).
A unique heterozygous COL22A1 variant was found in the case cat but is not present in human variant databases and not considered causal for the EDS phenotype.
Skin biopsy histopathology from the affected cat showed loosely arranged collagen bundles with shortened, irregularly arranged collagen fibers compared to a control cat.

Transmission electron microscopy of the affected cat's skin showed flower-like collagen fibrils with irregular edges and variable diameter, ultrastructural defects also reported in humans and other cats with COL5A1 mutations.

Giemsa staining showed increased cutaneous mast cell numbers in the affected cat's superficial dermis above published feline normal values, but this elevation was also present in the control sample, limiting attribution to the EDS phenotype.

Chronic pruritus in the affected cat was attributed to mast cell activation, referencing that up to 66% of human patients with EDS and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome experience related symptoms.
Hind limb declawing significantly reduced cutaneous self-trauma in the affected cat, with healthy intact skin observed 8 months post-procedure compared to prior recurrent lacerations and eschars.

Amitriptyline (1 mg/kg PO q12h, to reduce mast cell degranulation) and gabapentin (10 mg/kg PO q12h, for perceived neuropathic pain) were used to manage hyperesthesia, vocalization, and excessive grooming/biting behaviors in the affected cat.
Corticosteroids and fluoroquinolones were avoided in the affected cat because of the risk of further collagen damage in EDS.
Echocardiography of the affected cat revealed mild systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, with cardiovascular findings otherwise unremarkable.

In vitro cell culture data show that COL5A1 haploinsufficiency causes a 50% reduction in total collagen fibrils despite type V collagen comprising only 5% of total collagen mass, supporting a nucleating function for type V collagen in type I/V heterotypic fibril assembly.

Beyond skin signs, the affected cat exhibited mild lower motor neuron paraparesis, hyperesthesia, medial patellar luxation, mild dysphagia, and episodic constipation, reflecting multi-system involvement analogous to human cEDS.
The affected cat had a skin extensibility index (SEI) of 27.4%, above the ≥19% threshold used to screen for EDS in cats.

The COL5A1 splice acceptor site disrupted by the case variant is highly conserved across mammals, with 98% protein homology between cat and human COL5A1, supporting cross-species pathogenicity of the variant.
Superior popliteomeniscal fascicle abnormality was present in 94.4% of arthroscopically confirmed hypermobile lateral meniscus patients, significantly more often than in normal controls.
Inferior popliteomeniscal fascicle abnormality was present in 89.0% of hypermobile lateral meniscus patients, significantly higher than in normal controls.
Lateral meniscal abnormality, all involving the posterior horn meniscocapsular junction, was seen in 72.2% of hypermobile lateral meniscus patients.
Popliteus hiatus measurements were largest in patients with confirmed lateral meniscal tear compared to the hypermobile lateral meniscus and normal control groups.

A 7-year-old boy with esophageal stricture and scarred, atrophic skin was found to carry compound heterozygous mutations in the TNXB gene, consistent with classical-like Ehlers-Danlos syndrome due to tenascin-X deficiency.
The child presented clinically with an impacted foreign body in the esophagus attributable to esophageal stricture, and had a tendency toward atrophic skin scarring following trivial trauma.
Generalized joint hypermobility is associated with an increased risk of knee-related injury and osteoarthritis in the athletic population.

Gait signals (kinematic data of hip, knee, and ankle joints) show significant changes in individuals with generalized joint hypermobility compared to those without, as previously shown by the authors.

A deep neural network combining convolutional, residual, and attention blocks trained on 452 3D motion-capture gait samples (level, downhill, uphill walking of hip, knee, ankle) diagnosed generalized joint hypermobility with 95.77% accuracy, 98.68% specificity, and 76.84% recall, outperforming traditional machine learning methods in efficiency.

Systemic electroacupuncture (2/100 Hz) combined with auricular acupuncture at Nogier frequency did not significantly reduce pain intensity compared to control, as measured by the Numerical Pain Rating Scale.
The experimental acupuncture group showed a significant improvement in total Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ) score compared to control.
The FIQ pain domain showed a significant improvement in the experimental acupuncture group compared to control.
The FIQ anxiety domain showed a significant improvement in the experimental acupuncture group compared to control.
There was no significant difference between groups on the 2010 American College of Rheumatology diagnostic criteria for fibromyalgia after treatment.
Heart rate variability (HRV) parameters, reflecting cardiac autonomic function, did not significantly differ between the acupuncture and control groups.
Daily light consumption of red wine (15 g alcohol/day) for 4 weeks significantly reduced pain (VAS) in the wine group while the control group showed no change.
The number of tender points (Fibromyalgia Tender Points Graph) significantly decreased in the wine group after 4 weeks, while it did not change in controls.
Anxiety levels (Hamilton Anxiety Scale) significantly decreased in the wine group post-intervention compared to controls, whose levels remained unchanged.
Sadness (VAS) showed a significant group-by-time interaction favoring improvement in the wine group, though the between-group post-intervention comparison only approached significance.
Depression (Hamilton Depression Rating Scale) did not show a statistically significant group-by-time interaction, though mean levels appeared to improve descriptively in the wine group.

The Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ) total score decreased by an average of 3.5 points in the wine group, though the overall interaction and post hoc group differences were not statistically significant.

The paper cites prior evidence that fibromyalgia patients have decreased serotonin levels, which are proposed to be modulated by red wine's tryptophan and polyphenol content, though serotonin was not directly measured in this study.

The authors describe resveratrol, a polyphenol concentrated in red wine, as inhibiting expression of the enzyme PDE4 (influenced by corticosterone) and promoting endorphin/serotonin release, proposed as a mechanism underlying potential benefit in fibromyalgia.
No adverse effects were reported by any participant in the experimental group consuming light amounts of red wine daily under medical supervision.
Tibialis anterior muscle pH was significantly lower in rats 3-5 days after repeated cold stress (RCS) compared with untreated controls.

Subcutaneous bafilomycin A1 (V-ATPase inhibitor) dose-dependently reversed the RCS-induced decrease in muscular mechanical withdrawal threshold (MMWT) one week after RCS, with 40 nmol/kg almost completely reversing hypersensitivity.
The analgesic effect of bafilomycin A1 on RCS-induced hypersensitivity weakened over time, being nearly absent by 3 weeks after RCS, suggesting other mechanisms dominate at later stages.

The H+/K+-ATPase inhibitor PF3716556 only slightly and dose-restrictedly reversed RCS-induced MMWT decrease, with a much smaller maximal effect than bafilomycin A1, indicating H+/K+-ATPase plays a minor role compared with V-ATPase.
Bafilomycin A1 significantly increased muscle pH in RCS rats (toward normal) but had no effect on pH in control (non-RCS) muscle, confirming V-ATPase drives the RCS-induced acidification.
Single thin-fibre (C-fibre) recordings from the EDL muscle showed significantly larger mechanical response magnitude and significantly lower mechanical threshold in RCS rats compared with controls.

Intramuscular bafilomycin A1 injected near the receptive field decreased mechanical response magnitude and increased mechanical threshold of C-fibre afferents recorded from RCS rats, but had no effect in fibres from naïve rats.

Orally administered chondroitin sulfate (CS) dose-dependently reversed the RCS-induced decrease in mechanical withdrawal threshold, with higher doses acting faster and lower doses requiring longer exposure to reach maximal effect.

Intramuscular chondroitinase ABC (which cleaves chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans) dose-dependently and rapidly reversed the RCS-induced decrease in mechanical withdrawal threshold, supporting a role for extracellular matrix proteoglycans in mechanical hypersensitivity.
The ASIC3 antagonist APETx2, injected intramuscularly, reversed the RCS-induced decrease in mechanical withdrawal threshold in a dose-dependent manner.

The non-selective TRP antagonist ruthenium red (RR) did not significantly reverse the RCS-induced decrease in mechanical withdrawal threshold at either dose tested, indicating TRP channels are not involved in this mechanical hypersensitivity.
ASIC3 mRNA expression was significantly upregulated in dorsal root ganglia (DRG) one week after RCS, while TRPV1 mRNA was unchanged.
ASIC3 protein levels, measured by Western blot, were significantly increased in DRGs after RCS compared with controls.
FSS patients reported higher state negative affect than controls across all picture valences, independent of picture content.
FSS patients reported higher overall physical symptom ratings than controls across all picture valences.
The increase in physical symptom reporting after negative versus neutral picture viewing was significantly greater in FSS patients than in healthy controls.
Unlike physical symptom ratings, the negative-versus-neutral picture contrast did not differ between patients and controls for self-reported negative affect.

Whole-brain parcel-wise analysis showed significantly stronger negative-versus-neutral picture activation in FSS patients than controls in somatosensory/motor and pain-processing regions, plus cerebellar and higher-order visual cortex, with no regions showing the opposite pattern.

Controls showed a significant reduction in NPS pattern expression for negative versus neutral pictures, whereas this reduction was absent in FSS patients, yielding a significant between-group difference.
The between-group NPS difference was driven mainly by the positive-weight NPS subpattern, with controls showing a medium negative response and patients a small non-significant positive response.

The negative-weight NPS subpattern showed no significant between-group difference and no significant negative-versus-neutral effect within either group, though controls numerically showed stronger responses.

Within the positive NPS subpattern, patients showed significantly stronger negative-versus-neutral activation than controls specifically in right insula, right dorsal posterior insula, right S2/operculum, and aMCC, but not in cerebellar vermis, right V1, right thalamus, or left insula.

Both patients and controls showed strong, significant PINES activation for negative versus neutral pictures with no significant between-group difference, indicating equivalent neural affective processing.
Neither patients nor controls showed a significant SIIPS response to negative versus neutral pictures, and there was no between-group difference.
Mediation analysis showed that the NPS brain response partially mediates the relationship between FSS patient status and negative affect-induced physical symptom reporting.

A whole-brain multivariate 'principal directions of mediation' (PDM) analysis identified two independent brain activation patterns—a mediator pattern involving somatic stimulus-processing regions and a suppressor pattern involving affect/pain modulatory regions (PAG, cerebellum, right anterior insula)—that mediate the relationship between FSS patient status and negative affect-induced symptom reporting.
Six of the fifteen IBS patients also self-reported meeting ACR criteria for fibromyalgia, indicating substantial symptomatic overlap between the two functional somatic syndromes in this sample.
IgE-mediated mast cell activation was identified as a key regulator of food avoidance behavior in response to food allergens in mice.
Leukotrienes were identified as key regulators mediating avoidance responses to food allergens in mice.
Growth differentiating factor 15 (GDF15) was identified as a key regulator of the avoidance response to food allergens in mice.
A higher proportion of frail COVID-19 patients (~45%) reported a 'worse' health transition one month after infection compared to non-frail patients (~39%).
No significant difference in pre-existing comorbidities was found between frail and non-frail subgroups, ruling out comorbidity burden as a confounder of COVID-19 sequelae differences.

The 'worse' health-transition subgroup had a significantly higher number of long-COVID (PASC) sequelae than the 'same' subgroup, with this difference being more pronounced in the frailty group than the non-frailty group.
477 differentially expressed genes (294 up-regulated, 183 down-regulated) were identified in whole blood transcriptomes of frail COVID-19 patients with 'worse' versus 'same' health transition.

KEGG pathway analysis of DEGs revealed enrichment of inflammatory pathways including AGE-RAGE signaling, Rap1 signaling, cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, and rheumatoid arthritis pathway in the 'worse' versus 'same' comparison.
The authors note that AGE-RAGE interaction induces histamine production in mast cells, linking the enriched AGE-RAGE pathway to mast cell activation beyond its known role in diabetic complications.
GO enrichment analysis showed that nearly all top 20 terms (except cell proliferation and protein processing terms) were related to inflammation/immunity, with 'response to stress' as the top term.
NCAPG was identified as a hub gene from PPI network analysis of DEGs, implicated in cell division and proposed as a diagnostic biomarker for adverse long-COVID outcomes.
MCM10 was identified as a hub gene from PPI network analysis of DEGs, implicated in cell division and proposed as a diagnostic biomarker for adverse long-COVID outcomes.
CDC25C was identified as a hub gene from PPI network analysis of DEGs, implicated in cell division and proposed as a diagnostic biomarker for adverse long-COVID outcomes.
A combined biomarker panel of NCAPG, MCM10, and CDC25C showed superior diagnostic performance for distinguishing 'worse' from 'same' health transition, with an AUC of 0.808.

CIBERSORTx immune cell deconvolution of the gene expression matrix showed a significant increase in activated mast cell proportion in the 'worse' versus 'same' health-transition subgroup among frail COVID-19 patients.
Mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) and long-COVID share many overlapping signs and symptoms, including fatigue, anxiety, and depression, supporting a shared mast-cell-driven mechanism.

Citing prior literature, the authors note that famotidine's antihistamine mechanism alleviates long-COVID symptoms, supporting the role of mast cells and the clinical value of classifying COVID populations by frailty/mast cell activity.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (HαT), caused by increased copy numbers of the TPSAB1 gene encoding alpha-tryptase, is the most prevalent genetic cause of an elevated basal serum tryptase level.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia occurs in approximately 4% to 7.5% of the general Western population.
Serum tryptase levels correlate with the total copy number of the TPSAB1 gene in HαT-positive individuals.
Most individuals with HαT present with a slightly to moderately elevated basal serum tryptase level of 15 to 30 ng/mL.
The consensus proposes a normal basal serum tryptase range of 1 to 15 ng/mL for clinical practice, which encompasses asymptomatic individuals with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia.
A genetically-informed lower threshold of 8 ng/mL is proposed, below which the likelihood of HαT is low.

MCAS is diagnosed only when serum tryptase rises to at least 120% + 2 ng/mL above the individual's baseline during a suspected mast cell activation event, alongside compatible symptoms and treatment response.
Topical fluticasone therapy in eosinophilic esophagitis patients reduced serum tryptase levels from 4.7 to 3.8 ng/mL.
Patients with severely impaired kidney function often show basal serum tryptase levels slightly elevated over their individual baseline.

Serum tryptase levels were measured in a cohort of 110 patients with COVID-19 infection and compared with hepatic failure, renal failure, healthy controls, and pregnant women, with a statistically significant difference among the groups.
HαT prevalence is higher in patients with systemic mastocytosis (12.2%-20%) and idiopathic anaphylaxis (17%) compared with healthy controls (4%-7.5%).
A serum tryptase level of 20 ng/mL or higher has served as a minor WHO diagnostic criterion for systemic mastocytosis since 2001.

In 47 asymptomatic patients with bone marrow mastocytosis, indolent SM, or smoldering SM followed for a median of 5 years, basal tryptase levels remained stable and no severe mediator-related symptoms occurred.
Serum tryptase levels are modestly lower in children/younger adults than in older adults, ranging 0-15 ng/mL in ages 10-30 versus 4-16 ng/mL in adults over 50.
Tryptase levels show a positive correlation with body mass index and obesity in adults, but this correlation was not identified in children.

The consensus states that in asymptomatic individuals and in most patients presenting with dysautonomia, connective tissue abnormalities, or irritable bowel syndrome, there is generally no indication to test basal tryptase or tryptase gene (HαT) status.
During an anaphylactic reaction, serum tryptase peaks approximately 1-2 hours after the triggering event and has a serum half-life of approximately 2 hours, returning to baseline within 24 hours.

HαT-positive patients with systemic mastocytosis and/or IgE-dependent allergy have a higher likelihood of developing severe mediator-related symptoms during an allergic reaction compared with patients without HαT.

Wheatgrass-and-aronia-mixed extract at multiple mixing ratios significantly decreased TNF-α and IL-1β mRNA expression in LPS-stimulated RAW 264.7 macrophages and TNF-α/IFN-γ-stimulated HaCaT keratinocytes.
In anti-DNP IgE/DNP-BSA-sensitized RBL-2H3 mast cells, treatment with TAAR extract significantly decreased histamine and β-hexosaminidase secretion in a concentration-dependent manner.
TAAR extract significantly reduced mRNA production of TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-4, and IL-6 in IgE/DNP-BSA-activated RBL-2H3 mast cells, indicating anti-degranulation and anti-inflammatory activity.
TAAR extract significantly decreased phosphorylation of p38, ERK, and JNK MAPK pathway proteins that were activated by IgE/DNP-BSA stimulation in mast cells.
Nuclear NF-κB expression was upregulated by IgE/DNP-BSA stimulation in mast cells but significantly down-regulated by TAAR extract treatment, indicating blocked nuclear translocation.
TAAR extract notably reduced expression of the inflammatory mediators iNOS and COX-2, which had been increased by IgE/DNP-BSA stimulation in mast cells.

Nrf2, HO-1, and NQO1 expression, which was reduced by IgE/DNP-BSA stimulation, was increased in a concentration-dependent manner by TAAR extract treatment, indicating activation of the antioxidant Nrf2 signaling pathway.

Phosphorylation of Lyn, Fyn, and Syk, upregulated by IgE/DNP-BSA stimulation, was suppressed by TAAR extract treatment, with 40 and 80 µg/mL concentrations showing significant inhibitory effects on this proximal FcεRI signaling cascade.

PLCγ1 phosphorylation was significantly increased by IgE/DNP-BSA stimulation while PKCδ phosphorylation increased but not significantly; TAAR extract down-regulated the phosphorylation of both proteins.

In an IgE-mediated passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) mouse model, oral TAAR extract reduced ear pigmentation and thickness more effectively than single wheatgrass or aronia extracts at equivalent concentration.
HPLC analysis identified chlorogenic acid and GABA as the main index components of the TAAR extract, present at 0.2193 and 0.2155 mg/g respectively.
Antioxidant activity (DPPH, ABTS, FRAP) of wheatgrass-and-aronia-mixed extracts increased in a concentration-dependent manner and increased as aronia content increased at a given mixing ratio.

The mixed wheatgrass-and-aronia extract (TAAR) showed a synergistic anti-allergic effect compared to single extracts of wheatgrass (TA) or aronia (AR) alone, with 1:3 identified as the optimal mixing ratio.

Daily oral açaí berry treatment (500 mg/kg) beginning 2 weeks after STZ injection prevented behavioral changes, mast cell activation, and nerve deterioration in diabetic mice by regulating the NLRP3/ASC/CASP axis.
Açaí berry treatment reduced mast cell degranulation and associated histological damage in the diabetic neuropathy mouse model.
Açaí berry treatment improved the physiological antioxidant defense against reactive oxygen species in diabetic neuropathic mice.
Açaí berry inhibited/modulated the NLRP3/ASC/CASP inflammasome axis in diabetic neuropathic tissue.
Açaí berry ameliorated inflammation and oxidative stress overall in the STZ-induced diabetic neuropathy mouse model.
Five successive oral doses of dactolisib reduced serum anti-OVA antibody levels in OVA-sensitized mice, indicating suppressed sensitization.
Dactolisib treatment strongly diminished the anaphylactic drop in rectal temperature induced by OVA re-administration compared to vehicle-treated mice, consistent with reduced sensitization.
Dactolisib inhibited ex vivo splenic B cell activation, reducing Akt phosphorylation, CD69 expression, and proliferation upon anti-B cell receptor antibody stimulation.
A single oral dose of dactolisib attenuated the anaphylactic rectal temperature decrease in a mouse model of passive systemic anaphylaxis.
Pretreatment with dactolisib inhibited IgE/antigen-triggered degranulation in RBL2H3 mast cells in vitro.
Dactolisib inhibited cytokine production in RBL2H3 mast cells triggered by IgE and antigen.
Dactolisib treatment did not affect the viability of RBL2H3 mast cells, indicating its inhibitory effects were not due to cytotoxicity.

In mouse brain sections, tryptase-positive mast cells were found embedded within collagen fibers alongside PGP9.5-positive neurons, supporting the relevance of collagen gel as a culture substrate for brain mast cells.
Mast cells cultured in 3D collagen gels for 24 hours showed 95% viability, comparable to mast cells cultured in suspension.
Mast cell proliferation, measured by EdU incorporation over 2 hours, was similar (3-4%) between 3D collagen gel and suspension cultures.
IL-33 treatment (100 ng/mL, 24h) of mast cells in 3D collagen gel led to over 1000-fold induction of IL-6 release, the most highly elevated cytokine measured.
IL-33 treatment induced approximately 839-fold increase in IL-13 release from mast cells in 3D collagen gel culture.
IL-33 treatment induced approximately 438-fold increase in GM-CSF release from mast cells in 3D collagen gel culture.
IL-33 treatment also induced IL-2, IL-5, IL-8, RANTES, and TNF-α release from 3D-cultured mast cells, with induction ranging from 22- to 137-fold.
ELISA confirmation showed IL-33 induced a 25-fold increase in IL-1β release from 3D-cultured mast cells, higher than the 4-fold induction detected by the cytokine array.

IgE sensitization followed by anti-IgE stimulation significantly increased tryptase and chymase secretion from mast cells cultured in both suspension and 3D collagen gel, indicating that 3D-cultured mast cells retain degranulation capacity.

Fibrillar Aβ1-42 at 50 µM induced strong cytokine release from 3D-cultured mast cells, including GM-CSF (272-fold), IL-2 (390-fold), GRO (280-fold), IL-8 (98-fold), IL-1α (64-fold), IL-33 (27-fold), and IL-5 (26-fold).

Among the three amyloid-beta peptides tested, Aβ1-42 elicited the strongest mast cell cytokine response at 50 µM, while Aβ1-40 and Aβ25-35 were often similarly effective at the lower 10 µM concentration.
At the lower concentration (10 µM), Aβ1-40 and Aβ25-35 induced higher levels of some cytokines, including IL-5, IL-10, and TNF-α, than at higher concentrations or compared with Aβ1-42.
ELISA confirmed that IL-1β and TNF-α were induced most strongly by Aβ1-42, to a lesser extent by Aβ1-40, and Aβ25-35 did not induce production of either cytokine.
Comparing culture methods, mast cells in suspension showed greater induction of IL-6 and tryptase, whereas mast cells in 3D collagen gels showed greater induction of IFN-γ and MCP-1.
Fallopia japonica root extract (FJE) suppressed compound 48/80-induced degranulation of rat peritoneal mast cells (RPMCs) in vitro across a dose range.
FJE dose-dependently reduced the frequency of nasal rubbing and sneezing in OVA-induced CARAS mice compared with untreated CARAS mice.

FJE administration produced a dose-dependent reduction in total inflammatory cell numbers in nasal lavage fluid (NLF) and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF), with 100 and 200 mg/kg doses reaching significance versus CARAS mice.
FJE dose-dependently reduced differential inflammatory cell counts (epithelial cells, macrophages, eosinophils, neutrophils, lymphocytes) in NLF and BALF of CARAS mice.
Histopathology showed that FJE (especially 200 mg/kg) and Dexamethasone reduced nasal mucosal edema and subepithelial layer thickness compared with untreated CARAS mice.
PAS staining showed that FJE (100 and 200 mg/kg) and Dexamethasone reduced goblet cell hyperplasia and mucus hypersecretion in nasal and lung tissue of CARAS mice.
Toluidine blue staining showed fewer mast cells in nasal tissue of FJE-treated mice compared with CARAS mice.
CARAS mice showed a greater number of tissue eosinophils than FJE-treated mice, indicating eosinophilic infiltration as a feature of the CARAS model that is reduced by treatment.

FJE and Dexamethasone significantly reduced OVA-specific serum IgE and IgG1, while OVA-specific IgG2a was significantly improved in the FJE 200 mg/kg and Dex groups, indicating a shift away from Th2-dominant humoral response.
FJE (particularly 200 mg/kg) and Dexamethasone suppressed the Th2-associated cytokines IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, and IL-13 in NLF and BALF, which were significantly elevated in CARAS mice versus controls.
FJE and Dexamethasone treatment increased the Th1-associated cytokines IL-12 and IFN-γ in NLF and BALF, which had been significantly reduced in CARAS mice relative to controls.
FJE dose-dependently down-regulated the pro-inflammatory cytokine TNF-α in NLF and BALF, which was elevated in CARAS mice.

FJE treatment significantly reduced thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP) levels in NLF and BALF versus CARAS mice, with similar effects across FJE concentrations in NLF but dose-dependent reduction in BALF.
IL-33 levels were significantly elevated in NLF, BALF, and lung tissue of CARAS mice, and FJE and Dexamethasone significantly reduced IL-33 with a clear dose-dependent effect in lung tissue.
Immunohistochemistry showed significantly lower expression of ST2 (the IL-33 receptor) in nasal tissue of FJE- and Dexamethasone-treated CARAS mice compared with untreated CARAS mice.
FJE down-regulated phosphorylated NF-κB (P-NF-κB) and phosphorylated IκB (P-IκB) in NLF, BALF, and lung tissue of CARAS mice, indicating suppression of NF-κB pathway activation.
FJE treatment improved (increased) IL-10 levels in BALF and lung homogenate, consistent with an enhanced regulatory T cell/FOXP3-mediated anti-inflammatory response.
UPLC analysis identified emodin glucoside 1, emodin glucoside 2, procyanidin, and other polyphenols as major bioactive constituents of FJE, proposed as responsible for its anti-inflammatory effects.

Der f 40, a thioredoxin (TRX)-family protein cloned from Dermatophagoides farinae, was expressed as recombinant protein and confirmed as a novel HDM allergen listed by the WHO/IUIS Allergen Nomenclature Sub-committee.
Recombinant Der f 40 bound IgE in 9.68% (12/124) of HDM-allergic patient sera by ELISA, whereas none of 50 healthy control sera showed binding, confirmed by dot blot and western blot.
Amino acid sequence alignment showed Der f TRX shares 52% homology with Plo i 2, a thioredoxin allergen from Plodia interpunctella.
Purified rDer f 40 catalyzed the reduction of insulin disulfides in an enzymatic assay, confirming thioredoxin-like activity comparable to the natural protein.
Circular dichroism spectroscopy of purified rDer f 40 showed a spectrum consistent with a predominantly alpha-helical secondary structure, matching structural predictions.

rDer f 40 induced dose-dependent beta-hexosaminidase release from humanized IgE/FcεRI mouse bone-marrow-derived mast cells when pre-incubated with sera from Der f 40-sensitized HDM-allergic patients, but not with non-allergic control sera, demonstrating mast cell degranulation activity.

None of six overlapping 30-amino-acid linear peptide fragments (E1-E6) spanning Der f 40 showed IgE reactivity with Der f 40-binding allergic sera by western blot, dot blot, or ELISA, indicating the immunodominant epitope is not a simple linear sequence.

A hybrid protein containing the Der f 40 C-terminal region (Der f 40 C-hyb) fused to human thioredoxin showed IgE binding with HDM allergic sera, and a further truncated version (Der f 40 C-hyb1) localized the immunodominant conformational IgE epitope to amino acids 76-106 of the C-terminus.
Homology structural modeling using the Mala s 13 crystal structure as template predicted that Der f 40 adopts a fold with 4 alpha-helices and 4 beta-strands, consistent with the thioredoxin fold.

A Der f-derived heat shock cognate 70-like protein with 84.83% amino acid sequence homology to the mosquito allergen Aed a 8 elicited no IgE reactivity with HDM allergic sera, illustrating that high sequence homology does not guarantee allergenicity.

A 27-year-old man on infliximab for refractory Crohn disease developed leukocytoclastic small vessel vasculitis with renal involvement (IgA nephropathy), illustrating a rare drug-induced vasculitis presentation.
Skin biopsy demonstrated granular IgA deposition in superficial dermal blood vessels, consistent with an IgA-mediated small vessel vasculitis pattern.

Kidney biopsy revealed IgA nephropathy with mild mesangial expansion and increased cellularity, granular mesangial IgA (3+) and C3 (2+) staining, and nephrotic-range proteinuria (5 g/24h) with 2 g albumin.

TNF-α inhibitor therapy is reported to induce ANA in 23%-57% of patients and anti-dsDNA antibodies in 9%-33%, hypothesized to contribute to immune complex-mediated vasculitis via complement activation, though the link to vasculitis itself is unclear.
TNF-α inhibition is hypothesized to shift cytokine balance toward Th2 over Th1 responses, promoting an inflammatory state that may lead to autoimmune/vasculitic disease.
An FDA database analysis found that 67% of patients who restarted the same offending TNF-α inhibitor after developing vasculitis experienced relapse.
A cited study found that 33% of patients relapsed after being switched to a different anti-TNF-α agent following drug-induced vasculitis.

Among 41 patients who discontinued the offending TNF-α inhibitor, reintroduction of the same agent resulted in 71% reactivation of vasculitis, whereas switching to a different biologic among about half of these patients resulted in only 4 recurrences.
A systematic review of 72 cases of TNF-α inhibitor-induced vasculitis reported that 75% of patients achieved complete remission.
The patient's symptoms improved after treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin followed by high-dose IV methylprednisolone, and he was discharged on high-dose oral prednisone.

The patient exhibited profound allodynia and neuralgias in the bilateral lower extremities alongside the cutaneous vasculitis, with decreased range of motion in the hand and pain-limited foot movement.
In a large RCT, linagliptin reduced the incidence of small fibre peripheral neuropathy by 19.5% compared with placebo.
An observational study found liraglutide was associated with a higher incidence of neuropathy compared with sitagliptin, though this lost significance after correction for multiple testing.

The two largest human studies to date (an observational OptumLabs cohort, N=8252, and the GRADE RCT, N=5047) found no difference in neuropathy incidence with GLP-1RAs compared with other glucose-lowering therapies.
Two large observational studies of electronic medical records found decreased neuropathy incidence with vildagliptin and sitagliptin compared with sulfonylureas.

GLP-1RA use has been associated with signs of autonomic imbalance, including increased resting heart rate, decreased vagal tone, decreased 30:15 ratio on lying-to-standing testing, and decreased heart rate variability, though findings are inconsistent.
GLP-1 receptors identified in the carotid body may diminish sympathetic response to high plasma glucose and/or insulin upon activation.
Long-term intensive glucose control was associated with a lower incidence of gastroparesis in the follow-up of the DCCT/EPIC trials.
In the REWIND RCT, dulaglutide was associated with a small reduction in the incidence and severity of erectile dysfunction versus placebo.

Early rodent studies showed GLP-1RA treatment improved sensory and motor nerve electrophysiology, reduced intraepidermal nerve fibre density loss, restored myelin fibre size, prevented Schwann cell apoptosis, and reduced neuropathic pain.
Rodent studies with DPP-4 inhibitors showed decreased nerve fibre density loss and improved nerve conduction velocity.

DPP-4 inhibition increases circulating SDF-1, which may have beneficial end-organ effects particularly for neuropathy via enhanced tissue repair, though this benefit is debated and may carry offsetting harms elsewhere.

Attali et al. found that visceral osteopathic manipulative treatment decreased rectal sensitivity and provided short-term and long-term relief from abdominal distension and pain lasting up to one year.
Steiner's study showed that visceral manipulation significantly decreased daily IBS symptoms, with statistically significant improvements on both the IBS-QOL and IBS-SS instruments.

Florance et al. found that a combination of indirect and direct OMT techniques began reducing IBS symptom severity in the experimental group by day seven, with a recommendation for monthly sessions to maximize benefit.
Hundscheid et al. reported that OMT significantly improved overall IBS symptoms and quality of life in the osteopathy group.

Stiedl et al. found that OMT reduced VAS-rated pain levels from a mean of 64.5 to 12.9, compared to a control group without OMT that went from 63.7 to 49.7 — nearly a four-fold greater reduction in pain with OMT.
Stiedl et al. also demonstrated that OMT led to improvement in constipation intensity among participants.

The review proposes that OMT improves IBS symptoms via increased fluid dynamics and tissue nutrition, relaxation of smooth muscle in fascia and ligaments, increased blood flow, and improved lymphatic drainage, with effects amplified when multiple body regions (e.g., abdomen and sacrum) are treated.
Three of the five included studies (Attali et al., Florance et al., Hundscheid et al.) reported no adverse side effects from OMT, while Steiner and Stiedl et al. did not report on safety.

In a rat model of IBS induced by acetic acid plus chronic-acute stress (AA-CAS), abnormal fecal output, increased visceral sensitivity, depressive-like behaviors, and overexpression of inflammatory mediators were all reversed by vagus nerve stimulation (VNS).
Pharmacological activation of the α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (α7nAChR) reproduced the beneficial effects of VNS on IBS symptoms and inflammation in the rat model.
Blocking α7nAChR with the antagonist methyllycaconitine (MLA) reversed the therapeutic effects of VNS in the IBS rat model, confirming the receptor's necessity for the VNS effect.
VNS reduced the increased blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability that resulted from AA-CAS treatment in IBS rats.
Subdiaphragmatic vagotomy (SDV) showed only temporary efficacy against AA-CAS-induced IBS symptoms and had no effect on BBB permeability, contrasting with the sustained benefit of VNS.
In cultured human dermal fibroblasts, ALLN dose-dependently suppressed the TGF-β1-induced increase in ACTA2 (αSMA), COL1A2, and FN1 mRNA expression.
ALLN significantly suppressed TGF-β1-induced protein expression of αSMA, COL1A2, and FN1 in normal human dermal fibroblasts as shown by Western blot and immunocytochemistry.
ALLN markedly reduced collagen I concentration in the culture supernatant of dermal fibroblasts both with and without TGF-β1 stimulation, measured by ELISA.
ALLN treatment decreased mRNA expression of the mesenchymal transcription factors SNAI2, ZEB1, and ZEB2 in TGF-β1-stimulated dermal fibroblasts, with ZEB2 downregulated even without TGF-β1.
ALLN inhibited TGF-β1-induced Smad2/3 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of SNAIL2 and ZEB1 in dermal fibroblasts.
ALLN generally inhibited TGF-β1-induced increases in ACTA2, COL1A2, and FN1 mRNA/protein and myofibroblast filament formation in normal human lung fibroblasts.
ALLN inhibited expression and nuclear translocation of phosphorylated Smad2/3, SNAIL2, and ZEB1 in TGF-β1-stimulated lung fibroblasts, indicating inhibition of calpain-dependent fibrogenic activity.
ALLN significantly inhibited TGF-β1-induced mRNA expression of the mesenchymal markers CTGF, VIM, and SNAI2 in A549 lung epithelial cells undergoing EMT.
Protein expression of the epithelial marker E-cadherin increased following ALLN treatment in TGF-β1-induced A549 cells, indicating suppression of EMT.
Intraperitoneal ALLN administration for 4 weeks in mice showed no apparent adverse effects on body weight or activity.
ALLN significantly reduced bleomycin-induced dermal thickness, Masson's trichrome-stained collagen area, and total collagen content (Sirius Red assay) in mouse skin.
ALLN administration reduced the number of αSMA-positive spindle/star-shaped myofibroblast-like cells in bleomycin-injected mouse skin.
ALLN significantly reduced CD3-positive T cell infiltration in bleomycin-injected skin but had little effect on F4/80-positive macrophage infiltration.
ALLN reduced the number of p-Smad3-positive spindle-shaped cells and total p-Smad3 protein in bleomycin-injected mouse skin.
Calpain 2 (but not calpain 1) expression increased in mouse skin following bleomycin administration and was reduced by ALLN treatment.
Bleomycin injection or ALLN treatment did not affect calpain 1 expression in mouse skin, unlike calpain 2.
Intraperitoneal ALLN significantly reduced bleomycin-induced fibrotic stroma in mouse lungs as evaluated by H&E and Masson's trichrome staining.

ALLN treatment significantly reduced the αSMA-positive area and CD3-positive cells in bleomycin-injected mouse lungs, though the effect on F4/80-positive macrophage area was not emphasized as significant.
Bleomycin administration increased calpain 1 and calpain 2 positive area in mouse lungs, which was significantly suppressed by ALLN treatment.
In a survey of Brazilian Long Covid patients, 61% reported negative interactions with medical professionals while 22% reported positive interactions.
In a survey of U.S. Long Covid patients, 79% reported negative interactions with medical professionals while 21% reported positive interactions.
U.S. Long Covid patients frequently used the term 'medical gaslighting' to describe providers dismissing their symptom reports and refusing to attribute them to Long Covid.
Brazilian Long Covid patients commonly reported being told their symptoms were 'just anxiety,' reflecting psychologization of symptoms by physicians unfamiliar with Long Covid.
Due to a lack of local medical expertise and physician awareness, Long Covid patients in both the U.S. and Brazil turned to online patient communities for advice, information, and emotional support.

Brazilian respondents reported turning to overseas sources (U.S./European experts, French YouTube channels, U.K. studies, foreign newspapers) for credible Long Covid information, reflecting the global dominance of U.S. and European researchers in this field.
Veterans with ME/CFS and those with intermediate fatigue symptoms had significantly higher (worse) OSDI dry eye symptom scores than controls.
DEQ-5 dry eye symptom scores were significantly higher in ME/CFS and IF veterans than controls.
Current ocular pain ratings (NRS) were higher in ME/CFS and IF veterans than controls.
Neuropathic ocular pain scores (NPSI-E) were significantly higher in ME/CFS and IF veterans than controls, suggesting a neuropathic pain component.
Objective ocular surface signs on slit lamp examination were generally similar between ME/CFS, IF, and control groups despite differing symptom severity.
Blood markers of inflammation did not differ significantly across ME/CFS, IF, and control groups.
Of 33 ME/CFS patients interviewed, 26 reported partial recovery and 7 reported full recovery from their illness.

Participants reported spending substantial time and energy independently identifying, implementing, and adapting treatments, often without medical practitioner guidance, and formulated individualised treatment plans.
Most participants who achieved full recovery attributed their improvement to mind-body treatment approaches.
Participants described stigmatised and dismissive responses from clinicians that led them to disengage from the medical system and seek alternative treatments.
In Case 1, hydrogen gas inhalation reduced the Canadian Consensus Criteria (CCC) total severity score from 29 at baseline to 23 at 4 weeks, 15 at 6 weeks, and 13 by 20 weeks.

COVID-19 vaccination transiently worsened ME/CFS symptoms in Case 1, with the severity score rising to 27 after the second dose, before recovering to pre-vaccination levels (score 15) after continued H2 gas inhalation.
In Case 2, a 43-year-old woman with severe functional impairment, sleep disturbance, headaches, and migraines improved after 3 weeks of H2 gas inhalation and continued to improve at 9 weeks.

In Case 3, an 18-year-old woman had decreased fatigue, improved bowel movements, and increased motivation after 3 weeks of H2 gas inhalation, with more daytime activity by 8 weeks though residual tiredness persisted.

In Case 4, an 18-year-old man with ME/CFS and fibromyalgia had reduced headache and general pain after 3 weeks of H2 gas inhalation, sustained at 9 weeks with decreased analgesic use and improved brain fog.
Prior clinical studies of rituximab, NAD-H, coenzyme Q10, and acetyl L-carnitine for ME/CFS treatment found these agents were ineffective or had limited effect.
A single-blind randomized trial by Botek et al. in 50 post-COVID patients found that 14 days of H2 gas inhalation improved physical and respiratory functions in the acute phase of infection.

The authors propose that H2 gas selectively scavenges hydroxyl radicals and peroxynitrite, crosses the blood-brain barrier and biological membranes, reaches mitochondria, and protects cells from oxidative damage, which may underlie its anti-fatigue effects in ME/CFS.
Cognitive fatigue, measured by the FIS-40 cognitive domain, significantly decreased from baseline to the 36-week visit in the beta-glucan plus multivitamin intervention group.
Daytime dysfunction (PSQI domain) significantly improved at the 36-week visit compared to baseline in the active treatment group relative to placebo.
Anxiety and depression symptoms measured by HADS showed no statistically significant differences between the intervention and placebo groups over the course of the study.
Social role functioning (SF-36) improved significantly at the 36-week visit compared to baseline in the placebo group, but not in the active treatment group.
No treatment-related adverse events were recorded in the study population, indicating the 9-month intervention was safe and well tolerated.

Nine participants withdrew due to adverse events during the trial: five in the intervention group (three epigastralgias, one dizziness, one disease outbreak) and four in the placebo group (one epigastralgia, one tremor, two anxiety episodes).
Physical and psychosocial domains of the FIS-40 evolved in parallel between the intervention and placebo groups with no significant differences reported.
Other PSQI sleep quality domains besides daytime dysfunction showed no significant differences between groups over the course of the study.
Across pooled trials, CBT significantly reduced fatigue severity compared to control conditions.
CBT significantly reduced functional impairment across the pooled trials.
CBT significantly improved physical functioning across the pooled trials.
The beneficial effect of CBT on fatigue severity was moderated by patient age, with younger patients benefitting more.
The beneficial effect of CBT on fatigue severity was moderated by baseline functional impairment, with patients reporting less impairment benefitting more.
The beneficial effect of CBT on fatigue severity was moderated by physical activity pattern, with patients having a fluctuating activity pattern benefitting more.
The beneficial effect of CBT on physical functioning was moderated by self-efficacy, with patients with higher self-efficacy benefitting most.
CBT efficacy did not differ significantly by case definition met or by presence of additional symptoms including post-exertional malaise (PEM).

Long-read sequencing revealed a heterozygous ~42 kb inversion spanning the AKR1C1/AKR1C2 region that swaps the coding region of AKR1C1 with that of AKR1C2, which had been missed and misrepresented by short-read sequencing due to homology.

A heterozygous splice-donor loss SNV in the second intron of AKR1C2 transcript 1 was identified but reinterpreted, after refined breakpoint mapping, as lying outside the true inversion and part of the extended 5'UTR attached to AKR1C1.
RQ-PCR of stabilised whole blood from a luteal-phase sample showed AKR1C2 mRNA expression approximately 100-fold higher than controls, while AKR1C1 and AKR1C3 mRNA were comparable to controls.
AKR1C1 mRNA expression in patient whole blood was comparable to controls, despite the hypothesis of underactive AKR1C1 protein.

The ratio of inhibitory neurosteroids (allopregnanolone + pregnanolone) to the counter-inhibitory neurosteroid isopregnanolone was elevated in the patient relative to controls, consistent with disrupted neurosteroid homeostasis.

The ratio of 17α-hydroxyprogesterone to 17α,20α-dihydroxy-4-pregnen-3-one, a marker of AKR1C1 20α-reductase activity, was elevated in the patient except in one luteal sample with high cortisol, consistent with partial loss of AKR1C1 function.

The progesterone/20α-dihydroprogesterone ratio was elevated in the follicular phase but normal-to-slightly low in the luteal phase, suggesting compensatory diversion of progesterone to 5α-reduction pathways during the luteal phase.
The ratio of 5α- to 5β-reduced progesterone metabolites was high in the luteal phase, suggesting a shift toward extrahepatic 5α-reduction of accumulating intracellular progesterone.
The DHT/androstanediol ratio, an indicator of 3α-reduction by AKR1C2, was low in the patient, consistent with increased AKR1C2 activity.

Standard short-read WGS (100kGP pipeline with Manta/Canvas) falsely called an inversion ~10 kb larger than the true variant, due to a copy-and-paste homology artefact, and could not resolve the true breakpoints because of high sequence homology in the region.
Automated long-read SV calling with Sniffles detected several deep-intronic indels but failed to detect the large inversion, which was only identified through manual visual inspection in IGV.

The patient's family history showed unexplained fatigue in several relatives, including debilitating fatigue in the mother's early 20s (who also carries the inversion) and a maternal second cousin diagnosed with ME/CFS, suggesting a genetic predisposition.

The patient's clinical diagnoses include central adrenal insufficiency, partial central diabetes insipidus, renal salt wasting, and functional pan-enteric dysmotility, alongside a prior ME/CFS diagnosis, none of which fully explained her illness severity.

The authors propose that ursodeoxycholic acid, a selective AKR1C2 inhibitor that can penetrate the brain, may address excessive inhibitory neurosteroid synthesis as a potential treatment, though it has not been trialed in this patient.

Bioidentical isopregnanolone (Sepranolone) and GABAAR modulating steroid antagonist GR3027 (Golexanolone) are cited as showing promise in clinical trials for conditions associated with relative allopregnanolone excess.
Overall, patients infected with any of the studied potential pathogens had a significantly higher risk of subsequently developing CFS than uninfected controls.
Patients infected with varicella-zoster virus had significantly higher risk of CFS than uninfected controls.
EBV infection was not significantly associated with CFS risk in this cohort, likely due to the small number of identified cases.
Patients infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis had significantly higher risk of CFS than uninfected controls.
E. coli infection was significantly associated with increased CFS risk, supporting a role for typical (non-atypical) bacteria as CFS triggers.
Candida infection was significantly associated with increased risk of CFS, consistent with prior reports of chronic intestinal candidiasis in CFS patients.
Enterovirus infection was significantly associated with the highest hazard ratio for CFS among the pathogens studied.
Salmonella infection, an intracellular typical bacterium, was significantly associated with increased CFS risk.
Staphylococcus aureus infection was significantly associated with increased CFS risk, plausibly via its known T-cell immunomodulatory effects.
Chlamydia pneumoniae infection was not significantly associated with CFS risk, likely due to few identified cases.
Influenza virus infection (not limited to H1N1) was significantly associated with increased CFS risk.
Orientia tsutsugamushi infection was not significantly associated with CFS risk.
Mycoplasma infection was not significantly associated with CFS risk.
Dengue virus infection was not significantly associated with CFS risk in this cohort.
Borrelia burgdorferi infection showed a significantly elevated but imprecise association with CFS risk given very few cases.
Male sex was associated with lower CFS risk compared with female sex.
Older age groups (40–64 and ≥65 years) had progressively higher CFS risk than patients aged <40 years, and risk after infection also increased with age.
Pre-existing diabetes mellitus was associated with slightly increased CFS risk.
Pre-existing insomnia was associated with increased CFS risk.
Pre-existing depression was associated with increased CFS risk.
Pre-existing anxiety was associated with increased CFS risk.
Pre-existing peptic ulcer disease was associated with increased CFS risk.
Pre-existing gout was associated with increased CFS risk.
Pre-existing dyslipidemia was associated with increased CFS risk.
Pre-existing inflammatory bowel disease (labeled IBS in text) was associated with increased CFS risk.
Pre-existing hepatitis B was associated with increased CFS risk.
Pre-existing hepatitis C had the strongest comorbidity association with increased CFS risk.
Pre-existing fibromyalgia was associated with increased CFS risk, and fibromyalgia was one of the most common baseline comorbidities in the infection cohort (19.95%).
Pre-existing dementia was associated with lower CFS risk.
Hypothyroidism was not significantly associated with CFS risk after adjustment.
Obesity was not significantly associated with CFS risk after adjustment.
Psoriasis showed a borderline non-significant lower risk of CFS after adjustment.
History of burn injury was not significantly associated with CFS risk after adjustment.
Patients with pre-existing fibromyalgia had a significantly higher risk of developing CFS than those without fibromyalgia.
Patients taking doxycycline had a significantly lower risk of developing CFS compared with those not taking it.
Patients taking azithromycin had a significantly lower risk of developing CFS compared with those not taking it.
Clarithromycin use was not significantly associated with the risk of developing CFS.
Patients taking moxifloxacin had a significantly lower risk of developing CFS compared with those not taking it.
Patients taking levofloxacin had a significantly lower risk of developing CFS compared with those not taking it.
Patients taking ciprofloxacin had a significantly lower risk of developing CFS compared with those not taking it.

In stratified analyses by sex, age group, and comorbidity subgroup, patients with a potential pathogen infection consistently had a higher risk of CFS than those without infection, though the association was not significant in a few small comorbidity subgroups (e.g., hypothyroidism, dementia).

The paper states that over 35% of CFS patients have functional gastrointestinal disorders (FGIDs), which are associated with greater functional impairment.

Patients with isolated peptic ulcer and inflammatory bowel disease have a higher risk of developing CFS compared to patients with isolated nonorganic gastrointestinal diseases such as depression and diabetes.
CFS patients reportedly have intestinal barrier dysfunction, gut immune dysfunction, altered gut motility, altered gastrointestinal secretion, altered intestinal flora, and altered gut-brain axis.
Abnormal alterations to intestinal flora are reportedly linearly related to decreased motivation and increased levels of fatigue, anxiety, and depression in CFS patients.
Prior research by the authors' team found that 12-week PLWNT exercise effectively improved fatigue, sleep quality, anxiety and depression in CFS patients.

In a prior study, PLWNT further improved symptoms of functional dyspepsia on the basis of drug treatment, related to reducing plasma somatostatin content and increasing motilin content, which promotes gastrointestinal peristalsis.

Patients with SSD or any of the four FSS types had significantly higher adjusted hazard ratios for all-cause hospitalization compared to matched controls.
All SSD/FSS groups had significantly higher adjusted hazard ratios for suicide compared to controls, with SSD showing a particularly elevated risk.
