SSD and the four FSS conditions (fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome, IBS, functional dyspepsia) shared broadly similar patterns of clinical outcomes and medical costs, supporting their treatment as related diagnostic constructs.
Across the 10 included RCTs, oral NADH and NAD precursor supplementation was generally well tolerated with no serious adverse events reported.
In chronic fatigue syndrome patients, NADH supplementation trials evaluated quality of life, fatigue intensity, and sleep quality as outcome measures.
NADH/NAD precursor supplementation was associated with a decrease in anxiety and in maximum heart rate observed after a stress test.
NADH/NAD precursor supplementation was associated with increased muscle insulin sensitivity and improved insulin signaling, likely in overweight or prediabetic participants.
NADH supplementation was linked to a decrease in inflammatory cytokines measured in serum and cerebrospinal fluid.
All included studies reported some side effects with NADH use, most commonly muscle pain, nervous disorders, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and headaches, none of which were serious.
Across 18 RCTs using the PSQI, traditional Chinese exercise (TCE) significantly reduced (improved) sleep quality scores compared to control conditions, with high heterogeneity.
In the 2 studies using the VSHSS (a scale where higher scores indicate better sleep), TCE (Chan-Chuang Qigong and Chaoyi Fanhuan Qigong) significantly improved sleep quality with no heterogeneity.
In a subgroup analysis restricted to patients with chronic fatigue syndrome-like illness, TCE significantly improved (reduced) PSQI sleep quality scores.
In fibromyalgia patients, TCE significantly reduced PSQI sleep quality scores compared to control.
In breast cancer patients, TCE did not significantly improve PSQI sleep quality scores compared to control.
In older adults with unspecified medical conditions, TCE significantly improved PSQI sleep quality scores with no heterogeneity.
In stroke patients, TCE (Tai Chi) did not significantly improve PSQI sleep quality scores compared to control.
In patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma, TCE significantly improved sleep quality on the VSHSS with no heterogeneity.
In patients with knee osteoarthritis, TCE significantly improved PSQI sleep quality scores.
In patients with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, TCE significantly improved PSQI sleep quality scores.
In women with pausimenia (perimenopause-related symptoms), TCE significantly improved PSQI sleep quality scores.
In patients with a diagnosis of insomnia, TCE significantly improved PSQI sleep quality scores.
In normal college students, TCE did not significantly improve PSQI sleep quality scores.
In patients with episodic migraine, TCE did not significantly improve PSQI sleep quality scores.
Tai Chi produced a significantly larger improvement in sleep quality than Qigong, contrary to some prior reviews.
Practice location (home vs other settings) did not significantly moderate the effect of TCE on sleep quality.
Intervention duration (<12 weeks vs ≥12 weeks) did not significantly moderate the effect of TCE on sleep quality.
Participant age (≤61 vs >61 years) did not significantly moderate the effect of TCE on sleep quality.

A 35-year-old woman with a 23-year history of hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and Behçet's Disease underwent a 32-week multidisciplinary rehabilitation intervention guided by narrative medicine principles, resulting in decreased pain and improved function immediately post-intervention.

The patient presented with co-occurring hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and Behçet's Disease, described as two rare multisystemic chronic diseases producing a wide range of clinical symptoms, psychological distress, and poor quality of life.
Nailfold microhaemorrhages were more prevalent in adults with hEDS compared to matched controls.
Capillary number per linear millimetre at the nailfold was slightly higher in hEDS patients than controls, but this was not statistically significant.
The NVC score for abnormal shaped capillaries was slightly lower (i.e., less abnormal morphology) in hEDS patients than controls, but not statistically significant.
Peripheral blood perfusion measured by laser speckle contrast analysis was comparable between hEDS patients and controls.
Dermal thickness measured by high-frequency ultrasound was generally lower in hEDS patients than controls, with statistically significant reductions limited to the feet and thorax.
A statistically significant positive correlation was found between the Beighton hypermobility score and the microhaemorrhage score in hEDS patients.
A statistically significant positive correlation was found between the Beighton score and dermal thickness at the feet and thorax.
Genetic testing identified a heterozygous pathogenic COL3A1 variant (c.674G>A, p.(Gly225Asp)) confirming the diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in this patient.

The patient presented with metachronous bilateral iliac vascular events: dissecting aneurysms of the right iliac arteries with hemoperitoneum, followed three months later by an arteriovenous fistula between the left internal iliac artery and left common iliac vein.

A hybrid endovascular-open surgical approach (stent-graft placement combined with surgical cutdown/repair of access sites using interrupted sutures and felt pledgets rather than percutaneous closure devices) was used to manage bilateral iliac vascular events without further vascular manipulation of unaffected sites.

Use of a percutaneous vascular closure device (Perclose Proglide) in this vEDS patient caused vessel injury and femoral artery tearing, requiring emergency surgical repair, illustrating the risk of standard closure devices in fragile vEDS vasculature.

Deep vein thrombosis developed in both legs postoperatively (below right common femoral vein after first operation, below left mid common iliac vein after second operation), possibly related to coil migration into venous flow and stent-graft placement.

The patient was anticoagulated with rivaroxaban for bilateral proximal DVT (20 mg daily tapered to 15 mg then 10 mg over about a year), after which therapy was switched to aspirin 100 mg daily, with no further vascular events or bleeding complications observed after the second operation despite anticoagulation.

The patient was maintained on a beta-blocker (Carvedilol) to control blood pressure as part of medical management aimed at reducing risk of arterial dissection or rupture, consistent with standard vEDS management goals.
More than 60% of vEDS patients present with life-threatening vascular complications before age 40, per cited literature, contextualizing the young age (30 years) of this patient's presentation.

According to cited literature, endovascular treatment approaches for vEDS vascular complications show no noticeable improvement in outcomes compared with open repair, aside from a small reduction in mortality.

The patient displayed vEDS-characteristic physical features (easy bruising since childhood, thin/translucent skin with visible superficial veins, tooth decay, prominent eyes, long thin nose, spontaneous periorbital ecchymosis) but lacked classic-EDS features such as skin hyperextensibility or delayed wound healing.

Targeted sequencing excluded pathogenic variants in SMAD2, SMAD3, TGFB3, TGFBR1, TGFBR2, and COL1A1, ruling out Loeys-Dietz syndrome and Marfan syndrome as alternative diagnoses, with only the COL3A1 variant identified.
Among propensity-matched patients undergoing 1-3 level TLIF, those with EDS had a significantly higher rate of adjacent segment disease compared to those without EDS.
No significant difference in pseudoarthrosis diagnosis was found between EDS and non-EDS patients following TLIF.
No significant difference in all-cause medical and surgical complications was found between EDS and non-EDS patients following TLIF.
Genetic testing of the COL3A1 gene confirmed the diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in the patient after years of diagnostic uncertainty.

A two-stage free latissimus dorsi myocutaneous flap transfer strategy achieved optimal tissue coverage and full abdominal wall restoration while minimizing risk of lethal complications in a patient with vascular EDS and a voluminous full-thickness abdominal defect with enterocutaneous fistula.

Treatment with somatostatin (6 mg/day) combined with antibiotics, negative pressure therapy and nasogastric tube aspiration reduced enterocutaneous fistula output by one-third after one week, with complete fistula healing after six weeks.
Evisceration is described as a frequent and typical postoperative complication in patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, as occurred in this patient following bowel resection surgery.

Vascular EDS involves abnormal structure and production of type III procollagen, a major protein in vessel walls and hollow organs, resulting in fragile vessels and skin and an altered wound-healing process.
Among 36 adolescents with juvenile fibromyalgia, 13 (36.1%) met criteria for joint hypermobility based on a Beighton score ≥ 5.
Adolescents with JFM and joint hypermobility reported significantly lower functional disability than those with JFM but without joint hypermobility.
Pain intensity did not differ significantly between JFM adolescents with joint hypermobility and those without.
Higher Beighton hypermobility scores were associated with lower (better) functional disability scores among adolescents with JFM.
Adolescents with JFM and joint hypermobility demonstrated greater hip flexion throughout the drop vertical jump task compared to non-hypermobile peers.
Adolescents with joint hypermobility exhibited decreased hip abduction moment during the early landing phase of the drop vertical jump compared to those without joint hypermobility.

Adolescents with joint hypermobility showed greater hip and knee transverse plane moment during the late take-off (propulsion) phase of the drop vertical jump compared to those without joint hypermobility.
Higher Beighton scores may trend toward increased peak hip internal rotation angle during the drop vertical jump task.
Higher Beighton scores may be associated with higher knee flexion angle during the drop vertical jump task.
COL5A1 haploinsufficiency in humans causes classic Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome, presenting with hyperextensible skin and joint instability/laxity, with females more commonly affected.
Prior studies in Col5-deficient mice showed that reduced Col5a1 expression leads to lower tendon stiffness, reduced fibril deposition, and altered collagen fibril structure.
Male Col5-deficient tendons previously demonstrated altered healing compared to wild-type tendons, but female mice had not yet been studied in this model prior to the current work.
In female Col5a1+/- mice, patellar tendons demonstrated altered and decreased healing after injury compared to wild-type tendons.
Failure to normalize tendon cellularity by 6 weeks post-injury in Col5-deficient tendons was associated with the observed decrease in mechanical properties.
Tendon stiffness did not increase post-injury in Col5-deficient mice, unlike expected normal healing response.
Unlike wild-type tendons, Col5-deficient tendons failed to show an increase in stiffness following injury.
Collagen fiber realignment during mechanical loading was delayed in Col5-deficient female tendons compared to wild-type during healing.
The authors conclude that increased Col5a1 expression following injury is required to re-establish proper matrix engagement and cellularity during tendon healing.

Dermal collagen fibrils in Col1a1Jrt/+ (EDS-model) mice showed kinks, turns, non-linear paths and random orientation, whereas wildtype fibrils were straight, clearly bordered and unidirectional, despite D-banding still being detectable in both.
D-banding periodicity measured by computational (2D FFT/PSD) and manual methods did not significantly differ between wildtype and Col1a1Jrt/+ mice skin collagen.

2D FFT power spectrum density analysis showed wildtype mouse skin collagen produced a clear first-harmonic arc (indicating aligned fibrils), whereas Col1a1Jrt/+ mouse skin collagen produced a scatter pattern lacking a defined harmonic, indicating pathological anisotropy/disorganization.

Using constructed phantom AFM images with defined fibril orientations, the angle between discrete points in the 2D FFT matched the actual angular deviation between the fibril groups, confirming the method's validity for quantifying fibril angular distribution and anisotropy.

Eight blinded raters (clinicians untrained in AFM) classified 24 2D FFT images as wildtype or pathological with substantial inter-rater (Kappa=0.71) and intra-rater (Kappa=0.66) agreement, supporting the diagnostic potential of this image-analysis method.

Prior work (cited) showed Col1a1Jrt/+ mice have reduced skin tensile properties, more frayed tail tendon, and about one third of young adult mice develop kyphosis, consistent with an EDS-like connective tissue phenotype.

Most patients with generalized joint hypermobility achieved clinically important improvement in at least one patient-reported outcome measure after hip arthroscopy, though the proportion varied widely across studies.
No statistically significant differences were found between patients with and without generalized joint hypermobility for any described outcomes following hip arthroscopy.
One study found an association between generalized joint hypermobility and an increased risk of postoperative deep gluteal syndrome after hip arthroscopy.
One study found an association between generalized joint hypermobility and an increased risk of postoperative iliopsoas tendinitis after hip arthroscopy.
No complications were reported in any of the four studies that specifically assessed complication rates following hip arthroscopy in GJH patients.
The rate of revision arthroscopy among GJH patients ranged from 0% to 11.4% across included studies, and only two patients in a single study of 11 hips required conversion to total hip arthroplasty.

With effective labral repair and capsular closure, outcomes achieved in patients with generalized joint hypermobility undergoing hip arthroscopy are comparable to those reported in patients without hypermobility.
Long COVID symptoms persisting beyond 3 months after acute COVID-19 closely resemble fibromyalgia symptoms, with reported prevalence estimates varying widely.
Long COVID prevalence was much higher after the first pandemic wave and was linked to the belief that one had had COVID rather than to actual infection status.
The author proposes that psychological stress from the pandemic and lockdown, rather than direct effects of viral infection, probably caused the high frequency of long COVID.
Numerous studies attempting to identify objective biological abnormalities to explain long COVID have failed to produce replicated or convincing results.

The author argues that long COVID represents a historical repetition of relabeling fibromyalgia, paralleling past attempts to frame the condition as a well-understood somatic disease rather than acknowledge psychosomatic aspects.

AT-04 magnetic field irradiation significantly increased paw withdrawal threshold (reduced mechanical allodynia) compared to sham device in PSL neuropathic pain model rats, with the effect persisting after irradiation ended.

The 5-HT1A receptor antagonist WAY100635 partially blocked (~30%) the analgesic effect of AT-04, reaching statistical significance only on Day 12, indicating serotonergic receptor involvement in AT-04's mechanism.
The alpha-2 adrenoceptor antagonist Yohimbine significantly antagonized (~40%) the analgesic effect of AT-04 on Day 12, indicating noradrenergic receptor involvement.

Combined administration of WAY100635 and Yohimbine produced a significant ~50% antagonism of AT-04's analgesic effect, supporting involvement of both serotonergic and noradrenergic descending pain modulation pathways.
A single 30-minute AT-04 irradiation significantly increased extracellular serotonin levels in the spinal cord of PSL rats compared to sham device.
During a single AT-04 irradiation, extracellular noradrenaline in the spinal cord showed a non-significant increasing trend compared to sham device.
After 5 days of repeated AT-04 irradiation, a subsequent single irradiation session significantly increased extracellular 5-HT in the spinal cord compared to sham.
After repeated AT-04 irradiation, extracellular NA in the spinal cord was significantly increased compared to sham, unlike after a single irradiation.
The μ-opioid receptor antagonist naloxone significantly blocked approximately 60% of AT-04's analgesic effect, confirming involvement of endogenous opioid/μ-opioid receptor signaling.

Unpublished preliminary data showed that beta-endorphin levels did not increase in brain gray matter with AT-04 treatment, suggesting mechanisms other than beta-endorphin release may underlie the opioid-mediated analgesic effect.
Preliminary unpublished data indicated upregulation of opioid receptors in the brain of a repeated cold-stress mouse model of fibromyalgia and in microglial cell lines.

In an unpublished non-clinical fibromyalgia model induced by repeated cold stress, AT-04 demonstrated a significant analgesic effect in addition to the nerve ligation model, though detailed data were not shown.
The authors cite a prior clinical trial (Oka et al. 2020) using an AT-04 prototype device that reportedly showed a high analgesic effect in patients with fibromyalgia.
Mastocytosis is a rare disorder with an estimated prevalence of approximately 1 in 10,000 persons.
Darier's sign, the pathognomonic cutaneous finding of mastocytosis, has a sensitivity of over 90%.
US studies report anaphylaxis incidence of up to 40-50 per 100,000 person-years.
European studies report a lower anaphylaxis incidence of 1.5-7.9 per 100,000 person-years compared to the USA.
The lifetime prevalence of anaphylaxis is estimated at approximately 0.3%.
Fatal anaphylaxis occurs at a rate of approximately 1 per three million population per year.
Food-induced anaphylaxis is the most common cause of anaphylaxis in children, accounting for 80-92% of cases.
The consensus clinical diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis showed 95% sensitivity and 71% specificity in a prospective emergency department validation study.
The estimated overlap between anaphylaxis and mastocytosis is approximately 35%, though systematic overlap data for anaphylaxis and MCAS are lacking.
MCAS is diagnosed using a formula (1.2 × baseline serum tryptase + 2 ng/mL) to define the minimal tryptase rise during a suspected activation event.
Over 90% of systemic mastocytosis cases carry the activating KIT D816V mutation, and KIT ligand stem cell factor augments IgE-dependent mediator release in normal mast cells.
A study found that responsiveness of skin mast cells to morphine and airway mast cells to mannitol was similar between systemic mastocytosis patients and healthy controls in vivo.
Mast cells cultured from mastocytosis patients showed higher reactivity to mannitol when activated in vitro, compared to expected normal reactivity.
The prevalence of atopy (30%) and atopic disease (22%) in SM patients was not increased compared to the general population.
SM patients with anaphylaxis had significantly higher rates of atopy (42%) and atopic disease (33%) compared to SM patients without anaphylaxis.

HαT is two to three times more prevalent in patients with systemic mastocytosis than in the general population, and SM patients with concurrent HαT tend to have more severe/frequent MC activation and anaphylaxis symptoms.

The REMA score (male gender, sBT >25 ng/mL, hypotension, absence of urticaria) predicted underlying mastocytosis in anaphylaxis patients with 92% sensitivity and 81% specificity.
The Karolinska score, a modification of REMA using a lower tryptase cutoff (>20 ng/mL), showed improved sensitivity (93%) and specificity (94%) in idiopathic anaphylaxis patients.

Patients with indolent systemic mastocytosis (ISM) have been reported to have an increased susceptibility to developing malignant melanoma.
Darier's sign (swelling and redness after stroking lesional skin) has over 90% sensitivity for diagnosing cutaneous mastocytosis lesions.

The patient developed elevated anti-ACE-2 antibodies shortly after receiving the BNT162b2 SARS-CoV-2 vaccine.
Despite a clinical diagnosis of small fiber neuropathy, skin biopsies in this patient showed normal intra-epidermal nerve fiber density.
Serum tryptase was persistently elevated above the normal range, supporting a diagnosis of mast cell activation syndrome.
Chromogranin-A levels were elevated, contributing to the diagnosis of MCAS.
Urinary prostaglandin F2-alpha was elevated, supporting the MCAS diagnosis.
The patient tested negative for the KIT D816V mutation commonly associated with mastocytosis, and for hereditary alpha-tryptasemia gene mutations.
Following discontinuation of subcutaneous immunoglobulins, the patient's chest pain worsened and echocardiography revealed a moderate pericardial effusion, leading to a pericarditis diagnosis.
Total complement levels were persistently elevated above the normal reference range in this patient.
ALT was intermittently elevated, though extensive hepatology workup was negative.
A small transient IgA paraprotein with lambda light chains was detected on serum immunofixation, which resolved by follow-up in 2023.
Flow cytometry showed a markedly elevated CD4:CD8 ratio of 12 that normalized to 3.7 approximately 14 months later.
The patient developed POTS-type dysautonomia with a heart rate increase of 25-30 beats per minute upon standing along with dizziness, imbalance, urinary hesitancy, and profuse sweating.

Three courses of corticosteroids were ineffective at improving the patient's symptoms.
Oral cromoglicic acid at 800 mg/day did not lead to improvement of symptoms.
Colchicine and low-dose aspirin were started for pericarditis and led to improvement in chest pain.
Low dose naltrexone combined with time-restricted eating, started 16 months after symptom onset, provided some additional improvement though symptoms did not fully resolve.
Gabapentin, started for neuropathic pain, initially had no impact at doses up to 1200 mg/day.

A prior case report describes a 52-year-old male who developed SFN with orthostatic intolerance and syncope lasting more than 5 months after BNT162b2 vaccination.
Prestimulation of LAD2 mast cells with IL-33 and IL-6 significantly increased their responsiveness to IgE-mediated allergen stimulation compared to non-prestimulated cells.
LAD2 mast cell activation test (MAT) results correlated with basophil activation test (BAT) results in Hymenoptera venom allergy patients.
Patients with severe Hymenoptera sting reactions (Mueller grades III/IV) had a median 2-fold higher LAD2 MAT score than those with nonsevere reactions (large local reaction or Mueller grades I/II).
LAD2 MAT provided conclusive results in 20 of 37 (54.1%) Hymenoptera venom allergy patients whose basophils were nonresponsive in the BAT.
Omalizumab monoclonal antibodies with identical amino acid sequence but produced in CHO versus HEK293 cells showed slightly different human IgE binding and neutralizing features.
A known omalizumab variant carrying a three amino acid replacement in the Fab region exhibited lower IgE binding affinity than the original omalizumab.
The lower IgE binding affinity of the Fab variant translated into reduced IgE neutralizing capacity compared to original omalizumab.
The Fab-variant omalizumab showed a reduced ability to prevent mast cell activation compared to original omalizumab, demonstrated both in vitro and in vivo in mast cell-based models.

The developed orthogonal analytical/functional assay set was sensitive enough to detect Fab-linked differences between anti-IgE antibody versions with identical amino acid sequence, supporting biosimilar and novel anti-IgE agent assessment.

In patients with vertebrobasilar ischemia, phase of the BP-CBF velocity transfer function was significantly reduced in the very low frequency range compared to healthy controls, indicating impaired dynamic cerebral autoregulation.
Gain of the BP-CBF velocity transfer function was significantly increased in the very low frequency range in VBI patients compared to controls.
In the low frequency range, phase reduction of the BP-CBF velocity transfer function was significant only on the ipsilateral middle cerebral artery side in VBI patients.
In the high frequency range, phase reduction between VBI patients and controls was only marginally significant.
Blood pressure power spectral density was much higher across all frequency bands in VBI patients than in healthy controls.
Healthy controls, but not VBI patients, exhibited a strong heart rate variability power spectral peak around 0.11 Hz.
VBI patients, but not controls, exhibited a strong heart rate variability power spectral peak around 0.36 Hz.

Overall, patients with vertebrobasilar ischemia showed bilateral impairment of cortical cerebral autoregulation that was associated with autonomic nervous system disbalance rather than with vascular risk factors.
The authors argue that SARS-CoV-2 vaccination should only be attributed as a cause of small fiber neuropathy after all other differential diagnoses have been ruled out.
SCN9A-associated SFN patients showed significantly higher cortical thickness in sensorimotor brain regions compared to idiopathic SFN patients.
SCN9A-associated SFN patients showed lower cortical thickness than idiopathic SFN patients in functionally diverse regions including the posterior cingulate cortex.

Longer duration of pain was associated with lower right thalamic volume in SFN patients.

Hypermobility spectrum disorders were present as a comorbidity in 20% of dyspeptic children, following mental health (32%) and neurologic (27%) comorbidities.
Solid and liquid gastric emptying rates were concordant (both normal or both abnormal) in 61.23% of dyspeptic children.
A small subset (2.5%) of dyspeptic children had delayed solid emptying with normal liquid emptying.
About one quarter (26.16%) of dyspeptic children had delayed liquid emptying with normal solid emptying, indicating liquid-phase testing captures additional abnormalities missed by solid-phase alone.
Abdominal pain showed a trend toward association with either delayed or normal solid gastric emptying, though this did not reach statistical significance.
Nausea was most often reported by children with normal solid gastric emptying, a statistically significant association.
Nausea was underreported (29%) among younger children (<12 years) presenting with vomiting, suggesting nausea is an unreliable symptom indicator in this age group.
Abnormal solid gastric emptying (either rapid or delayed) occurred more frequently in children with mental health disorders.
Only 2.5% of dyspeptic children had delayed solid emptying with normal liquid emptying, while 26.16% had delayed liquid emptying with normal solid emptying.
Abdominal pain showed a borderline trend for association with delayed or normal (i.e., not rapid) solid gastric emptying.
Nausea was most often reported in children with normal solid gastric emptying rather than delayed or rapid emptying.
In children under 12 years old with vomiting, nausea was underreported, being noted in only 29% of these patients.
Abnormal solid gastric emptying, either rapid or delayed, was significantly more common among children with mental health comorbidities.
Rapid liquid gastric emptying was significantly more common in children with genetic disorders compared to those without.

Immunohistochemistry showed significantly decreased TRPV1 expression in the spinal cord of SNS-treated IBS-D rats compared with sham rats.
Immunohistochemistry showed significantly decreased TRPV1 expression in the colon of SNS-treated IBS-D rats compared with sham rats.

Ultra-short (15-s) RMSSD and SDSD showed strong agreement with standard 6-min HRV measures in the NSHD cohort.
Ultra-short PHF showed only moderate agreement with 6-min PHF, with a small positive bias and wider limits of agreement compared to RMSSD/SDSD.
In cross-sectional analysis, increasing age, BMI, diabetes, beta-blocker use, male sex, and smoking were each independently associated with lower usHRV.
usHRV decreased with increasing resting heart rate, consistent with the known interaction between HRV and heart rate.

Lower PHF (ultra-short HRV) was associated with increased long-term risk of atrial fibrillation independent of resting heart rate and cardiovascular risk factors, showing the strongest association among usHRV indices.
Lower RMSSD, SDSD, and PHF were each similarly associated with increased long-term risk of stroke, independent of resting heart rate and standard cardiovascular risk factors.
In unadjusted linear Cox regression models, all usHRV markers were significantly associated with cardiovascular outcomes, with hazard ratios per SD decrease ranging from 1.25 to 1.40.
A one SD decrease in heart rate recovery from exercise was associated with increased risk of MACE and mortality, but not with atrial fibrillation or stroke.
A U-shaped (non-linear) association was found between RMSSD/SDSD and both MACE and mortality, such that both very low and very high usHRV were associated with increased risk.
Compared with participants in the 2nd-4th RMSSD quintiles, those in the lowest RMSSD quintile had significantly higher risk of MACE and mortality.

Inclusion of a small number of individuals with premature atrial contractions artifactually inflated HRV values and could reproduce a spurious association between high usHRV and atrial fibrillation, potentially explaining prior reports of U-shaped HRV-AF associations.
RMSSD and SDSD measured from 10-s and 5-s ECG segments correlated well with 15-s values and showed similar, though slightly attenuated, associations with cardiovascular outcomes.

Overall, reduced ultra-short HRV (from ECGs as short as 5-15 s) was independently associated with increased long-term risk of atrial fibrillation, major adverse cardiac events, stroke, and all-cause mortality after adjustment for resting heart rate and standard cardiovascular risk factors, in a cohort without prevalent cardiovascular disease.
Male sex was associated with a lower likelihood of developing post-COVID-19 condition.
Tertiary education or higher was associated with a lower likelihood of developing post-COVID-19 condition.
A prior history of headache was strongly associated with increased risk of developing PCC.
Tachycardia at COVID-19 onset was associated with increased risk of developing PCC.
Fatigue at COVID-19 onset was associated with increased risk of developing PCC.
Neurocognitive complaints at COVID-19 onset were strongly associated with increased risk of developing PCC.
Neurosensitive alterations at COVID-19 onset had the strongest association with increased risk of developing PCC.
Dyspnea at COVID-19 onset was associated with increased risk of developing PCC.
A combined model of preexisting conditions and acute-phase symptoms discriminated PCC development with excellent accuracy (AUC 0.931).
Preexisting fibromyalgia, headache or insomnia history, autoimmune disease, and prior arrhythmia episodes were associated with increased risk of PCC.

Three sub-syndromic PCC clusters were identified by hierarchical clustering, characterized by an additive accumulation of overlapping symptoms rather than mutually exclusive syndromes, consistent with the US RECOVER study.
Cardiac MRI-confirmed myocardial perfusion abnormalities were more frequent among PCC patients in the most symptomatic cluster (C) than in less symptomatic clusters.
Only a small minority of PCC patients recovered during the 2-year follow-up period, with a median time to recovery of 11.4 months.
Male sex was associated with a higher likelihood of subsequent recovery from PCC.

Four weeks of fluoxetine injection produced fatigue-like behavior in mice, shown by reduced latency to fall in the rota-rod test compared with saline-treated mice.
Fluoxetine-treated mice showed decreased exercise duration and distance traveled in the fatigue rotating wheel test compared with saline controls.
Fluoxetine reduced locomotor activity and increased immobility time after waking in the home-cage activity test, modeling unrefreshing sleep.
Fatigue-like behavior induced by fluoxetine was abolished after 6 weeks of drug withdrawal, indicating reversibility.
Fluoxetine-treated mice showed reduced nest building scores, indicating general malaise similar to ME/CFS.
Fluoxetine-treated mice showed increased pain sensitivity, with faster paw withdrawal from infrared irradiation than saline controls.
Fluoxetine-treated mice spent significantly less time in the center of the open field, indicating anxiety-like behavior, though total distance traveled was unchanged.
Fluoxetine slightly decreased the grip strength-to-weight ratio but the difference was not statistically significant compared with saline, supporting brain-specific rather than muscular fatigability.
Fluoxetine markedly increased extracellular serotonin concentrations in the dorsal raphe nucleus (over 3-fold) and hypothalamus (about 2-fold) as measured by microdialysis/LC-MS.
Fluoxetine increased 5-HT/c-Fos double-positive neuronal signal in the dorsal raphe nucleus, indicating serotonergic neuronal activation.
Fluoxetine increased serotonergic innervation from the dorsal raphe nucleus to the hypothalamus, shown by increased retrograde tracer (FG)/5-HT co-stained cells.
Fluoxetine-evoked serotonergic overactivation was not due to quantitative changes in 5-HT1A receptor protein or mRNA, nor its transcriptional repressors (freud-1, deaf1) or promoter (pet-1).

8-OH-DPAT (5-HT1A agonist) challenge failed to increase TPH2 and c-Fos expression in the raphe nucleus of fluoxetine-treated mice as it did in saline controls, evidencing functional desensitization/loss of function of the 5-HT1A receptor.
8-OH-DPAT challenge rapidly increased plasma corticosterone in saline mice but produced a much blunted response in fluoxetine-treated mice, indicating HPA axis dysfunction.
The blunted HPA axis response in fluoxetine-treated mice was also observed following a 15-minute forced exercise challenge compared with pre-exercise levels.
8-OH-DPAT-induced lowering of rectal temperature seen in saline mice was absent in fluoxetine-treated mice, indicating impaired thermoregulatory response.
Fluoxetine-treated mice showed a significantly lower CRH neuronal response (CRH receptor 2/c-Fos double-positive signal and CRH-related protein expression) to 8-OH-DPAT than saline controls.

In fluoxetine-treated mice, hypothalamic membrane GIRK1 (but not GIRK2) protein and downstream signaling (phospho-ERK1/2, phospho-CREB, BDNF) were reduced compared to saline, confirming impaired 5-HT1A-GIRK signaling.
Serum cortisol levels were significantly lower in 17 ME/CFS patients than in 10 healthy controls, supporting the hypocortisolism seen in the animal model.
CRISPR-mediated Htr1a knockdown mice had significantly lower plasma corticosterone than wild-type or Htr1a+/+ mice.
Htr1a knockdown mice exhibited fatigue-like behavior in the rota-rod test compared to wild-type/Htr1a+/+ mice.
Htr1a knockdown mice showed augmented pain sensitivity in the plantar test compared to wild-type/Htr1a+/+ mice.
Htr1a knockdown mice exhibited anxious behavior in the open-field test compared to wild-type/Htr1a+/+ mice.

The serotonin synthesis inhibitor pCPA significantly reversed fluoxetine-induced fatigue-like (rota-rod) and malaise (nest building) behaviors, supporting the causal role of serotonergic hyperactivity.
Plasma TGF-β1 (active form) was elevated in both the fluoxetine-injected and Htr1a-knockdown mouse models, mirroring the elevated serum TGF-β1 reported in ME/CFS patients.

Reactive astrocytes (GFAP-positive) were increased in the fluoxetine/Htr1a-knockdown mouse brain, consistent with reported neuroinflammation in ME/CFS patients, while microglial (Iba-1) levels were unchanged.
Fluoxetine-treated mice showed no significant alteration in cognitive function on the novel object recognition test, a limitation of the model.
Overall, plasma C4a levels did not significantly differ between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls when the ME/CFS group was not stratified by immune status.

After stratifying by immunodeficiency status, plasma C4a concentrations were significantly reduced in ME/CFS patients with immunodeficiencies compared to both ME/CFS patients without immunodeficiencies and healthy controls.
Serum IL-1-beta levels were significantly lower in ME/CFS patients without immunodeficiencies compared to healthy controls.

Serum IL-33 was elevated (non-significantly) in ME/CFS patients without immunodeficiencies compared to both healthy controls and ME/CFS patients with immunodeficiencies, suggested to reflect mucosal barrier leakage.
Serum IL-6 levels were significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients without immunodeficiencies compared to healthy controls.
No statistically significant differences were found between ME/CFS subgroups and healthy controls in serum TNF-alpha, IL-8, IFN-gamma, or FGF21 levels.
Serum EDN levels were numerically higher in both ME/CFS subgroups (with and without immunodeficiency) than in healthy controls, but the difference was not statistically significant.
When ME/CFS patients were not stratified by immune status, serum LBP levels did not significantly differ from healthy controls.
After stratification, serum LBP levels were significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients without immunodeficiencies compared to healthy controls, indicating mucosal barrier leakage.
Serum soluble CD14 levels did not differ significantly between ME/CFS subgroups and healthy controls.

The LBP/sCD14 ratio was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients without immunodeficiencies compared to both ME/CFS patients with immunodeficiencies and healthy controls, consistent with barrier leakage-driven low-grade inflammation.
I-FABP levels were slightly, but not significantly, reduced in ME/CFS patients without immunodeficiencies compared to healthy controls.

Endotoxin-core IgG antibody levels were numerically highest in ME/CFS patients with immunodeficiencies, while ME/CFS patients without immunodeficiencies had levels similar to healthy controls; differences were not statistically significant.
Ten percent of ME/CFS patients with immunodeficiencies in this cohort had a diagnosed complement deficiency.
All ME/CFS patients enrolled in this cohort had disease onset attributed to EBV infection, supporting EBV as a post-infectious trigger of ME/CFS.

A pilot GWAS study found that approximately 70-80% of 383 ME/CFS subjects carry variant alleles in mucin genes MUC16, MUC19, and MUC22 at 1.60 to 3.75 times the frequency seen in the 1000 Genomes reference population.
The MUC19 SNP rs10784618, present in 77% of ME/CFS subjects versus 48% of the reference population, introduces a premature stop codon predicted to be highly deleterious with a CADD score of 36.

The MUC19 missense SNP rs11564109 (cysteine to tyrosine at residue 1411), present in 24% of ME/CFS subjects versus 8% of the reference population, has a CADD score of 24.7 and is predicted to disrupt disulfide bond formation important for gel-mucin structure.
The MUC16 variant rs7245949, found in ME/CFS patients, has separately been associated with lower expression of T-cell response markers in a tumor mutation burden study.

Three additional MUC16 SNPs found in ME/CFS (rs1862462, rs1867691, rs2547072) have been significantly associated with changes in grey matter volumes across ten brain regions in an Alzheimer's disease genetic biomarker study.
Two MUC19 SNPs found in ME/CFS (rs2588401 and rs2588402) have separately been associated with the chronic inflammatory disorder asthma.
MUC19 SNP rs2588401 has also been associated with acute lymphocytic leukemia in an external study.
MUC22 SNP rs10947121, found in ME/CFS subjects, has been associated with ankylosing spondylitis in an external study.
MUC22 SNP rs3094672 has been associated with a protective role against multiple sclerosis in an external study.
Depletion of mucin-16 in vitro increases binding of Staphylococcus aureus to cultured corneal epithelial cells, illustrating mucin-16's role in restricting microbial invasion.

Mucin-16, whether detached or cell-surface bound, has been shown to directly inhibit the natural cytotoxicity mechanism of NK cells, offering a potential mechanistic link to the reduced NK cell function reported in ME/CFS.

A literature-based logic model of the mucosal-immune system predicted three stable states, and the resting plasma cytokine profile of female ME/CFS patients most closely aligned with SS1, an inflammatory state marked by increased pro-inflammatory cytokines and a Th1 shift.

The male ME/CFS cytokine profile aligned nearly equidistant between the healthy state (SS0) and SS1, but was closest to SS2, a mixed inflammatory state with increases in some pro-inflammatory cytokines and decreases in anti-inflammatory cytokines and Th2/Th17/Treg activity.
In male subjects, none of the 12 measured plasma cytokines showed a statistically significant difference between ME/CFS patients and healthy sedentary controls at rest.

Female ME/CFS patients showed statistically significant differences in some resting plasma cytokines compared to healthy sedentary controls, with the overall profile being furthest from the modeled healthy steady state.

Serum mucin-16 levels are increased in women with endometriosis, although endometrial tissue expression of mucin-16 is unchanged, suggesting a possible link relevant to female-predominant ME/CFS comorbidities.

Dexamethasone, a synthetic glucocorticoid similar to cortisol, has been shown to upregulate mucin-16 expression, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between stress hormone signaling and mucin-16-driven immune dysregulation in ME/CFS.
Reduced NK cell function in ME/CFS correlates with illness severity, though the underlying cause of this reduced function remains unknown.

Flow cytometry evidence indicates significant deficits in the expression of receptors and adhesion molecules on subsets of CD8+ T cells in ME/CFS patients, which may contribute to disease pathogenesis, potentially via mucin-mediated disruption of immune synapse formation.
Circulating EV concentration in plasma was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than controls at baseline and 15 minutes post-exercise.

Control subjects showed a significant increase in EV concentration after exercise (1.4-fold at 15 min, 2.2-fold at 24 h) while ME/CFS patients showed no significant change in EV concentration in response to exercise.
ME/CFS patients showed significantly lower oxygen consumption at ventilatory threshold and longer time to peak on CPET, indicating decreased physiological exercise capacity compared to controls.
At 15 min post-exercise, 13 EV proteins had lower abundance and 3 had higher abundance in ME/CFS patients compared to controls after FDR correction, whereas no proteins were significant at baseline.
EMILIN1 was the only EV protein significantly increased 24 hours post-exercise in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.

Platelet degranulation/activation/aggregation was the most enriched Reactome pathway among EV proteins differentially abundant 15 min post-exercise, with F8, F13A1, FN1 and HSPA5 decreased and ORM1 increased in ME/CFS versus controls.
Myosin light chains MYL9 and MYL12A, associated with muscle contraction and EPH-Ephrin signalling pathways, were decreased in EVs from ME/CFS patients versus controls at 15 min post-exercise.
IPA canonical pathway analysis showed the complement system pathway was significantly inhibited in ME/CFS patients versus controls at baseline.
LXR/RXR activation and RHOGDI signalling pathways were significantly inhibited in ME/CFS patients versus controls at 24 h post-exercise.
The 14-3-3-mediated signalling pathway was significantly activated in ME/CFS patients compared to controls at 15 min post-exercise, but not at 24 h.
Glycolysis I and gluconeogenesis I canonical pathways, linked to energy metabolism, were significantly activated in ME/CFS patients versus controls at baseline.

Far fewer EV proteins increased with exercise in ME/CFS patients (63 DAPs, all increased) than in controls (187 DAPs, 178 increased and 9 decreased), with only 45 proteins overlapping between groups, indicating a blunted post-exercise EV proteomic response in ME/CFS.

Six members of the 14-3-3 protein family increased in abundance post-exercise uniquely in ME/CFS patients and were associated with G2M/checkpoint, cell cycle checkpoint, and TP53 transcriptional regulation pathways.
Three integrin EV proteins (ITGB1, ITGB3, ITGA2B) increased post-exercise uniquely in ME/CFS patients and were associated with the neural cell adhesion molecule L1 signal transduction pathway.

In the control group only, EV proteins overrepresented after exercise included TRiC chaperonin complex/tubulin components (actin and tubulin folding) and muscle contraction proteins, unlike ME/CFS patients where no muscle-related pathway enrichment was observed.

Muscle-related tissue enrichment categories (myoblasts, smooth muscle, kidney, heart) seen among controls' post-exercise EV proteins were absent in ME/CFS patients, suggesting disrupted systemic muscle-EV signalling in ME/CFS.
Lung tissue was the only broad category exclusively enriched among the post-exercise increased EV proteins in ME/CFS patients.

Despite fewer total DAPs, post-exercise increased EV proteins in ME/CFS patients were uniquely and significantly associated with a broader range of immune cell types (mast cells, CD4 memory T cells, non-classical monocytes, interstitial and resident macrophages, basophils, multiple dendritic cell subsets) than in controls.
Only in ME/CFS patients were post-exercise EV protein changes uniquely enriched for proteins expressed in the subthalamic nucleus and amygdala (basal ganglia brain regions).

Eight EV proteins including coagulation factor VIII (F8), muscle proteins ATP2A2, MYL6, MYL9, WDR1, and chaperones PDIA6, HSPD1 and HSPA8 had a significantly lower 15 min/0 h fold-change ratio in ME/CFS patients than controls after FDR correction.
At 24 h versus baseline, PDIA6 and CCT6A had lower fold-change ratios while COLEC11, CLDN5, VWF, SAA2-SAA4 and FN1 had higher fold-change ratios in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.

Clusterin (CLU) was the only EV protein whose increased abundance from baseline to 24 h post-exercise positively correlated with both average myalgia and arthralgia severity, and its 15 min/0 h ratio also positively correlated with fatigue severity, in ME/CFS patients.

Seven EV proteins (DBN1, GSTP1, HSPB1, THBS1, TMOD3, TPM4, CAPZB) had 24 h/0 h fold changes that strongly and significantly positively correlated with the change in myalgia severity post-exercise in ME/CFS patients, correlations absent in controls.
Increases in fibrinogen chains FGA and FGB from baseline to 15 min post-exercise positively correlated with post-exertional malaise severity 24 h post-exercise in ME/CFS patients.
EV size measured by nanoparticle tracking analysis did not significantly differ between ME/CFS patients and controls at any of the three time points.
TEM imaging confirmed isolated particles had characteristic saucer-shaped, bilayered EV morphology consistent with NTA size distribution.
At baseline, none of the six proteins with nominal differences between ME/CFS and controls remained significant after FDR correction, indicating minimal EV proteomic differences prior to exercise.

In control subjects, mean EV plasma concentration significantly increased 1.4-fold at 15 minutes and 2.2-fold at 24 hours after exercise compared to baseline, whereas ME/CFS patients showed no significant change in EV concentration in response to exercise.

Within-group analysis showed 63 EV proteins increased post-exercise (15 min vs baseline) in ME/CFS patients, all with higher levels, whereas 187 DAPs were found in controls (178 increased, 9 decreased), with only 45 proteins common to both groups.

Tissue enrichment analysis found myoblast, smooth muscle, kidney and heart tissue categories were uniquely enriched among EV proteins changing post-exercise in controls but not in ME/CFS patients, suggesting disrupted muscle-derived EV signalling in ME/CFS.
Lung tissue was the only category exclusively enriched among EV proteins responding to exercise in ME/CFS patients but not controls.

Despite a smaller number of DAPs, the ME/CFS-specific exercise-responsive EV proteins were uniquely and significantly associated with a broader range of immune cell types, including mast cells, CD4 memory T cells, non-classical monocytes, interstitial and resident macrophages, basophils, and multiple dendritic cell types.

Only ME/CFS patients showed exercise-responsive EV proteins expressed in the subthalamic nucleus and amygdala, brain regions within the basal ganglia, suggesting possible CNS-derived EV signalling unique to ME/CFS.

Proteins whose EV levels correlated strongly with average myalgia severity were enriched for leukocyte-mediated immunity, neutrophil-related processes, and platelet degranulation/aggregation pathways.

Proteins whose EV levels correlated strongly with arthralgia severity were enriched for cytoskeleton organization, cellular component assembly/biogenesis, and regulation of cellular protein localization pathways.
IPA canonical pathway analysis showed 'glycolysis I' and 'gluconeogenesis I' pathways were significantly activated in ME/CFS patients versus controls at baseline, prior to exercise.

ME/CFS patients showed significantly lower oxygen consumption at ventilatory threshold and lower time to peak exercise compared to controls during the maximal CPET, despite similar peak oxygen consumption and heart rate.

ME/CFS patients had lower Bell Disability Scale scores and lower SF-36 Physical and Mental Component Summary scores than controls, reflecting worse functional status and health-related quality of life.

Tubulin proteins and members of the TRiC chaperonin complex were significantly increased in EVs from controls 15 minutes post-exercise, contributing to actin/tubulin folding pathway enrichment and myoblast tissue enrichment unique to controls, a response not seen in ME/CFS.

The largest number of significant clinical correlations with EV protein fold changes in ME/CFS patients occurred in the 24h vs baseline comparison, with 878 significant correlations (648 negative, 230 positive) at q<0.1.

ANXA2, B2M, and ORM1 were found increased in ME/CFS versus controls 15 minutes post-exercise and are members of immune pathways including antigen presentation, cytokine signalling, and adaptive immune system.
The 24h/0h ratio of B2M was negatively correlated with general myalgia severity in ME/CFS patients, and B2M contributed to uniquely enriched immune, brain, and bone marrow tissue terms in ME/CFS.
More than 87% of patients continue to experience at least one symptom two months after onset of COVID-19 infection.

Post-acute COVID-19 patient reports and early observational studies suggest development of a syndrome resembling myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), a chronic multisystem disease previously associated with other infections.
In the general population, chronic fatigue prevalence ranges from 10% to 40%, while full ME/CFS diagnosis prevalence is much lower at 0.17-0.89%, and ME/CFS is reported to be more common in females.
Higher fatigue symptom levels in ME/CFS patients were associated with higher connectivity between the somatomotor network (SMN) and premotor network (PMN).
Higher fatigue symptom levels in ME/CFS patients were associated with lower connectivity between the somatomotor network (SMN) and default mode network (DMN).
Higher pain symptom levels in ME/CFS patients were associated with lower connectivity between the premotor network (PMN) and default mode network (DMN).
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) improved (increased) SMN-DMN connectivity in ME/CFS patients compared to a waiting-list group.
Among ME/CFS patients treated with CBT, larger clinical improvements were associated with larger increases in frontal SMN-DMN connectivity.
CBT did not produce significant changes in PMN-DMN or SMN-PMN connectivity relative to the waiting-list group.
Pooling four studies identified 56 circulating miRNAs differentially expressed between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, with 37 elevated and 19 decreased, mostly unique to individual studies.
Genes targeted by miRNAs elevated in ME/CFS formed a large, statistically robust cluster of functional interconnectivity by STRING analysis, holding up even at very high confidence thresholds.

Genes targeted by decreased ME/CFS miRNAs did not have high negative scores and showed virtually no functional clustering via STRING even at a low confidence threshold, suggesting they are unlikely to be central to disease pathology.
A simulation with 10000 random miRNA sets showed the ME/CFS miRNA set's target gene convergence and STRING interconnectivity were highly statistically significant and unlikely due to chance.

VEGFA ranked highest by both miRNA targeting frequency and Katz centrality, predicting strong translational suppression consistent with previously reported decreased VEGF-A protein levels in ME/CFS patients.

MDM2 scored highly in the final combined ranking and is predicted to be inhibited by circulating miRNAs, a gene known to play a key role in exercise-induced angiogenesis and skeletal muscle capillary maintenance.

Predicted miRNA targets include both pro-apoptotic (Bim, c-Myc, PTEN, Foxo3, Noxa/PMAIP1) and anti-apoptotic (Bcl-2, Mcl-1, MDM2, Akt1) proteins, making the net effect on apoptosis in ME/CFS unclear and possibly near-neutral.

Predicted suppression of c-Myc, Bcl-2, Mcl-1, MDM2, E2F1 and Sirt1 by circulating miRNAs converges on increased mitochondrial fission, consistent with Schreiner et al.'s report of increased mitochondrial fission in cells exposed to ME/CFS plasma.
SOD2 was among the highest-scoring genes predicted to be suppressed by circulating miRNAs, corroborating a prior report of reduced SOD2 levels in ME/CFS and suggesting impaired antioxidant defense.
Predicted downregulation of Sirt1 by circulating miRNAs may help explain sleep and circadian dysfunctions reported in ME/CFS patients, given Sirt1's regulatory role in the circadian clock.
MKNK2, a highly scoring predicted miRNA target, exhibits high circadian rhythmicity and may contribute to sleep dysfunction if inhibited in ME/CFS.

TGF-beta receptors (TGFBR1, TGFBR2, TGFBR3) and multiple Smad effectors were identified among predicted miRNA targets, suggesting TGF-beta signaling may be suppressed at the translational level despite consistently elevated circulating TGF-beta cytokine levels in ME/CFS, possibly as a compensatory response.

E2F1, normally upregulated by herpesviruses including HHV-6 to drive viral gene expression, was strongly predicted to be inhibited by ME/CFS circulating miRNAs, suggesting a mechanism enforcing herpesvirus latency.

Eight of the top 10 miRNAs ranked by predicted influence on the disease phenotype have been reported to be upregulated by herpesviruses (EBV, HHV-6A, CMV, KSHV), supporting a possible herpesvirus origin for circulating miRNA changes in ME/CFS.

A small cluster of AGO1, DICER1, DDX6, and TNRC6A—proteins central to miRNA biogenesis—was found among the predicted miRNA target genes, suggesting circulating miRNAs in ME/CFS might suppress the host's own miRNA production machinery.
Reanalysis of plasma metabolomics data from the Su et al. INCOV cohort showed reduced acetylcarnitine levels in PASC patients compared with healthy controls.
A plasma metabolomics study found increases in medium- and long-chain acylcarnitines in PASC patients compared with healthy controls, while short-chain acylcarnitines were unchanged.
Kovarik et al. found a significant decrease in short-chain C3-carnitine in patients with long COVID compared with healthy controls.
The ratio of neuroprotective to neurotoxic kynurenine metabolites differs between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
Plasma tryptophan levels were significantly decreased in PASC patients.
Alterations in kynurenine pathway metabolites have been associated with cognitive impairment in long COVID patients and with anxiety/depressive symptoms in COVID-19 survivors 6 months post-infection.
During exercise, long COVID patients showed decreased rates of fatty acid oxidation compared with expected/healthy metabolism.
A large meta-analysis found an association between depression risk and different lipid classes.

An open-label randomized trial found that acetylcarnitine supplementation had a significant main effect on mental fatigue in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome, differentiating responders and non-responders.
A randomized cross-over trial in MS patients with fatigue found that 3 months of acetylcarnitine supplementation had a more favourable effect on fatigue severity than amantadine.
A placebo-controlled randomized trial in relapsing-remitting MS patients found only a trend-level improvement in fatigue impact on daily life after 1 month of acetylcarnitine supplementation.

A meta-analysis of twelve randomized controlled trials found that acetylcarnitine monotherapy significantly decreased depression severity compared with placebo or no intervention, with adverse effects comparable to placebo and lower than antidepressants.

An observational case-control study found improvements in quality of life, depressive complaints, and pain scores after 1 month of combined physical exercise and acetylcarnitine supplementation compared with exercise alone in long COVID patients.
A study of long COVID patients reported decreased fatigue and increased subjective energy levels after 2 weeks of a supplement containing 150 mg of acetylcarnitine.
Multiple studies measuring blood acetylcarnitine levels in COVID-19/post-COVID-19 patients found no significant differences compared with healthy subjects.
Blood acetylcarnitine levels showed no significant differences between CFS/ME-CFS patients and healthy controls in the cited studies.
Blood acetylcarnitine concentrations were increased in heart failure patients compared with controls without heart failure.
Blood acetylcarnitine concentrations were higher in sepsis non-survivors than in survivors.
In elderly patients with fatigue, acetylcarnitine supplementation reduced physical and mental fatigue and improved cognitive status and physical function.
Patients with hepatic encephalopathy treated with acetylcarnitine showed decreased severity of mental and physical fatigue and increased physical activity.

In animal models of depression, acetylcarnitine epigenetically regulates metabotropic glutamate receptor 2 (mGluR2), negatively modulating neurotransmitter release and producing rapid antidepressant effects.
Acetylcarnitine treatment increased levels of norepinephrine and serotonin in the cortex of healthy mice.
Post-COVID-19 cardiovascular dysfunction is mechanistically linked to cardiac mitochondrial dysfunction.
Post-COVID-19 sarcopenia, driven by immunosenescence, endothelial damage, and mitochondrial dysfunction, causes loss of muscle mass/function and exercise intolerance.
Sleep disturbances observed three months after COVID-19 may relate to persistent infection, inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction.
Improving mitochondrial function has been reported to accelerate resolution of post-COVID-19 symptoms.
Acetylcarnitine has relatively low oral bioavailability, with absorption as low as 5–10% of a ~2000 mg saturating dose, and bioavailability decreases further at higher doses.
Acetylcarnitine is metabolized by gut microbiota to trimethylamine, which the liver converts to trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a cardiometabolic risk biomarker.

OCTN2 (SLC22A5) is the main carnitine transporter and also efficiently transports acetylcarnitine into cells, from the gut, and across the blood-brain barrier, with lower expression in brain than in high-energy-demand tissues.
Organic cation transporter 1 (OCT1/SLC22A1) promotes hepatic efflux of acetylcarnitine, contributing to the plasma acetylcarnitine pool.
Carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase (CACT) in the inner mitochondrial membrane exchanges acylcarnitines for carnitine to enable acetylcarnitine transfer across the mitochondrial membrane.

In an animal study, direct brain injection of radiolabeled acetylcarnitine showed rapid metabolism, with 60% recovered as exhaled 14CO2 by 22 hours and only 0.9-1.9% remaining in brain tissue across 1-22 hours.
Acetylcarnitine treatment further upregulates heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1) expression in aged rats, potentially via the Nrf2 pathway.
Studies measuring blood acetylcarnitine levels in chronic fatigue syndrome/ME-CFS and COVID-19/post-COVID-19 patients found no significant differences compared with healthy subjects.
Blood acetylcarnitine concentrations were significantly increased in heart failure patients compared with controls without heart failure.
Blood acetylcarnitine concentrations were higher in patients who did not survive sepsis compared with survivors.

In a CFS acetylcarnitine supplementation trial (2 g/day for 24 weeks), acetylcarnitine had a main effect on mental fatigue and post-treatment blood levels differed between responders and non-responders.
Acetylcarnitine supplementation has been shown to reduce fatigue associated with aging, cancer, and chronic hepatitis.
Patients with hepatic encephalopathy treated with acetylcarnitine (2 g twice daily for 90 days) showed decreased severity of mental and physical fatigue and increased physical activity.
A randomized cross-over trial in 36 MS patients with fatigue found that 3 months of acetylcarnitine had a more favourable effect on fatigue severity than amantadine.

In a placebo-controlled RCT of 60 people with relapsing-remitting MS, 1 month of acetylcarnitine supplementation showed only a trend-level, non-significant improvement in fatigue's impact on daily life.
Reanalysis of plasma metabolomics data from the INCOV cohort showed reduced plasma acetylcarnitine (C2) levels in PASC patients compared with healthy controls at 2-3 months post-infection.
Pathways related to hypoxia and dysregulated immune activity are proposed as strong drivers of neurological complications in PASC, based on post-mortem brain and observational studies.
Post-COVID-19 cardiovascular dysfunction is mechanistically linked to cardiac mitochondrial dysfunction.
Post-COVID-19 sarcopenia, involving muscle mass and function loss driven by mitochondrial dysfunction and autophagy, leads to exercise intolerance.
Sleep disturbances observed 3 months after COVID-19 may be linked to persistent viral infection/inflammation and mitochondrial dysfunction.
Blood acetylcarnitine concentrations did not differ between COVID-19 patients and non-COVID-19 subjects (7.4 vs 6.6 µmol/L).
Normalized blood acetylcarnitine data showed no difference between healthy subjects and patients with mild or moderate COVID-19.
Blood acetylcarnitine levels did not differ between chronic fatigue syndrome patients and controls (5.5 vs 5.8 µmol/L).
Blood acetylcarnitine levels did not differ between ME/CFS patients and controls in either males or females.
In a CFS supplementation trial, acetylcarnitine had a main effect on mental fatigue, with responders showing higher post-supplementation acetylcarnitine levels than non-responders.
Combined exercise and acetylcarnitine supplementation was reported as an effective management strategy for post-COVID syndrome.
In elderly patients with fatigue, acetylcarnitine supplementation reduced both physical and mental fatigue and improved cognitive status and physical function.
Patients with hepatic encephalopathy treated with acetylcarnitine showed decreased severity of mental and physical fatigue and increased physical activity.
Blood acetylcarnitine concentrations were increased in patients with heart failure compared to controls without heart failure.
Blood acetylcarnitine was higher in sepsis non-survivors than survivors.
Oral acetylcarnitine has low bioavailability, with absorption rates as low as 5-10% at an approximately 2000 mg saturating dose, and even lower relative bioavailability at higher doses.
Acetylcarnitine is metabolized by gut microbiota to trimethylamine, then hepatically converted to trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a cardiometabolic risk biomarker.

OCTN2 (SLC22A5) transports carnitine and acetylcarnitine across cell membranes, the gut, and the blood-brain barrier, but is expressed at lower levels in the brain than other tissues, limiting brain acetylcarnitine transport.
OCT1 (SLC22A1) promotes hepatic efflux of acetylcarnitine, contributing to the plasma acetylcarnitine pool.
Carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase (CACT), located on the inner mitochondrial membrane, mediates exchange of acylcarnitines for carnitine to transport acetylcarnitine across the membrane.

After direct brain injection in animal studies, most acetylcarnitine acetyl groups were rapidly metabolized, with 60% recovered as exhaled CO2 by 22 hours and brain retention declining from 1.9% at 1 hour to 0.9% at 22 hours.
In aged rats, acetylcarnitine treatment further upregulated heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1) protein expression, potentially via the Nrf2 pathway.
Many in vitro studies use acetylcarnitine concentrations exceeding physiological levels by up to 1000-fold, limiting translation of in vitro findings to human supplementation effects.
Acetylcarnitine supplementation improved mental fatigue in an open-label randomized trial in patients with ME/CFS.
In a randomized cross-over trial of 36 MS patients with fatigue, 3 months of acetylcarnitine had a more favourable effect on fatigue severity than amantadine.
In a placebo-controlled randomized trial of 60 people with relapsing-remitting MS, 1 month of acetylcarnitine supplementation showed only a trend-level improvement in fatigue impact on daily life.
Acetylcarnitine treatment has shown benefit in general and senile major depressive disorder patients across multiple studies.
A meta-analysis of twelve RCTs found a significant decrease in depression severity after acetylcarnitine monotherapy compared with placebo or no intervention.

The incidence of adverse effects with acetylcarnitine was comparable to placebo and lower than with antidepressants, and acetylcarnitine has been reported as effective as antidepressants in meta-analyses.
Multiple studies reported mitochondrial abnormalities in skeletal muscle cells of ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
A study reported lower mitochondrial respiration rates and increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species production in immune cells of ME/CFS patients.
Studies in fibromyalgia patients showed reduced mitochondrial ATP production, impaired oxidative phosphorylation, and increased oxidative stress biomarkers in muscle cells.
Emerging research indicates mitochondrial dysfunction in the blood immune cells of COVID-19 patients.
SARS-CoV-2 ORF-9 protein interacts with mitochondrial antiviral signalling proteins (MAVS) to suppress the host innate immune/interferon response.

An open study by Barletta et al. found that supplementation with CoQ10 (200 mg/day) plus alpha-lipoic acid (200 mg/day) for 2 months substantially reduced fatigue severity in 116 chronic COVID-19 patients compared with 58 untreated patients.
A randomised controlled trial of 121 chronic COVID-19 patients supplemented with 500 mg/day CoQ10 for 6 weeks found no significant benefit on the number or severity of post-COVID-19 symptoms.

Fibromyalgia patients have depleted tissue CoQ10 levels, typically 40–50% of normal, along with increased mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress and inflammation in both adults and children/adolescents.

In a randomised controlled trial of 20 fibromyalgia patients, CoQ10 (300 mg/day for 40 days) significantly reduced chronic pain and fatigue by more than 50%, with improved mitochondrial energy generation and reduced oxidative stress, inflammation, and psychopathological symptoms.

Cordero et al. correlated headache symptoms with reduced CoQ10 levels and increased oxidative stress in fibromyalgia patients, and both headache and oxidative stress significantly improved after CoQ10 supplementation (300 mg/day for 3 months).
In adolescent fibromyalgia patients (aged 8-17), CoQ10 supplementation (100 mg/day for 3 months) significantly improved fatigue.
An open-label crossover study found that a water-soluble form of CoQ10 (400 mg/day for 6 months) resulted in significant reductions of 20-40% in chronic fatigue and pain.

A double-blind randomised crossover trial found that adding CoQ10 to pregabalin produced significantly greater reductions in pain and anxiety/depression, plus reduced oxidative stress, inflammation and mitochondrial dysfunction, compared with pregabalin plus placebo, whereas pregabalin alone had no effect on inflammation or mitochondrial function.
An open uncontrolled study of 23 fibromyalgia patients found that CoQ10 (200 mg) plus ginkgo biloba (200 mg) significantly improved health-related quality of life.
A randomised controlled trial in 21 fibromyalgia patients supplemented with CoQ10, vitamin D, alpha-lipoic acid, magnesium, and tryptophan for 3 months found a significant reduction in pain.
CoQ10 intake was associated with a significantly reduced risk of hospitalisation among COVID-19 patients.
A computational study identified CoQ10 as capable of inhibiting SARS-CoV-2 by binding to the active site of the main viral protease.
A study of ~150,000 patients found both hospitalised and non-hospitalised COVID-19 individuals had substantially increased risk of developing heart conditions including myocarditis and heart failure.

A study of 100 COVID-19 patients using PET/myocardial blood flow imaging found infection doubled the risk of unhealthy endothelial cells lining the heart and blood vessels, increasing likelihood of heart failure.
In a study of more than 1000 patients, one in eight individuals hospitalised due to COVID-19 were later diagnosed with myocarditis.

In a randomised controlled trial of 207 ME/CFS patients, supplementation with 200 mg/day CoQ10 plus 20 mg/day NADH for 3 months significantly improved fatigue perception, health-related quality of life, and sleep quality compared with placebo.

In an open-label study, 27 ME/CFS patients supplemented with 400 mg/day CoQ10 and 200 mcg/day selenium for 8 weeks showed significant improvement in overall fatigue severity and global quality of life compared to baseline.

In a randomised controlled trial, 43 ME/CFS patients supplemented with ubiquinol (150 mg/day for 3 months) showed no improvement in perceived fatigue on Chandler's fatigue scale, though several other symptoms such as night-time awakenings improved.

A bioavailability study in 14 healthy individuals found that a crystal-modified ubiquinone CoQ10 formulation (Myoqinon) had the highest bioavailability, while the same CoQ10 material without crystal modification had bioavailability reduced by 75%.
Increased susceptibility to COVID-19 infection in people over 65 years old coincides with the age at which endogenous CoQ10 levels become substantially depleted.
COVID-19 infection may cause virus-induced oxidative stress leading to mutations in genes responsible for CoQ10 biosynthesis, resulting in mitochondrial dysfunction.
Anti-M3 receptor autoantibody levels did not differ significantly between healthy controls and ME/CFS patients across severity groups.
Anti-M4 autoantibody levels were significantly higher in mild, moderate, and severe ME/CFS groups compared with healthy controls, though not increasing monotonically with severity.
Anti-β2AdR autoantibody levels were markedly and significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls across all severity groups.
IL-2 plasma levels showed significant intergroup differences across healthy controls and ME/CFS severity groups.
IL-21 plasma levels showed significant intergroup differences across healthy controls and ME/CFS severity groups.
IL-6 plasma levels showed significant intergroup differences across healthy controls and ME/CFS severity groups.
IL-17A levels differed significantly overall across groups, with only the moderate group significantly different from controls.
Activin-B levels differed significantly overall, with moderate and severe groups significantly different from controls.
IgG4 levels decreased progressively with increasing ME/CFS severity, from mild to moderate to severe.
IgA levels were significantly lower in the severe ME/CFS group compared with healthy controls.
IgM levels rose in mild and moderate ME/CFS compared with controls but fell sharply in the severe group.
IgG3 levels were significantly lower in the severe ME/CFS group compared with controls.
IgG1 levels were significantly lower in the severe ME/CFS group compared with controls.
IgG2 median levels varied non-monotonically across groups (Ctrl, Mild, Moderate, Severe) without a reported statistically significant overall difference.

In the severe ME/CFS group, inflammatome and immunome biomarkers fused into a single positively correlated cluster (IFN-γ, IL-17A, IL-2, IL-21, IL-23, TNF-α, anti-M4, IgM, IgG1, IgG3, IgG4, IgA), whereas these were separate clusters in healthy controls.
Linear discriminant analysis efficiently separated healthy controls from ME/CFS cases overall, but could not distinguish between different severity groups.

Principal component factoring identified three underlying components corresponding to inflammatome, immunome (Ig classes), and receptor biomarkers (anti-M4, anti-β2AdR), with anti-M4 bridging the inflammatome and immunome factors.
Random forest variable importance analysis identified anti-β2AdR as the most relevant biomarker for classifying healthy controls versus ME/CFS cases and severity groups, followed by anti-M4.
High random forest variable importance scores for IgG4 and IL-2 were interpreted as suggestive of an underlying autoimmune process in ME/CFS onset.

The authors present KombOver, a graph-based (k-core and K-truss) computational tool that scales to large metagenomic cohorts and can characterize microbial community dynamics/perturbations from short-read gut microbiome sequencing data.

Applying KombOver's graph-based (k-core/K-truss) analysis to a myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) cohort was informative for pinpointing microbial community dynamics, suggesting detectable gut microbiome perturbations in ME/CFS.

TCR clonotype diversity (Rényi entropy metric) did not significantly differ between people with ME (severe and mild/moderate combined) and healthy controls across CD4+ and CD8+ cells and α/β/γ chains after multiple-testing correction.
TCR clonotype diversity did not significantly differ between ME cases and Multiple Sclerosis (disease control) cases.
TCR clonotype diversity did not significantly differ between severely affected (house/bed-bound) ME patients and mildly/moderately affected ME patients.
CMV seropositivity, assessed in 98 of 160 samples, was not significantly associated with disease group (ME, MS, or healthy control) status.

Among 21 tested variables, donor age (binned by decade) was strongly negatively correlated with MDS x-axis values of the CD8+ TCR chain distance matrix, likely reflecting age-related narrowing of immune repertoire diversity rather than disease status.
MDS y-axis values of the CD8+ chain distance matrix were negatively correlated with the total number of TRB (β-chain) locus coding junctions per sample.
Age group was found to be a significant predictor of CD8+ TREC count, consistent with age-related decline in thymic output.
CD8+ cell number showed an association with sample group in ANOVA, but this did not remain significant after correcting for multiple tests.

Four pairwise group comparisons (out of 54 secondary tests) achieved nominal significance (p<0.05) via permutation testing of P-SVM classifications, but none remained significant after Bonferroni correction.

The P-SVM permutation-testing approach used to detect group differences in TCR repertoire perfectly distinguished simulated sample groups at a 1% p-value threshold, validating the method's sensitivity in principle.

Two patients with Long COVID treated with the Lightning Process, a positive-psychology-based self-management programme, reported improvements in fatigue and a range of physical and emotional symptoms immediately post-treatment and at 3 months follow-up.
In the observation group, physical fatigue, mental fatigue, and total FS-14 scores decreased significantly after acupoint massage at Shenque (CV 8) compared with before treatment.
After treatment, FS-14 scores in the observation group were lower than those in the untreated control group of CFS patients.
In the observation group, most PSQI item scores and the total PSQI score (except sleep time and hypnotic use) decreased after treatment compared with before treatment.
After treatment, each PSQI item score and the total PSQI score in the observation group were lower than those in the control group.
The overall clinical effective rate in the acupoint massage group was superior to that in the untreated control group.
Before treatment, CFS patients with anxiety and depression comorbidity had higher MFI-20 total and subscale scores than healthy controls.
Before treatment, CFS patients had higher SDS (depression), SAS (anxiety), and PSQI (sleep quality) scores than healthy controls.
Mind-regulation electroacupuncture reduced MFI-20 subscale and total scores (except reduced motivation) after treatment compared to before treatment.
The reduced motivation subscale of MFI-20 did not improve significantly after electroacupuncture treatment.
After electroacupuncture treatment, regional homogeneity (ReHo) increased in the right precuneus compared to before treatment.
After electroacupuncture treatment, ReHo decreased in the left inferior temporal gyrus and left angular gyrus compared to before treatment.
Before treatment, CFS patients showed increased ReHo in the left inferior cerebral lobe, the interhemispheric region, the right occipital lobe and the thalamus compared with healthy controls.

Before treatment, CFS patients showed reduced ReHo in the left middle temporal gyrus, right posterior central gyrus, right middle temporal gyrus, right orbital middle frontal gyrus, paracentral lobule and right fusiform gyrus compared with healthy controls.

Before treatment, CFS patients with anxiety and depression comorbidity showed reduced ReHo values in the left middle temporal gyrus, right postcentral gyrus, right middle temporal gyrus, right orbital middle frontal gyrus, paracentral lobule and right fusiform gyrus compared with healthy controls.

Within the observation group, functional connectivity between the right thalamus and the left postcentral gyrus, right hippocampus and right fusiform gyrus was decreased before treatment and partially re-established after electroacupuncture treatment.

Before treatment, functional connectivity between the right thalamus and the left postcentral gyrus, right hippocampus and right fusiform gyrus was reduced in the observation group compared with healthy controls.
After treatment, functional connectivity between the right thalamus and the right hippocampus remained reduced in the observation group compared with the control group.
