ReHo values in the left middle temporal gyrus, paracentral lobule, right precuneus and left inferior temporal gyrus showed a partial positive correlation with clinical scale scores (MFI-20, SAS, SDS, PSQI).
ReHo values in the interhemispheric region, thalamus, right fusiform gyrus and right middle temporal gyrus showed a partial negative correlation with clinical scale scores (MFI-20, SAS, SDS, PSQI).

EDS is an umbrella term for 14 types, of which 13 are rare and monogenic, sharing overlapping features of joint hypermobility, skin and vascular fragility, and generalised connective tissue friability, while hypermobile EDS lacks an identified genetic cause.
Hypermobile EDS currently has no identified genetic cause, distinguishing it from the other 13 monogenic EDS types.
Most of the rare monogenic EDS types can present with neurological features, which are often part of the major or minor diagnostic criteria for each specific type.

The different EDS types have distinct clinical features, genetic causes, and pathogenic mechanisms, each requiring bespoke management and surveillance, so defining the specific EDS type is crucial since 'EDS' alone is not a diagnosis.

In four EDS patients treated with adjuvant conventional or hypofractionated breast radiation therapy, no increase in acute or late radiation toxicity was observed over a median follow-up of 13.2 months.
All four EDS patients experienced grade 1 radiation dermatitis as an acute toxicity following breast radiation therapy, with no cases of grade 2 or higher.

A prior case report by Holodny et al. described a patient with EDS who developed severe grade 3 pericarditis, pleuritis, and mediastinitis during post-mastectomy radiation therapy, requiring treatment discontinuation at 10Gy, and later died of a ruptured basilar artery aneurysm.
An in vitro study by Aghajanyan et al. found increased radiation-induced chromosomal aberrations in irradiated lymphocytes from children with EDS compared to control subjects.

A heterozygous de novo missense variant in COL3A1, c.146C>T (p.Pro49Leu), was identified by trio whole-exome sequencing as the likely pathogenic cause of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in the proband and was also found in his affected son but not in his parents or sister.

The proband presented with multiple arterial aneurysms and dissections (bilateral internal carotid, vertebral, celiac trunk, hepatic, splenic, and renal arteries), ulnar artery rupture, non-traumatic ecchymoses, joint hypermobility, and characteristic slender build, ultimately dying from arterial rupture and hemorrhagic shock.

The proband's 3-year-4-month-old son, who carries the same COL3A1 variant, exhibited mild early-onset symptoms including short stature, low body weight, skin pigmentation, deep palm prints, poor wound healing, and occasional gastrointestinal bleeding (blood in stools), suggesting early childhood manifestation of vEDS complications rarely reported in the literature.

A literature review of published cases identified three non-glycine missense COL3A1 variants (c.1351G>A p.(Glu451Lys), c.2791G>A p.(Glu931Lys), c.3511G>A p.(Glu1171Lys)) that were associated with digestive tract symptoms, contradicting a prior review's claim that gastrointestinal events in vEDS arise only from glycine substitutions, splicing variants, and in-frame indels, not non-glycine missense variants.

Approximately two-thirds of published genetically diagnosed vEDS cases are caused by point mutations at glycine residues, which destabilize the collagen triple helix and, in related collagen genes (COL1A1, COL2A1, COL7A1), have been reported to cause more severe disease than other single-amino-acid mutations.

Epidemiological data cited indicate that 25% of vEDS patients have their first symptom by age 20 and over 80% have at least one symptom by age 40, with median age at first major vascular event of 24.6 years and median age at death of 48 years.

A previously reported variant, c.145C>G p.(Pro49Ala), affecting the same residue as the proband's variant, has been found homozygous in at least four patients with an autosomal recessive disorder (polymicrogyria with or without vascular-type EDS, OMIM 618343), but evidence supporting its pathogenicity specifically for vEDS was insufficient, so the PM5 criterion was not applied to the proband's variant.
Genetic testing identified a heterozygous pathogenic splice-site variant in COL3A1 (c.582+1G>C), confirming a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Vessel-wall MRI showed fusiform aneurysmal dilatation and stenosis of both vertebral arteries and eccentric stenosis of the left proximal posterior cerebral artery, consistent with dissecting aneurysms attributable to vascular EDS-related arterial fragility.

The patient had persistently elevated anticardiolipin IgG and anti-β2-glycoprotein I IgG antibodies at initial presentation and again at 3-month follow-up, meeting criteria for a definitive diagnosis of antiphospholipid syndrome co-occurring with EDS.

Because full anticoagulation carries bleeding/rupture risk in EDS while APS guidelines recommend anticoagulation, clinicians chose aspirin monotherapy, and the patient had no recurrent embolic or vascular rupture events over 1 year of follow-up.

The authors cite prior observations of elevated inflammatory markers, including transforming growth factor-β and interleukin-8, in individuals with EDS, proposed to contribute to tissue fragility and mechanical stress on blood vessels.

The patient exhibited dissociated sensory loss with 50% reduction in pain and temperature sensation in the right arm and leg but intact vibration and proprioception, localizing the lesion to the spinothalamic pathway following left thalamic/occipital infarction.
A patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and intestinal pseudo-obstruction was successfully treated with linaclotide for ten years, with sustained symptomatic benefit.
Two related patients studied were found to be heterozygous for the pathogenic COL3A1 p.G588S variant (c.1762G>A), located in coding exon 25, causing vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Global proteomic profiling of vEDS versus normal fibroblasts identified 1685 proteins with statistically significant expression changes out of 4980 proteins detected.
Protein family analysis identified 64 ECM family proteins with statistically significant changes between vEDS and normal fibroblasts.

Among the top 10 significantly changed ECM proteins, COL8A1 (basement membrane component), COL12A1 (fibril-associated collagen), and COL2A1 (fibral collagen) were upregulated in vEDS fibroblasts compared to normal.
COL5A1 and COL5A2, genes associated with classical (hypermobility-related) Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, were both upregulated in vEDS fibroblasts, suggesting overlapping function with COL3A1.
TIMP1, ADAMTSL4, THSD4, and SERPINE2, proteins involved in inhibition of matrix proteases, were downregulated in vEDS fibroblasts versus normal.
The profibrotic factor WNT5A was upregulated in vEDS fibroblasts compared to normal fibroblasts.
TGFBR3, a TGFβ decoy receptor, was downregulated in vEDS fibroblasts versus normal fibroblasts.
MMP-1 mRNA was significantly upregulated approximately 7-fold in vEDS fibroblasts compared to normal fibroblasts, consistent with increased protein levels.

Collagen III protein was increased in vEDS fibroblast cell lysates compared to normal fibroblasts but was below quantifiable limit in conditioned culture media, suggesting intracellular retention of mutant/misfolded Collagen III.
COL3A1 gene expression by qPCR array did not differ significantly between vEDS and normal fibroblasts, despite increased Collagen III protein.
Fibronectin was increased in vEDS fibroblasts as measured by proteomics, mRNA expression, and quantitative ELISA.
LOXL2 protein was increased in vEDS fibroblast media compared to normal fibroblast media, as measured by LC/MS and ELISA.
LOX enzymatic activity, measured with a fluorogenic substrate, was increased in vEDS fibroblast media compared to normal fibroblasts.
Treatment of fibroblasts with recombinant TGFβ was used to upregulate LOXL2 protein and LOX activity, supporting a mechanistic link between TGFβ signaling and collagen cross-linking enzymes.

Cross-linked C-Telopeptide of Type III collagen (CTXIII) was significantly increased in vEDS fibroblast conditioned media compared to normal fibroblasts, consistent with increased LOX-mediated collagen cross-linking.
The irreversible LOX inhibitor BAPN reduced LOX activity and reduced CTXIII levels in treated vEDS fibroblasts, supporting LOX as a therapeutic target.
TGFβ has been reported elevated in plasma from vEDS subjects in prior literature, supporting a role in vEDS pathogenesis via upregulation of LOX enzymes, collagens, and fibronectin.

In a transgenic vEDS mouse study cited by the authors, celiprolol accelerated rather than reduced death from aortic rupture in both severe (Col3a1 G938D/+) and mild (Col3a1 G209S/+) vEDS mouse models, despite achieving the predicted heart-rate effect.
Losartan, propranolol, atenolol, and amlodipine did not rescue death from aortic rupture in the vEDS transgenic mouse models cited by the authors.
Prior studies cited in this paper report that COL3A1 mutations altering glycine residues correlate with more severe vEDS disease manifestations.

Prior studies cited indicate that individuals with COL3A1 deletion (null) mutations have less severe vEDS manifestations because the non-mutant allele can partially compensate, albeit with reduced Collagen III fibers.

A cited cohort study of over 200 confirmed vEDS individuals found that only 25% had a first complication by age 20, more than 80% had at least one complication by age 40, and the calculated median survival of the cohort was 48 years, with most deaths due to arterial rupture.
A 23-week fetus with a 6q25.1 (TAB2) deletion presented with cardiomegaly, redundant myxomatous tricuspid and mitral valve leaflets, thickened pulmonary valve, and bicuspid aortic valve.

6q25.1 (TAB2) deletion is noted as one of the notable genetic causes of myxomatous degeneration of cardiac valves, alongside conditions such as trisomy 18, Noonan, Marfan, and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes.
The authors recommend that whole exome sequencing be considered in similar cases of myxomatous cardiac valve degeneration to enable effective prenatal genetic counselling.
Occipito-cervical fusion (OCF) was associated with a significant reduction in headache and neck pain severity from a preoperative mean of 4.3/5 to a postoperative mean of 3.3/5.
There was no significant difference in pain improvement after OCF between patients with CSF flow obstruction (Chiari malformation/low-lying tonsils) and those without.
Functional status measured by the Karnofsky Performance Scale improved significantly after OCF, from a median of 50 preoperatively to 60 postoperatively.
Orthostatic symptoms, measured by the Orthostatic Grading Scale, significantly improved in frequency, severity, and standing time after OCF.
Mental fatigue and cognitive symptoms ("brain fog") measured by the Wood Mental Fatigue Inventory significantly improved after OCF, from a median score of 23 to 18.
Intraoperative open reduction significantly corrected the kyphotic clival axial angle (CXA) from a pathological mean to within the normal range.
Ventral brainstem compression, measured by the pBC2 (Grabb-Oakes) metric, was significantly reduced from a pathological preoperative mean to a normal postoperative mean.
Syncope and presyncope symptoms significantly improved after OCF.
Fatigue severity significantly improved after OCF, from a mean of 4.3 to 3.7.
POTS was a highly prevalent comorbid condition among adults with EDS and craniocervical instability, present in 58% of the surgical cohort.
Mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) was a highly prevalent comorbid condition, present in 45% of the surgical EDS/CCI cohort.
Migraine was a common comorbid condition, present in 28% of the surgical EDS/CCI cohort.
Chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) was present in 15% of the surgical EDS/CCI cohort.
Fibromyalgia was present in 15% of the surgical EDS/CCI cohort.
Autonomic neuropathy was documented in 11% of the surgical EDS/CCI cohort, and small-fiber/peripheral neuropathy in 9%.
IBS was documented in 13% of the surgical EDS/CCI cohort as part of a high overall gastrointestinal comorbidity burden (53%).

Atlantoaxial instability (AAI), characterized by excessive rotational subluxation/lateral translation and >80% facet overlap loss with preserved atlanto-dental interval, was present in the majority of surgical patients and was frequently a key factor in the decision to proceed with OCF.
The mean basion-axis interval (BAI, Harris Measurement) in this EDS surgical cohort was 11 mm, consistent with prior reports in patients with 'complex Chiari' who benefited from OCF.
Wound dehiscence requiring re-operation occurred in 4 of 53 patients (2-4 weeks postoperatively), a recognized complication attributed to slow wound healing and skin fragility in EDS.

The large majority of patients reported satisfaction with OCF surgery, with 94% stating they would repeat it, though only 75% reported overall global quality-of-life improvement given the high comorbidity burden.

Chiari malformation/low-lying cerebellar tonsils with CSF flow obstruction was common in this EDS/CCI cohort (60%), and was treated with limited suboccipital decompression at the time of OCF, without added intraoperative complication.
Tethered cord syndrome was the single most common comorbid neurospinal condition, present in nearly half of the EDS/CCI surgical cohort.
Connective tissue diseases including Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome are cited as recognized predisposing factors for spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD).
In this patient with extensive SCAD and a Marfanoid appearance, genetic testing for connective tissue disorders (including Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) was negative.

The authors report an asymptomatic 33-year-old man with prior Hodgkin's lymphoma treated with chemoradiotherapy who was incidentally found on angiography (before planned PFO closure) to have spontaneous coronary artery dissection involving the left main and all three major coronary arteries, described as the first reported case of this extent that was asymptomatic.
Coronary artery tortuosity on angiography is more common in SCAD patients than controls and severe tortuosity is a marker for recurrent SCAD events.
Chemotherapy agents such as cisplatin and capecitabine (5-fluorouracil) can cause vasospasm and oxidative stress that may predispose to SCAD even without other coronary risk factors.
The left anterior descending artery is the most frequently affected vessel in SCAD (about 60% of cases), followed by RCA and LM, with multivessel dissection occurring in 20-25% of cases.
Beta-blocker use is significantly associated with reduced risk of recurrent SCAD, whereas hypertension is associated with increased risk of recurrence.

The patient was managed conservatively with antiplatelets, anti-lipid therapy, a beta-blocker, and citalopram; at 3-month follow-up CT angiography showed no progression of coronary lesions, and he remained asymptomatic through 12 months of follow-up.
General joint hypermobility (GJH) was over-represented in this TMJ surgical cohort (25%) compared to reported general adult European population prevalence of 5-15%.
All patients in the GJH group were women, a significantly higher female proportion than in the NJM group.
GJH patients were significantly younger than NJM patients at the time of TMJ surgery.
Preoperative TMJ disability (VAS) was significantly higher in GJH patients compared to NJM patients.
Preoperative maximum interincisal opening (MIO) was higher in GJH patients but the difference versus NJM patients was not statistically significant.
Surgical outcome at six-month follow-up did not differ significantly between GJH and NJM patients, refuting the hypothesis that GJH predicts inferior outcome.
Synovial tissue FAP-α (fibroblast activation protein alpha) concentration was significantly higher in GJH patients compared to NJM patients on univariate analysis.
Synovial tissue OPG concentration was significantly higher in GJH patients compared to NJM patients on univariate analysis, but this association did not persist after multivariate adjustment.
Synovial tissue TIMP-3 concentration was significantly lower in GJH patients (higher in NJM patients) on univariate analysis, and also differed significantly by sex.
In multivariate quantile regression adjusting for age, sex, and TMJ diagnosis, none of the 28 analysed ECM/ECM-turnover proteins correlated significantly with joint mobility status (GJH vs NJM).
TMJ diagnosis (e.g., disc displacement without reduction vs with reduction) showed strong correlation with protein profile changes in 20 of 28 analysed proteins, more than joint mobility status.

In a subgroup analysis restricted to patients aged 18-29 (to control for age-related under-scoring of hypermobility), no significant differences in any of the 28 ECM proteins were found between GJH and NJM patients.
Only one GJH patient in the cohort had a formally diagnosed connective tissue disorder (Ehlers-Danlos syndrome), and this patient had a good surgical outcome.
OVA-sensitized allergic mice showed increased serum levels of mucosal mast cell protease 1 (mMCP1), a marker of mucosal mast cell degranulation, compared to non-allergic sham mice.

Mice fed a 0.5% 2'FL supplemented diet had significantly lower serum mMCP1 levels than OVA-allergic mice on control diet, reaching levels comparable to non-allergic mice, despite no reduction in clinical allergy symptoms.
Lower serum mMCP1 levels showed a non-significant trend toward correlating with reduced acute allergic skin response (ear swelling).

Mice receiving a 0.5% 2'FL supplemented diet had significantly higher total cecal SCFA levels (acetate, propionate, butyrate, iso-butyrate, valeric acid, iso-valeric acid) than OVA-allergic mice on control diet.
Mice receiving a 0.1% 3FL diet showed a non-significant trend toward lower total cecal SCFA levels compared to OVA-allergic mice on control diet.
Mice receiving a 0.1% 2'FL diet had higher cecal acetate and butyrate levels than mice receiving a 0.1% 3FL diet.
Mice receiving 0.5% HMO supplemented diets (2'FL or 3FL) had higher cecal propionate levels compared to lower-dose groups.
Mice receiving a 0.1% 2'FL supplemented diet had significantly lower serum OVA-specific IgG2a compared to OVA-allergic mice on control diet.
Mice receiving a 0.5% 3FL diet showed a non-significant trend toward higher serum OVA-specific IgG1 compared to OVA-allergic mice on control diet.
Neither 2'FL nor 3FL supplemented diets significantly affected anaphylactic shock symptoms or serum OVA-specific IgE levels compared to OVA-allergic mice on control diet.

Mesenteric lymph nodes from mice receiving a 0.5% 3FL diet showed a lower percentage of total and activated Th2 cells and a minor but significant increase in Treg population compared to OVA-allergic mice on control diet.
OVA-allergic mice had an increased proportion of Th2 and activated Th2 cells in mesenteric lymph nodes compared to sham mice, while Th1, Th17, and Treg proportions were unaffected.
Combined butyrate and 3FL exposure of intestinal epithelial cells significantly enhanced relative RALDH mRNA expression compared to control cells, an effect not seen with either compound alone.
Combining butyrate with 2'FL pre-incubation of IEC led to a tendency toward decreased IL12p70 and increased IL6 secretion by dendritic cells cocultured with these IEC, compared to butyrate alone.
3FL exposure alone inhibited IL12p70 secretion by dendritic cells cocultured with pre-exposed IEC, an effect that remained stable when combined with butyrate.
Combined butyrate and 3FL exposure of IEC reduced regulatory IL10 secretion in the IEC/dendritic cell coculture compared to control.

Dendritic cells primed by 2'FL-exposed IEC enhanced T cell IL13 secretion, whereas dendritic cells primed by 3FL-exposed IEC instead enhanced T cell IFNγ, IL17, and IL10 secretion, indicating divergent, isomer-specific downstream T helper skewing.

Adding butyrate to 2'FL preserved the increase in T cell IL13 secretion and additionally increased IFNγ and IL10; butyrate combined with 3FL preserved elevated IFNγ and IL10 (trend p=0.0534) while keeping IL17 low, compared to control and butyrate alone.
Butyrate pre-incubation of IEC tended to prevent OVA-induced TSLP release, though this did not reach statistical significance.
2'FL pre-incubation alone increased RALDH mRNA in OVA-stimulated IEC, but this increase was prevented when combined with butyrate.
OVA-allergic mice showed significant anaphylactic shock symptoms and ear swelling 1 hour after intradermal OVA challenge compared to sham mice.
Dietary supplementation with 2'FL or 3FL did not impact allergic shock symptoms or OVA-specific IgE levels compared to OVA control diet.
Mice receiving a 0.5% 3FL supplemented diet showed a trend toward higher OVA-specific IgG1 levels compared to OVA-allergic mice on control diet.
Mice receiving a 0.1% 2'FL supplemented diet showed significantly lower OVA-specific IgG2a levels compared to mice receiving control diet.
The proportion of Th2 and activated Th2 cells in mesenteric lymph nodes was enhanced in OVA-allergic mice compared to sham, while Th1, Th17, and Treg percentages were unaffected.

Mice receiving 0.5% 3FL diet had a lower percentage of Th2 and activated Th2 cells and a minor but significant increase in Tregs in mesenteric lymph nodes compared to OVA-allergic mice on control diet.
Serum mMCP1, a marker of mucosal mast cell degranulation, was increased in OVA-allergic mice compared to sham mice.
Mice fed a 0.5% 2'FL diet had significantly lower serum mMCP1 levels, reaching levels seen in non-allergic mice, despite no effect on allergy symptoms.

Mice receiving 0.5% 2'FL diet had significantly higher total SCFA levels (including acetate, propionate, butyrate, iso-butyrate, valeric acid, iso-valeric acid) in cecum content compared to OVA control mice.
Mice receiving 0.1% 3FL diet showed a trend toward lower total cecal SCFA levels compared to OVA-allergic mice on control diet.
Mice receiving 0.1% 2'FL diet had higher cecal acetate and butyrate levels than mice receiving 0.1% 3FL diet.
Mice receiving 0.5% supplemented diets (2'FL or 3FL) showed higher cecal propionate levels.
Lower serum mMCP1 levels tended to correlate with fewer clinical symptoms measured by acute skin response, but this correlation was not statistically significant.
Butyrate pre-incubation of IEC tended to prevent OVA-mediated TSLP release, though this did not reach statistical significance.
2'FL pre-incubation alone enhanced RALDH mRNA levels in OVA-exposed IEC, but this enhancement was prevented when butyrate was combined with 2'FL.
3FL pre-incubation lowered IL12p70 secretion in OVA-IEC/DC cultures compared to control, an effect also seen without OVA, and combined 2'FL+butyrate produced a similarly lower IL12p70 level.
Combined butyrate and 3FL pre-incubation significantly enhanced IL6 and TGFβ secretion in OVA-IEC/DC cultures, an effect not seen with either compound alone.
IL10 secretion was significantly enhanced only in but-2'FL-OVA-IEC/DC cocultures compared to OVA-IEC/DC, an effect not observed without OVA or without butyrate.
3FL pre-incubation prevented OVA-IEC/DC-mediated IL13 secretion by T cells, an effect maintained in the presence of butyrate.
IL17 levels were enhanced by 2'FL and 3FL pre-incubation in OVA-IEC/DC/T cell cultures, and this enhancement remained significant when combined with butyrate.
3FL-OVA-IEC/DC/T cells showed significantly enhanced IL10, but this increase was lost when butyrate was combined with 3FL pre-incubation.
The review estimates that food intolerances account for approximately 30-40% of IBS-D cases.
Bile acid diarrhea is estimated to explain approximately 20-30% of IBS-D cases.
Disturbed microbial flora is estimated to account for approximately 15-20% of IBS-D cases.
Mastocytosis/mast cell activation is noted as a less frequent condition that can cause IBS-like symptoms or be confused with IBS-D.
Oral administration of valerate ameliorated passive systemic anaphylaxis and passive cutaneous anaphylaxis in mice.
Oral administration of butyrate ameliorated passive systemic anaphylaxis and passive cutaneous anaphylaxis in mice.
Propionate, butyrate, valerate, and isovalerate suppressed IgE-mediated degranulation of bone marrow-derived mast cells in vitro.

SCFA-mediated suppression of mast cell degranulation was abolished by Gi protein inhibition (pertussis toxin) and by knockdown of Gpr109a, indicating GPR109A/Gi signaling is required for the SCFA effect.
The HDAC inhibitor trichostatin A suppressed IgE-mediated mast cell activation and reduced surface expression of FcεRI on mast cells, implicating epigenetic regulation in SCFA effects.
Acetylsalicylic acid and indomethacin (COX inhibitors) attenuated the suppressive effects of SCFAs on mast cell degranulation, indicating a COX-dependent mechanism.
Mast cell degranulation was significantly reduced by PGE2 treatment but not by PGD2.
PGD2 treatment did not significantly reduce mast cell degranulation, unlike PGE2.
Pertussis toxin, a Gi protein inhibitor, abolished the suppressive effect of SCFAs on IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation, implicating Gi-coupled receptor signaling.
Knockdown of Gpr109a eliminated the suppressive effect of SCFAs on IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation, confirming GPR109A as the receptor mediating this effect.
The HDAC inhibitor trichostatin A suppressed IgE-mediated mast cell activation, suggesting an epigenetic regulatory mechanism analogous to SCFA action.
Trichostatin A reduced the surface expression level of FcεRI on mast cells, linking HDAC inhibition to reduced IgE receptor expression.
Acetylsalicylic acid attenuated the suppressive effects of SCFAs on mast cell degranulation, implicating COX activity/prostaglandin production in the SCFA mechanism.
Indomethacin attenuated the suppressive effects of SCFAs on mast cell degranulation, consistent with a COX-dependent mechanism.
PGE2 significantly reduced mast cell degranulation, whereas PGD2 had no such effect.
Unlike PGE2, PGD2 did not significantly reduce IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation.
Short-chain fatty acids enhanced the release of PGE2 from IgE-stimulated mast cells.
COX inhibitors reversed and exacerbated anaphylaxis despite SCFA treatment, indicating COX activity is required for the SCFA-mediated protective effect.
An EP3 receptor antagonist exacerbated anaphylaxis despite SCFA treatment, implicating EP3 signaling in the protective mechanism.
In contrast to the EP3 antagonist, an EP4 receptor antagonist did not affect the SCFA-mediated amelioration of anaphylaxis.
Administration of niacin, a GPR109A ligand, alleviated the symptoms of passive cutaneous anaphylaxis in mice.
The protective effect of niacin on passive cutaneous anaphylaxis was blocked by cyclooxygenase inhibitors.
The protective effect of niacin on passive cutaneous anaphylaxis was blocked by an EP3 antagonist.
AnxA1-deficient mice with LPS-induced endometritis showed significantly more degranulated mast cells than AnxA1-deficient sham mice.
Lack of AnxA1 promoted upregulation of NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β protein levels in acute endometritis compared to wild-type LPS animals.
LPS-induced endometritis increased peripheral blood leukocyte counts in both wild-type and AnxA1-/- mice compared with sham mice.
AnxA1-/- mice showed significantly increased plasma IL-1β levels following LPS-induced endometritis.
AnxA1-/- mice showed significantly increased plasma IL-6, IL-10, IL-17, and TNF-α levels following LPS-induced endometritis compared with wild-type animals.
Endometrium inflammatory scores were significantly increased in the LPS-treated group compared to sham.
Solar urticaria skin biopsies showed early and marked neutrophil infiltration after solar-simulated UV exposure, which was not seen in healthy controls.
IL20 gene expression was upregulated in solar urticaria skin following UV exposure.
IL6 gene expression was upregulated in solar urticaria skin following UV exposure.
CXCL8 (IL-8) gene expression was upregulated in solar urticaria skin and was identified as a transcript unique to solar urticaria compared with chronic spontaneous urticaria datasets.
CSF2/3 transcripts were identified as unique to solar urticaria when compared with chronic spontaneous urticaria transcriptomic datasets.
TNF was identified as an upstream regulator of the gene expression changes seen in solar urticaria skin after UV exposure.
IL-1β was identified as an upstream regulator of the gene expression changes seen in solar urticaria skin after UV exposure.
IFN-γ was identified as an upstream regulator of the gene expression changes seen in solar urticaria skin after UV exposure.
IgE and its high-affinity receptor FcεRI were identified as upstream regulators of the transcriptomic changes in solar urticaria, indicating FcεRI engagement as an early event.
FcεRI was identified as an upstream regulator in solar urticaria skin following SSR exposure, implicating IgE-receptor engagement in early mast cell activation.
Phosphorylated STAT3 expression in mast cells was increased in solar urticaria skin at 30 minutes and 3 hours after SSR exposure, indicating rapid mast cell activation.
Clinical resolution of solar urticaria symptoms by 24 hours after SSR exposure corresponded with resolution of the inflammatory gene expression signature.
Comparison of solar urticaria transcriptomic data with existing chronic spontaneous urticaria datasets showed overlapping immune activation signatures.
CXCL8 and CSF2/CSF3 transcripts were identified as unique to solar urticaria and not shared with chronic spontaneous urticaria datasets.
Total mast cell infiltration (by CIBERSORT deconvolution) was lower in breast cancer tissue compared with adjacent normal breast tissue.
Eosinophil infiltration was lower in breast cancer tissue than in normal breast tissue.
Follicular helper T cell infiltration was higher in breast cancer tissue than in normal breast tissue.
Regulatory T cell infiltration was higher in breast cancer tissue than in normal breast tissue.
Macrophage M0 infiltration was higher in breast cancer tissue than in normal breast tissue.
Among the 22 immune cell subtypes examined, macrophage M1 showed the strongest (negative) correlation with activated dendritic cells in breast cancer tissue.
High infiltration of resting (dormant) mast cells was associated with better overall survival in breast cancer patients compared with low infiltration.
High infiltration of activated mast cells was associated with worse overall survival in breast cancer patients compared with low infiltration.
High macrophage M0 infiltration was associated with worse overall survival and was confirmed as an independent risk factor in both univariate and multivariate Cox regression.
Resting mast cells were confirmed as an independent protective prognostic factor for breast cancer in multivariate Cox regression, after adjustment for other variables.
Resting mast cells and activated mast cells were negatively correlated with each other in breast cancer tissue, suggesting a reciprocal relationship between the two states.
The EMT marker DDR2 was positively correlated with resting mast cell infiltration and negatively correlated with activated mast cell infiltration in breast cancer tissue.
The EMT marker CDH1 (E-cadherin) was positively correlated with resting mast cell infiltration and negatively correlated with activated mast cell infiltration in breast cancer tissue.
DDR2 expression was negatively correlated with macrophage M0 infiltration in breast cancer tissue.

The cancer stem cell marker Nanog was positively correlated with resting mast cell infiltration, and negatively correlated with activated mast cell infiltration and macrophage M0 infiltration in breast cancer tissue.

The authors hypothesize, based on prior literature, that activated mast cells may promote tumor invasion and migration via histamine secretion, and that resting mast cells may be protective in breast cancer by limiting histamine release.

Citing prior work, the authors note macrophage M0 distribution in breast cancer tissue is positively correlated with VEGF and microvessel density (MVD), potentially promoting tumor progression via angiogenesis, and that M0 may reduce chemosensitivity via IL-10 production.

High macrophage M2 infiltration was associated with better survival in Kaplan-Meier analysis, but this association was not confirmed in univariate or multivariate Cox regression, and the authors caution against drawing firm conclusions.
The overall ratio of headaches did not significantly differ between rosacea patients and controls.
Migraine-type headaches were more common in rosacea patients than in controls.
Among rosacea patients with migraine, 61% had migraine without aura, 37% had migraine with aura, and 2% had menstrual migraine.
Rosacea severity was positively correlated with migraine severity.
Headache prevalence was higher among rosacea patients with the predominant ETR subtype compared to PPR and RhR subtypes.
Migraine and secondary-type headaches (STHs) were more frequent in the predominant ETR subtype, while tension-type headaches (TTHs) were more frequent in the predominant phymatous (RhR) subtype.
Rosacea patients with headaches were younger and had higher ratios of female sex and peptic ulcer compared to those without headaches.
Burning, stinging, and itching symptoms of rosacea were more prevalent in patients with headaches than those without.
The proportion of patients with moderate and severe rosacea was higher among those with headaches than those without.
Among rosacea triggering factors, only sunlight exposure was found to be associated with headache occurrence.
Patients with secondary-type headaches were older on average than those with other headache types.
Burning, stinging, itching, and facial edematous symptoms, as well as severe rosacea, were more common in patients with migraine-type headache compared to other headache types.
Stress was more frequently reported as a trigger in the TTH group, coffee/menstruation/cheese in the migraine group, and hypertension in the STH group.
Stress, alcohol, coffee, and menstruation were identified as common triggering factors shared by both rosacea and headaches.
Multivariable logistic regression identified lower age, female gender, and moderate-to-severe rosacea severity as independent predictors of increased headache likelihood in rosacea patients.
Prior literature cited in the discussion reports that mast cell counts are raised in all predominant subtypes of rosacea, especially the papulopustular (PPR) subtype, from early disease onset.
Prior literature indicates mast cells contribute to rosacea inflammation by producing LL-37 and matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9).

Prior literature reports activation of the Th17 pathway and increased IL-17 in rosacea, associated with inflammation, angiogenesis, and stimulation of LL-37/MMP-9, and that IL-17/MMP activity is also increased in migraine independent of aura.

Prior literature indicates rosacea patients show increased density of TRPV receptors and a lower stimulation threshold, located in dermal nerve endings, trigeminal ganglion, and scalp arteries, suggesting therapeutic relevance for both rosacea and migraine.
In a retrospective review of an SFN clinic, 53.9% of patients had a physician-diagnosed functional gastrointestinal disorder before their SFN diagnosis.
SFN patients with and without a prior FGID diagnosis did not differ in gender, age, topographical distribution of neuropathic symptoms, or rate of positive autoimmune blood tests.
Among SFN patients with GI symptoms, 41.6% carried a formal diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome, making IBS the most common FGID in this population.
Functional constipation was the second most common FGID among SFN patients with GI symptoms, present in 30.6%.
Functional dysphagia and dyspepsia was the third most common FGID among SFN patients with GI symptoms, present in 13.9%.
A previously published study cited in this letter reported that 49% of fibromyalgia patients also had small fiber neuropathy.
A previously published study cited in this letter reported that 30% of chronic fatigue syndrome patients had definite small fiber neuropathy.

The authors propose that SFN causes IBS-like GI symptoms through involvement of the autonomic and enteric nervous systems, producing GI dysautonomia with bloating, constipation, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting.
Skin biopsy for intra-epidermal nerve fiber density, the gold-standard diagnostic test for SFN, confirmed most of the SFN diagnoses in this cohort as definite.
Serum neurofilament light chain (sNfL) levels did not differ between patients with SFN and healthy controls.
sNfL levels showed a strong positive correlation with age in both the SFN patient group and the healthy control group.
Both proximal and distal intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) were significantly lower in SFN patients compared to healthy controls.
Quantitative sensory testing revealed predominant loss of thermal perception (cold detection threshold, warm detection threshold, thermal sensory limen) in SFN patients relative to controls.
Sural nerve conduction studies (SNAP and NCV) did not differ between SFN patients and healthy controls, confirming absence of large fiber neuropathy.

In SFN patients, sNfL levels correlated negatively with sural nerve SNAP even though SNAP values were within the normal range, suggesting subtle preclinical large fiber involvement, whereas no such correlation was seen in healthy controls.

The authors note that a prior study found increased plasma phosphorylated neurofilament heavy chain (NfH) in patients with diabetic SFN who also had significantly lower sural SNAP compared to controls, contrasting with the current study's null sNfL and sural SNAP findings.
Across all SFN patients, widespread frontal brain regions showed reduced gray matter volume compared to healthy controls.
Both whole-brain and region-based analyses showed reduced gray matter volume in the left caudate of SFN patients compared to controls.
SFN patients showed reduced gray matter volume in the insula relative to healthy controls.
SFN patients showed reduced gray matter volume in the superior parietal lobule relative to healthy controls.
Surface-based morphometry revealed reduced cortical thickness in the right precentral gyrus of SFN patients compared to controls.

In a homogeneous subsample of SFN patients carrying rare heterozygous missense variants in voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav), whole-brain and region-based analyses revealed gray matter volume reductions in the bilateral caudate.
Total activity-dependent slowing (ADStotal) of CMi-fibers was similar across SFN patients with pain, without pain, and healthy controls.

Normalization of latency after high-frequency stimulation was significantly faster (i.e., relative hyperexcitability) in SFN patients with pain compared to healthy controls, with a similar but non-significant trend versus non-pain patients.
Non-pain SFN patients showed normalization of latency nearly identical to healthy subjects, distinct from pain patients.

In the computational model, increasing Na-K-pump rate speeds normalization of latency but simultaneously alters ADS substantially, so this single-parameter change alone could not reproduce the patient phenotype.
Model simulations showed that Kdr conductance, alongside Na-K-pump rate and RMP, most strongly affects ADStotal, with increased Kdr conductance increasing ADS.
Despite being a large persistent sodium current, Nav1.9 conductance was found not to influence ADS under the low-frequency stimulation protocol used.
Na-K-pump rate, the h current, and RMP were identified as the mechanisms with the most pronounced influence on normalization of latency in the model.
Different potassium channel subtypes had opposing effects on normalization of latency: reducing Ks conductance slowed normalization while reducing KNa conductance sped it up.

The best-fitting model combination reproducing unchanged ADS with faster normalization, matching SFN pain patients, was a 50% reduction in h conductance combined with a 37.5% increase in Kdr conductance.
A previously unknown parameter combination — increased Na-K-pump rate by 37.5% plus increased Kdr conductance by 50% — was discovered via grid search to also reproduce the SFN pain phenotype.

Based on prior evidence of depolarized RMP and reduced Na-K-pump function in diabetic neuropathy, the authors favor a combination of depolarized RMP, decreased Na-K-pump rate (-25%), and increased Kdr conductance (+50%) as the most biologically plausible mechanism underlying SFN pain.
Grid search analysis showed Nav1.7 and Kf channel conductance had negligible effect on ADS or normalization of latency and could be excluded from the optimal parameter combinations.

A computational C-fiber model with a 1 μm axon diameter best reproduced the electrically-stimulated conduction velocity changes of healthy human CMi-fibers, validating the model against microneurography data.
A gain-of-function Nav1.7 I848T mutation in an erythromelalgia patient caused frequency-dependent speeding of conduction velocity rather than the normal slowing seen in healthy controls.
An erythromelalgia patient with a Nav1.8 mutation exhibited exaggerated activity-dependent slowing.
Healthy elderly volunteers showed more activity-dependent slowing and slower normalization of latency than younger subjects, mirroring the effect of reduced Na-K-pump rate in the model.

In the original smaller cohort (Kleggetveit et al., 2012), ADS was similar between pain and non-pain SFN patients but normalization of latency was significantly faster in patients with pain, forming the basis for this study's model targets.

Reduced function of some Kdr channels is associated with less mechanical and heat pain in prior literature; the authors speculate the converse (increased Kdr conductance) may be associated with more pain via the mechanisms identified in their model.

Rodent studies cited show that blocking the h current (Ih) reduces discharge frequency and pain behavior/mechanical hyperalgesia, though other studies suggest opposite effects depending on RMP, consistent with the model's finding that RMP determines the direction of h's contribution.
Laser-evoked potentials were the most sensitive neurophysiologic test for detecting small fiber involvement in AOSFN patients.
Quantitative sensory testing (warm detection threshold) showed low sensitivity for detecting small fiber involvement.
Electrochemical skin conductance testing showed poor sensitivity for detecting small fiber involvement in AOSFN.
Skin biopsy showed reduced epidermal nerve fiber density in over half of patients tested, more often affecting the thigh than the calf, consistent with a non-length-dependent neuropathy.
A precipitating event (infection, new treatment, or vaccination) preceded symptom onset in 80% of AOSFN patients, including one case following COVID-19.
Most patients with AOSFN reported neuropathic pain and paresthesia at onset.
Autonomic symptoms, mainly faintness and tachycardia, were reported in the majority of AOSFN patients.
The majority of AOSFN patients presented with a non-length-dependent clinical pattern, contrasting with typical chronic SFN.
Anti-CASPR2 IgG autoantibodies were detected in one of 20 AOSFN patients.
Anti-FGFR3 IgG antibodies were positive in 4 of 18 tested AOSFN patients, though their extracellular immunostaining pattern did not match anti-FGFR3 reactivity observed in vitro.
Antithyroid antibodies were present in 2 of 7 tested AOSFN patients.

In vitro immunostaining of mouse sciatic nerve fibers or dorsal root ganglia was observed with sera from 70% of AOSFN patients but not with sera from healthy or diseased controls, supporting an immune-mediated mechanism.

Patient sera produced heterogeneous immunostaining patterns including paranodal Schwann cell/axon staining, juxtaparanodal staining (associated with anti-CASPR2), unmyelinated fiber staining, and DRG neuron surface staining.
Disease course was heterogeneous: 65% of patients showed recovery (complete in 4, partial in 9), 25% had a chronic steady course, and 20% experienced relapses.
A one-month course of oral corticosteroids given during the acute phase was associated with complete or partial recovery in three patients.
IV immunoglobulin given after the acute phase showed no efficacy in two AOSFN patients treated for chronic symptoms.
Plasma exchange was ineffective in a patient with anti-CASPR2 antibody-associated AOSFN.
Combining neurophysiologic tests and skin biopsy findings, 90% of patients met criteria for definite SFN, with the remainder classified as probable SFN.
None of the 20 AOSFN patients developed large fiber involvement over a median follow-up of 4.8 years, supporting AOSFN as a distinct entity from length-dependent large-fiber neuropathies.
Monocyte levels differed significantly between MSA patients and healthy controls.
NLR was significantly different between MSA patients and healthy controls.
MPV was significantly different between MSA patients and healthy controls.
Uric acid levels, along with monocyte levels, differed significantly between MSA and Parkinson's disease patients.
A combination of NLR and MPV distinguished the MSA-parkinsonian subtype from healthy controls with an AUC of 0.824.
Complement component C4 was significantly correlated with autonomic symptom severity (SCOPA-AUT) and Wexner constipation scores in MSA patients.
Complement component C3 was significantly correlated with autonomic symptom severity (SCOPA-AUT) and Wexner constipation scores in MSA patients.
Serum complement component C3 levels were significantly correlated with autonomic symptom severity (SCOPA-AUT) and bowel symptom severity (Wexner scale) in MSA patients.
Serum IgG levels were significantly correlated with disease severity as measured by the Unified Multiple System Atrophy Rating Scale (UMSARS) in MSA patients.
The monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio (MLR) was found to significantly correlate with disease severity in MSA patients.
Four studies found no significant difference in preoperative patient-reported outcome scores between patients with at least one functional somatic syndrome and controls prior to TKA.
One study found that patients with at least one FSS had lower preoperative PROMs than controls prior to THA.
Two studies reported that patients with at least one FSS had worse SF-36 Physical Functioning Scores following TKA compared to controls.
Three studies found that patients with at least one FSS had worse SF-12 scores after TKA than controls.
Patients with at least one FSS demonstrated worse Oxford Knee Scores and American Knee Society Scores following TKA compared to controls (2 studies each).
Four studies found that patients with at least one FSS had worse WOMAC scores after TKA compared to controls.
Mehta et al. (2015) found that patients with an FSS diagnosis had worse KOOS pain and function scores at 6 months and 1 year following TKA.
Three studies found that patients with an FSS diagnosis were significantly less satisfied postoperatively than controls after TJA.
Skrejborg et al. (2019) found markedly worse postoperative Numeric Rating Scale pain scores among fibromyalgia patients compared to controls after TKA.
Loth et al. (2017) found that patients with at least one FSS had worse SF-12, Oxford Hip Score, and Forgotten Joint Score-12 scores following THA compared to controls.
Quintana et al. (2009) reported that patients with an FSS diagnosis had worse SF-36 Physical Functioning Scores and WOMAC scores following THA than controls.
All 11 studies reporting postoperative opioid use concluded that patients with at least one FSS are at increased risk for higher opioid use after total joint arthroplasty.
Brummett et al. (2013) reported that higher patient scores on the ACR fibromyalgia criteria were independently associated with greater inpatient opioid consumption following THA and TKA.
Bedard et al. (2017) found that fibromyalgia and chronic back pain significantly increased the risk of continued opioid use at 6 and 12 months after THA.
Chronic back pain and migraine headaches were significant risk factors for new persistent opioid use following THA, even among patients who were not prior opioid users.
Moore et al. (2019) found that patients with fibromyalgia were nearly twice as likely to develop any medical complication after TKA compared to propensity-matched controls.
Cregar et al. (2021) found fibromyalgia was associated with increased risk of undergoing lysis of adhesions for arthrofibrosis within 1 year of primary TKA in the Humana database.
Cregar et al. (2021) found fibromyalgia patients were more likely to undergo revision TKA within 2 years of index TKA than controls in the Medicare database.
D'Apuzzo et al. (2012) reported an overall revision rate of 6% among patients with fibromyalgia who underwent primary TKA at a mean 7-year follow-up.

Sodhi et al. (2019) found that patients with fibromyalgia had significantly increased odds of surgical complications following TKA including bearing wear, periprosthetic osteolysis, mechanical loosening, infection, dislocation, and revision of tibial insert.

Patients with fibromyalgia had lower readmission costs but greater management costs for medical and surgical complications after TKA, resulting in net financial losses compared to non-fibromyalgia patients.
A cited study (Agger et al., 2018) reported that prescription opioids are used at baseline by 26% of patients with multiple functional somatic syndromes.
At baseline, plasma S-Klotho levels were not significantly associated with heart rate or any heart rate variability parameter.
Exercise-induced increases in plasma S-Klotho levels after the 12-week intervention were positively associated with increases in SDNN, a marker of overall heart rate variability.
Exercise-induced increases in S-Klotho were negatively associated with changes in stress score, indicating reduced physiological stress with higher S-Klotho gains.
Exercise-induced increases in S-Klotho were negatively associated with changes in the sympathetic/parasympathetic ratio, suggesting reduced sympathetic dominance with higher S-Klotho gains.

Overall, the study concludes that higher S-Klotho plasma levels achieved through exercise training are related to increased vagal influence and reduced sympathetic tone in the autonomic nervous system.

In a fibromyalgia RCT, patients receiving electro-acupuncture with somatosensory input had a greater reduction in pain severity than those receiving mock laser acupuncture with no somatosensory input.

Electro-acupuncture recipients in the fibromyalgia trial showed increased resting-state functional connectivity between the leg region of primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and the anterior insula, associated with reduced pain severity.
Following electro-acupuncture therapy, fibromyalgia patients showed increased GABA+ levels in the anterior insula, which correlated with lower pain severity.
Changes in anterior insula GABA+ levels statistically mediated the relationship between S1 leg-anterior insula connectivity changes and pain severity reduction after electro-acupuncture.
Prior literature cited in the review notes that fibromyalgia patients show decreased anterior insula GABA levels along with compensatory upregulation of GABA type A receptors.
The anterior insula is described as hyperactive in fibromyalgia patients, per cited literature.
In constipation-predominant IBS patients, both electro-acupuncture and moxibustion at ST25/ST37 were therapeutically effective in relieving abdominal pain, bloating, and abdominal discomfort.

Electro-acupuncture was more effective than moxibustion in improving defecation frequency, difficulty in defecation, constipation, and psychological symptoms (depression, anxiety) in constipation-predominant IBS patients.

After electro-acupuncture treatment, constipation-predominant IBS patients showed significantly decreased activity in the anterior cingulate cortex, an area related to pain perception and chronic pain regulation.
Constipation-predominant IBS patients in the study exhibited increased insular cortex activation, consistent with the insula's role in interoception, visceral sensation, and pain regulation.
Prefrontal cortex activity, which was elevated in constipation-predominant IBS patients before treatment, significantly decreased after electro-acupuncture treatment.
Other cited clinical trials support electro-acupuncture's benefit in IBS by down-regulating abnormally increased colonic mucosa-associated substance P and vasoactive intestinal peptide expression.

In a carpal tunnel syndrome RCT, all electro-acupuncture arms (local, distal, and sham) reduced symptom severity, but verum electro-acupuncture (local and distal) was more effective than sham in improving neurophysiological outcomes.

Using diffusion tensor imaging, carpal tunnel syndrome patients had elevated fractional anisotropy in specific white matter regions near S1 compared to healthy adults, and improvement in median nerve latency was associated with decreased fractional anisotropy in region-specific patterns depending on acupuncture site.

In Crohn's disease remission patients, electro-acupuncture at bilateral ST25, CV6, and CV12 significantly increased resting-state functional connectivity between the hippocampus, anterior middle cingulate cortex, and insula, which was negatively correlated with Crohn's Disease Activity Index scores.

In an obesity RCT, after the first electro-acupuncture treatment, patients showed decreased activity in the right insular cortex and increased activity in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, with baseline BMI positively related to right insular cortex activity.

Long-term electro-acupuncture treatment in obese patients led to significant improvements in weight, BMI, emotional eating, and food addiction, along with increased activity in the right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex and altered connectivity to orbitofrontal cortex and thalamus.
In the multicentric cross-sectional cohort, 25% of ax-SpA patients met Rome IV criteria for IBS.
Meta-analysis of 10 studies (8395 SpA patients) found an overall pooled IBS prevalence of 15.4%.
Diagnostic method affected estimated IBS prevalence in SpA: much lower when based on ICD disease codes than when based on Rome criteria questionnaires.
Meta-analysis of five studies showed a significantly increased risk of IBS in SpA patients compared with healthy controls.
Sensitivity analysis excluding one outlier study (Ozgocmen) showed an even larger increase in IBS risk for SpA patients versus controls and removed the significant heterogeneity.
In multivariate analysis, anxiety was independently associated with more than double the risk of IBS in ax-SpA patients.
Higher physical activity was independently associated with a reduced risk of IBS in ax-SpA patients.
Fibromyalgia was twice as frequent in ax-SpA patients with IBS compared with those without, with a significant interaction between fibromyalgia and anxiety.
Female gender was significantly associated with IBS in ax-SpA patients on univariate analysis.
Unemployment was significantly associated with IBS in ax-SpA patients on univariate analysis.
Higher axial disease activity (BASDAI) was significantly associated with presence of IBS.
Worse functional impairment (BASFI) was significantly associated with presence of IBS.
Having received multiple prior lines of biologic therapy was significantly associated with presence of IBS.
Depression was significantly associated with presence of IBS in ax-SpA patients on univariate analysis.
The prevalence of IBS was not significantly different between ax-SpA patients with versus without concomitant inflammatory bowel disease.
CRP levels did not differ between ax-SpA patients with and without IBS symptoms, and IBS was not associated with NSAID use.
No significant difference was found in dietary habits or treatment adherence between ax-SpA patients with and without IBS.
Across two meta-analysis studies reporting disease activity, SpA patients with IBS had significantly higher BASDAI and BASFI scores than those without IBS.
The authors hypothesise that gut microbiota and related environmental factors may explain the observed link between SpA, gastrointestinal disorders and comorbidities such as IBS.
Compared with the contemporary comparison group, individuals who survived 30 days post-COVID-19 had a significantly increased long-term risk of functional gastrointestinal disorders (GI dysfunction).
COVID-19 survivors showed an increased long-term risk of peptic ulcer disease (PUD) compared with contemporary controls.
COVID-19 survivors had a significantly increased long-term risk of gastro-esophageal reflux disease (GERD) compared with contemporary controls.
COVID-19 survivors had an increased long-term risk of gallbladder disease compared with contemporary controls.
COVID-19 survivors had an increased long-term risk of severe liver disease compared with contemporary controls.
COVID-19 survivors had an increased long-term risk of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) compared with contemporary controls.
COVID-19 survivors had an increased long-term risk of pancreatic disease compared with contemporary controls.
30-day survivors of COVID-19 did not show a statistically significant increased risk of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) compared with contemporary controls.

The increased risks of GI dysfunction and GERD in the COVID-19 group persisted beyond 1 year of follow-up, while risk of gallbladder disease was only observed within 6 months and other digestive diseases showed no increased risk after 6 months.
Increased risks of GI dysfunction, PUD, GERD, and NAFLD were evident even among non-hospitalized (mild) COVID-19 patients compared with contemporary controls.
A dose-dependent (severity-related) relationship was observed between COVID-19 severity and GERD risk, with increasing risk from non-hospitalized to hospitalized to severe COVID-19.
SARS-CoV-2 reinfected patients had a markedly higher long-term risk of pancreatic disease compared with the non-infected group, greater than the risk seen in single-infection patients.
In a head-to-head comparison, reinfected COVID-19 patients had a significantly higher risk of pancreatic disease than patients with a single infection.
No sex-based differences in digestive disease risk between COVID-19 patients and comparison groups were observed in subgroup analyses by sex.

Sensitivity analysis restricting the COVID-19 cohort to before vaccine availability in the UK (pre-December 2020, n=8431) yielded results largely consistent with the main analyses, suggesting findings are not primarily driven by vaccination status.

Using a historical (pre-pandemic) comparison group as a sensitivity analysis, the trend of elevated digestive disease risks following COVID-19 was similar to that found with the contemporary comparison group.
Meta-analysis of six studies showed a significant 34% reduction in gut microbiome alpha-diversity in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.

Five of six studies reporting beta-diversity found significant differences in overall gut microbiome community structure between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, while one study found no difference.
At the phylum level, ME/CFS patients showed a significant increase in Bacteroidetes and a decrease in Firmicutes compared to healthy controls.
Firmicutes phylum abundance was notably reduced in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Potentially beneficial genera including Bifidobacterium, Roseburia, and Faecalibacterium showed a notable decrease in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.

Despite overall reduction in Firmicutes, certain Firmicutes-belonging genera (Phascolarctobacterium, Blautia, Coprobacillus, Oscillospira, Lactococcus, Anaerotruncus) were significantly increased in ME/CFS patients.

Four studies showed a significant increase of opportunistic pathogenic bacterial species, including Erysipelatoclostridium ramosum, Enterocloster citroniae, Hungatella hathewayi, and Eggerthella lenta, among ME/CFS patients.

Beneficial lactic acid and species-level bacteria such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Bifidobacterium angulatum, Lactobacillus ruminis, and Roseburia intestinalis were notably decreased in ME/CFS patients.
Short-chain fatty acids including butyrate, acetate, and branched SCFA isobutyrate were significantly reduced in feces, blood, or urine of ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum alpha-tocopherol (Vitamin E), an antioxidant vitamin potentially metabolized by gut microbes, was extensively reduced in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Gastrointestinal comorbidities were substantially more common in ME/CFS patients than healthy controls, with IBS reported in 64.8% vs 3.6% and general GI disturbances in 34.7% vs 19.5%.

Decreased abundance of butyrate-producing bacteria (Ruminococcus, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Eubacterium rectale) was negatively correlated with the severity of fatigue symptoms in ME/CFS patients.

Patients with severe ME/CFS have excessive antibodies against flagellins, a pathogen-associated molecular pattern from Lachnospiraceae, compared to healthy controls, suggesting direct involvement of commensal microbiome in ME/CFS pathogenesis.
A clinical trial demonstrated that probiotic administration (Lactobacillus casei strain Shirota and Bifidobacterium infantis 35624) reduced anxiety and inflammatory biomarkers in ME/CFS patients.
Fecal microbiome transplantation (FMT) failed to ameliorate symptoms and health-related quality of life in ME/CFS patients in a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled clinical study.

The reviewed ME/CFS cohort was predominantly female (77.6% overall, ~83% among ME/CFS patients specifically), consistent with known female-dominant prevalence of ME/CFS, though none of the included studies analyzed gut microbiome differences by sex.
wIRA irradiation (39°C, 60 min) induced autophagy in healthy fibroblasts and in PBMCs from both healthy donors and ME/CFS patients.
ME/CFS patients showed higher mitochondrial function compared to healthy donors at baseline.
wIRA treatment slightly reduced mitochondrial function in PBMCs from ME/CFS patients, bringing it closer to the level seen in healthy donors.
wIRA treatment activated mRNA expression of the autophagy-related gene MAP1LC3B.
wIRA treatment activated mRNA expression of the autophagy-related gene SIRT1.
wIRA treatment activated mRNA expression of HSPA1, a gene encoding a heat shock protein.

Epipharyngeal abrasive therapy (EAT) for chronic epipharyngitis was followed by resolution of chronic fatigue, tinnitus and insomnia, allowing the patient to return to work about six months after starting treatment.

Nasopharyngeal endoscopy revealed diffuse erythema, swelling, Eustachian tube orifice obstruction, Rosenmuller fossa compression, internal hemorrhage and deep vascular congestion, confirming chronic epipharyngitis in a patient previously diagnosed with ME/CFS without recognized epipharyngeal disease.
Before EAT, salivary cortisol diurnal variation was abnormal, with loss of the morning surge and an increasing trend in the afternoon.
After chronic epipharyngitis improved with EAT, the diurnal variation of salivary cortisol normalized, with restoration of the morning surge.
Salivary alpha-amylase activity (SAA), a marker of sympathetic/acute stress reactivity, showed a stimulated trend in the patient after EAT stimulation compared to healthy adults.
During active orthostatic stress testing, systolic, mean arterial, and diastolic blood pressures, which were decreased before treatment, tended to increase with EAT over the follow-up period.
Heart rate, which was elevated before treatment during orthostatic testing, decreased following EAT treatment.
Despite an ME/CFS diagnosis and orthostatic symptoms, the patient did not meet the diagnostic criteria for orthostatic dysregulation (OD) or POTS on active standing testing.

Heart rate variability indices (⊿ccv HF, L/H, ⊿L/H, CVRR) showed a trend toward recovery of parasympathetic activity and suppression of excessive sympathetic reflexes over the course of EAT treatment, improving overall autonomic balance.
Following return to work, the patient had no relapse of ME/CFS over approximately eight years of follow-up, using intermittent EAT when epipharyngitis flare symptoms recurred.
Prior standard ME/CFS treatments (high-concentration IV vitamin C, DHEA, and oral magnesium/nutritional therapy) produced no improvement in the patient's symptoms before EAT was tried.
The paper cites literature reporting that baseline heart rate is elevated in ME/CFS due to suppression of parasympathetic activity.
The paper notes literature indicating that approximately half of patients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 infection meet ME/CFS criteria post-infection (long COVID).
The paper cites literature reporting gender differences in the SAM system stress response, with a greater salivary amylase stimulatory effect observed in women.
The great majority of ME/CFS patients reported that people in their social circles have limited knowledge or complete unawareness of their disease.
Sixty-three participants who avoided discussing their disease cited misunderstanding/disbelief (77.8%) and avoidance of negative reactions (44.4%) as the main reasons.
The great majority of participants reported that ME/CFS had a negative impact on their mental health.
Male ME/CFS patients reported being mentally affected by the disease more often than female patients.
Sadness and hopelessness for possible relief were the two most commonly reported negative feelings among ME/CFS patients.
Nearly 40% of ME/CFS patients reported experiencing suicidal thoughts at least once because of the disease.
Half of male ME/CFS patients reported suicidal ideation at least once, significantly more than women, and far exceeding general-population male suicidal ideation rates.

Four of 169 patients registered with the Swiss physician-assisted suicide organization EXIT as a consequence of ME/CFS, with one additional patient stating they would register if the disease worsened.
About one-fifth of patients reported suffering from depression at the time of the study, most having developed it after ME/CFS onset (reactive/secondary depression).
Disease severity (bed-bound status) was not significantly associated with depression; the large majority of severely bed-bound patients were not depressed.
Suicidal thoughts, fear, hopelessness, feeling of becoming less, social isolation, and belief life is not worth living were significantly associated with secondary depression after ME/CFS onset.
Being told the disease is only psychosomatic, feeling not understood, worthless life, and clinical depression were significantly associated with suicidal thoughts among ME/CFS patients.
Two-thirds of ME/CFS participants reported experiencing stigmatization, most commonly misperception about the disease, followed by blame/judgment, discriminatory behavior, and inappropriate behavior.
Stigmatization did not differ significantly by gender or age group among ME/CFS patients.
Close family members were the largest source of coping support for ME/CFS patients, followed by close friends, physicians, faith/spirituality and the Swiss ME/CFS association.
The great majority of respondents stated they were no longer able to do what they wanted or had planned in life and constantly felt at the end of their strength.
Over half of patients reported social isolation, financial stress, and the perception that life was not worth living as contributors to negative mental health.
Pre-onset depression/anxiety prevalence (7.7%) among ME/CFS patients was similar to general population lifetime prevalence rates and other chronic diseases, with no significant gender difference.

The study authors argue that ME/CFS-related depression is reactive (secondary to disease burden) rather than a primary psychiatric cause, distinguishing it clinically from classical depression by the absence of typical worthlessness/guilt/anhedonia symptoms and by post-exertional symptom worsening rather than improvement with activity.
People with ME/CFS and people with long COVID performed similarly on the Purdue pegboard test of dexterity and bimanual coordination.
People with ME/CFS performed worse on the Purdue pegboard test than age-matched healthy controls, indicating impaired dexterity and bimanual coordination.
People with long COVID (~16-month illness duration) performed worse on the Purdue pegboard test than age-matched healthy controls, indicating impaired dexterity and bimanual coordination.

Blood cells in long COVID/PCS patients show multiple pathological changes including decreased lymphocyte stiffness, increased monocyte and neutrophil size, reduced erythrocyte deformability, and reduced natural killer cell function.
Long COVID and ME/CFS patients showed similarly impaired endothelial function in a direct comparison, suggesting shared vascular pathogenesis between the two post-viral illnesses.
Cardiac output was found increased in a subgroup of ME/CFS patients, likely due to left-to-right peripheral shunting diverting blood from skeletal muscle to other organs (a steal effect).
Autoantibodies targeting vasoregulators, including alpha1-adrenergic receptors (the main mediator of venous contraction), have been found in these patients.
Antihistamine treatment has been reported to alleviate long-term symptoms of Post-COVID-19 infection, supporting a role for histamine-driven venous dilation in disease mechanisms.
Several endothelial cell-related biomarkers (VWF, Factor VIII, ET-1, angiopoietin-2) are strongly correlated with COVID-19 and PCS.
Disturbed retinal microcirculation was strongly associated with PCS and ME/CFS and may serve as a marker of microcirculatory disorder.
A muscle biopsy study found patients with post-COVID exertion intolerance had fewer capillaries, thicker capillary basement membranes, and increased numbers of CD169+ macrophages.
Cerebral blood flow measured over a large cerebral artery was found decreased in both ME/CFS and PCS patients.
A clinical study found a marked increase in arterial stiffness and carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity predicting COVID-19-related cardiovascular complications.

In a study of 256 ME/CFS patients, orthostatic challenge revealed decreased cognitive efficiency, narrow pulse pressure (less than 25% of systolic pressure), and increased heart rate, confirming a negative effect of low stroke volume and tachycardia on diastolic capillary perfusion.
A study of COVID-19 patients echocardiographically detected impaired left ventricular diastolic function and impaired right ventricular function.
The bradycardic drug Ivabradine has a beneficial effect in PCS patients, pharmacologically confirming the negative role of tachycardia in impairing capillary perfusion.
23-Na+ MRI demonstrated a rise in intracellular sodium in skeletal muscles of ME/CFS patients, elevated at rest in some muscle types or only after exercise in others.
Increased ROS production with evidence of inhibited Na+/K+-ATPase activity was found in ME/CFS patients.
Cortisol and aldosterone levels are reported to be in the low-to-normal range in both ME/CFS and PCS patients, potentially contributing to reduced Na+/K+-ATPase stimulation.
Low oxygen consumption on cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) is considered a biomarker in ME/CFS patients, consistent with combined perfusion and mitochondrial dysfunction.
Connective tissue disorders affecting the vasculature, such as Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and Marfan Syndrome, are reported to be related to ME/CFS.
Small fiber neuropathy (SFN) occurs in a subset of ME/CFS and PCS patients, potentially contributing to CGRP deficiency and muscular malperfusion.

At the primary endpoint of 6 months, physical function (SF-36-PFS) improved only slightly in both groups with no significant difference between graded exercise therapy (GET) and activity management (AM).
At the 12-month secondary assessment, modest increases in SF-36-PFS scores were seen in both groups with no evidence of a difference between GET and AM.
A pre-specified subgroup analysis found no evidence that the relative treatment effect of GET versus AM on physical function differed between males and females.
A pre-specified analysis found no evidence that attending more treatment sessions was associated with improved physical function by 6 months.
Fatigue, measured by the Chalder Fatigue scale, improved similarly over time in both the GET and AM groups.
At 6 months there was some evidence of greater improvement (reduction) in anxiety symptoms (HADS) among participants allocated to GET compared to AM.
Self-reported school attendance did not change from baseline at either 6 or 12 months in either treatment group.
Global self-rated improvement (Clinical Global Impression Scale) was similar between groups: 30% overall felt much/very much better at 6 months (26% GET, 34% AM), rising to 40% at 12 months.

Accelerometer-derived physical activity (counts per minute) was similar between GET and AM groups at baseline, 3 and 6 months, and both groups showed reduced moderate-to-vigorous activity over follow-up.
Clinically significant deterioration in physical function (a 20-point drop) occurred in a similar minority of participants in both groups: 19% of GET and 23% of AM participants.
A composite measure combining CGI, withdrawal, and functional deterioration showed a higher (though not statistically significant) rate of deterioration in the GET group compared to AM.
A serious adverse event, a psychiatric hospital admission due to suicidal ideation, was judged possibly related to GET.
Withdrawal from allocated therapy due to feeling worse was more common with GET (3%) than AM (1%).
There was no evidence of a difference in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) between GET and AM over 12 months.
GET was not shown to be cost-effective compared to AM, with a negative incremental net monetary benefit and low probability of cost-effectiveness at standard willingness-to-pay thresholds.
Participants allocated to AM attended more healthcare appointments overall and incurred slightly higher specialist care costs than those allocated to GET.

Adherence to allocated treatment was high, with 96% of GET and 94% of AM participants starting their allocated intervention, and treatment fidelity (delivery of mandatory/prohibited components) was also high in both arms.
Approximately half of people infected with SARS-CoV-2 worldwide develop long COVID, with regional prevalence estimates of 51% in Asia, 44% in Europe, and 31% in the USA.
Cognitive dysfunction ('brain fog') was present in 22% of COVID-19 patients 19 weeks after diagnosis and persisted in 19.7% at 9 months post-infection.
Women and individuals with chronic underlying conditions were reported to be more susceptible to the detrimental effects of long COVID.
Using ME/CFS diagnostic criteria, up to 43% of long COVID patients met criteria for ME/CFS, with fatigue, post-exertional malaise, and insomnia as main symptoms.
COVID-19 has substantially increased the number of ME/CFS cases, and bioinformatics analysis identified a shared network of genetic interactions between long COVID and ME/CFS.
One year after rehabilitation, COVID-19 survivors had a 4.16-fold increased risk of myocarditis and mortality of 1.36–5%.
Within 2-3 months of SARS-CoV-2 infection, 19% of patients developed persistent myocarditis symptoms.
Post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis prevalence among survivors exceeds 9.3% across multiple studies.
Chronic cough was present in approximately 23-57% of COVID-19 survivors across countries, in both mild and severe cases.
COVID-19 survivors have a 64-66% higher risk of developing diabetes compared with uninfected individuals.
During the first year of the pandemic, new pediatric type 1 diabetes and DKA incidence surged by 9.5% and 25%, respectively, alongside rising blood glucose levels.
After 3.8 months of recovery, sexual dysfunction was found in 35.9% of men and 27.7% of women, with different underlying mechanisms by sex.
COVID-19 survivors showed 2-3 times higher incidence of thrombophilia, pulmonary embolism (2.5-6.3%), and deep vein thrombosis (1.2-6.4%) than uninfected individuals.
Post-infection follow-up of COVID-19 survivors found general pain in 13.40%, joint pain in 28.25%, muscle pain in 13.30%, headache in 9.50%, and chest pain in 12.12%.
In critically ill COVID-19 patients, naringenin showed excellent IL-6 inhibition compared to synthetic monoclonal antibodies.
Naringenin was shown by molecular docking to bind SARS-CoV-2 NSP3 macrodomain, NSP12 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, 3-chymotrypsin-like protease, and the ACE2 receptor, suggesting antiviral activity.
Naringin promotes M2 (anti-inflammatory/repair) microglial activation and inhibits M1 (pro-inflammatory) activation via modulation of the JAK/STAT3 signaling pathway.

By stabilizing redox status and elevating blood glucose, naringin reduces MMP-9 and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) concentrations, prolonging fatigue-inducing exercise duration and relieving post-exercise discomfort.

Naringin stabilizes mitochondrial membrane potential, preserves mitochondrial integrity, and sustains mitochondrial complex activity, potentially reducing mitochondrial dysfunction relevant to ME/CFS.
Naringin's anti-inflammatory properties reduce cardiovascular injury-associated inflammatory factors NF-κB, IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α.
Naringin inhibits cellular fibrosis by suppressing TGF-β overexpression and reducing downstream regulatory factor phosphorylation.
Naringin interacts with TRPV1 to suppress nervous system hyperexcitability and mitigate nerve pain by inhibiting oxidative stress.
Naringenin inhibits platelet aggregation via the PI3K/Akt pathway, preventing FeCl3-induced carotid artery thrombosis and vascular occlusion.
Naringin significantly reduces the abundance of gastrointestinal disease-related bacteria (Lachnoclostridium and Bilophila) and enhances probiotic content.
Naringenin alleviates rheumatoid arthritis symptoms in rats by modulating lymphocyte polarization, reducing Th1 and Th17 cell differentiation and IL-6/TNF-α levels.
Gut microbes remained significantly different from healthy controls after 3 months of recovery from COVID-19 and correlated with persistent long COVID symptoms.
COVID-19 survivors have a 64-66% higher risk of developing diabetes compared to uninfected individuals.
The risk of developing diabetes within three months of COVID-19 infection was as high as 95%, with a greater relative risk for type 2 diabetes (70%) than type 1 diabetes (48%).
During the first year of the pandemic, new pediatric type 1 diabetes and diabetic ketoacidosis diagnoses rose 9.5% and 25% respectively, alongside a rise in blood glucose levels.
ACE2 is proposed to be elevated in exocrine glands and pancreatic islets, allowing SARS-CoV-2 entry and induction of pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction or apoptosis that impairs insulin signaling.
Naringenin protects pancreatic beta-cells from streptozotocin-induced stress by activating Nrf2, substantially lowering blood glucose and restoring normal insulin levels.
