Naringin increases pancreatic beta cell mass and improves diabetes by upregulating the FoxM1 transcription factor that governs beta-cell proliferation.

In type 2 diabetes patients, naringin improved glucose metabolism, increased residual insulin secretion, and stimulated glycogen synthesis, and could reverse type 1 diabetes-induced diabetic ketoacidosis even though it could not regulate glucose in absolute insulin deficiency.
Naringenin combined with insulin modulates matrix metalloproteinases to reduce diabetic neuropathic pain.
Ten percent of COVID-19 survivors still experience persistent musculoskeletal pain two months after recovery, with pain duration unrelated to initial COVID-19 severity.
Post-infection follow-up of COVID-19 survivors found general pain in 13.40%, joint pain in 28.25%, muscle pain in 13.30%, headache in 9.50%, and chest pain in 12.12%.
Naringin attenuates iodoacetate-induced osteoarthritis pain by inhibiting the secretion of adrenaline and pro-inflammatory factors including IL-6, NO, and TNF-α.
Naringenin inhibits glial cell activation and reduces TNF-α, IL-1β, and monocyte chemotactic protein 1 in a rat model of nerve-ligation-induced neuropathic pain.
Naringin interacts with TRPV1 to suppress nervous system hyperexcitability and potentially mitigate nerve pain by inhibiting oxidative stress.
Naringenin effectively blocks TRPM3 ion channels in vivo and in vitro, supporting an analgesic effect.
After 3.8 months of recovery from COVID-19, 35.9% of men and 27.7% of women had sexual dysfunction, via differing mechanisms in each sex.
ACE2 and TMPRSS2 are highly expressed in the gonads, especially male gonads, with detectable SARS-CoV-2 infection in the testis, suggesting gonadal susceptibility to viral damage.
Naringenin reduces bisphenol A-induced testicular damage by suppressing oxidative stress and mitochondrial apoptosis.
In vivo naringin treatment inhibits steroidogenic enzymes and controls ovulation, restoring ovarian morphology and reducing cystic follicle levels in a polycystic ovary syndrome rat model.
COVID-19 survivors had significantly higher incidence of thrombophilia, pulmonary embolism (2.5-6.3%), and deep vein thrombosis (1.2-6.4%), 2 to 3 times higher than uninfected individuals.
Naringin protects endothelial cell function by upregulating nitric oxide bioavailability, decreasing inflammatory factors (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-18), and reversing YAP downregulation.
Naringin inhibits excessive autophagy in endothelial cells by activating the PI3K-Akt-mTOR pathway.
Naringenin inhibits platelet activation by targeting the PI3K/Akt pathway, preventing FeCl3-induced carotid artery thrombosis and vascular occlusion, demonstrating antithrombotic properties.
Molecular docking shows naringenin is strongly attracted to thrombin and can bind its active core, potentially impeding thrombin activity.
Naringin can affect thrombus formation and stabilization by binding to protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) and inducing conformational changes.
Applying the CDC/Fukuda 1994 criteria to symptom responses, 24% of the 225 MS patients would meet diagnostic criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome.
20.9% of MS patients reported having received a prior physician diagnosis of chronic fatigue syndrome.
Agreement between CDC/Fukuda criteria-based CFS status and patients' physician-reported CFS diagnosis was poor (Cohen's kappa = 0.146), a discordance that was statistically significant.
CDC criteria-defined CFS diagnosis rates differed significantly by age group among MS patients, with higher rates in those under 25 and over 40 years compared with the 25–40 age group.

No significant differences were found between CFS-diagnosed and non-CFS MS patients regarding sex, age group overall trend within subgroups, employment status, MS type, or physical disability (EDSS) level.
MS patients with a CFS diagnosis reported effort-related exhaustion far more often than those without a CFS diagnosis.
A significantly higher proportion of CFS-diagnosed MS patients reported that fatigue impacted their daily performance compared with non-CFS patients.
Severe headaches were significantly more common in CFS-diagnosed MS patients than in those without a CFS diagnosis.
MS patients with a CFS diagnosis more often reported worsening headaches over time than those without the diagnosis.
Feeling groggy upon waking was significantly more common among CFS-diagnosed MS patients than those without CFS.
Postexertional malaise, a CDC/Fukuda criterion for CFS, was reported by 29.8% of the overall MS patient sample.
Among the CDC/Fukuda symptom checklist, memory or concentration impairment was reported by 52.4% and muscle pain by 50.7% of the overall MS sample.
Comparing current and past functional status, 7% of MS patients showed a deterioration in EDSS score.
More than half of MS patients reported fatigue lasting longer than 6 months, meeting the duration criterion for CFS.
Prior research found higher levels of D-lactic acid-producing enterococci and streptococci in the gut flora of CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
A previous study by the same authors found that PLWNT practice reduced fatigue and improved quality of life in patients with CFS.
A previous published study reported a mean difference of 1.634 (SD 3.238) in MFI-20 fatigue scores between groups, which was used to calculate this trial's sample size.
According to Institute of Medicine data, 42.2% and 33.3% of US patients with CFS presented with anxiety and depression, respectively, in 2015.
The majority (82%-95%) of patients with CFS experience lifelong symptoms of mental and sleep disorders.
A cited recent study found differences in the composition and function of the gut microbiota between patients with CFS and healthy controls.
Previous fMRI studies have shown abnormal brain network structure and connectivity in patients with CFS.
Changes in the composition profile of the intestinal flora are reported to be related to changes in cingulate and cerebellum signals involved in brain activity in CFS.
Several cited studies have shown that Qigong exercise can substantially increase the diversity of intestinal flora and the content of beneficial bacteria.
Compared with healthy individuals, individuals with CFS exhibit altered emotion regulation, somatic and sensory processing, and motor control activities.
PLWNT abdominal massage techniques are proposed to reduce sympathetic nerve excitability and enhance parasympathetic nerve excitability, thereby reducing anxiety.
At the post-treatment (12-week) assessment, no significant differences were observed between the aquatic therapy and land-based therapy groups on any outcome measure.
At the 18-week follow-up (6 weeks after treatment ended), women who received aquatic therapy had significantly lower pain intensity than those who received land-based therapy.
At the 18-week follow-up, women who received aquatic therapy had significantly better sleep quality scores than those who received land-based therapy.
During gait, the hEDS group exhibited a significantly lower peak hip extensor moment compared to asymptomatic controls.
Isometric hip extensor strength testing showed a 40% deficit in peak hip extensor strength in the hEDS group relative to controls.
Both hEDS and control groups exhibited similar walking speeds and similar hip, knee, and ankle joint kinematics.
Knee and ankle joint moments during gait did not significantly differ between hEDS and control groups.
A majority of the hEDS cohort self-reported at least weekly joint subluxations, most commonly at the hip, followed by knee/patella and ankle.

Functional neurological signs (motor and/or sensory) were present in 92% of hEDS/HSD patients compared to healthy controls, with sensory signs (e.g., splitting of vibration sense) significantly more frequent in patients.
Among hEDS/HSD patients with FNS, sensory signs occurred either in isolation (N=12) or combined with motor signs (N=10), while no patient showed isolated motor FNS.
The number of positive FNS did not significantly differ between patients with definite, possible, or excluded small-fiber neuropathy (SFN) likelihood groups.
Patients with a higher number of functional neurological signs (≥3) reported significantly greater pain interference with daily life than those with fewer FNS (<3).
Patients with more functional neurological signs (≥3) also showed a trend toward higher pain intensity compared to those with fewer signs.
The majority of hEDS/HSD patients in this cohort reported neuropathic pain characteristics and a large proportion met criteria for definite or possible small fiber neuropathy.

Prior literature reviewed by the authors reports generalized joint hypermobility (GJH) is more prevalent in patients diagnosed with functional neurological disorders (functional seizures, fixed dystonia, digestive functional syndromes) than in the general population.
Nearly 90% of surveyed EDS Association members reported symptoms of temporomandibular disorders (TMD).
Bite splint therapy, counselling, jaw training and occlusal adjustment were the most frequently reported TMD treatments among EDS patients.
There was no statistically significant difference in perceived good treatment effect for TMD between hypermobile EDS and classical EDS subsamples.

A heterozygous missense variant in THBS2 (c.2686T>C, p.Cys896Arg) was identified as the disease-causing variant, segregating with a novel EDS phenotype with prominent vascular features in a three-generation family.

The index patient presented with joint hypermobility (Beighton score 5/9), multiple joint dislocations, tendon rupture, easy bruising, prolonged wound healing, atrophic scarring, and piezogenic papules.

Affected family members displayed prominent vascular involvement, including a dilated aortic arch (4.2 cm) and thickened mitral valve in patient II:1, and fatal abdominal aortic dissection with cerebral aneurysms in the deceased grandfather (I:1).

Affected individuals showed a bleeding diathesis, with patient III:1 bleeding continuously for over 20 minutes after skin punch biopsy compared to no bleeding in a healthy age-matched control, despite normal platelet counts and coagulation testing.

Despite the observed bleeding phenotype, testing of von Willebrand factor, clotting factor VIII, fibrinogen, and platelet function (PFA-200) did not indicate any clotting abnormalities in the affected patients.
Heterozygous Thbs2 p.Cys896Arg knock-in mice developed remarkably flexible tails that could be knotted without distress by 3-4 months of age, unlike wild-type littermates.

Pregnancy accelerated onset of the hyperflexibility phenotype in heterozygous female mice, which became hyper-flexible as early as 2 months of age post-partum, compared to 4 months in males and non-pregnant females.

Bleeding time assay showed markedly prolonged bleeding in heterozygous Thbs2 mutant mice (over 11 minutes, with three of four exceeding the 12-minute cutoff) compared to wild-type littermates (under 4 minutes).

Skin biopsy histology from patient III:1 showed thin, disorganized and fragmented collagen fibers with mucinous material in the reticular dermis and increased dilated blood vessels compared to healthy control skin.

Electron microscopy of the patient's skin showed abnormally-shaped fibroblasts and endothelial cells with excess irregular ECM near blood vessels, while collagen fibrils themselves appeared unremarkable; in contrast, mutant mouse tail and skin collagen fibrils were larger with irregular contours compared to wild-type mice.

Thrombospondin-2 directly binds MMP2 and mediates its clearance; THBS2 loss-of-function has been shown to increase ECM MMP2 levels, enhancing MMP2-mediated cleavage of decorin and producing ECM abnormalities resembling those observed in this THBS2-related EDS.
Patient III:1 was diagnosed with bilateral greater saphenous vein insufficiency and patient II:1 with unilateral greater saphenous vein insufficiency.

The heterozygous knock-in mouse phenotype (connective tissue laxity, bleeding diathesis, abnormal collagen fibers) recapitulates features previously reported in homozygous Thbs2 null mutant mice, despite the human disease being caused by a heterozygous variant.

Unlike the dilated cardiomyopathy seen with age in homozygous Thbs2 knockout mice, echocardiography of the affected human family members did not reveal age-related cardiomyopathy, possibly due to their relatively young age or partial penetrance.
Patient III:2 suffered from symphysiolysis during childbirth and reported increased joint flexibility while breastfeeding, mirroring the pregnancy-related exacerbation seen in mutant mice.

No pathogenic variants were identified in a panel of 15 known EDS-related genes or in whole-exome sequencing for other genes previously associated with EDS, supporting THBS2 as a novel causative gene for this phenotype.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome is primarily caused by COL3A1 gene mutations resulting in abnormal type III collagen production, leading to fragile blood vessels and connective tissue.
Spontaneous carotid-cavernous fistula is described as pathognomonic of vEDS, occurring in approximately 9.8% of individuals with vEDS.

The patient with vEDS presented with multiple concurrent vascular pathologies including a left CCF, superior mesenteric artery dissection, 34 mm abdominal aortic aneurysm, multiple splenic artery aneurysms (up to 11 mm), left renal artery aneurysm (7 mm), and inferior gluteal artery aneurysm (8 mm).

Endovascular embolization of the left CCF using coils and balloon-assisted technique via a transvenous route through the superior ophthalmic vein successfully achieved cessation of flow through the fistula.

During femoral artery access for the endovascular procedure, an unrecognized anatomical variant (corona mortis, an anastomosis between the obturator artery, inferior epigastric artery, and distal external iliac artery) led to arterial rupture and significant haemorrhage requiring emergency stent graft placement and later embolization.

A new 9 mm common hepatic artery aneurysm developed and increased to 22 mm within two weeks, prompting embolization with coils in the gastroduodenal artery and Onyx-34 liquid embolic in the aneurysmal sac, resulting in complete exclusion of the aneurysm on follow-up imaging.

Anticoagulation with low molecular weight heparin for incidental pulmonary emboli was later stopped by patient preference due to recurrent bleeding complications (rectus sheath and pararenal haematomas, raised INR to 3.17) in the context of underlying vEDS vessel fragility.
In a prior series, vEDS patients undergoing angiography had major complications in 22% and a mortality rate of 5.6% among 18 patients.
Open surgical repair of arterial complications in vEDS carries a higher mortality rate (30%) compared with endovascular procedures (24%).

Endovascular interventions for CCF in the general population offer a 90-100% cure rate with mortality less than 1%, but vEDS patients have much higher complication rates due to underlying vascular fragility.
A multi-institutional study of 86 genetically confirmed vEDS individuals identified 139 aortic/arterial pathologies in 53 individuals (61.6%), with 37.4% presenting as emergencies.

In vEDS, mesenteric arteries were most commonly affected by arterial pathology (31.7%), followed by cerebrovascular (16.5%), iliac (16.5%), and renal arteries (12.2%), with arterial embolization (13.4%) and stenting (2.5%) being the predominant endovascular interventions when treatment was undertaken.
vEDS patients have a median life expectancy of 51 years, with arterial rupture being the most common cause of death.

The patient experienced significant psychological impact from multiple hospital admissions, life-threatening bleeds, and frequent follow-ups, compounded by anxiety over her children's confirmed EDS diagnoses, requiring psychological support.
vEDS is an autosomal dominant condition with a 50% chance of inheritance, and genetic counselling is recommended to help families understand inheritance patterns and risks to children.
The Beighton score and Sachse scale showed poor agreement in classifying joint hypermobility among 30 female fitness instructors, as measured by Spearman and Kendall tau non-parametric correlations.

The authors conclude that the expanded correlation analysis indicates poor compliance between the Beighton and Sachse hypermobility tests, highlighting a need to standardise hypermobility spectrum disorder diagnostics.
Children with achondroplasia had a 2-fold higher risk of ligamentous laxity compared to age- and sex-matched healthy controls, with 55% meeting diagnostic criteria for hypermobility.
No significant difference in ligamentous laxity was found between male and female children with achondroplasia.
Joint involvement analysis showed that knee hypermobility was common, observed in 67% of children with achondroplasia.
Elbow hypermobility was rare among children with achondroplasia, in contrast to the frequent knee involvement.
Longitudinal assessments showed a decreasing trend in ligamentous laxity scores over time, suggesting hypermobility issues may lessen in adulthood.
Among 530 patients undergoing primary inflatable penile prosthesis placement, 139 (26.2%) were retrospectively found to have glans hypermobility.
Using the newly developed grading scale, glans hypermobility severity was classified as grade 1 in 86 cases (16.2%), grade 2 in 29 cases (5.5%), and grade 3 in 24 cases (4.5%).
Larger implant size was associated with a lower likelihood of detecting glans hypermobility, with each 1 cm increase in implant size decreasing GH incidence by 11.0%.

Of 11 patients who underwent primary glans hypermobility repair using the modified glanspexy technique, one required repeat glanspexy for recurrent bothersome GH and one developed a suture granuloma requiring unilateral cylinder explant at one-year follow-up.

Unilateral pectineal suspension (UPS), a mesh-free technique using a single nonabsorbable suture connecting the pectineal ligament to the anterior cervix, restored physiologic uterine and vaginal position in a woman with pelvic floor hypermobility and vaginal laxity after four vaginal deliveries.

In a previously published short-term follow-up case series of patients with POP-Q stage 2-4 prolapse treated with UPS, apical correction was 100% successful and 93.6% of patients reported satisfaction with the operative result, with no unexpected complications.

Across an unpublished case series of over 400 UPS procedures since 2020, the authors report no cases of bowel disorders, ureter or bladder complications, de novo incontinence, or need for re-operation.
More than half of premenopausal primiparous women have some form of clinically significant pelvic floor symptoms after vaginal delivery.
Pregnancy is associated with bladder neck lowering, increased bladder neck mobility, pelvic organ descent, decreased levator ani strength, and decreased urethral resistance.
Dynamic magnetic resonance imaging studies demonstrated increased mobility of pelvic floor structures after first pregnancy.

Women who gave birth vaginally have longer genital hiatus, lower anterior and posterior vaginal walls, and significantly decreased perineal body length, while POP-Q points Ba and Bp remain within normal range.
A longitudinal cohort study demonstrated a worsening in general sex score after vaginal deliveries.
Wandering spleen results from elongation or maldevelopment of the spleen's suspensory ligaments, predisposing to splenic torsion and detorsion.
Wandering spleen is a rare clinical entity that primarily affects children but shows higher prevalence among adult females of reproductive age.

A 14-year-old female initially misdiagnosed with gastroenteritis later developed acute abdomen due to splenic torsion, confirmed by ultrasonography, CT, and exploratory laparotomy showing an infarcted spleen.

The patient underwent total splenectomy for the infarcted wandering spleen, while the authors recommend splenopexy as a spleen-preserving alternative when feasible, particularly in pediatric patients, given the spleen's role in the reticuloendothelial system.
Fatigue was the most strongly intercorrelated FIQ item and the dominant feature driving the first principal component that separated fibromyalgia patients from controls.
A classifier trained using only the fatigue item achieved balanced classification accuracy up to 86% in an independent validation sample, comparable to using the full FIQ.
Machine-learning classifiers (SVM, random forest, logistic regression) trained on full FIQ data distinguished patients from controls with balanced accuracy up to 88%.
Fibromyalgia patients had significantly higher BMI than healthy controls, with fewer patients being normal weight.
At baseline (fasting), fibromyalgia patients had higher blood cAMP levels than controls, one of the metabolites with the largest effect sizes.
Cytidine, carnosine, and inosine showed the largest baseline effect sizes distinguishing patients from controls, linking fibromyalgia to tyrosine and purine metabolism.
Xanthine showed a different pattern of stress-induced change between fibromyalgia patients and controls after both glucose and exercise challenges.
In response to the exercise challenge (CPET), fibromyalgia patients showed an increase in glutamine levels, unlike controls whose glutamine remained stable, representing an abnormal stress response.
Unlike controls, fibromyalgia patients failed to show the expected rise in glutamate after exercise, indicating a blunted glutamatergic stress response.
Aspartate, hypoxanthine, spermidine, histidine, normetanephrine, and allantoin changed differently between fibromyalgia patients and controls specifically after the oral glucose tolerance test.
Baseline 5-HIAA levels were negatively correlated with fatigue severity across the cross-validated analysis, with lower 5-HIAA associated with more fatigue.
Larger exercise-induced increases in glutamine were associated with higher fatigue levels in fibromyalgia patients.
Exercise-induced changes in kynurenine concentration were strongly correlated with fatigue severity in fibromyalgia patients.
Metabolite set enrichment analysis showed the largest pathway-level differences between patients and controls were in the purine and tyrosine pathways in the fasting state.
Purine and pyrimidine pathway enrichment differences between patients and controls emerged in response to the oral glucose tolerance test.
Pyrimidine pathway differences between patients and controls were manifest specifically in response to the cardiopulmonary exercise test, a difference not evident at baseline.

A combined metabolomic panel reflecting purine, pyrimidine, and tyrosine pathways discriminated fibromyalgia patients from controls with 79% balanced accuracy and 84% ROC-AUC in a held-out validation sample.
Consistent with prior literature, systemic glutamate was elevated in fibromyalgia patients, potentially due to reduced bacterial conversion of glutamate to GABA.

Elevated purine metabolites (inosine, hypoxanthine, xanthine) were found in fibromyalgia patients, consistent with previously reported reduced conversion of inosine to adenosine possibly involving gut bacteria.
Reduced 5-HIAA in fibromyalgia patients indicates reduced serotonin, consistent with tryptophan being shunted into the kynurenine pathway rather than serotonin synthesis.
The metabolites associated with fatigue (5-HIAA, glutamine, kynurenine) were not correlated with BMI, suggesting the metabolic-fatigue association is not simply explained by body weight.

A study identified candidate genes (SLC64A4, TRPV2, MYT1L, NRXN3) associated with fibromyalgia risk and found a hypomethylated DNA pattern in genes related to stress response, DNA repair, autonomic system response, and subcortical neuronal abnormalities.

A case-control study of 130 women with fibromyalgia versus 35 healthy women controls found significantly lower serum serotonin levels in fibromyalgia patients, with a positive correlation between serotonin levels and tender point count.

In a double-blind controlled study, 80% of fibromyalgia patients experienced norepinephrine-evoked forearm pain compared to 30% of rheumatoid arthritis patients and 30% of healthy controls, with significantly greater pain intensity in the fibromyalgia group.

A study found disrupted release of endogenous dopamine in the basal ganglia of fibromyalgia patients in response to both painful and nonpainful stimulation, potentially explaining widespread pain and bodily tenderness.

Central sensitization in fibromyalgia is linked to alterations in NMDA receptor function and an imbalance in excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitter systems, contributing to widespread and persistent pain.
An immune function study found lower percentages of CD19+ B-cells in the fibromyalgia group compared to controls, alongside differences in monocyte CD14/CD16 populations.
The fibromyalgia group showed lower IFN-γ stimulation indices, which negatively correlated with cold pain threshold.
Mitochondrial dysfunction with increased ROS production has been associated with fibromyalgia, suggesting disrupted energy metabolism and contribution to heightened pain sensitivity.

A study by Coppens et al. found that fibromyalgia patients showed blunted cortisol responsivity to the Trier Social Stress Test compared to controls, an effect especially pronounced when early childhood adversity was accounted for.
Fibromyalgia shows a striking gender disparity, with approximately 80-90% of diagnosed individuals being women.

A study found an inverse relationship between pain severity and both progesterone and testosterone levels in fibromyalgia patients, with pain being greatest when progesterone was low and cortisol was high.

Heritability of fibromyalgia is estimated at around 50%, indicating substantial genetic influence, with variations in genes involved in pain perception, neurotransmitter regulation, and immune function implicated.

A multi-case family study of 116 families and 342 siblings found a sibling recurrence risk of 27.2% (λs=13.6) for fibromyalgia, with a genome scan identifying suggestive linkage to chromosome 17p11.2-q11.2 (LOD score 2.52 at marker D17S2196).
Obesity is associated with an increased risk and severity of fibromyalgia, linking body weight to symptom development or exacerbation.

A Cochrane systematic review of 29 RCTs of mixed exercise (aerobic, resistance, flexibility) found moderate-quality evidence supporting positive effects on health-related quality of life, pain, fatigue, stiffness, and physical function compared to controls.
Studies support the efficacy of Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT) in reducing tender points count and enhancing function in fibromyalgia patients.
Cognitive behavioral therapy has been shown to be effective in managing fibromyalgia-related symptoms and improving overall quality of life.

A study by Vambheim et al. found relaxation techniques advantageous for chronic pain management programs, but noted that efficacy decreases over time, requiring continuous practice for sustained pain reduction.

A study found that individuals with fibromyalgia adhering to a vegan diet experienced notable enhancements in reported pain, and those following a low-FODMAP diet also reported significant pain improvements.
Supplementation with Chlorella green algae, coenzyme Q10, acetyl-l-carnitine, or a combination of vitamin C and E demonstrated significant improvements in pain measures in fibromyalgia.

A cross-sectional web-based survey found that approximately 66% of fibromyalgia patients used complementary and alternative medicine (CAM), with those combining CAM and pharmacologic treatments reporting higher quality of life, and CAM-only users reporting lower pain than pharmacologic-only users.

Standard pharmacologic treatments for fibromyalgia include TCAs (amitriptyline, nortriptyline), SSRIs/SNRIs (duloxetine, milnacipran), anticonvulsants (gabapentin, pregabalin), and muscle relaxants (cyclobenzaprine) to improve sleep, mood, and reduce pain.
Investigational therapies such as ketamine, targeting glutamate/NMDA receptors, have shown promise in early studies for modulating pain perception in fibromyalgia.
Cannabinoids are being investigated for analgesic and anti-inflammatory properties, with some studies suggesting they may offer pain relief and improve sleep in fibromyalgia.

Growing evidence links the gut microbiome to fibromyalgia, with investigational therapies focusing on modulating gut microbiota through dietary changes, probiotics, or fecal microbiota transplantation.
Intermittent cold stress induced mechanical hyperalgesia (lower von Frey withdrawal threshold) in mice, which was substantially reversed by electroacupuncture but not sham electroacupuncture.
Intermittent cold stress induced thermal hyperalgesia (shortened paw withdrawal latency), which was reversed by electroacupuncture but not sham electroacupuncture.

Plasma levels of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines/chemokines were elevated in FM mice compared to normal mice, and this elevation was reversed by electroacupuncture but not sham electroacupuncture.
The microglial marker Iba1 was increased in the thalamus of FM mice by Western blot, and this increase was attenuated by electroacupuncture but not sham electroacupuncture.
TLR4 and its downstream signaling proteins (MyD88, TRAF6, pERK, pp38, pJNK, pNFκB) were increased in the thalamus of FM mice and attenuated by electroacupuncture but not sham electroacupuncture.

Immunofluorescence showed increased TLR4/Iba1 colocalization in the thalamus of FM mice, indicating microglial TLR4 expression, which was abrogated by electroacupuncture but not sham electroacupuncture.

TLR4 and downstream Iba1-associated proteins (MyD88, TRAF6, pERK, pp38, pJNK, pNFκB) were increased in the medial prefrontal cortex of FM mice and attenuated by electroacupuncture but not sham electroacupuncture.
Immunofluorescence showed increased TLR4/Iba1 colocalization in the medial prefrontal cortex of FM mice, abolished by electroacupuncture but not sham electroacupuncture.
TLR4 and downstream Iba1-associated proteins were increased in the somatosensory cortex (SSC) of FM mice and attenuated by electroacupuncture but not sham electroacupuncture.
Immunofluorescence showed increased TLR4/Iba1 colocalization in the SSC of FM mice, alleviated by electroacupuncture but not sham electroacupuncture.
TLR4 and downstream Iba1-associated proteins were increased in the amygdala of FM mice and attenuated by electroacupuncture but not sham electroacupuncture.
Immunofluorescence showed increased TLR4/Iba1 colocalization in the amygdala of FM mice, abrogated by electroacupuncture but not sham electroacupuncture.
Chemogenetic (hM4Di DREADD/CNO) inhibition of the somatosensory cortex significantly reduced mechanical hyperalgesia induced by FM in mice.
Chemogenetic (hM4Di DREADD/CNO) inhibition of the somatosensory cortex significantly alleviated thermal hyperalgesia induced by FM in mice.

Chemogenetic inhibition of the SSC reduced TLR4, MyD88, TRAF6, pERK, pp38, pJNK, and pNFκB levels in the SSC of FM mice, while Iba1 levels were unchanged, suggesting the analgesic effect acts on neuronal TLR4 signaling downstream of microglial activation.
Administration of the S. amarissima aqueous extract alone produced significant changes in EEG frequency bands and spectral power compared to baseline.
SAAE produced dose-dependent anticonvulsant effects, reducing the incidence and severity of PTZ-induced seizures and increasing seizure latency/survival.
Amarisolide A (AMA), a metabolite of S. amarissima, produced dose-dependent anticonvulsant effects similar to the extract in the PTZ seizure model.
Pretreatment with the GABAA receptor antagonist picrotoxin prevented the anticonvulsant effects of amarisolide A on seizure severity and survival, implicating GABAergic mechanisms.
Pretreatment with the 5-HT1A receptor antagonist WAY100635 prevented the anticonvulsant effects of amarisolide A on seizure severity and survival, implicating serotonergic 5-HT1A mechanisms.
In BMS patients receiving active cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES), longer stimulation duration significantly predicted decreased pain intensity on the NRS.
Sham (inactive) stimulation was also associated with a significant decrease in pain intensity over time, similar in direction to the active group.
Using a 30% pain reduction cut-off, responder rates were identical (36%) in both the active and sham stimulation groups, with no significant between-group difference.
Somatic symptom disorder scores significantly decreased over the 28-day study period across the whole cohort, but with no significant difference between active and sham groups.
Anxiety scores did not significantly change over the study period in either group.
Depression scores did not significantly change over the study period in either group.
Sleep quality significantly improved over the study period in both active and sham groups, with no significant advantage of active over sham stimulation.
At baseline, patients in the active stimulation group reported significantly better sleep quality than the sham group.
No severe adverse events occurred during CES or TENS use in either group, and stimulation was never discontinued due to side effects; localized tingling was the most common side effect.

Only 28% of both active and sham groups would recommend CES as a treatment option, with subjective ratings between 'no change' and 'mild improvement' and no significant between-group differences in patient satisfaction.
In prior randomized, double-blind, controlled trials cited by the authors, CES showed a positive effect on pain in patients with fibromyalgia.
Prior clinical studies cited by the authors demonstrated positive effects of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) on pain in patients with fibromyalgia.

A biopsy study cited by the authors found significantly reduced epithelial and subpapillary nerve fiber density in the lingual mucosa of 12 patients with burning mouth syndrome, supporting a small-fiber polyneuropathy mechanism.
Psychosocial and psychological comorbidities, particularly anxiety and depression, are reported in up to 85% of burning mouth syndrome cases according to the cited literature.

This BMS cohort had high prevalence of poor sleep and psychiatric comorbidity at baseline, with 77% of subjects showing bad or clinically relevant sleep disturbance and the majority reporting mild-to-severe somatic, anxiety, and depressive symptoms.
AME treatment reduced ovalbumin-induced food allergy symptoms in a mouse model.
AME reduced serum histamine release in the mouse food allergy model.
AME treatment considerably reduced the mast cell population in the spleen and mesenteric lymph nodes of allergic mice.
In RBL-2H3 mast cells, AME inhibited the release of beta-hexosaminidase, a marker of degranulation.
AME inhibited histamine release from RBL-2H3 mast cells in vitro.
Transcriptomic analysis showed that AME altered expression of genes associated with mast cell function.
AME suppressed mast cell activation by modulating the MAPK and NF-kB signaling pathways, as shown by Western blotting.
Bladders from patients with recurrent UTI showed a notable increase in neuropeptide content in the lamina propria compared to expected normal levels.
In mice with recurrent UTI, sensory nerve sprouting occurred and was linked to NGF produced by recruited monocytes and tissue-resident mast cells.
Treatment of rUTI mice with an NGF-neutralizing antibody prevented sensory nerve sprouting and alleviated pelvic sensitivity.
Instillation of native NGF into bladders of naïve mice was sufficient to mimic sensory nerve sprouting and pain behavior seen in rUTI mice.
Nerve activation, pain, and urinary frequency in rUTI mice were each linked to the presence of proximal mast cells, as mast cell deficiency was therapeutically effective.
Pharmacological antagonism of receptors for several direct or indirect mast cell products was each effective in reducing nerve activation, pain, and urinary frequency in rUTI mice.
SBF treatment dose-dependently reduced β-hexosaminidase release from IgE-sensitized, antigen-stimulated RBL-2H3 mast cells, whereas PSBF showed an opposite (increasing) trend.

SBF, PSBF, and the five flavonoid compounds markedly decreased histamine secretion in antigen-stimulated RBL-2H3 mast cells, with quercitrin, quercetin, isorhamnetin (40 μmol/L), SBF (100 μg/mL), and PSBF (25 μg/mL) showing the strongest effects.

Toluidine blue staining showed that treatment with quercitrin, SBF, PSBF, or the reference drug ketotifen fumarate restored normal elongated cell morphology and intracytoplasmic granule distribution in IgE/antigen-stimulated RBL-2H3 cells, indicating inhibition of degranulation.
IgE sensitization and antigen challenge significantly increased IL-4 secretion from RBL-2H3 cells while significantly decreasing IFN-γ production.

Treatment with quercitrin, isorhamnetin (40 μmol/L), and SBF (100 μg/mL) significantly reduced IL-4 levels, while only quercitrin and SBF significantly increased IFN-γ levels in stimulated RBL-2H3 cells.
Quercitrin and SBF treatment restored the IFN-γ/IL-4 ratio in stimulated RBL-2H3 cells to levels comparable to unstimulated controls, indicating normalization of Th1/Th2 balance.
Antigen stimulation of IgE-sensitized RBL-2H3 cells markedly increased intracellular calcium ([Ca2+]i) levels compared with unstimulated controls.
SBF, PSBF, and quercetin (especially SBF and PSBF at 100 μg/mL and quercetin at 40 μmol/L) reduced the antigen-induced increase in intracellular Ca2+ influx in RBL-2H3 cells.
SBF, PSBF, and the flavonoid compounds significantly reduced phosphorylation of p38 MAPK in IgE/antigen-stimulated RBL-2H3 cells, with quercitrin showing a strong effect.
Among all tested treatments, only PSBF at 100 μg/mL significantly downregulated ERK phosphorylation in IgE/antigen-stimulated RBL-2H3 cells.
SBF, PSBF, rutin, quercitrin, quercetin, and isorhamnetin markedly reduced phosphorylation of both p38 and JNK MAPK proteins in stimulated RBL-2H3 mast cells.
Mice immunized with the IgE-Fc-coupled VLP vaccine developed high titers of anti-IgE antibodies in serum and elevated numbers of anti-IgE secreting plasma cells in lymphoid organs.
Vaccine-induced anti-IgE antibodies reduced levels of free IgE in serum of immunized mice.
Vaccination reduced the amount of IgE bound to FcεRI receptors on the surface of basophils.
Immunized mice were protected from systemic and local allergen challenge compared to unimmunized/control mice, consistent with reduced effector-cell-bound IgE.

Despite induction of anti-IgE antibodies, immunized sensitized (allergic) mice showed no acute or chronic allergic response, indicating the vaccine does not itself trigger mast cell/basophil activation via IgE cross-linking.
Osteoporosis prevalence was substantially lower in cutaneous mastocytosis (3.7%) than in monoclonal mast cell activation syndrome (30.8%) or systemic mastocytosis (34.1%).
Vertebral fracture prevalence was also lower in CM (0.0%) compared with MMAS (15.4%) and SM (20%).
Most patients with OP and VFs in the non-systemic-mastocytosis (CM/MMAS) groups had the usual known risk factors for osteoporosis, rather than mastocytosis-specific bone disease.

One non-SM patient with an SM-like osteoporosis phenotype had elevated bone marrow tryptase, later developed a bone marrow KIT mutation on follow-up, and had a family history of systemic mastocytosis.

Osteoporosis is not a common clinical finding in cutaneous mastocytosis but is frequent in monoclonal mast cell activation syndrome, suggesting differing bone disease mechanisms across clonal mast cell disorder subtypes.

Corneal nerve fiber density (CNFD) was significantly lower in diabetic patients compared with healthy controls, with differences seen both in those with overt polyneuropathy and those with neuropathic symptoms alone.
Corneal nerve fiber length (CNFL) was found to be lower in diabetic patients compared with healthy controls.
The authors conclude that CCM can identify small fiber neuropathy in diabetic patients with neuropathic symptoms but normal EMG, enabling earlier diagnosis.
Anti-plexin-D1 antibody seropositive small fiber neuropathy predominantly affects female patients.
Patients with anti-plexin-D1 seropositive SFN typically show normal skin biopsy findings despite clinical neuropathic pain and dysautonomia symptoms.
Nerve conduction studies are typically normal in anti-plexin-D1 seropositive SFN patients, consistent with isolated small fiber involvement.
Anti-plexin-D1 seropositivity shows an association with concurrent chronic pain conditions.
Nearly half of the anti-plexin-D1 seropositive SFN patients underwent an interventional pain procedure as part of management.
Anti-plexin-D1 seropositive SFN represents a distinct subgroup of SFN defined by unique demographics, clinical phenotype, biopsy findings, and treatment approach.
SFN and PPN groups did not differ on clinical measures of neuropathic pain duration, frequency, and intensity.
Cognitive profiles were similar across SFN, PPN, and healthy control groups.
SFN patients showed higher levels of anxiety compared to both PPN patients and healthy controls, even accounting for pain intensity.
SFN patients showed higher levels of alexithymia compared to both PPN patients and healthy controls, even accounting for pain intensity.
Both SFN and PPN patient groups showed maladaptive pain coping strategies compared to healthy controls.
Only SFN patients showed higher levels of acceptance of pain compared to the other groups.
Pain intensity and neuropathic symptoms were associated with mood disturbance, lower quality of life, and catastrophism.
Higher perceived pain intensity correlated with greater use of maladaptive coping strategies.
Personality assessment revealed significant feelings of worthlessness and somatization traits in both SFN and PPN patients compared to healthy controls.
No abnormal p-syn aggregates were detected in skin nerves of the 11 very elderly healthy subjects (including centenarians) who showed no clinical signs of synucleinopathy.
No abnormal p-syn deposits were found in skin nerves of the 20 elderly patients suspected of acquired small fiber neuropathy, despite predisposing causes for peripheral neuropathy.

Skin biopsy confirmed small fiber neuropathy in 18 of the 20 elderly patients who had predisposing causes for peripheral neuropathy (diabetes, autoimmune connective disease, hepatitis C, B12 deficiency).

Two elderly subjects (aged 102 and 98) excluded from the healthy group due to subclinical parkinsonian signs (bradykinesia, rigidity) showed abnormal p-syn deposits in skin nerves, supporting detection of synucleinopathy in an early/preclinical phase.

A literature review of 490 healthy subjects across studies using immunofluorescence for skin p-syn found positivity in only 4 subjects (from a single study), indicating virtual absence of p-syn deposits in the healthy population.

Combining the reviewed literature and original very elderly/centenarian data, the authors estimate skin p-syn immunofluorescence has ~99% specificity for differentiating healthy controls from patients with synucleinopathy.

Autopsy literature indicates incidental Lewy body (ILB) prevalence in the brain increases with age, reported as 4.7% in the sixth decade, 9.3% in the seventh decade, and 12.8% in the eighth decade, with an overall autopsy prevalence of roughly 10%-15%.

A previously identified chromosome 5q22 risk allele associated with heart failure mortality lies in an enhancer upstream of TSLP and increases NHLH1 transcription factor binding, resulting in increased TSLP expression in human heart tissue.
Increased mechanical strain of primary human myocardial fibroblasts induces increased TSLP expression, suggesting a mechanotransduction pathway linking cardiac strain to TSLP production.

Single-nuclei RNA sequencing of human heart tissue shows that the TSLP receptor is expressed specifically in myocardial mast cells, identifying a candidate cellular target for TSLP signaling in the heart.

Overexpression of TSLP induces increased transforming growth factor beta expression in myocardial mast cells and results in tissue fibrosis, linking the TSLP genetic risk pathway to fibrotic remodeling.
The authors describe diabetic gastroparesis as a common manifestation of autonomic neuropathy occurring in patients with long-standing, poorly controlled diabetes.
The authors suggest that choice of insulin preparation and timing of administration can be tailored to the predominant gastroparesis symptomatology in diabetic patients.
The authors advise careful selection of oral glucose-lowering drugs in patients with diabetic gastroparesis due to symptom considerations.
Mast cells are increasingly recognized as contributing to the pathophysiology of irritable bowel syndrome, providing rationale for mast cell-directed therapies.
Treatment with disodium cromoglycate produced a significant overall improvement in key IBS symptoms compared to control groups across included trials.
Treatment with ebastine produced a significant overall improvement in key IBS symptoms compared to control groups across included trials.
Treatment with ketotifen produced a significant overall improvement in key IBS symptoms compared to control groups across included trials.
Mast cells are increasingly implicated in the underlying pathophysiology of irritable bowel syndrome.
Of the 11 included trials on mast cell directed therapies for IBS, only three were judged to be at low risk of bias, indicating limited overall evidence quality.
TGF-β1 stimulation downregulated miR-29b expression in cardiac fibroblasts, while addition of choline upregulated it, and the M3 receptor antagonist 4-DAMP reversed choline's effect.

Overexpression of miR-29b (mimics) reversed the TGF-β1-induced upregulation of collagen I, α-SMA, and CTGF protein levels in cardiac fibroblasts, but inhibition of miR-29b alone did not affect these fibrosis markers.

The anti-fibrotic effect of choline (reduced collagen I, α-SMA, CTGF) was blocked when miR-29b was knocked down using an inhibitor, showing miR-29b mediates choline's effect via M3 receptor activation.

Immunofluorescence confirmed choline reduced TGF-β1-induced upregulation of collagen I and α-SMA, and this benefit was lost when miR-29b was inhibited; separately, overexpressing miR-29b countered the fibrotic effect of blocking M3 receptor with 4-DAMP.
TGF-β1 promoted migration/invasion of cardiac fibroblasts (scratch and transwell assays), an effect suppressed by choline but restored when miR-29b was inhibited.

Bioinformatic screening across four miRNA-target prediction databases (miRDB, miRTarBase, TargetScan, PicTar) identified 19 common candidate genes, from which BACE1 was selected as a novel miR-29b target relevant to cardiac fibrosis based on expression, cardiac abundance, and cross-species conservation of binding sites.
BACE1 protein was increased by TGF-β1 stimulation and this increase was reduced by miR-29b mimics, while miR-29b inhibition did not further affect TGF-β1's effect on BACE1.

Choline reduced TGF-β1-induced BACE1 protein levels in cardiac fibroblasts, and this reduction was reversed by the M3 receptor antagonist 4-DAMP, indicating BACE1 is downstream of M3 receptor activation.
Overexpression of BACE1 via plasmid transfection reduced miR-29b expression levels, and BACE1 overexpression also abolished the anti-fibrotic (collagen I-reducing) effect of miR-29b mimics.

Overall, the study proposes a signaling cascade whereby choline activates the M3 receptor to upregulate miR-29b, which in turn downregulates BACE1, reducing collagen I and inhibiting cardiac fibrosis.
Females predominated among ME/CFS patients at every specialty clinic, with an overall female-to-male ratio of 2.9, ranging from 1.6 to 5.6 across sites.

Socio-demographic variables differed statistically by clinical site, but distributions overlapped extensively and trended in the same direction (predominantly insured, white, highly educated women) across all seven clinics.
Mean duration of fatigue (used as a surrogate for ME/CFS illness duration) varied substantially across clinics, ranging from 9.4 to 17.9 years.
The number of medications prescribed per patient showed the largest cross-site variation of any general characteristic, with means ranging from 4.1 to 8.2, a statistically significant difference.

Across all seven clinics, SF-36 Role Physical and Vitality subscales were consistently the most impaired domains, while Mental Health and Role Emotional were the least impaired, with no significant differences between sites.
ME/CFS patients spent about half as many hours per day in vertical activity (sitting, standing, walking) as healthy controls, averaging 7.5 hours versus a reported 14 hours in healthy controls.

The large majority of patients could tolerate only mild exercise, with 73.6% reporting mild exercise engagement, compared to just 29.5% for moderate and 7.8% for strenuous exercise at least once weekly.
Patients reported markedly more physically unhealthy days (mean 23.2 of past 30 days) than the 2017 U.S. general population average of 4.0 days.

Patients reported markedly more mentally unhealthy days (mean 9.2 of past 30 days) than the U.S. general population average of 4.0 days, alongside clinically significant PHQ-8 and Zung depression scores.

Post-exertional malaise (PEM) was identified concordantly by all three assessment methods (Illness Abstraction Form, CDC Symptom Inventory, DePaul Symptom Questionnaire) in 81% of participants, with only 1.3% failing to show PEM by any method.
The CDC Symptom Inventory identified PEM presence in 94.7% of patients overall, with a mean symptom score of 11.7, consistent across clinics.

PROMIS sleep-related impairment T-scores varied by site with a 3.8-point difference that would ordinarily be considered clinically meaningful, but the within-site standard deviations were nearly twice this difference, indicating the site variation was not clinically important relative to individual heterogeneity.
Cognitive symptoms — concentration, memory, only focusing on one thing, and word-finding difficulty — were consistently the highest-scoring DSQ symptoms across all clinics and overall.
Muscle-related pain symptoms consistently scored higher than joint pain symptoms in both the CDC Symptom Inventory and DePaul Symptom Questionnaire at every clinic.
Among immunologic/inflammatory symptoms, sinus problems and tender lymph nodes had the highest mean scores while fever had the lowest, a pattern consistent across nearly all clinics.

Applying standardized algorithms, the 1994 CFS research case definition was met by the highest proportion of patients (83.4%), while the 2003 Canadian ME/CFS case definition was met by the lowest proportion (50.1%), demonstrating that case definitions capture different, non-overlapping proportions of clinically diagnosed patients.

Among 449 patients with complete data, 70.2% met two or more of the three ME/CFS case definition algorithms, while 9.1% met none of the algorithms, illustrating incomplete overlap between case definitions.

Despite substantial differences in clinical practice characteristics (board certification, practice size, location, payment structure) across the seven specialty clinics, standardized measures of ME/CFS symptoms and function showed few statistically significant and no clinically meaningful differences between clinics, suggesting expert clinicians recognize the same, albeit heterogeneous, clinical entity.
Patients with post-COVID ME/CFS had significantly lower SF-36 physical function scores compared to PCS patients without ME/CFS.

ME/CFS patients had significantly higher disability as measured by the Bell score compared to non-ME/CFS PCS patients (higher Bell score value indicates less restriction, so lower Bell score = more disability; text reports higher degree of disability).
ME/CFS patients showed more severe orthostatic intolerance than non-ME/CFS PCS patients.
ME/CFS patients showed more severe vasomotor symptoms than non-ME/CFS PCS patients.
ME/CFS patients had significantly higher fatigue severity scores (Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire) than non-ME/CFS PCS patients.
ME/CFS patients had significantly higher postexertional malaise (PEM) severity than non-ME/CFS PCS patients.
The immune symptom score (painful lymph nodes, throat pain, flu-like feeling) was significantly higher in the ME/CFS group compared to non-ME/CFS PCS.
Median maximum hand grip strength (Fmax 1), adjusted for age and sex, was below normal population values in both PCS patient groups.
Most HGS parameters showed little difference between the ME/CFS and non-ME/CFS PCS groups, except fatigue ratio 2 which was higher in ME/CFS.
In ME/CFS patients, lower hand grip strength strongly correlated with worse SF-36 physical function and Bell disability score.
In ME/CFS patients, lower hand grip strength correlated with more PEM, pain, fatigue, cognitive impairment, and orthostatic intolerance.
In ME/CFS patients, higher HGS fatigue ratios correlated with more PEM, fatigue, and cognitive and orthostatic symptoms.
In non-ME/CFS PCS patients, HGS correlated only with SF-36 physical function and pain, but showed no correlation with PEM, fatigue, cognition, orthostatic intolerance, or Bell score.
A correlation between SF-36 physical function and cognitive impairment was observed only in the ME/CFS cohort, not in non-ME/CFS PCS, despite similar cognitive symptom severity between groups.

Correlations of more impaired cognition with more pain, PEM, and lower Bell score were found only in the ME/CFS group, not in non-ME/CFS PCS patients, despite similar cognitive symptom severity between groups.

Jäkel et al. previously showed HGS to be a sensitive diagnostic test for muscular fatigue, fatigability, and disease severity in ME/CFS, and lower HGS was associated with lower Bell score, more severe PEM, and myalgia in prepandemic postinfectious ME/CFS.
In a prior 2023 study, impaired HGS six months after COVID-19 onset was identified as a risk factor for symptom persistence in PCS.
An MRI study found higher muscle sodium content in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, correlating with HGS, suggesting impaired ion transport related to hypoperfusion.
In prior work, autoantibodies against vasoregulatory GPCRs (e.g., adrenergic receptors) were associated with fatigue and impaired peripheral perfusion in ME/CFS but not in PCS.

A recent study comparing mitochondrial function and morphology in muscle found that both PCS and ME/CFS patients had fatigue and impaired mitochondrial function, but distinct morphological changes indicating mitochondrial damage were found only in ME/CFS.
A proangiogenic biomarker pattern was observed in PCS but not in ME/CFS in prior work by this group.
A large proportion of ME/CFS patients (35-90%) have gastrointestinal complaints, often associated with comorbid IBS and IBD.
The Firmicutes phylum is often decreased in the gut microbiome of ME/CFS patients relative to homeostatic composition.
The Bacteroidetes phylum is often increased in the gut microbiome of ME/CFS patients relative to homeostatic composition.
In a controlled study, pathological bacterial translocation occurred in 6 of 9 main bacterial genera 72 hours after a defined stress test in ME/CFS patients, versus 2 of 9 genera in controls.
ME/CFS patients show increased IgA and IgM antibody levels against LPS, a marker of gram-negative bacterial translocation, correlating with disease severity.

Metagenomic profiling identified distinct fecal bacterial clusters in ME/CFS with concomitant IBS (increased unclassified Alistipes, decreased Faecalibacterium) versus ME/CFS without IBS (increased unclassified Bacteroides, decreased Bacteroides vulgatus), alongside differing metabolomic pathways (unsaturated fatty acid synthesis, atrazine degradation, vitamin B6 synthesis, pyrimidine ribonucleoside degradation).
A study examining viral taxa in feces, blood, and saliva found no differences between ME/CFS patients and controls.
ME/CFS patients show less gut microbiome biodiversity compared to healthy individuals, thought to contribute to disease onset and progression.
An 8-week pilot study of multiple probiotics in CFS/ME patients led to improved well-being and reduced inflammatory and oxidative markers.

In 15 CFS patients given a Lactobacillus/Bifidobacterium probiotic combination for 4 weeks, neurocognitive function improved but fatigue and physical activity scores showed no significant change; 6 of 15 patients reported subjective improvement.
A systematic review of 25 studies (including 24 RCTs) found the evidence for probiotic interventions on gastrointestinal/IBS symptoms in CFS/ME to be poor and limited.
A study reported reduction in ME/CFS symptoms after rectal infusion of bacteria, though the majority of patients (52 of 60) had concomitant IBS as an underlying condition.

In a non-randomized study, 21 CFS patients received 10 FMT infusions via rectal catheter over 10 days; 17 reported 65-95% self-assessed improvement, and 7 reported normalization of quality of life and performance.
A small randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study found FMT to be safe but it did not relieve symptoms or improve health-related quality of life in CFS patients.

A meta-analysis of 24 studies on FMT found that clinical response correlated with the extent of donor microbiome engraftment; antibiotic pretreatment and combined upper/lower gastrointestinal administration improved engraftment, and Bacteroidetes/Actinobacteria showed higher engraftment rates than Firmicutes/Proteobacteria.
Tryptophan levels, a neurotransmitter influenced by the gut microbiome, have been linked to ME/CFS.

Increased TGF-β production has been reported as part of gut-brain axis immune changes in ME/CFS, though these findings remain controversial as chronic inflammation may reflect an underlying disease rather than a primary cause.
A Danish study found that ME/CFS patients have a lower quality of life than patients with cancer, stroke, or multiple sclerosis.
Glutamate levels in the posterior cingulate cortex were significantly higher in long COVID patients than in healthy controls.
Glutamate levels in the posterior cingulate cortex were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
No significant difference in brain neurochemical levels, including glutamate, was found between the long COVID and ME/CFS cohorts.
N-acetyl-aspartate levels in the posterior cingulate cortex were significantly higher in long COVID patients compared with healthy controls.
Brain neurochemical levels measured by MRS were associated with self-reported severity measures in both long COVID and ME/CFS patients.

There was no statistically significant difference between MS patients, ME/CFS patients, and healthy controls in fatigue- or physical activity-related attentional bias as measured by the Visual Probe Task.
Both MS and ME/CFS patients showed a stronger tendency than healthy controls to interpret ambiguous information in a somatically threatening way (interpretation bias).
The somatic interpretation bias was significantly stronger in MS patients than in ME/CFS patients.
In MS patients, interpretation bias was significantly correlated with cognitive responses to symptoms.
Fatigue and brain fog were the most severely rated long COVID symptoms, with mean severities of 9.6 and 8.9 out of 10 respectively.
Chest pain, dizziness/vertigo, shortness of breath, and cough were the most frequently reported long COVID symptoms after applying an individual median cutoff.
Otalgia and skin rashes were the least frequently reported long COVID symptoms in the cohort.
Hierarchical cluster analysis identified 'Cluster A' consisting of insomnia, headache, brain fog, fatigue, muscle pain, joint pain and paresthesia, uniting rheumatologic and neurological symptoms.
'Cluster B' groups neurological symptoms (confusion, dizziness/vertigo, loss of smell/taste) and psychological symptoms (anxiety, depression) together with cardiologic and pulmonary symptoms.
'Cluster C' shows co-occurrence of gastrointestinal symptoms with tinnitus/otalgia, skin rashes, and infection-associated symptoms such as fever and loss of appetite.
In the combined heatmap clustering of participants and symptoms, 1424 participants displayed symptoms spanning all three clusters (A, B, and C) simultaneously.
A separate subgroup of 899 participants in the heatmap predominantly showed symptoms belonging to clusters A and B rather than all three clusters.

Fatigue clustered with pain and musculoskeletal symptoms similarly in both this study's Cluster A and in the study by Kenny et al., which used an identical long COVID definition and similar age distribution, though this study's much larger sample additionally confirmed the cardiorespiratory cluster and its association with neurological symptoms like loss of smell/taste and confusion.

The paper discusses that a large symptom overlap exists between long COVID and ME/CFS core criteria (fatigue, reduced daily activity, post-exertional malaise), with both syndromes hypothesized to originate from a dysregulated immune response and hyperinflammation.

Citing the COVID Human Genetic Effort consortium, the authors note a hypothesis that persistent viral reservoirs cause fever spikes (part of Cluster C) while autoimmunity targeting G-protein-coupled receptors on neurons may underlie neurological symptoms such as loss of smell/taste and confusion (as in Cluster B).
Approximately 30-60% of individuals infected with COVID-19 go on to develop long COVID.
LC patients showed significantly decreased cortisol levels compared to matched control groups in an immunological study by Klein et al.
LC patients had elevated antibody responses to spike protein compared to recovered or uninfected individuals, suggesting persistent viral antigen stimulation.

Using US Veterans Affairs healthcare databases, Xie et al. found COVID-19 survivors had increased risk of cardiovascular outcomes including heart failure, myocarditis, pericarditis, dysrhythmias, ischemic/non-ischemic heart disease, and thromboembolic disease, even in non-hospitalized patients.

The same VA database analysis found increased risk of gastrointestinal disorders in LC including peptic ulcer disease, pancreatitis, hepatic/biliary disease, motility disorders, dyspepsia, indigestion, bloating and reflux.

Gut microbiota studies in LC patients found lower levels of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and higher levels of Bacteroides vulgatus and Ruminococcus gnavus, with butyrate-producing Bifidobacterium pseudocatenulatum and F. prausnitzii inversely correlated with LC at 6 months.
Human subjects with LC-related cognitive impairment showed elevated plasma CCL11 (eotaxin-1) levels compared to control groups.
In a mouse model, systemic injection of CCL11 activated hippocampal microglia, causing myelin loss and inhibited neurogenesis linked to cognitive impairment.
In a retrospective cohort of 140 LC patients assessed using IOM 2015 criteria, about 43% met criteria for the ME/CFS phenotype.

Klein et al. found LC patients had increased non-classical monocytes, activated B cells, double-negative B cells, exhausted T cells, and IL-4/IL-6-secreting T cells compared to matched controls, correlating with EBV antibody reactivity.

Phetsouphanh et al. reported persistent immunological dysfunction for eight months in LC patients, with activated innate immune cells and elevated expression of type I IFN (IFN-β) and type III IFN (IFN-λ1).
A triad of elevated cytokines - IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α - has been reported to remain dysregulated in LC patients.
A Danish cohort study found that persistent symptoms at two months post-SARS-CoV-2 infection were more common in children of all ages compared with matched uninfected controls.

A Swedish study of over 162,000 children found girls had a higher incidence of long COVID than boys, along with higher risk in older adolescents and those with chronic conditions or prior hospitalization.
Long COVID incidence in children was six times higher when the child's parents also had long-term COVID-19, though similar across parental education levels.

In a Canadian multi-site pediatric emergency study, the proportion of children reporting LC symptoms and quality-of-life changes was very low and similar between SARS-CoV-2 positive and negative groups at 6 and 12 months.
In a German household study, infected adolescent girls and infected adult women and men had increased risk of negative long COVID outcomes that appeared to cluster within families.

A meta-analysis of 40 studies (12,424 participants) found about one-quarter of pediatric COVID-19 patients had long COVID symptoms across multiple organ systems, more common in females and older/adolescent age groups.
Machine-learning clustering of over 6000 RECOVER/N3C long COVID patients identified a 'Multisystem + lab' phenotype with multiple laboratory abnormalities that was associated with worse prognosis.
Patients coded with the U09.9 long COVID ICD-10 code in EHR data were predominantly female, White, non-Hispanic, and from low-unemployment/low-poverty areas, suggesting diagnostic disparities.
An XGBoost machine-learning model trained on N3C EHR data from 597 long COVID patients identified LC patients among COVID-19 patients with high precision.
Analysis of two British birth cohorts found that elevated lifetime BMI, and earlier age of onset of obesity/overweight, increased the risk of developing long COVID.

Single-cell multi-omic profiling showed COVID-19 promotes age-induced immune cell polarization and senescence-related gene expression, with age-associated dendritic cells showing increased IFN-stimulated gene expression but decreased antigen-presenting ability.
PBMCs from long COVID patients showed persistently high IFN-γ release mediated by CD8+ T cells, compared to PBMCs from patients recovered from acute COVID-19, without ex vivo peptide stimulation.

IFN-γ levels significantly decreased after vaccination in long COVID patients, and reduction to baseline correlated with symptom improvement/resolution, though it is unclear if IFN-γ is a mediator or merely a biomarker.
Serotonin levels were found to be reduced in people with long COVID, suggesting that restoring circulating serotonin might improve symptoms.

Three highly functioning individuals with severe fatigue and cognitive impairment from long COVID experienced rapid remission following casirivimab/imdevimab monoclonal antibody cocktail infusions, regardless of age, sex, or vaccination status.
Long COVID patients showed markedly slower reaction times (about three standard deviations) than age-matched controls without LC on a brief web-based psychomotor cognitive test.

In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, the synbiotic SIM01 given twice daily for six months alleviated neuropsychiatric long COVID symptoms including concentration difficulties and memory loss.

In a prior (non-LC) study, Lactobacillus Plantarum 299v supplementation improved vascular endothelial function and reduced inflammatory biomarkers in men with stable coronary artery disease, motivating its investigation for LC-associated endothelial dysfunction.
In a randomized placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, outpatient metformin treatment for acute COVID-19 reduced the incidence of subsequent long COVID by 42%.
In a rat single-cell transcriptomic study of aging, caloric restriction reversed excessive inflammation in immune cells.

In murine models, ketone bodies (β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate) serve as essential fuels for CD8+ T cell metabolism, with ketolysis acting as a metabolic and epigenetic driver of optimal CD8+ T cell effector responses.
In a randomized crossover multi-omics trial, a vegan diet substantially affected the innate immune system and antiviral immunity, while a ketogenic diet significantly affected adaptive immunity.
Patients with hypertension, obesity, diabetes, chronic lung disease, and heart disease are more dramatically impacted by COVID-19 and more likely to develop long COVID.

Deficiencies in vitamins B and C, coenzyme Q, sodium, magnesium, zinc, folic acid, tryptophan, and essential fatty acids are reported to contribute to the progression and severity of chronic fatigue syndrome.

Adjusted mean levels of psychological flexibility were lowest in the Somatic Symptom Disorder group, intermediate in the central sensitivity syndromes group, and highest in controls without SSD or CSS.
A markedly higher proportion of SSD patients (74%) had low psychological flexibility compared to CSS patients (42%) and controls (21%).
Within the SSD group, higher psychological flexibility was significantly associated with better mental health.
Interaction analysis found no evidence that psychological flexibility buffered the impact of more severe somatic symptoms on mental health.
A quarter of autistic adults reported at least one perceived misdiagnosis of a psychiatric condition diagnosed prior to their autism diagnosis.
Autistic women were more likely than autistic men to report having received at least one psychiatric diagnosis prior to their autism diagnosis.
Autistic women were more likely than autistic men to perceive at least one prior psychiatric diagnosis as a misdiagnosis.
Among only those participants who had received a prior psychiatric diagnosis, gender no longer predicted the likelihood of reporting a perceived misdiagnosis.
Personality disorders were the most frequently perceived misdiagnosis among autistic adults, with women far more likely than men to report this misdiagnosis.
Anxiety disorders were a commonly perceived misdiagnosis, with autistic women more likely than men to report this.
Mood disorders were a commonly perceived misdiagnosis, with autistic women more likely than men to report this.
A perceived misdiagnosis of chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS)/burnout-related disorder was reported by 4% of autistic adults, with no significant difference between men and women.
A perceived misdiagnosis of ADHD/ADD was reported by 2.8% of autistic adults, with no significant difference between men and women.
A later age of autism diagnosis was associated with greater odds of reporting at least one prior psychiatric diagnosis and at least one perceived misdiagnosis.
Participants diagnosed with autism between ages 18 and 54 were more likely to report at least one perceived misdiagnosis compared with those diagnosed before age 18 or at/after age 55.
Autistic women reported a significantly greater average number of perceived misdiagnoses than autistic men.
The prevalence of temporomandibular disorders (TMD) is higher among EDS patients, particularly the hypermobile subtype (hEDS), compared with the general population.
In a cohort combining Marfan syndrome and EDS patients with generalized joint hypermobility, 69% reported myofascial pain.
A case-control study of hEDS patients (n=26) found higher rates of myalgia (5 vs 0), arthralgia (5 vs 0), and headache attributed to TMD (13 vs 0) compared with controls, using DC/TMD criteria.
A systematic review of 12 studies estimated the mean prevalence of TMD manifestations in EDS patients at approximately 65% (range 26.6-100%), with hEDS most commonly affected.
In hEDS patients (n=14), myalgia was diagnosed in 97%, arthralgia in 64%, and disc-related disorders in 57%, compared with 1.7% of non-EDS controls diagnosed with disc-related disorders.
In a large case-control study, 62% of hEDS/Hypermobile Spectrum Disorder patients exhibited TMJ pain.
TMD symptoms were more frequent (87.7%) among patients with comorbid fibromyalgia and hEDS/HSD than in hEDS/HSD patients without fibromyalgia.
In a study of 114 women with EDS in Sweden, there was significantly greater orofacial pain compared with controls.
47% of EDS patients reported masticatory muscle pain compared with 4% of matched controls, and 65% of EDS patients had TMJ hypermobility during mouth opening.
A study of 17 patients with vascular EDS (vEDS) found a significantly higher prevalence of arthralgia compared with controls.
A cohort of 38 EDS patients showed 71% with arthralgia and 92% with myalgia based on DC/TMD criteria.
In over 250 participants with classical or hEDS, 85% reported pain in the masticatory muscles, and those with TMD had 2.5-fold higher likelihood of chronic pain.
EDS patients with TMD were 2.5 times more likely to suffer from chronic pain than those without TMD.
In 38 EDS patients, 60% were diagnosed with disc displacement with reduction, 79% had subluxations, and 22% had degenerative joint disease based on DC/TMD.
A vEDS cohort matched to healthy controls showed a significantly higher prevalence (71%) of TMJ disc disorders.
Radiological assessment showed a greater proportion (44%) of early arthritic remodelling of TMJ articulating surfaces in vEDS patients compared with controls.
In 18 female EDS patients with TMD, clicking/locking occurred in one-third of cases, seven experienced dislocations, and all reported TMJ pain.
49% of patients with cEDS/hEDS reported pain or restricted movement of the jaw.
In a case-control study, individuals with hEDS had reduced pain-free mouth opening and reduced maximum mouth opening compared with controls.

A single patient with dermatosparaxis EDS exhibited limited horizontal movement but an increased mouth opening of more than 50 mm, compared with normative Turkish population means (44.2 mm male, 40.29 mm female).
EDS patients with TMD showed significantly reduced oral health-related quality of life (OHRQoL) compared with EDS patients without oral involvement, measured by Oral Health Impact Profile.
EDS participants reporting frequent pain had significantly reduced OHRQoL, highlighting the influence of pain on quality of life.
A study on eating behaviour in EDS suggested that TMD could be a potential co-factor contributing to the development of an eating disorder.

A case report of a 33-year-old woman with hEDS, TMJ subluxation, myalgia and arthralgia treated with splint therapy and osteopathic therapy reported complete resolution of TMJ and masseter pain after 18 months.
Splint therapy resulted in positive outcomes for over 50% of hEDS/cEDS participants, and jaw training and occlusal adjustments were each effective in 50% of cases.
16 of 18 EDS patients benefitted from habit unlearning, heat/massage application, and physiotherapy for TMD.

18 female EDS patients with TMD who did not respond to conservative treatment underwent arthroscopy, arthrocentesis, balloon dilation and intra-articular morphine, and were symptom-free at a mean 62-month follow-up.
Arthrocentesis performed for recurrent acute TMJ locking with reduced mouth opening and joint pain in an EDS patient resulted in an uneventful follow-up.
Arthroscopic discopexy performed on an EDS patient with masticatory pain and TMJ luxation tendency significantly reduced hypermobility and pain symptoms without complications.

A 40-year-old EDS patient with recurrent anterior disc dislocation, posterior ligament laxity and complete disc disruption underwent discectomy with reconstruction using a temporalis muscle osteofascial flap, chosen to reduce soft-tissue healing complications, and showed improved symptoms and increased range of motion at 2.5-year follow-up.

Two EDS patients with subluxation, clicking, locking and chronic TMJ pain underwent myofascial temporalis flap surgery with condyle recontouring and recovered without complications, reporting no recurring TMJ symptoms at 1.5-year follow-up.

An 18-year-old EDS patient with TMJ laxity underwent TMJ arthroplasty using a cryopreserved cranial bone cube secured under the zygomatic arch, resulting in no complications and increased oral aperture with no recurrent dislocations at one-year follow-up.

An EDS patient with 26 prior left-sided TMJ dislocations underwent condylectomy after failed conservative and minimally invasive treatments, with intermaxillary fixation for 4 weeks, and reported no additional dislocations or symptoms at 18-month follow-up, though the procedure was later noted to be controversial in the literature.

A 47-year-old woman with hEDS and bilateral TMJ pain, disc displacement and degenerative joint disease underwent bimaxillary surgery, with an uneventful post-operative course and resolution of TMJ pain and decreased orofacial pain during mastication at one-month follow-up.

A female EDS patient with refractory TMD who failed conservative and invasive therapy underwent total TMJ replacement in end-stage degenerative joint disease; while one side healed uneventfully, the other side developed repeated prosthesis complications requiring replacement and eventual free fibular flap reconstruction, with chronic pain persisting despite these efforts, hypothesized to relate to EDS-associated impaired soft-tissue healing.

The review notes that only one clinical trial (NCT05757960) is currently recruiting to assess the effectiveness of conservative, TMD-specific physiotherapy in EDS patients, highlighting a scarcity of treatment literature, especially regarding conservative approaches.

The review concludes that TMD is a frequent diagnosis among EDS patients, compromising them with pain and disc/capsule-related symptoms, and that oral health-related quality of life is generally lower than in the general population, while treatment remains an ongoing challenge due to scarce literature.

There was no significant difference in spirometric parameters (FVC, FEV1, IVC) between hEDS patients and matched healthy controls, consistent with prior literature showing normal lung function in hEDS.
At 30% of inspiratory vital capacity (IV30), hEDS patients showed significantly reduced accuracy of lung volume perception compared to healthy controls, both in absolute (mL) and percentage error.

At 50% of inspiratory vital capacity (IV50), there was no significant difference in lung volume perception accuracy between hEDS patients and controls, suggesting increased stretch provides better sensory information at higher volumes.

In free breathing (no cognitive task), breathing frequency (fB) was significantly higher in hEDS patients compared to controls, consistent with a clinical tendency toward hyperventilation in this population.

During a cognitive task (Trail Making Test part B), hEDS patients showed significantly greater spatial and temporal ventilatory variability than controls, including increased VT,SD, CoefVar_V, PPSD, and CoefVar_t, indicating erratic breathing patterns including episodes of apnea.
During the free breathing condition (no cognitive task), there was no significant difference between hEDS and control groups in most ventilatory variability parameters, except breathing frequency.
Self-reported subjective ability to perceive lung volume on a 0-10 scale did not differ significantly between hEDS patients and controls, despite objective differences found with the device.

The novel lung volume perception device (IVCfm) was strongly and significantly correlated with standard spirometer measurements of inspiratory vital capacity, supporting its validity as a measurement tool.

The critique discusses occipito-cervical fusion as a surgical treatment for craniocervical instability in EDS patients, noting the original study's limitations including small sample size, lack of a control group, and absence of long-term follow-up.
