Diazinon inhibited A23187-induced ERK phosphorylation, a signaling event downstream of calcium influx, while having little effect on p38 phosphorylation.
Diazinon significantly inhibited IgE cross-linking-mediated degranulation and Tnf/IL4 expression while having little effect on calcium influx.

MRGPRX2 is a promiscuous mast cell receptor mediating IgE-independent degranulation and is implicated in multiple mast cell-mediated disorders including chronic urticaria, atopic dermatitis, and pain disorders.

Novel small molecule MRGPRX2 antagonists potently inhibited agonist-induced MRGPRX2 activation and mast cell degranulation across cell lines overexpressing MRGPRX2, LAD2 mast cells, peripheral stem cell-derived mast cells, and isolated skin mast cells.
Orally administered MRGPRX2 antagonists inhibited agonist-induced skin mast cell degranulation and associated vascular permeability in human MRGPRX2 knock-in mice.
MRGPRX2 antagonist treatment dose-dependently inhibited agonist-induced mast cell degranulation and histamine release in ex vivo human skin tissue as assessed by microdialysis.
AAT1 knockdown in HMC-1 mast cells reduced AAT activity and endogenous SO2 content, and SO2 donor supplementation restored SO2 levels.
AAT1 knockdown significantly increased β-hexosaminidase release (mast cell degranulation) in HMC-1 cells, and this was reversed by SO2 donor supplementation.
The thiol-reducing agent DTT abolished the SO2-mediated suppression of β-hexosaminidase release, implicating a thiol-dependent (sulfenylation) redox mechanism.

Venn analysis intersecting a SO2-sulfenylome dataset with GO datasets for positive/negative regulation of mast cell activation identified LGALS9 (Gal-9) as the sole candidate gene whose protein is both sulfenylated by SO2 and involved in mast cell activation regulation.
SO2 increased sulfenylation of Gal-9 protein in HMC-1 cells (reduced by AAT1 knockdown, restored by SO2 donor), and this modification was reversed by DTT.
In a cell-free system, SO2 treatment directly increased sulfenylation of purified human Gal-9 protein, an effect blocked by DTT.
LC-MS/MS analysis of SO2-treated purified Gal-9 protein identified cysteine 74 as the site of sulfenylation, consistent with high evolutionary conservation of Cys74 across species.
Site-directed mutation of Cys74 to serine (Gal-9-C74S) abolished SO2-induced Gal-9 sulfenylation, whereas the Cys312Ser (C312S) mutant did not, confirming Cys74 as the functional sulfenylation site.
IgE stimulation of RBL-2H3 mast cells significantly reduced SO2 content, AAT1 protein expression, and AAT activity compared with unstimulated controls.
IgE stimulation increased mast cell degranulation in RBL-2H3 cells, and SO2 donor supplementation restored intracellular SO2 and reduced IgE-induced degranulation.

In a mouse IgE-mediated passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) model, IgE/DNP-HSA challenge caused marked dye extravasation and ear swelling accompanied by reduced ear tissue AAT activity and SO2 content.
Pretreatment with SO2 donor recovered ear tissue SO2 content and prevented dye extravasation and ear swelling in the IgE-challenged PCA mouse model.

In a chronic hypoxia/SU5416 (SuHx) mouse model of pulmonary vascular remodeling, lung tissue showed decreased SO2 content and AAT activity along with increased numbers of degranulated mast cells compared with normoxic mice.
Exogenous SO2 supplementation significantly reduced the number of degranulated mast cells and reduced pulmonary arteriole media thickness and area in SuHx mice.

SO2 suppressed IgE-stimulated degranulation in RBL-2H3 cells expressing Gal-9-WT and Gal-9-C312S, but failed to suppress degranulation in cells expressing the Gal-9-C74S mutant, indicating that Cys74 sulfenylation is required for SO2's inhibitory effect on IgE-mediated degranulation.
Hypoxic stimulation decreased AAT activity in mast cells compared with normoxic cells.

SO2 suppressed hypoxia-induced degranulation in HMC-1 cells expressing Gal-9-WT and Gal-9-C312S, but not in cells expressing Gal-9-C74S, confirming Cys74 sulfenylation is required for SO2's suppression of non-IgE (hypoxia)-induced mast cell degranulation.

C48/80, a non-IgE-dependent mast cell degranulation inducer, inhibited AAT activity and SO2 content in HMC-1 cells; SO2 donor supplementation restored intracellular SO2 levels in C48/80-treated cells.

SO2 failed to prevent C48/80-induced mast cell degranulation only in HMC-1 cells transfected with the Gal-9-C74S mutant plasmid, further confirming that Cys74 sulfenylation of Gal-9 mediates SO2's suppressive effect on non-IgE-stimulated MC degranulation.

In scramble-transfected (non-perturbed/uninjured) mast cells, SO2 donor increased intracellular SO2 content but did not affect baseline mast cell degranulation, suggesting exogenous SO2 does not disrupt normal MC homeostasis.
Three concurrent SCN9A variants were identified in two patients from both cohorts, both presenting with classical SFN and burning pain in the lower legs, and classified as Pathogenic.
WFS1 variants causing complete loss of WFS1 protein were identified in patients ITA42 and NET11 and classified as Pathogenic, with NET11 also showing glucose intolerance.
Variants in voltage-gated sodium channel genes were found in 23.8% of the EO-SFN cohort.
Variants in TRP channel genes were observed in 19.3% of the EO-SFN cohort.

Six heterozygous ATP7B variants were identified and classified as Likely Pathogenic; ATP7B affects copper transport and is linked to Wilson's disease and MEDNIK syndrome, both of which can present with peripheral neuropathy and itch.
In individual ITA04, two Likely Pathogenic variants in ATP7B and COL6A2 co-segregated with SFN and distal myopathy in affected family members.

Two COL7A1 variants classified as Likely Pathogenic, previously linked to Epidermolysis Bullosa, were identified in patients with SFN, one of whom also had itch, suggesting a possible role in SFN beyond EB.
Two genetic variants in LZTR1, previously linked to schwannomatosis, were identified in the EO-SFN cohort.

Five TRPA1 variants of uncertain significance were identified in six individuals, all located in the ankyrin repeat hotspot domain, and were associated with cold allodynia in two patients and sheet intolerance in two others.

The Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptor Signaling (NARS) pathway was the only pathway significantly enriched in EO-SFN cases compared to healthy controls, with no pathways significantly enriched in controls.

Two variants of uncertain significance in CHRNA6 and CACNA1S genes, part of the NARS pathway, were identified as causative in the cohort, with CHRNA6 loss-of-function linked to increased allodynia and CACNA1S variants associated with myalgic myopathy and pain transmission.

The SCN10A: c.41G>T variant was observed in two individuals in this cohort and had previously been reported in four SFN patients, though family co-segregation analysis for this variant was inconclusive.
KIF1A and NAGLU were the most frequently selected inherited peripheral neuropathy genes in patients presenting with burning pain and sheet intolerance.
Among 119 heterozygous VUS variants identified across 86 genes, the majority were categorized in the 'Neurotransmission' functional group, followed by 'Ion channels'.
19 of 50 SLE patients with painful symptoms were diagnosed with Small Fiber Neuropathy, predominantly with a non-length-dependent pattern.
7 of 50 SLE patients had a mixed neuropathy involving both large and small nerve fibers.
Patients with SFN were significantly younger than patients with mixed (large and small fiber) neuropathy.
SFN in SLE patients was significantly associated with a history of hypocomplementemia, suggesting a pathogenic role of the complement system.
SFN patients were more likely than patients without neuropathy to be treated with cyclosporine A, suggesting SFN may be influenced by disease-modifying therapies.
There were no significant differences in painful and autonomic symptoms between SLE patients with and without SFN.

The type I interferon response blood transcription module was increased during acute infection in monocyte, B cell, and T cell subsets of patients who later developed Long COVID compared to those who recovered.

The 'chromosome Y linked' blood transcription module was decreased across many cell types during acute infection in patients who would develop Long COVID, driven by XIST, DDX3Y, UTY/KDM6C, KDM5D, PRKY, and USP9Y.
DDX3Y, the Y-linked homolog of DDX3X involved in interferon responses, was downregulated across most cell subsets at 12 months in males with persistent Long COVID.

XIST, a gene implicated in autoimmunity, showed higher expression in several innate and adaptive immune cell subsets in females who developed Long COVID during acute infection, persisting less prominently at 3 and 12 months.
In this cohort, a greater proportion of females than males progressed to Long COVID after acute infection (75% vs 67%, respectively).

Males who developed Long COVID showed reduced expression of the 'leukocyte activation and migration' module in several T cell subsets during acute infection, with prominent BTM differences also in proliferating NK cells; affected BTMs in females were less cell-type restricted, spanning multiple lymphoid and myeloid subsets.

In acutely infected males who would develop Long COVID, proliferating NK cells showed predominant bidirectional TGFβ1 (and IFNγ) signaling, predicted to upregulate CCL3, DAPK1, IFIT2, ZNF395, FURIN, IGFBP7, and GALNT10 and downregulate ADAMTS6, SMAD3, TRAP1, and ETS1.

IL-7 signaling toward proliferating NK cells was upregulated in acutely infected males who would develop Long COVID, predicted to downregulate IL7R; IL7R expression was indeed reduced across most cell types in males (but not females) who developed LC.

TGFβ1 gene expression was increased across the majority of cell types during acute infection, at 3 months, and at 12 months in males who developed and had persistent Long COVID, and plasma LAP-TGFβ1 was significantly higher in acutely infected males who would develop LC compared to those who recovered.
TGFβ1 gene expression was decreased during acute infection and at 3 months in females who developed Long COVID, but became increased across most cell types by 12 months in females with persistent LC.

In males, monocytes from recovered subjects received CD40 ligand co-stimulatory signaling from T cells during acute infection, whereas CD14+ monocytes in males who developed Long COVID instead received proinflammatory IFNG and IL15 signaling as well as pro-apoptotic TNFSF10 (TRAIL) signaling.

CD16+ monocytes in males who developed Long COVID received CD226 signaling from NK and T cells directed at PVR (CD155) and Nectin2, receptors previously associated with poor antiviral response and monocyte tissue infiltration.

CD14+ monocytes in females who developed Long COVID received increased CCL5 signaling and showed increased expression of chemokine receptors CCR1 and CCR3 during acute infection, a combination expected to promote chemotaxis.

Gene network analysis of CD14+ and CD16+ monocytes in females who developed Long COVID revealed upregulation of interferon-stimulated and antiviral genes including MX1, MX2, TRIM22, OAS2, OAS3, IFI44, DDX60L, EPSTI1, PARP14, and IFIT3.
CD16+ monocytes in females who developed Long COVID received increased TNF signaling, including TNFSF8 (CD30L), and complement C5 signaling, compared to those who recovered.

Both CD14+ and CD16+ monocytes showed increased IL1β expression in females with persistent Long COVID at 12 months (not in males), and plasma IL-1α was significantly elevated in females with persistent LC at 12 months but not in males.

Expression of the co-stimulatory molecule CD86 was reduced at 3 and 12 months post infection in both CD14+ and CD16+ monocytes in subjects with Long COVID in both sexes, suggesting impaired antigen-presenting cell function.

Plasma proteomic markers of T cell anergy/exhaustion, including LILRB4, IL-10, IL-10RB, and LAG3, were higher in males with persistent Long COVID at 12 months, with LAG3 reaching statistical significance.
NFKB1 expression was higher during acute infection in those who would develop Long COVID, and remained elevated at 3 and 12 months in those with persistent Long COVID, with sexes combined.

RELB (non-canonical NF-κB activator) was upregulated in most cell types except CD8+ TEM and naive B cells during acute infection in those who developed Long COVID, and c-REL was similarly upregulated in acute samples and in persistent LC at 12 months.

NFKB1, a primary component of canonical NF-κB signaling, showed higher expression during acute infection in those who developed LC and at 3 and 12 months in those with persistent LC, in both sexes combined.
RELB, an activator of the non-canonical NF-κB pathway, was upregulated in nearly all cell types during acute infection in those who developed LC.

c-REL, primarily expressed in B and T lymphocytes and implicated in autoimmune conditions, had higher expression in acute samples of those who developed LC and in those with persistent LC at 12 months.
The AP-1 transcription factor complex genes FOS, FOSB, JUN, and JUNB, which drive T cell activation, showed increased transcriptional expression across many cell types in those with persistent LC.

ETS1 expression during acute infection was reduced in males who progressed to LC but increased in several lymphocyte subsets in females who progressed to LC, indicating sex-specific direction of this transcription factor.

ETS1 expression was lower at 3 months in subjects who would have persistent LC at 12 months and remained lower at 12 months across most B and T cell subsets in both sexes, marking it as a predictor of LC persistence.

Intracellular IL-4, a major Th2 cytokine, was higher in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells at 3 and 12 months in subjects with persistent LC at 12 months, a pattern that persisted across naive and memory CD4+ and CD8+ subsets when separated by sex.

Plasma proteomics showed higher levels of Th2 cytokines IL-13, IL-33, IL-4, and IL-5 in subjects with persistent LC at 12 months versus those who recovered, with only IL-33 reaching unadjusted statistical significance (p<0.05).
CD86, a co-stimulatory molecule on antigen-presenting cells, showed reduced expression at 3 and 12 months post infection in CD14+ and CD16+ monocytes for those with LC in both sexes.

LILRB4, which induces immune tolerance in antigen-presenting cells and an immunosuppressive T cell phenotype, was higher in plasma of male subjects with LC at 12 months, supporting reduced monocyte co-stimulatory function.
Plasma LAG3, a marker of T cell anergy/exhaustion, was higher in those with persistent LC at 3 and 12 months, reaching statistical significance specifically in males.
Pseudobulk IL1β expression was increased in CD14+ and CD16+ monocytes of females with LC, but this pattern was not observed in males.
Plasma proteomic analysis demonstrated upregulation of IL-1α in females with persistent LC at 12 months, but not in males, consistent with sex-specific IL1 pathway involvement.

Single-cell proteomics showed intracellular IL-6 and IP-10 (CXCL10) were higher in CD14+ and CD16+ monocytes at 3 and 12 months in males with LC, and IP-10 was higher in CD14+ monocytes at 3 months in females, indicating a pro-inflammatory monocyte state.

In males, CD16+ monocytes of those who developed LC received CD226 signaling from NK and T cells directed toward PVR (CD155, an inhibitory protein linked to poor antiviral responses) and Nectin2, both of which promote tissue infiltration of monocytes.

In females, CD14+ monocytes of those who developed LC received increased CCL5 signaling from NK and T cell subsets and showed increased CCR1/CCR3 receptor expression, a combination expected to promote chemotaxis and previously linked to increased acute COVID-19 severity.

Gene network analysis of CD14+ monocytes in females revealed a subnetwork of interferon-stimulated and antiviral genes (MX1, MX2, TRIM22, OAS2, OAS3, IFI44, DDX60L, EPSTI1, PARP14, IFIT3) upregulated in those who developed LC.

CD16+ monocytes in females who developed LC received increased TNF signaling including TNFSF8 (CD30L), which induces NF-κB activation and is implicated in autoimmunity, as well as increased complement C5 signaling, previously implicated in LC pathogenesis.
A greater proportion of females than males in the cohort progressed to LC after acute infection (75% vs 67%, respectively).

Secreted LAP TGFβ1 in plasma appeared increased in both males and females with persistent LC at 12 months compared to recovered counterparts, though these differences did not reach statistical significance.
Abdominal withdrawal reflex (AWR) scores, a measure of visceral sensitivity, were higher in visceral hypersensitivity (VH) and sodium butyrate (NaB) enema rats than in controls.
Probiotic VSL#3 administration reduced AWR scores in VH rats back toward normal levels.
VH rats had higher fecal water content and shorter total gastrointestinal transit time (TGITT) than controls.
VSL#3 restored fecal water content and TGITT toward normal in VH rats.
Direct sodium butyrate enema (NaB group) increased visceral sensitivity and shortened time to first white stool compared with controls, and also produced higher fecal water content and shorter TGITT.
Total fecal output did not differ significantly between control, VH, NaB, and VSL#3 groups.
Fecal abundance of the butyrate-producing genus Clostridium sensu stricto 1 was higher in VH rats than controls, and was reduced by VSL#3 treatment.
Fecal butyrate concentration was higher in VH rats than controls, and was reduced back down by VSL#3 treatment, while propionate and acetate levels did not differ between groups.
Colonic mast cells showed increased degranulation (irregular shape, decreased granules, vacuolated cytoplasm) in VH and NaB rats, which was reduced by VSL#3 treatment.
TRPV1 immunofluorescence optical density in DRG neurons was higher in VH and NaB rats than controls, and lower in the VH+VSL#3 group compared with VH.
Western blot confirmed higher TRPV1 protein levels in DRGs of VH and NaB rats than controls, and levels were reduced in the VH+VSL#3 group.
LincRNA-01028 expression in DRG neurons was increased in VH and NaB rats compared with controls, and decreased in the VH+VSL#3 group.
miR-143 expression in DRG neurons was decreased in VH and NaB rats compared with controls, and increased back up in the VH+VSL#3 group.
PKC (PRKCE) expression in DRG neurons was higher in VH and NaB rats than controls, and lower in the VH+VSL#3 group compared with VH.
Luciferase reporter assays confirmed that miR-143 directly binds and represses lincRNA-01028 via its predicted target site.
Luciferase reporter assays confirmed miR-143 directly targets the PRKCE (PKC) 3'-UTR binding site.
In DRG-mast cell co-culture, treating mast cells with butyrate increased TRPV1 channel current in DRG neurons, and this increase was reversed by a lincRNA-01028 inhibitor.
In co-culture, butyrate treatment of mast cells increased lincRNA-01028 and PKC while decreasing miR-143 in DRG neurons; these changes were prevented by a lincRNA-01028 inhibitor.

The authors propose an overall model wherein increased Clostridium sensu stricto 1 and butyrate induce mast cell degranulation via GPR receptors, activating DRG neurons through a lincRNA-01028-miR-143-PKC-TRPV1 ceRNA axis to drive visceral hypersensitivity.
Promethazine (first-generation antihistamine) administration significantly increased iNOS mRNA expression in rat parotid glands compared to controls.
Cetirizine (second-generation antihistamine) administration significantly increased iNOS mRNA expression in rat parotid glands compared to controls.
Promethazine significantly increased caspase-3 gene expression in the parotid gland, indicating enhanced apoptosis compared to control.
Cetirizine increased caspase-3 gene expression in the parotid gland, but the increase was not statistically significant compared to control.
Promethazine caused a non-significant decrease in α-SMA gene expression in the parotid gland compared to control.
Cetirizine caused a non-significant decrease in α-SMA gene expression in the parotid gland compared to control.
A significant positive correlation was found between caspase-3 and iNOS gene expression across the treated groups, suggesting a link between oxidative stress and apoptosis.
A significant positive correlation was observed between caspase-3 and iNOS gene expression in the parotid glands of antihistamine-treated rats.
An inverse correlation was noticed between caspase-3 and α-SMA gene expression in the parotid glands of antihistamine-treated rats.

Histological degenerative changes in the parotid gland (acinar degeneration, connective tissue widening, vacuolization, inflammatory infiltration) were similar in the cetirizine group but less severe than in the promethazine group.
A 21-day heterotypic chronic stress paradigm in mice induced anxiety- and depression-like behaviors.

Chronic heterotypic stress produced long-lasting wide-spread hyperalgesia across multiple body regions (orofacial area, hindpaw, thigh, upper back, abdomen) in female mice, modeling comorbid chronic primary pain.
CCK receptor expression was significantly increased in the L4-L5 spinal dorsal horn of female mice after 14 and 21 days of heterotypic stress compared with unstressed control animals.
Intrathecal injection of the CCK receptor antagonist CR-1505 blocked stress-induced pain hypersensitivity in subcervical body regions including the upper back, thigh, hindpaw, and abdomen.

Under physiological conditions, cholinergic (VAChT-positive) neurons were the most numerous enteric neuron population in mouse jejunum, comprising roughly half of all PGP 9.5-positive neurons in both plexuses.
BPA administration caused a dose-dependent increase in the percentage of VIP-immunoreactive neurons in both the myenteric and submucous plexuses of mouse jejunum.
BPA administration increased the percentage of nNOS-immunoreactive (nitrergic) neurons in both plexuses in a dose-dependent manner.
BPA administration increased the percentage of galanin-immunoreactive neurons in both the myenteric and submucous plexuses.
BPA administration increased the percentage of substance P-immunoreactive neurons in both plexuses in a dose-dependent manner.
BPA administration decreased the percentage of cholinergic (VAChT-positive) neurons in both the myenteric and submucous plexuses in a dose-dependent manner.
Both low and high doses of BPS increased the percentage of nNOS-immunoreactive neurons in the myenteric and submucous plexuses.
Both low and high doses of BPS increased the percentage of substance P-immunoreactive neurons in the myenteric and submucous plexuses.
Low-dose BPS did not significantly change the percentage of VIP- or GAL-immunoreactive neurons compared to control, whereas the higher BPS dose significantly increased both.
BPS administration decreased the percentage of cholinergic (VAChT-positive) neurons in both plexuses, with more pronounced decreases at the higher dose.

At lower doses BPA produced more pronounced neurochemical changes in enteric neurons than BPS, but at higher doses both bisphenols produced similarly pronounced changes, suggesting BPS may be less toxic than BPA at low exposure but comparably toxic at high exposure.
No clinical signs, behavioral changes, or differences in feed consumption were observed in mice given BPA or BPS at either dose over the three-month exposure period.
Purified total IgG from Long COVID participants showed increased reactivity to human pons compared with control IgG.
LC patient IgG cross-reactivity to mouse meninges was significantly associated with headache and enriched among participants reporting loss of memory, weakness, and disorientation.
IgG staining of meninges predominantly co-localized with pericytes (NG2-dsRed) and partially with endothelial cells (CD31), suggesting pericytes as a target of cross-reactive antibodies.
LC patients with tinnitus showed increased (non-statistically-significant) mean fluorescence staining of IgG against mouse sciatic nerve.
LC participants had a significantly increased number and diversity of autoreactive antibodies on a >21,000 protein human proteome array compared to controls, many targeting CNS antigens.
MED20 was identified as a top autoantigen target by HuProt array and validated by mass spectrometry and ELISA in a subset of LC participants.
USP5 was identified as a top autoantigen target by HuProt array and validated by mass spectrometry and ELISA; USP5 deubiquitinates Cav3.2 T-type calcium channels involved in nociceptor excitability.
After intraperitoneal injection of purified human IgG, approximately 5% of the human IgG crossed the mouse blood-brain barrier and was detectable in brain homogenate at day 5.

Mice injected with IgG from LC participants displayed increased thermal pain sensitivity (hot plate test) at day 3 post-injection, and this phenotype was more common in mice receiving IgG from donors with self-reported chronic/new-onset pain.
Hot plate pain phenotype in mice was also associated with donor-reported weakness (55% of positive mice) and dysautonomia (90% of positive mice).
Grip strength testing showed a trend toward muscle weakness in mice injected with LC IgG, associated with donor-reported tinnitus (54.5%) and headache (90.9%).

Rotarod motor coordination testing showed no overall significant difference between groups, but mice with loss of balance/coordination were predominantly (88.88%) those that received IgG from donors reporting dizziness.
Mice injected with LC IgG showed reduced number and volume of intraepidermal nerve fibers compared to mice injected with healthy control IgG, a marker consistent with small fiber neuropathy.

Passive transfer of LC, convalescent, or healthy control IgG produced no significant differences in anxiety-like behavior/locomotion (open field, elevated zero maze) or blood pressure/heart rate between groups.

In the neurological Long COVID subgroup (n=55), the most common symptoms were brain fog (80.0%), headache (65.4%), memory loss (64.4%), dizziness (58.2%), sleep disturbance (58.2%), and confusion (54.5%), with 63.6% experiencing five or more neurological symptoms.

Four large independent retrospective studies of medical records from millions of COVID-19 patients reported a 20-40% increased risk of multiple new-onset autoimmune diseases after SARS-CoV-2 infection.

A cited analysis of 130 IVIg-treated neuro-COVID cases and a review of 76 case reports found IVIg generally beneficial for post-COVID neurological disorders and for LC/ME-CFS, though only 16% had unequivocal autoimmune encephalitis diagnoses and 26% lacked diagnostic evidence.
IC/BPS patients with higher autonomic symptom burden (COMPASS-31 score ≥20.36) were significantly less likely to have Hunner lesions than those with lower symptom burden.
IC/BPS patients with higher autonomic symptom burden had significantly greater anesthetic bladder capacity than those with lower symptom burden.
IC/BPS patients with higher autonomic symptom burden scored significantly higher on the Pelvic Pain and Urgency/Frequency (PUF) scale than those with lower symptom burden.
IC/BPS patients with higher autonomic symptom burden had a significantly greater number of comorbid nonurologic associated syndromes than those with lower symptom burden.
Linear Mendelian randomization using the focused genetic score found no evidence that genetically-predicted 25(OH)D concentration causally affects fibromyalgia risk in the population as a whole.
Linear Mendelian randomization using the focused genetic score found no evidence that genetically-predicted 25(OH)D concentration causally affects clinical fatigue risk.
Linear Mendelian randomization using the focused genetic score found no evidence that genetically-predicted 25(OH)D concentration causally affects chronic widespread pain risk.

Linear Mendelian randomization using the focused genetic score showed a weak, non-significant inverse association between genetically-predicted 25(OH)D concentration and probable lifetime major depression across the whole population.

Non-linear Mendelian randomization revealed that among individuals with the lowest genetically-predicted 25(OH)D levels, higher vitamin D was associated with markedly reduced odds of probable lifetime major depression, whereas no association was seen in higher strata or for the other three outcomes.

When the population was divided into three strata instead of five, the inverse association between low genetically-predicted 25(OH)D and probable lifetime major depression persisted, with a slightly attenuated but more statistically significant estimate due to larger stratum sample size.
Using a pleiotropic genome-wide genetic score for 25(OH)D, linear Mendelian randomization found no significant causal effect on fibromyalgia risk.
Using the pleiotropic genome-wide genetic score, linear Mendelian randomization found no significant causal effect of 25(OH)D on clinical fatigue risk.

Using the pleiotropic genome-wide genetic score, higher genetically-predicted 25(OH)D was significantly associated with reduced risk of chronic widespread pain, in contrast to the null result from the focused four-gene score.
Using the pleiotropic genome-wide genetic score, the inverse association between 25(OH)D and probable lifetime major depression did not reach conventional statistical significance.

Negative control analyses testing the doubly-ranked stratification method against age and sex found no clear associations with age but some slight associations with sex in certain strata, raising a possible but likely limited concern about instrument validity in the non-linear analyses.
Genetically predicted major depressive disorder (MDD) was associated with an increased risk of chronic regional pain.
Genetically predicted MDD was associated with an increased risk of fibromyalgia.
Genetic liability to MDD increased the odds of insomnia.
Genetic liability to MDD was associated with a modest increase in the odds of self-reported short sleep duration.

MDD showed no significant association with several other sleep-related phenotypes, including self-reported chronotype, being a morning person, sleep duration, accelerometer-based sleep duration, number of sleep episodes, and least-active-5-hour (L5) timing.
Insomnia was found to mediate the causal pathway from MDD to chronic regional pain, accounting for approximately 12.8% of the total effect.

A second sleep-related mediator (reported alongside insomnia, likely short sleep duration) showed a mediation effect of 1.03 with a mediation proportion of 15.2% in the pathway from MDD to chronic regional pain.
Insomnia mediated the causal pathway from MDD to fibromyalgia, accounting for 15.2% of the total effect.
Self-reported short sleep duration did not significantly mediate the relationship between MDD and fibromyalgia.
No differences in circadian rhythm, sleep, or activity variables were found between ME/CFS patients and post-COVID ME/CFS patients.
ME/CFS and post-COVID ME/CFS patients showed lower motor activity levels than matched healthy controls on actigraphy.
ME/CFS and post-COVID ME/CFS patients had worse sleep quality than matched healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients showed a worse lipid profile than healthy controls, which was associated with disturbances in the circadian wrist temperature rhythm.
ICAM-1 levels were associated with plasma lipids in healthy controls but not in ME/CFS/post-COVID patients.
ME/CFS and post-COVID ME/CFS patients showed higher levels of endothelin-1 than healthy controls, suggestive of endothelial dysfunction.
ME/CFS and post-COVID ME/CFS patients showed higher levels of VCAM-1 than healthy controls, suggestive of endothelial dysfunction.

At 3 months, the weighted prevalence of ME/CFS-like illness was similar in COVID-19-positive (3.4%) and COVID-19-negative (3.7%) participants, with no statistically significant difference at any follow-up time point through 12 months.

At 12 months, 2.8% of the COVID-19-positive group and 4.5% of the COVID-19-negative group met ME/CFS criteria, and the marginal incidence rate ratio for ME/CFS symptom count was not significantly different between groups.

Weighted and adjusted models showed no statistically significant differences in the odds of ME/CFS between COVID-19-positive and COVID-19-negative participants at any time point, with marginal odds ratios ranging from 0.84 to 1.18.
Across both COVID-19 groups, unrefreshing sleep was the most frequently reported individual ME/CFS symptom, followed by postexertional malaise and orthostatic intolerance.

Participants who ever met ME/CFS criteria consistently reported more severe symptoms (sleep, pain, anxiety, depression, fatigue, physical function) than those who never met criteria, with moderate to very large effect sizes, and effect sizes tended to be larger in the COVID-19-positive group than the COVID-19-negative group.
Overall, 6.8% (322 of 4738) of INSPIRE participants ever met ME/CFS criteria at some point during 12 months of follow-up after an acute illness prompting COVID-19 testing.

The ME/CFS-like illness prevalence found in this study (≤4.5%) was lower than in previous studies following specific infections, such as 27% after SARS (4-year follow-up) and 13% after acute Epstein-Barr virus infection (6-month follow-up), possibly due to differences in population sampling, case ascertainment, and preceding infection type.

Given that ME/CFS-like illness prevalence estimates in this study translate to a large absolute burden, the authors estimate 2.8 to 3.6 million individuals in the US may be affected with ME/CFS associated with COVID-19.

Health-related quality of life in ME/CFS patients is markedly lower than the general population average and lower than that reported for 20 other conditions including lung cancer and multiple sclerosis.
Diagnosed ME/CFS prevalence in Germany rose from 350,000-400,000 in 2018-2019 to nearly 500,000 patients nationwide in 2021.
A prospective ME/CFS drug is projected to yield approximately 29,000 QALYs gained in the German population, valued at roughly €2.5 billion using the German health-system opportunity-cost threshold.

Beyond QALY gains, a prospective ME/CFS drug is estimated to reduce productivity losses by about €142 million and direct medical costs by about €13 million over the relevant lifetime, yielding a total societal value of about €2.7 billion.

The optimal public R&D investment to achieve a marginal return equal to the average return at full investment is estimated at about 25% of total costs (~€676 million), corresponding to roughly 18% of total drug development cost being justified for German government funding.
Sensitivity analysis identified the extent of diminishing returns of R&D investment as the most influential parameter on the estimated societal value of ME/CFS drug R&D in Germany.
The willingness-to-pay threshold used for valuing health outcomes in Germany was €88,107 per QALY gained, based on health system opportunity costs.
The minimally important difference (MID) for ME/CFS health outcomes was set at 15% of the range of the respective morbidity/quality-of-life scale, per IQWiG methodology.

Government research spending required per drug approval was estimated at roughly $3 billion (reducing to ~$1.8 billion with a 3% discount rate), rising to about €3.3 billion when accounting for the fact that only 53% of new non-orphan drugs in Germany demonstrate added benefit over standard care.
Pyridostigmine, originally used to treat POTS, has shown promise as a repurposed treatment in ME/CFS by improving exercise capacity.
NIH funding for ME/CFS research has remained static at $13-17 million annually since 2017, totaling $103 million through 2022, despite the disease burden.
The German Federal Ministry of Education and Research has allocated 15 million euros over three years to research the fundamental disease mechanisms of ME/CFS.

The friction cost method used to estimate productivity losses incorporated German labor market vacancy data: over 52% of vacancies were filled in under three months as of March 2022, and there were 3.7 vacancies per 100 demanded positions in Q1 2023, plus a two-week replacement training period.

Only 53% of new non-orphan drugs assessed under Germany's early benefit assessment (AMNOG) have demonstrated added clinical benefit over standard care, informing an adjustment to the government R&D cost-per-approval estimate.
Thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1) was significantly increased in ME/CFS plasma compared to healthy controls, with fold changes of ~3.5-3.75 across three detected peptides.
Platelet factor 4 (PF4), a chemokine released from activated platelet alpha-granules, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS plasma.
Vitamin K-dependent protein S (PROS), an endogenous anticoagulant, was significantly decreased in ME/CFS plasma compared to controls.
Complement C1s, a subunit of the C1 complex, was significantly downregulated in the ME/CFS group.
Complement component C9, part of the membrane attack complex, was significantly downregulated in ME/CFS plasma with a fold change of 0.17.

Ficolin-3, a lectin-pathway pattern recognition receptor, was significantly decreased in ME/CFS plasma across multiple peptides, contrasting with a prior report of increased ficolin-3 in ME/CFS leukocytes.
Lactotransferrin (LF) was markedly elevated in ME/CFS plasma with large fold changes across three peptides, potentially indicating ongoing inflammation.
Protein S100-A9, a proinflammatory damage-associated molecular pattern protein, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS plasma and may contribute to endothelial and platelet dysfunction.
An immunoglobulin heavy constant gamma 1 variant was significantly elevated in ME/CFS plasma relative to controls.
Complement factor C1q, previously reported as elevated in a subgroup of ME/CFS patients, showed no significant difference between the ME/CFS and control groups in this study.
No significant differences were found between ME/CFS and control groups for classical proinflammatory cytokines/mediators TNF-α, NF-κB, and IL-1β.

The HHV6-H viral protein UL29 was significantly downregulated in the ME/CFS group, the only significant herpesvirus-related finding, though likely limited by detection difficulty for low-abundance viral proteins.

Combined elevations in TSP-1 and PF4 with reduced PROS indicate an overall procoagulant, prothrombotic profile in the ME/CFS cohort, consistent with prior findings of platelet hyperactivity and endothelial dysfunction.

Downregulation of complement proteins (C1s, C9, ficolin-3) forming membrane attack complex and lectin pathway components suggests broader complement system dysfunction in ME/CFS, potentially increasing infection susceptibility.
Gastrointestinal symptoms were reported as a comorbidity in 6 of 15 (40%) ME/CFS participants.
Orthostatic symptoms consistent with POTS were reported in 5 of 15 (33%) ME/CFS participants, and POTS is listed as a comorbidity in 33% of the cohort.
Fibromyalgia was reported as a comorbidity in 3 of 15 (20%) ME/CFS participants.
Mast Cell Activation Syndrome was reported as a comorbidity in 7% of the ME/CFS cohort (Table 1).
A lack of scientific consensus and limited research on ME/CFS diagnosis and care contributes to healthcare system barriers for Canadians with the illness.
Long-standing stigma, disbelief, and sexism toward people with ME/CFS were identified as a healthcare system barrier affecting care quality in Canada.
Inadequate or inconsistent healthcare provider education and training on ME/CFS was identified as a key barrier to appropriate care in Canada.
Heterogeneity in how family physicians coordinate care for ME/CFS patients was identified as a contributing healthcare system barrier in Canada.
Approximately 40% of patients with severe SARS-CoV-associated SARS developed reversible secondary adrenal insufficiency, suggesting pituitary inflammation.
SARS-CoV-infected patients showed reduced immunostaining of corticotropic, somatotropic and thyrotropic pituitary cells.
Adenohypophysitis observed during acute COVID-19 is reported to have higher rates of secondary adrenal insufficiency in patients with long COVID.

Vitamin D supplementation is proposed to reduce T-cell hyperactivation, decreasing inflammation, and may improve insulin sensitivity.

The authors argue that ICI therapy would not be beneficial for immune exhaustion in ME/CFS/LC, as it could exacerbate inflammatory cytokine production, worsen pre-existing hypophysitis, and increase T-cell exhaustion.

CTLA-4 blockade has been observed to increase expression and activity of the enzyme indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), which may further contribute to immune exhaustion by depleting tryptophan needed for T-cell function.

Both long COVID and ME/CFS exhibit CD8 T-cell hyperactivation, T-cell exhaustion, and hypopituitarism.

Isolated case reports document ME/CFS developing after hepatitis B vaccination meeting ASIA syndrome criteria, and suspected chronic dysautonomia resembling ME/CFS after HPV vaccination in genetically susceptible individuals.
Leow et al. observed that approximately 40% of patients with SARS associated with SARS-CoV infection may develop reversible secondary adrenal insufficiency, suggesting pituitary inflammation.
Wei et al. observed reduced immunostaining of corticotropic, somatotropic, and thyrotropic cells in the pituitary of SARS-CoV-infected patients.

Lio et al. found that individuals with HLA-DR2 (HLA-DR15/DR16) showed significantly increased antiviral antibody titers against herpes simplex type 1, cytomegalovirus, EBV and rubella virus compared with other HLA-DR types.

In humanized mice, HLA-DR15+ animals had higher EBV viral load and CD8 T-cell expansion, and only HLA-DR15+ mice developed myelin basic protein-specific CD4 T cells, indicating impaired CD4-mediated EBV control.

HLA-Cw12, HLA-DR15, HLA-DQ7 and HLA-DPw9 allele prevalence was significantly higher in patients with isolated ACTH deficiency due to immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment, and HLA-Cw12/HLA-DR15 were significantly higher in patients with ICI-induced hypophysitis.

Multiple HLA class II alleles (HLA-DQA1*01, HLA-DQB1*06, DQB1*0303, HLA-DQ3, HLA-DR4, HLA-DR5) have been associated with increased risk of developing ME/CFS, though the strength of evidence is limited.
In neurotypical adults, a single session of low-to-moderate intensity physical activity usually transiently improves feelings of energy.

In people with chronic multisymptom illnesses such as Long-COVID, Gulf War Illness, and ME/CFS, a similar bout of exercise produces the opposite effect, worsening feelings of fatigue rather than improving energy.

Short-term adoption of regular moderate intensity physical activity (typically 1 to 6 months) in neurotypical adults results in small-to-moderate improvements in self-reported fatigue, energy, and vitality.

For chronic multisymptom illnesses, regular chronic physical activity produces only small improvements in fatigue-related feelings, or no change at all, though limited data preclude strong conclusions.

The mechanisms underlying acute exercise-induced fatigue worsening in chronic multisymptom illnesses may involve unknown pathophysiological processes possibly including brain, immune, and autonomic system dysfunction and their interactions.
In the CycloME trial, mean SF-36 Physical Function continued to improve slightly from 18 months to six years after cyclophosphamide treatment.
At six-year follow-up there were no significant differences in outcome measures between the rituximab and placebo groups, either during the trial or from 2 to 6 years.

Repeated-measures analysis adjusted for age, sex, study centre and baseline severity showed a significantly better course of SF-36 PF and Function level over six years in CycloME participants compared to RituxME participants.
A significantly greater proportion of CycloME patients reached SF-36 PF of 70 or more at six years compared with RituxME patients overall.
The proportion of patients reaching a near-normal SF-36 PF of 90 or more at six years did not differ significantly between CycloME and RituxME.
In logistic regression, being in the CycloME trial (versus RituxME) independently predicted achieving SF-36 PF of 70 or higher at six years.
The proportion of cyclophosphamide-treated patients meeting Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS fell markedly from baseline to six years, indicating symptomatic improvement.

At six years, a substantial proportion of both rituximab- and placebo-treated RituxME patients no longer fulfilled Canadian Consensus Criteria, without a clear group difference reported as significant.

Among patients who no longer met Canadian Consensus Criteria at six years, roughly half still reported core ME/CFS symptoms such as PEM, cognitive problems, fatigue or sleep disturbance at moderate severity or worse.

More than half of patients in both trials received new diagnoses or comorbidities by six-year follow-up, including irritable bowel syndrome and postural tachycardia syndrome, with similar rates across treatment arms.
Cyclophosphamide treatment was associated with premature menopause in a subset of women in the CycloME trial.
Two rituximab-treated patients reported symptom exacerbation (pain, muscle spasms) that they attributed to rituximab treatment.
Citing prior studies, the authors note that some research has found a higher frequency of T regulatory cells in ME/CFS patients, which may relate to cyclophosphamide's mechanism of action.

Cyclophosphamide infusions at the CycloME trial doses were associated with moderate depletion of CD4 and CD8 T cells, CD19 B cells and CD56/16 NK cells, along with modest reductions in serum immunoglobulin levels.
The six-year follow-up did not identify any serious long-term toxicity from either rituximab or cyclophosphamide treatment beyond known fertility risks with cyclophosphamide.
The proportion of patients with a large drop (≥30 points) in SF-36 PF from baseline to six years was lowest in the cyclophosphamide group and highest in the placebo group.
Mean DSQ-SF symptom burden score decreased significantly from baseline to six years in the cyclophosphamide group.
The symptom network of chronic fatigue syndrome showed significantly lower connectivity, greater fragmentation, and more symptom clusters compared to the long-COVID symptom network.
The symptom network of irritable bowel syndrome showed significantly lower connectivity, greater fragmentation, and more symptom clusters compared to the long-COVID symptom network.
The symptom network of fibromyalgia showed significantly lower connectivity, greater fragmentation, and more symptom clusters compared to the long-COVID symptom network.
The number of statistically related symptom clusters varied widely across the six diagnostic groups, ranging from 9 clusters in CFS to 3 clusters in severe asthma.
Of 33 total symptom clusters identified across the six groups, 30 were unique to a particular group, indicating that symptom cluster content differs substantially by diagnosis.

The pattern of variable, largely non-overlapping symptom clusters across long-COVID, CFS, IBS, fibromyalgia and severe asthma is inconsistent with a modular causal structure but is consistent with a connectionist (parallel distributed processing) biological basis for medically unexplained symptoms, which could explain symptom overlap between syndromes, absence of a diagnostic biomarker, and efficacy of psychological/behavioral interventions.
The molecular weight distribution ranges of raw licorice polysaccharides and honey-processed licorice polysaccharides were essentially the same.

Honey-processed licorice polysaccharides contained significantly higher levels of mannose, rhamnose, glucuronic acid, galacturonic acid and glucose than raw licorice polysaccharides, though monosaccharide types were the same.
High-dose honey-processed licorice polysaccharides produced significantly greater improvement in IL-2 levels in a chronic fatigue syndrome model than raw licorice polysaccharides.
High-dose honey-processed licorice polysaccharides produced significantly greater improvement in IFN-γ levels in a chronic fatigue syndrome model than raw licorice polysaccharides.
High-dose honey-processed licorice polysaccharides produced significantly greater improvement in IgA levels in a chronic fatigue syndrome model than raw licorice polysaccharides.

Multi-omics analysis showed that both raw and honey-processed licorice polysaccharides could affect the immune system by regulating immunoglobulin levels, B-cell signaling pathway, and T cell phenotypic differentiation in a chronic fatigue syndrome model.

Unlike raw licorice polysaccharides, honey-processed licorice polysaccharides additionally affected natural killer cell-mediated cytotoxicity, suggesting a mechanism for its superior immune-modulating activity in chronic fatigue syndrome.
Adults with pulmonary infection (pneumonia) had a significantly higher incidence of subsequent chronic fatigue syndrome than those with non-pulmonary infection.

Patients infected with specific pathogens (Pseudomonas, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and influenza virus) showed a significantly higher risk of developing chronic fatigue syndrome compared to those without these pathogens.
Patients with pneumonia had a significantly higher risk of developing thromboembolism compared to the control group.
Urinary incontinence prevalence in EDS patients is estimated at 50-60% based on the reviewed literature.
Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) prevalence in EDS patients is estimated between 29% and 75% across the reviewed literature.
Bladder diverticula are frequently reported as a urological manifestation in EDS patients.
Urinary incontinence prevalence in JHS patients is estimated between 40% and 73%.
Generalized JHS (g-JHS) patients are almost three times more likely to be affected by pelvic organ prolapse (OR=2.37), with 73% having stage greater than 2, and the prolapses appear more severe.
Patients with vesicoureteral reflux, most often severe, are more likely to have joint hypermobility (OR=2.79).
Few studies have been carried out on urological assessment and treatment modalities for EDS/JHS patients, indicating a gap in the literature.
Most women with EDS in this Australian survey experienced a prolonged diagnostic delay, with the majority first noticing symptoms more than 15 years before receiving a formal diagnosis.
The large majority of survey respondents were diagnosed with the hypermobile subtype of EDS (hEDS), consistent with its known predominance among EDS diagnoses.
Having a family member already diagnosed with EDS did not shorten the time to diagnosis compared to those without a family history.
The large majority of participants reported having received one or more alternative (misdiagnoses) diagnoses before their formal EDS diagnosis.
The most common misdiagnosis reported by women prior to their EDS diagnosis was anxiety and/or depression.
Nearly half of participants reported having been previously diagnosed with ME/CFS before their EDS diagnosis was established.
Fibromyalgia was reported as a prior misdiagnosis in nearly one-fifth of participants before their EDS diagnosis, raising concerns about disability support recognition in Australia.
Over one tenth of participants reported receiving more than nine alternative diagnoses before their EDS diagnosis was confirmed, higher than rates reported in comparable prior studies.
Almost all participants who reported being misdiagnosed described experiencing negative emotions, most commonly frustration/anger, feeling dismissed, or feeling hopeless.

Three-quarters of participants sought self-diagnosis online prior to formal diagnosis, and most found this information helpful, with websites, Facebook groups and medical journal articles being the most valued resources.
Rheumatologists formally diagnosed the majority of EDS cases, followed by geneticists, with only a small proportion diagnosed by GPs or physiotherapists.
The Beighton scale was the most frequently used assessment tool during the EDS diagnostic process, while the International Diagnostic Checklist (IDC) for hEDS was used in only around 61% of cases.
The great majority of participants reported having to educate health professionals about EDS during their diagnostic journey.

During the diagnostic process itself, nearly half of participants felt validated and listened to, though a similarly large proportion also reported feeling stressed or overwhelmed about the diagnosis and its future implications.
A prior cited study reported that nearly a third of women with hEDS had attempted suicide at least once, with over 40% showing some suicide risk on assessment.

A previously cited survey found that most hypermobile EDS patients enrolled in a physical therapy program reported a positive treatment effect, though physiotherapists themselves have reported low confidence managing hEDS.

Two-thirds of participants suggested that increased training, education, and awareness among health professionals would improve the EDS diagnostic journey, with nearly a third specifically emphasising the need for clinicians to listen to and believe patients.
Adults with EDS had total healthcare costs $21,100 higher than matched patients without EDS or HSD in 2021.
Adults with HSD had total healthcare costs $11,600 higher than matched patients without EDS or HSD in 2021.
Children with EDS had total healthcare costs $17,000 higher than matched patients without EDS or HSD in 2021.
Children with HSD had total healthcare costs $11,000 higher than matched patients without EDS or HSD in 2021.
Gastrointestinal comorbidity was associated with more than double the total healthcare costs in EDS patients, the largest cost driver among comorbidities examined.
Patients with vascular type EDS had higher mean healthcare costs than those with non-vascular EDS types across nearly all cost categories.
Patients with hypermobile EDS (hEDS) had higher mean total healthcare costs than patients with hypermobility spectrum disorder (HSD), across all categories except inpatient claims which were similar.
The majority of EDS patients had at least one comorbid condition, at a higher rate than HSD patients, in both adults and children.
A substantial proportion of EDS patients had 3 or more comorbid conditions, at higher rates than HSD patients.
Patients with EDS had roughly twice the rate of inpatient claims compared to patients with HSD.
Emergency department claims were common in EDS and HSD cohorts, with about one-third of EDS patients and one-quarter of HSD patients having ED claims.
Most EDS patients in the database were coded with the nonspecific ICD-10 diagnosis 'Unspecified' (Q79.60), limiting ability to analyze EDS by subtype.
Broad genetic exome testing of the decedent revealed a mutation consistent with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The patient had a 10-mm aneurysm of the right internal carotid artery discovered on imaging 3 years prior to death, later understood in the context of underlying vascular EDS.

Autopsy following CPR revealed catastrophic injuries including subarachnoid hemorrhage, bilateral hemothoraces, hemopericardium, laceration of the interatrial septum, laceration of the left pulmonary artery, and chronic alveolar hemorrhage changes in the lungs, attributed to underlying vascular fragility from vascular EDS.
Genetic testing revealed a COL3A1 abnormality confirming the diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in this patient with recurrent thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm.

The patient underwent successful redo open thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm replacement surgery using deep hypothermia circulatory arrest 14 years after her first descending aorta replacement, without intra- or post-operative complications observed 13 months post-surgery.

The authors conclude that vascular fragility shows considerable individual differences among patients with vEDS, and this patient's relatively low vascular fragility was the major reason for successful surgery.
Over 90% of Classic Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (Type I/II) cases are associated with heterozygous mutations in COL5A1 or COL5A2, with rarer cases due to COL1A1 mutations.

Vascular-type EDS (Type IV), caused by COL3A1 mutations, is associated with poor average life expectancy due to spontaneous pneumothorax, pulmonary hemorrhage, aneurysm rupture, arterial dissection, and hollow organ rupture.
In vascular-type EDS, uterine rupture is more frequent in late-stage pregnancy, while the sigmoid colon is the intestinal segment most commonly affected by spontaneous perforation.

Autopsy histology in vascular-type EDS often shows reduced dermal skin thickness, thin collagen bundles with large interstitial spaces in the reticular dermis, increased thickness of cutaneous elastic fibers, and thinning of the aortic adventitia, though these findings are less specific than in other vascular syndromes.

In EDS, accidental injuries typically occur over the knees, anterior tibial area, and other bony prominences as small, single bruises, which helps differentiate accidental trauma from non-accidental injury (child abuse).
The estimated prevalence of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome overall is approximately 1 in 5,000 individuals.

Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in FBN1, which encodes fibrillin-1, a large structural macromolecule contributing to connective tissue integrity, and is primarily autosomal dominant with 25-30% of mutations arising sporadically.
FBN1 mutations located in exons 24-32 are associated with neonatal mortality and a severe Marfan syndrome phenotype, significantly linked to lower life expectancy (death before 40 years of age).

FBN1 mutations causing haploinsufficiency confer a higher risk of cardiovascular death than dominant-negative mutations, and phenotype severity depends more on truncating/splicing mutations than missense variants.

Missense mutations that substitute a cysteine residue in FBN1 carry a higher probability of ascending aortic dilation and mitral valve prolapse than mutations that create a cysteine, suggesting a critical role of cysteine in fibrillin-1 protein structure.

In a postmortem genetic testing study of 17 thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection sudden death cases, molecular autopsy identified two pathogenic variants, two likely-pathogenic variants, and six variants of unknown significance (VUS).

In an analysis of 134 athletes who died of cardiovascular causes, 115 had undergone standard physical evaluation; of these, only four (3%) were suspected of having cardiovascular disease, and one (0.9%) was found to have a dilated aorta with postmortem diagnosis of Marfan syndrome.

Approximately 90% of Osteogenesis Imperfecta cases involve heterozygous dominant or sporadic mutations in COL1A1/COL1A2, IFITM5 mutations specifically cause OI type V, and the remaining 10% of cases are due to recessive mutations in genes such as FKBP10, LEPRE1, PLOD2, PPIB, SERPINH1, SP7, TMEM38, BCRTAP, BMP1, WNT1, CREB3L1, SPARC, and TENT5A.

Rib fractures, especially posteromedial and in children under three years of age, have a 95% predictive value for child abuse and are extremely rare in OI, occurring generally only in the most severe forms and on lateral sides.
A review found that 25.5% (44/172) of OI type IV subjects were confused with non-accidental injury (NAI), compared to 13.1% (77/589) of subjects with other OI types.

In a retrospective study of 43 children with fractures suspected to be from physical abuse, molecular testing for OI genes revealed only 2 pathogenic COL1A1/COL1A2 mutations associated with clinical features.

Best practice guidelines recommend that variants of unknown significance (VUS) in OI genetic testing should remain classified as unclassified until family segregation analysis and/or functional evidence becomes available, which has direct forensic implications in suspected child abuse cases.
Patients with EDS had a higher rate of hip dislocation at 90 days after total hip arthroplasty compared to matched non-EDS controls.
At 2 years post-THA, EDS patients had significantly greater odds of dislocation compared to matched controls.
EDS patients had significantly greater odds of aseptic loosening 2 years after THA compared to matched controls.
EDS patients had significantly greater odds of undergoing aseptic revision surgery 2 years after THA compared to matched controls.
HybridPoseNet's thumb joint angle estimates correlated more strongly with gold-standard measurements than manual goniometry did.
HybridPoseNet's elbow joint angle estimates showed higher correlation with gold-standard measurements compared to manual goniometry.
HybridPoseNet's knee joint angle estimates correlated substantially better with gold-standard measurements than manual goniometry did.
HybridPoseNet's fifth finger joint angle estimates showed the strongest correlation with gold-standard measurements among all joints tested, exceeding manual goniometry.
HybridPoseNet achieved higher diagnostic classification accuracy for EDS than manual measurement in both training and testing phases, with perfect accuracy on the small test set.
Overall, the authors report that HybridPoseNet's joint angle estimation performance represents an approximate 20% improvement over traditional pose estimation approaches for EDS evaluation.

Both calcaneal lengthening osteotomy (CLO) and double arthrodesis (DA) significantly improved radiographic parameters of planovalgus foot deformity in patients with generalised joint hypermobility, except for the lateral talocalcaneal angle in the CLO group.
The lateral talocalcaneal angle did not significantly improve following calcaneal lengthening osteotomy, in contrast to the other radiographic parameters that improved with both procedures.
Pedobarographic study demonstrated elevation of the medial longitudinal arch and improved foot-pressure distribution after both CLO and DA surgeries.
Plantar pressure in the lateral forefoot significantly increased only after double arthrodesis (DA), not after calcaneal lengthening osteotomy.
Medial forefoot and hindfoot plantar pressures and the arch index improved only in the CLO group, not in the DA group.

In the targeted high-risk population (including patients with hypertension, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, atherosclerosis, peripheral vascular disease, aneurysmal disease, or age ≥65), the December 2018 FDA warning was not associated with a significant immediate (level) or sustained (trend) change in fluoroquinolone prescription rates.

In the non-targeted (low-risk) falsification population, the FDA warning was associated with a significant flattening (trend change) of the pre-existing declining fluoroquinolone prescribing trend, though the immediate level change was not significant.

In a secondary analysis restricted to the subgroup most vulnerable to aortic aneurysm/dissection (patients with Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, or existing AA/AD), there was no statistically significant level or trend change in fluoroquinolone prescribing after the FDA warning.

Among targeted patients with other vascular risk factors (hypertension, atherosclerosis, peripheral vascular disease, without Marfan/EDS/AA-AD), there was a statistically significant increase (flattening) in the fluoroquinolone prescribing trend after the warning, although the level change was not significant.

Both targeted older adults (≥65) and targeted non-older adults showed a similar prewarning declining trend in fluoroquinolone prescribing that flattened after the warning, with no other significant age-stratified level or trend changes.

Cephalosporin prescribing trends (used as an active comparator antibiotic class not linked to AA/AD risk) remained flat before and after the warning in both targeted and non-targeted populations, with no significant level or trend changes.

Fluconazole (a non-antibiotic falsification comparator) showed no change in trend or level in the targeted population, but an unexpected drop in level of use (with no trend change) in the non-targeted population after the warning.

The proportion of fluoroquinolone prescriptions relative to all other antibiotics decreased significantly from the prewarning to postwarning period in both the targeted and non-targeted populations, but this decline reflected a pre-existing downward trend rather than an effect of the December 2018 warning.
Joint hypermobility score was significantly correlated with emotion dysregulation (DES-II) score across the sample.
Joint hypermobility score correlated significantly with neurodivergent characteristics (compound RAADS/WURS z-score).
Joint hypermobility score correlated significantly with proprioceptive surprise (Glasgow Sensory Questionnaire proprioceptive sub-score).
Emotion dysregulation was strongly correlated with neurodivergent characteristics.
Emotion dysregulation correlated significantly with proprioceptive surprise.
Neurodivergent characteristics were strongly correlated with proprioceptive surprise.
Mediation analysis showed that hypermobility was linked to emotion dysregulation through proprioceptive surprise as a mediator.
The hypermobility-proprioception-emotion mediation effect remained significant when emotion regulation was analyzed as a binarized (above/below clinical threshold) variable.
Mediation analysis showed that likely neurodivergence was linked to emotion dysregulation through proprioceptive surprise as a mediator.
The neurodivergence-proprioception-emotion mediation effect remained significant when emotion regulation was binarized.
In the integrated moderated mediation model, joint hypermobility moderated the strength of the pathway linking neurodivergence to emotion dysregulation through proprioceptive surprise.
The moderated mediation effect of hypermobility on the neurodivergence-emotion pathway remained significant when emotion regulation was binarized.

Half of the purposively sampled participants screened positive for generalized joint hypermobility, 45% screened above threshold for likely neurodivergence, and 24% scored above threshold for significant dissociative/emotional dysregulation on the DES-II.
Participants scoring above the DES-II dissociation/emotion dysregulation threshold were significantly younger than those scoring below threshold, with no significant sex difference between groups.
Within the complex chronic condition clinical subsample, fibromyalgia and ME/CFS were common co-occurring diagnoses, frequently overlapping with BPD/C-PTSD.

Genetic panel testing for familial aortopathies/connective tissue disorders confirmed a known inherited connective tissue disorder in 5.1% of a major SCAD registry, most commonly due to pathogenic mutations in COL3A1.
A large genetic study found the non-coding variant rs9349379 at the PHACTR1/EDN1 locus, a locus shared with FMD and coronary artery disease, was associated with increased risk of SCAD.
A study identified five replicated risk loci and positional candidate genes for SCAD, most of which are also linked to extra-coronary arteriopathies.

Isolated case reports have described SCAD occurring in association with known inherited vascular/connective tissue disorders including Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, and Loeys-Dietz syndrome, though these instances are rare and their causal contribution to SCAD is undetermined.
FMD is the most common extra-coronary vascular abnormality identified in SCAD patients, with reported prevalence varying widely between 11% and 86% depending on cohort and screening completeness.

The prevalence of intracranial aneurysms among SCAD patients (14-23%) is significantly higher than in the general population, supporting recommendations for systematic brain aneurysm screening in all SCAD patients.
SCAD patients diagnosed with FMD are significantly older than SCAD patients without FMD, possibly because FMD's angiographic appearance evolves over time.

In a large MRA-screened SCAD cohort, at least 27% had an extra-coronary vascular abnormality; the majority of patients with positive vascular screening (73.3%) had myocardial infarction, with an odds ratio of 7.0 versus those with negative screening.
Patients with negative extra-coronary vascular screening were more likely to have single-territory coronary involvement rather than multiple territories (odds ratio 4.0).
Severe coronary tortuosity may be a risk factor for recurrent SCAD symptomatology, though it is unclear if it is causal or merely a marker of higher-risk vascular phenotype.
Hypertension has been identified as a significant predictor of recurrent cardiac events in SCAD patients, while beta-blocker use appears to confer a significant protective effect.
The presence of extra-coronary arterial involvement, whether FMD or non-FMD, has not been found to be related to the risk of SCAD recurrence.
During 5-year follow-up of 173 SCAD patients, no primary extra-coronary vascular events were recorded, whereas recurrent coronary events occurred in 20% during the same period.
MRA has shown 96% sensitivity and 93% specificity for diagnosis of renal FMD compared with conventional angiography, particularly in the presence of a string-of-beads appearance.
Rare familial SCAD cases involving two or more affected relatives have been reported, implicating a hereditary predisposition to the disease.
Children with OI showed reduced external foot progression angle when walking with foot orthoses compared to walking barefoot.
Peak ankle dorsiflexion angle increased when children with OI walked with foot orthoses compared to barefoot.
Peak plantarflexion moment increased with foot orthoses compared to barefoot walking in children with OI.
Peak knee flexion angle during swing phase increased when children with OI walked with foot orthoses compared to barefoot.
No significant differences were found in sagittal plane knee joint moments between barefoot and foot-orthoses walking conditions.
No significant differences were found in pelvic rotation range or peak hip rotation between barefoot and foot-orthoses conditions.
With foot orthoses, children with OI walked with longer steps than barefoot, while overall walking speed and step width remained unchanged.
The five children excluded from kinetic analysis due to lack of clean force-plate strikes were significantly younger, shorter, and had shorter legs than the remaining children.
Pain was reported by 20 of the 23 included children with OI.
Patient-reported maximal walking distance varied widely among children with OI, ranging from 25 meters to 10 kilometers.
All 23 included children with OI reported daily wear of their prescribed foot orthoses.
Twelve of the 23 included children with OI received bisphosphonate treatment.
All included children with OI presented with forefoot abduction in standing (no toes visible medially), and the vast majority also presented with hind-foot valgus.
Osteogenesis Imperfecta is, in most affected individuals, caused by dominantly inherited pathogenic variants in the collagen genes COL1A1 or COL1A2.
Modified Lapidus arthrodesis with plantar plate fixation achieved bone union in 79 of 80 feet (98.75%) in patients with hallux valgus and first ray hypermobility.
The hallux valgus angle (HVA) significantly improved from a mean of 30.5° preoperatively to 10.1° at follow-up after modified Lapidus surgery.
The intermetatarsal angle (IMA) significantly improved from a mean of 13.4° preoperatively to 5.6° at follow-up after modified Lapidus surgery.
The sesamoid position improved from stage 5.9 preoperatively to stage 2.6 at follow-up after modified Lapidus surgery.
Radiological measurements (HVA, IMA, sesamoid position) showed no significant difference between the 3-month and 12-month postoperative time points.
FMS patients had significantly greater total retinal parafoveal thickness on OCT compared to healthy controls.
Foveal density measured by OCTA was significantly higher in FMS patients compared to healthy controls.
There was no significant difference between FMS patients and controls in total retinal foveal thickness, foveal avascular zone area, or foveal avascular zone perimeter.
Superficial capillary plexus foveal and parafoveal vascular density (including all quadrant subfractions) did not differ significantly between FMS patients and controls.
Deep capillary plexus foveal and parafoveal vascular density (including all quadrant subfractions) did not differ significantly between FMS patients and controls.
Choriocapillaris flow area and outer retinal flow area were not significantly different between FMS patients and controls.
Average, temporal, superior, nasal, and inferior RNFL thickness measurements showed no significant difference between FMS patients and healthy controls.
No significant correlation was found between FIQ disease severity scores and any OCTA parameter or RNFL thickness measurement.
No significant correlation was detected between FMS symptom duration and any ophthalmologic (OCT/OCTA) parameter.
Food-induced abdominal pain in IBS is driven by histamine released from mast cells that sensitizes colonic pain-sensing neurons following a local IgE response to food.
Mast cell activation plays an important role in the development of visceral hypersensitivity underlying abdominal pain in IBS.
The authors propose antihistamines as a novel treatment option to manage chronic abdominal pain in patients with IBS.
The authors state that Bruton's Tyrosine Kinase inhibitors show potential as disease-modifying treatments in CSU.
The authors state that IL-4-targeting therapies show potential benefit as disease-modifying treatments in CSU.
The authors state that IL-13-targeting therapies show potential benefit as disease-modifying treatments in CSU.
The paper proposes that reducing mast cell-activating IgE autoantibodies is a target criterion for disease-modifying treatments in CSU.
The paper proposes that normalizing the gut microbiome and barrier is a target criterion for disease-modifying treatments in CSU, implying gut dysbiosis is relevant to disease mechanism.
Mast cells were found to accumulate in the intestinal tissue of both human IBD patients and DSS-induced colitis mice.
Colitis mice showed increased expression of mast cell-related tryptase compared to controls.
IL-33 was upregulated in the intestines of DSS-induced colitis mice.
ST2/IL1RL1 receptor was suppressed in DSS-induced colitis mice.
Intestinal mucosal barrier function, related to tight junction proteins, was weakened in colitis mice.
Treatment with HucMSC-Ex significantly reduced mast cell infiltration and intestinal damage in colitis mice.
In the co-culture model, interaction between mast cells and the epithelial barrier triggered activation of the IL-33/IL1RL1 (ST2) pathway with subsequent release of inflammatory factors and trypsin.
Activation of the IL-33/ST2 pathway and mast cell mediator release in the co-culture model led to aberrant expression of tight junction proteins in epithelial cells.
Supplementation with hucMSC-Ex alleviated the aberrant tight junction protein expression caused by mast cell-epithelial interaction and IL-33/ST2 activation in the co-culture model.
The authors conclude that hucMSC-Ex may reduce release of mast cell mediators via the IL-33/IL1RL1 (ST2) axis, thereby mitigating detrimental effects on intestinal barrier function.

Using EPOS2020 composite criteria (blood eosinophils ≥250 cells/mcL, tissue eosinophils ≥10/HPF, or total IgE ≥100 IU/ml), 99.7% of CRSwNP patients met criteria for type 2 inflammation, with only one patient (0.3%) classified as non-type 2.

Based on tissue eosinophil count alone (≥10/HPF), 93.4% of CRSwNP patients had type 2 disease, with most falling into the severe (>100/HPF) subgroup (41.2%), followed by mild (31%) and moderate (21.3%).
Using total serum eosinophil count (≥250 cells/mcL) alone, 61.7% of CRSwNP patients were classified as type 2, compared to 38.3% non-type 2.
Based on total serum IgE (≥100 IU/ml) alone, 89.5% of CRSwNP patients were classified as type 2, compared to 10.5% non-type 2.
Among type 2 patients stratified by tissue eosinophil severity (mild, moderate, severe), no significant differences were found in demographics, comorbidities, olfactory status, or CT findings.
Comorbid allergic rhinitis (55.4%) was more prevalent than bronchial asthma (33.1%) among CRSwNP patients, consistent with shared type 2/atopic inflammatory mechanisms.

Bacterial and fungal culture swabs from CRSwNP sinonasal cavities most frequently grew Staphylococcus aureus (9.2%), followed by Aspergillus flavus (5.6%), Klebsiella (4.9%), and Bipolaris (3.5%), with MRSA and Pseudomonas aeruginosa each at 3% and E. coli at 2.1%.
Olfactory dysfunction was highly prevalent among CRSwNP patients, with 47.5% reporting hyposmia and 38.8% reporting anosmia, while only 13.6% had normal olfaction.
The cited European prevalence of diagnosed small fiber neuropathy exceeds that of multiple sclerosis.
Passive transfer of IgG from patients with initially idiopathic SFN reproduced SFN symptoms and pathology in mice, supporting autoimmune causality.
A lower-leg skin biopsy showed markedly reduced epidermal neurite density confirming pure small fiber neuropathy.
A second skin biopsy during remission showed partial normalization of epidermal nerve fiber density, consistent with axonal regeneration.
Empiric high-dose oral prednisone during the first episode produced major improvement within 2 weeks and complete remission within 2 months.
In Episode 2, restarting prednisone rapidly reduced validated symptom scores from moderate severity to complete resolution.
Standard composite autonomic function testing was normal despite active small fiber neuropathy symptoms.
Cyclosporine A, an anti-T-cell therapy, was ineffective and was stopped after worsening leg pain and erythromelalgia, a reported side effect.
Rituximab, a B-cell-depleting therapy, stopped worsening of whole-body symptom spread and produced about 25% improvement but incomplete pain control.
Daratumumab, a CD38-targeting antibody, repeatedly induced rapid, near-total symptom remission across multiple episodes, consistent with predominant plasma-cell-mediated pathology.
Belimumab, which targets B-cell activating factor (BAFF), produced slow symptom improvement and was used safely into pregnancy and postpartum breastfeeding.
IV immunoglobulin maintained remission but caused severe, long-lasting meningeal headaches with nausea, requiring dose tapering and eventual switch to subcutaneous immunoglobulin.
Subcutaneous immunoglobulin maintained remission in several episodes, but tapering or discontinuing it precipitated relapses.
Plasmapheresis produced only transient (2-3 day) complete or partial remission during a late-pregnancy flare and was discontinued due to limited durability.
Pregnancy and the postpartum period repeatedly precipitated symptom flares in this patient over multiple pregnancies.
Each of the first four disease episodes began 10-14 days after a viral upper respiratory infection, supporting a dysimmune postinfectious trigger.
Symptom exacerbations occurred within days of influenza vaccination on two separate occasions, once at onset of Episode 2 and once postpartum.
Amyloid neuropathy was diagnosed in 55 of 19,081 peripheral nerve biopsies (0.28%) over a 39-year period at the institute.
Duration of symptoms at presentation ranged from 3 months to 10 years, with a mean of 2.31 years.
