The majority of amyloid neuropathy patients presented with a small fiber neuropathy phenotype (85%).
Pure sensory symptoms predominated in 23% of patients, while 72% had combined sensorimotor neuropathy.
Autonomic involvement was present in 35.8% of amyloid neuropathy patients, with isolated autonomic failure in one patient.
Amyloid neuropathy was clinically suspected prior to biopsy in only 22.6% of nonfamilial cases, indicating frequent diagnostic delay.
Familial amyloid neuropathy was suspected clinically in eight patients within the cohort.
Genetic testing identified an ATTR (transthyretin) mutation in one tested patient with suspected familial amyloid neuropathy.
Pure sensory symptoms were the presenting feature in 23% of amyloid neuropathy cases.
Amyloid neuropathy was clinically suspected prior to biopsy in only 22.6% of nonfamilial cases, indicating frequent underdiagnosis.
Familial amyloid neuropathy was clinically suspected in eight patients within the cohort.
On nerve biopsy, Congo red-positive birefringent amyloid deposits stained mahogany brown were found predominantly around endoneurial microvessels in 34.5% of cases.
Amyloid deposits were also identified in the perineurium and epineurium in 25.45% of biopsied cases.
Nerve biopsy showed preferential loss of small diameter myelinated fibers in amyloid neuropathy cases.
Axonal degeneration or regeneration was notably absent in the nerve biopsies of amyloid neuropathy patients.
Duration of symptoms at presentation of amyloid neuropathy ranged from 3 months to 10 years, with a mean of 2.31 years.
Microarray analysis of MFS patient skin fibroblasts showed reduced expression of the TGF-β repressor VDR compared to healthy controls.
The same MFS fibroblast study found increased expression of the TGF-β activator TSC2.
Genome-wide microarray analysis of MFS patient skin fibroblasts identified over 260 differentially expressed genes compared to healthy controls.
In the mgR/mgR MFS mouse model, 159 genes were deregulated in the ascending aorta, of which 140 were upregulated, with gene ontology showing enrichment for immune-related terms.
RNA-seq of mgR/mgR mouse aortic tissue confirmed induction of Igfbp2, which is proposed to promote ERK1/2 signaling relevant to Marfan cardiomyopathy.
Mfap4, which directly interacts with fibrillin-1 and maintains microfibrils, was down-modulated in mgR/mgR mouse aortic tissue.

RNA-seq of Fbn1C1039G/+ mouse aortas showed reduced expression of fatty acid β-oxidation and mitochondrial complex genes, including Tfam, alongside reduced mitochondrial respiration confirmed by Fbn1 silencing in VSMCs and in MFS patient tissue.
Treating Fbn1C1039G/+ mice with an NAD+ precursor boosted Pgc1-α and Tfam expression and rapidly reversed established aortic aneurysm by restoring mitochondrial metabolism.

Multi-omics analysis of aortic tissue from MFS patients (HI and DN variant groups) versus healthy donors found over 1500 modulated genes with strong overrepresentation of inflammatory and mitochondrial pathways, without a distinctive TGF-β signature.

Peripheral blood miR-200c levels correlated significantly with aortic root Z-score in MFS patients, while seven other miRNAs correlated with left ventricular end-diastolic diameter, whereas no mRNA correlated with clinical parameters.
In dilated MFS aortic tissue, the lncRNA XIST was the most strongly induced lncRNA and was linked to TIMP4 expression in a co-expression network.
The lncRNA H19 was highly upregulated in the aortic tissue of mgR/mgR Marfan mice, consistent with its induction in heart failure and coronary artery disease.
RNA profiling of MFS TAA tissue identified 25 down-modulated miRNAs and a single upregulated miRNA, miR-632, versus non-MFS TAA tissue.

Upregulated miR-632 correlated with DNAJB6 inhibition and induction of Wnt/β-catenin signaling, endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and fibrosis markers in MFS TAA tissue; TGF-β treatment induced miR-632 and activated these processes, and miR-632 overexpression in non-MFS aorta reproduced the effect.

In Fbn1mgR/mgR mice, miR-122 showed the strongest down-modulation at the late (10-week) TAA stage, with post-transcriptional induction of its targets Ccl2, IL1β, and MMP12, and similar results were found in a milder MFS model at 70 weeks.
Digoxin treatment inhibiting HIF1α induced miR-122 levels in Fbn1mgR/mgR mice, reducing Ccl2 and MMP12, diminishing elastic laminae fragmentation and ameliorating aortic dilation.
scRNA-seq identified a MFS-specific 'modSMC' cluster with overexpression of Serpine1 and Klf4, distinguishing it from similar SMC modulation seen in an atherosclerosis mouse model.

scRNA-seq of human MFS aortic tissue (Dawson et al.) showed increased de-differentiated, proliferative SMCs with reduced contractile markers MYOCD and MYH11, while COL1A1/2 was induced in fibroblasts.

In Dawson et al.'s scRNA-seq study, TGF-β receptors and SMAD were reduced in SMCs, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells, contrasting with the enriched TGF-β signaling reported in Pedroza's modSMC study.
Losartan treatment of Fbn1mgR/mgR mice, which inhibits AT1R signaling, eliminated the MFS-specific MFSmod (SMC3/EC4) aortic cell cluster associated with dissecting aneurysm.

An epigenome-wide association study in ~200 MFS patients found 28 differentially methylated positions correlating with aortic diameter, 7 of which mapped to CVD-relevant genes (HDAC4, IGF2BP3, CASZ1, SDK1, PCDHGA1, DIO3, PTPRN2); no FBN1-proximal methylation loci were associated with phenotype.

Integrated scRNA-seq/ATAC-seq in a second-heart-field lineage-traced MFS mouse identified enrichment of Twist1 and Smad2/3/4 binding motifs in SHF-derived modulated SMCs, linked to overactive collagen synthesis in the aortic root.
TWIST1 overexpression in vitro increased collagen and small leucine-rich proteoglycan production, consistent with a TWIST1-driven mechanism of focal collagen deposition in the Marfan aortic root.

Time-course miRNA profiling in Fbn1mgR/mgR mice showed 17 deregulated miRNAs at early-stage (4 weeks) TAA versus 129 differentially expressed miRNAs at late-stage (10 weeks) TAA, both stages enriched for inflammatory and ECM-related pathways.

miR-122 showed the strongest down-modulation at the late (10-week) TAA stage in Fbn1mgR/mgR mice, and this reduction was shown to post-transcriptionally induce Ccl2, IL1β, and MMP12, a pattern also confirmed in 70-week-old Fbn1C1041G/+ mice.

Upstream of miR-122, disruption of integrin signaling and upregulation of HIF1α was observed in the aortic wall of Fbn1mgR/mgR mice, connecting FBN1 deficiency to a hypoxia response that drives miR-122 downregulation.
Digoxin treatment (a HIF1α inhibitor) of Fbn1mgR/mgR mice induced miR-122 levels, reduced Ccl2 and MMP12, diminished elastic laminae fragmentation, and ameliorated aortic dilation.

scRNA-seq of aortic tissue from Fbn1C1041G/+ mice and a MFS patient identified an MFS-specific 'modSMC' cluster with phenotypic modulation toward a fibroblast-like state, and overexpression of Serpine1 and Klf4 specific to MFS (unlike a similar cluster in atherosclerosis mice).

scRNA-seq of TAA tissue from three MFS patients (Dawson et al.) showed increased de-differentiated, proliferative SMCs with reduced contractile markers MYOCD and MYH11, while ECM marker COL1A1/2 was induced in fibroblasts, with MYOCD/MYH11 modulation opposite to that reported by prior MFS studies.

In the Dawson et al. scRNA-seq study, although TGFB1 was induced in fibroblasts, TGF-β receptors and SMAD were reduced in SMCs, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells, contrasting with prior studies reporting enhanced canonical TGF-β signaling in MFS.

scRNA-seq of Fbn1mgR/mgR mouse aortic tissue identified two MFS-specific subpopulations (SMC3 and EC4, together termed 'MFSmod'), with SMC3 enriched for ECM formation and nitric oxide signaling genes and EC4 enriched for SMC/fibroblast/immune-related genes; no association with TGF-β signaling was found, unlike in the non-dissecting Fbn1C1041G/+ model.

Losartan treatment of Fbn1mgR/mgR mice, which inhibits angiotensin II type I receptor signaling and mitigates TAA progression, resulted in the absence of MFSmod cells, linking this cell state to dissecting TAA and to losartan-responsive mitigation.

The first epigenome-wide association study in ~200 MFS patients' peripheral whole blood identified 28 differentially methylated positions correlated with aortic diameter, 7 of which were associated with CVD-relevant genes (HDAC4, IGF2BP3, CASZ1, SDK1, PCDHGA1, DIO3, PTPRN2).
Differentially methylated region analysis in the MFS EWAS uncovered a previously unreported protocadherin gene cluster on chromosome 5 related to cell adhesion.

No methylation loci near the FBN1 gene were found to be associated with the MFS phenotype in the EWAS study, and no significant correlations were observed with non-cardiovascular phenotypic features, suggesting specificity of the identified DMPs to cardiovascular manifestations.

In a second heart field (SHF) lineage-traced Fbn1C1041G/+ mouse strain, SMCs of SHF origin overexpressed collagen synthetic genes and small leucine-rich proteoglycans while neural crest-derived SMCs activated chondrogenic genes, suggesting embryological origin drives distinct transcriptomic responses contributing to focal aortic root aneurysm formation.

Integrated scRNA-seq and ATAC-seq analysis identified enrichment of TWIST1 and Smad2/3/4 binding motifs in SHF-derived modulated SMC, and TWIST1 overexpression in vitro increased collagen and small leucine-rich proteoglycan production, implicating TWIST1 as a driver of collagen synthesis in SHF-derived SMC in MFS aneurysm.

RNA-seq of aortic tissue from two Col3a1 mutant mouse models of vEDS (Col3a1G209S/+ and Col3a1G938D/+), which recapitulated spontaneous vascular rupture and death, showed excessive PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK signaling, implicating this pathway as a major mediator of vEDS vascular pathology.

Pharmacological inhibitors of ERK1/2 or PKCβ prevented death from aortic rupture in Col3a1G938D/+ vEDS mice, whereas drug-induced reduction of blood pressure (unlike in MFS/LDS mice) did not improve survival in this vEDS model.

In Col3a1G209S/+ vEDS mice, inhibition of oxytocin signaling (previously shown to trigger PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK signaling and aortic dissection during lactation in MFS mice) led to decreased ERK activation, downregulation of ERK target genes, and reduced risk of vascular rupture, paralleling the increased vascular risk observed with pregnancy in vEDS patients.

In Col3a1G938D/+ mice, treatment with androgen receptor antagonists rescued the elevated vascular dissection risk observed at sexual maturity in adolescent males, correlating with changes in ERK1/2 activation in the aortic wall, paralleling the higher TAA occurrence/severity in male MFS patients.

RNA- and miRNA-seq of dermal fibroblasts from vEDS patients identified deregulated miRNAs linked to autophagy, proteostasis, and mTOR signaling, and 52 lncRNAs potentially sponging miR-29a-3p/miR-29b-3p, with NEAT1 being the most significantly downregulated ncRNA.

miR-29b, also induced in the aortic tissue of Fbn1C1039G/+ MFS mice and implicated in early aneurysm development, was proposed to have an analogous role in vEDS pathophysiology based on the vEDS fibroblast ncRNA network findings.

Yu et al. found overexpression of lncRNA AK056155 in peripheral blood circulating endothelial cells of LDS patients, confirmed in patients' aortic aneurysm tissue, with expression enhanced by TGF-β1 and reduced by PI3K or AKT inhibitors.

An early epigenetic study of patient-derived VSMC from MFS and BAV TAA revealed TGF-β1-independent, SMC-specific heritable activation and overexpression of Smad2, associated with histone H3 modifications near the transcription start site on the Smad2 promoter, without an MFS- or BAV-specific epigenetic pattern.

Genome-wide DNA methylation and expression analysis of BAV versus TAV aortic tissue identified 27 CpG probes in 9 genes with significant differential methylation specific to BAV, with the strongest differences observed for PTPN22, which showed hypermethylation and decreased expression in BAV relative to TAV tissue.
Several cardiovascular development genes, including ACTA2 and GATA4, showed differential methylation in BAV versus TAV tissue but no corresponding differences in expression levels.

Mucosal biopsy supernatants from IBS-D patients strongly activated guinea pig submucous plexus neurons across all four intestinal regions (proximal/distal duodenum, proximal/distal colon), significantly more than supernatants from non-IBS/non-MC patients.
Supernatants from MC-D patients evoked a higher spike frequency than those from non-IBS/non-MC in all four regions, but only a small percentage of neurons responded.
The percentage of responding neurons was significantly increased for IBS-D supernatants compared to both non-IBS/non-MC and MC-D supernatants, while MC-D did not differ from non-IBS/non-MC.

The neuroindex (spike frequency x percentage of responding neurons) was significantly higher in response to IBS-D supernatants compared to both non-IBS/non-MC and MC-D supernatants, with no difference between the latter two groups.
In female-only subgroup analysis, the neuroindex remained significantly higher in IBS-D patients compared to MC-D and non-IBS/non-MC in the duodenum, proximal colon, and distal colon.

Mast cell density (measured by c-Kit and tryptase immunostaining) did not differ significantly between IBS-D, MC-D, and non-IBS/non-MC patients in the duodenum, proximal colon, distal colon, or rectum.

The proportion of tryptase-positive to c-Kit-positive mast cells (an indirect measure of mast cell degranulation/reactivity) showed no significant difference between IBS-D, MC-D, and non-IBS/non-MC patients in any of the analyzed regions.
Histamine concentrations in mucosal biopsy supernatants did not differ significantly between IBS-D, MC-D, and non-IBS/non-MC patients in proximal or distal duodenum, or proximal or distal colon.

The nerve-activating effect of duodenal (small bowel) mucosal biopsy supernatants from IBS-D patients was comparable to that of colonic biopsy supernatants, demonstrating that nerve activation in IBS-D is a general phenomenon throughout the gut and not restricted to the descending colon.

Diarrhea per se was not linked to nerve activation, as MC-D patients with diarrhea and some non-IBS/non-MC patients with diarrhea did not show the same nerve-activating supernatant properties seen with IBS-D.

The authors state that these findings support their prior conclusion that proteases signaling via PAR-1 on submucous enteric neurons, rather than mast cell mediators, are the most decisive components in IBS-associated nerve activation.
Restraint stress significantly increased the number of fecal pellet outputs compared to unrestrained control rats.
Fecal water content collected after isolation was significantly higher in restraint rats than controls, indicating stress-induced diarrhea.
The first stool collected during isolation showed no significant difference in water content between restraint and control rats.
Total small intestinal length did not differ significantly between restraint and control rats.
Restraint-stressed rats showed a significantly higher small intestinal transit rate than control rats, indicating enhanced small intestinal motility.
CRH mRNA expression in small intestine and colon tissue did not differ significantly between restraint and control rats.
Mast cell mRNA expression in small intestine and colon did not differ significantly between restraint and control rats.
5-HTR3a mRNA expression (whole tissue, real-time PCR) in small intestine and colon did not differ significantly between restraint and control rats.
5-HTR3a mRNA expression was significantly higher in the distal small intestine than the proximal small intestine in both restraint and control groups.
In the distal small intestine specifically, 5-HTR3a expression did not differ significantly between restraint and control groups.
The number of 5-HT-positive enterochromaffin cells was significantly higher in the small intestine of restraint rats compared to controls.
The number of 5-HT-positive enterochromaffin cells in the colon did not significantly differ between restraint and control rats.
Within both the restraint and control groups, the number of enterochromaffin cells did not differ significantly between the proximal and distal small intestine.
In the distal small intestine, the number of enterochromaffin cells was significantly increased in restraint rats compared to controls.
In the proximal small intestine, the number of enterochromaffin cells did not differ significantly between restraint and control rats.
Immunostaining showed no significant difference in 5-HTR3a expression between restraint and control groups in either the small intestine or colon.

In control/sham rats, blocking nNOS with L-NPA increased sympathetic nerve-evoked vasoconstriction in rectal submucosal arterioles, indicating tonic nitrergic inhibition of sympathetic vasoconstriction.
The PDE5 inhibitor tadalafil (10 nM) diminished EFS-induced sympathetic vasoconstriction in control/sham rats, consistent with cGMP-mediated nitrergic inhibition of sympathetic tone.

In phenylephrine-constricted, guanethidine-treated arterioles, EFS-induced vasodilatation was blocked by the CGRP receptor antagonist BIBN-4096 but not affected by the nNOS inhibitor L-NPA, indicating this vasodilator response is CGRP-mediated and NO-independent.

Immunohistochemistry showed perivascular nNOS-immunoreactive nitrergic fibres co-expressing the parasympathetic marker VAChT were intermingled with tyrosine hydroxylase-immunoreactive sympathetic fibres expressing soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC), the receptor for NO, supporting an anatomical basis for parasympathetic-to-sympathetic nitrergic modulation.
Rats exposed to chronic water avoidance stress (10 days, 1 h/day) developed augmented sympathetic vasoconstriction in rectal arterioles compared to controls.
In WAS-stressed rats, the nNOS inhibitor L-NPA failed to further increase sympathetic vasoconstriction, unlike in controls, indicating loss of tonic nitrergic inhibition after chronic stress.

In WAS-stressed rats, the vasoconstriction-inhibiting effect of the PDE5 inhibitor tadalafil was attenuated compared to controls, consistent with reduced nitrergic (NO-cGMP) signaling after chronic stress.

Water avoidance stress did not alter vasoconstrictions induced by phenylephrine (α-adrenoceptor agonist) or α,β-methylene ATP (P2X-purinoceptor agonist), indicating post-junctional receptor sensitivity was unchanged.

Acetylcholine-induced (endothelium-dependent) vasodilation was unaffected by water avoidance stress, indicating the endothelial vasodilator pathway remained intact despite impaired nitrergic inhibition of sympathetic vasoconstriction.

The authors conclude that chronic psychological stress augments sympathetic vasoconstriction in rectal submucosal arterioles primarily through diminished pre-junctional nitrergic (NO-mediated) inhibition of sympathetic transmitter release, without altering post-junctional adrenoceptor/purinoceptor signaling or endothelial vasodilator function.
The number of MCT-positive mast cells in colonic biopsies did not change from baseline to post-treatment with ReFerm.
Total MCT protein levels measured by Western blot were significantly reduced after 14 days of ReFerm treatment compared to baseline.
MCT protein levels did not change from baseline to post-treatment in the placebo group.
The number of extracellular MCT granules per mast cell, a marker of degranulation, was significantly decreased after ReFerm treatment compared to baseline.
The size of extracellular MCT granules was significantly reduced after ReFerm treatment compared to baseline.
Neither the number nor size of extracellular MCT granules changed after placebo treatment compared to baseline.
The number of GFAP-positive enteric glial cells did not change after ReFerm or placebo treatment.
The number of S100β-positive enteric glial cells did not change after ReFerm or placebo treatment.
Total GFAP protein levels by Western blot showed a non-significant trend toward decrease after ReFerm treatment (p=0.0726), with no change in the placebo group (p=0.6202).
Total S100β protein levels by Western blot showed a non-significant trend toward decrease after ReFerm treatment (p=0.0709), with no change in the placebo group (p=0.297).

The authors propose, citing prior in vitro work, that SCFAs such as propionate and butyrate inhibit human mast cell activation, which may explain the reduction in mast cell degranulation observed with ReFerm despite its low propionate/butyrate content, as lactic acid can be converted to butyrate in the intestine.
miRNA microarray showed miR-21 was the most notably upregulated miRNA (4-fold) in denervated mouse gastrocnemius muscle compared to normal muscle.
Fibrosis markers TGF-β1, α-SMA and CTGF were significantly increased at both mRNA and protein levels 2 weeks after denervation, correlating temporally with miR-21 upregulation.
TGF-β1 stimulation of C2C12 and NIH3T3 cells upregulated miR-21 expression, which correlated with increased α-SMA and CTGF at mRNA and protein levels.
Transfecting C2C12 and NIH3T3 cells with miR-21 mimics significantly increased α-SMA and CTGF expression, while anti-miR-21 reversed these fibrosis-related changes.

Intramuscular injection of a miR-21-targeting lentiviral vector reduced CTGF/α-SMA expression and attenuated Masson's trichrome-stained fibrosis in mouse gastrocnemius muscle after denervation, compared to the negative control vector.
SMAD7 protein was suppressed in denervated gastrocnemius muscle of pLKO-NC treated mice, and this suppression was reversed by anti-miR-21 treatment, indicating miR-21 represses SMAD7 in vivo.

A dual-luciferase reporter assay in HEK293T cells demonstrated that miR-21 significantly inhibited luciferase activity of a construct containing the wild-type SMAD7 3'-UTR, confirming SMAD7 as a direct target of miR-21.

In C2C12 and NIH3T3 cells, the miR-21 inhibitor reduced α-SMA/CTGF and reduced SMAD2/3 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation, but co-transfection with SMAD7 siRNA reversed these effects, demonstrating that miR-21 acts through SMAD7 suppression to activate SMAD2/3 signaling.

The discussion notes that a direct miR-21 inhibitor (RG-012) has already passed clinical phase I testing and is being evaluated in a phase II study for renal fibrosis, supporting miR-21 as a therapeutic target class relevant to fibrosis broadly.
Current short-read sequencing and MLPA approaches provided a precise molecular diagnosis for 81.7% (680/832) of the 21-hydroxylase deficiency cohort, leaving the remainder unresolved.
Long-read sequencing was applied to resolve 144 cases with complex chimeric variants and 8 cases with pathogenic variants located on multiple gene copies that could not be solved by standard methods.
Combining LRS with prior genetic testing identified chimeric alleles (CYP21A1P/CYP21A2 or TNXA/TNXB) in 16.9% (281/1664) of alleles across the 832-patient cohort.
The three most common chimeric alleles (CYP21 CH-1, TNX CH-1, TNX CH-2) accounted for 77.2% (217/281) of all chimeric alleles found in the cohort.
Eight patients carrying pathogenic variants located on multiple copies of CYP21A2, which are typically undetectable by conventional methods, were accurately identified using long-read sequencing.
Continuous deletions of CYP21A2 extending into TNXB (CAH-X) were found in 12.1% of the cohort, and CAH-X patients showed a high frequency of connective tissue-related symptoms.
Covalent conjugation of beta-lactoglobulin with EGCG altered its protein structure, reduced IgE-binding capacity, and increased digestibility in a dose-dependent manner.
In vivo studies showed that covalent conjugation of beta-lactoglobulin with EGCG reduced allergic symptoms along with reduced levels of IgE.
Covalent conjugation of beta-lactoglobulin with EGCG reduced histamine levels in an allergy model.
Covalent conjugation of beta-lactoglobulin with EGCG reduced levels of mast cell protease-1 (mMCP-1), a marker of mast cell activation, in an allergy model.
Covalent conjugation of beta-lactoglobulin with EGCG reduced the percentage of sensitized mast cells in an allergy model.
Saturated βLG-EGCG conjugates reduced allergenicity more effectively than semisaturated conjugates, indicating a dose-dependent effect of EGCG conjugation degree.
Changes in cytokine levels (IFN-γ, IL-4, IL-5, IL-10, TGF-β) following βLG-EGCG conjugate exposure suggested a shift toward Th1/Th2 immune balance.

Systematic harmonization of over 12 million UK Biobank primary care and hospitalisation records into 1448 disease terms identified 679 diseases associated with increased risk of severe COVID-19 (n=672) and/or Long COVID (n=72).
Disease associations with severe COVID-19 risk were strongly enriched in clusters of cardio-respiratory and endocrine-renal conditions.
For 57 diseases, consistent evidence for predisposition to severe COVID-19 was established using both survival analysis and genetic susceptibility analysis.
Pre-existing symptoms of malaise and fatigue emerged as a largely overlooked risk factor predisposing to severe COVID-19.

At known severe COVID-19 risk loci, partially opposing genetic risk estimates were observed for etiologically related diseases such as post-inflammatory pulmonary fibrosis versus rheumatoid arthritis, suggesting divergent underlying disease mechanisms.
TTMV9 RNA was significantly overexpressed in PBMCs of the ME/CFS subgroup 2 patients compared to ME/CFS subgroup 1, FM, co-diagnosed, and healthy control groups.
CNOT3 gene expression showed a moderate positive correlation with TTMV9 RNA levels in the ME/CFS patient cohort.
XIAP gene expression showed a moderate positive correlation with TTMV9 RNA levels.
CNOT3 and XIAP, the genes most correlated with TTMV9 levels, were also strongly correlated with ME/CFS diagnosis in subgroup 2.
The HERV element MLT1_14q32.33, located within the lncRNA LINC02298, showed a moderate-to-strong correlation with TTMV9 RNA levels.
The HERV element MLT1_5q11.2, near the COX6C gene, showed a moderate-to-strong correlation with TTMV9 RNA levels.
Genes significantly correlated with TTMV9 levels were functionally enriched for pathways involved in CD4 T-cell commitment toward T-helper 17 cells and other leukocyte differentiation processes.
Plasma cell proportions (estimated by digital cytometry) positively correlated with TTMV9 RNA levels.
γδ T cell proportions negatively correlated with TTMV9 RNA levels, suggesting reduced γδ T cells with higher viral RNA.
ROC analysis showed TTMV9 RNA levels discriminate ME/CFS subgroup 2 from all other study groups with high accuracy (AUC >0.9, 100% sensitivity, 78.9% specificity).
ME/CFS subgroup 2 patients had significantly higher (worse) MFI general fatigue scores than the ME/CFS+FM co-diagnosed group.

Analysis of viral RNA aggregated by family (e.g., Coronaviridae, Gammapapillomavirus, Retroviridae) showed no significant differences associated with ME/CFS subgroup 2 versus other groups, except isolated differences between FM and subgroup 2.
The 289-virus microarray ruled out differential expression of EBV, herpesviruses, enterovirus, or other exogenous viruses previously implicated in ME/CFS in this cohort.
HPV5 was one of the few viruses showing increased presence in ME/CFS subgroup 2, cited as supporting evidence of compromised immunocompetence.

The authors infer (hedged) that increased TTMV9 levels may relate to worsening of Role Emotional and Mental Health domains of the SF-36 quality-of-life questionnaire, via associated gene expression correlations.
miR-152 expression was significantly decreased in NK cells of ME/CFS patients compared to non-fatigued controls, potentially contributing to reduced NK cytotoxicity via HLA-G targeting.
miR-23a was found to be downregulated in fibromyalgia patients compared to controls, and is implicated in muscle atrophy via targeting atrogin-1/MAFx.
miR-320a was reported to be upregulated in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls, targeting FKBP5 in the HPA axis and TGFBR2/SMAD2 in neuroinflammation.
miR-320b was reported to be downregulated in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
miR-103a-3p was underexpressed in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls and was associated with pain and sleep quantity.

miR-103 expression was lower in NK cells of ME/CFS patients compared to non-fatigued controls, and its downregulation has been linked to pain hypersensitivity via L-type calcium channel regulation in an animal model.
miR-99b was overexpressed in blood and NK cells of ME/CFS patients, suggesting activation of the mTOR signaling pathway and reduced NK cell cytotoxic and cytokine effector function.
miR-128-3p upregulation has been reported in fibromyalgia patients; it suppresses bone formation via SIRT6 and targets the cholinergic system.

miR-374b-5p was found to be underexpressed in both fibromyalgia and ME/CFS patients, targeting VEGFA and potentially linking impaired capillary supply in skeletal muscle to post-exertional malaise and fatigue.
miR-766-3p was underexpressed in blood samples from fibromyalgia patients, and miR-766 more broadly regulates apoptosis, extracellular matrix, and inflammatory pathways.
A deficiency in CoQ10 has been reported in both ME/CFS and fibromyalgia, contributing to mitochondrial dysfunction, decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, ROS production, and mitophagy.
Increased NF-kB activity and decreased tumor suppressor p53 were suggested as key mechanisms in ME/CFS driving pro-inflammatory cytokine release, ROS production, and mitochondrial exhaustion.

ME/CFS patients showed a decreased post-occlusive hyperemic response of the brachial artery and forearm skin microcirculation compared to healthy controls, indicating endothelial/vascular dysfunction.
Fibromyalgia patients showed reduced brachial artery flow-mediated dilatation in response to increased blood flow or nitric oxide, attributed to NO unavailability or muscle cell dysfunction.
Women with fibromyalgia were found to be 5.5 times more likely than healthy women to develop metabolic syndrome and to have a larger waist circumference.
A high prevalence (17.3%) of GH/IGF-1 signaling deficiency was described in obese fibromyalgia patients.

Metabolic profiling of plasma from ME/CFS patients revealed altered fatty acid and lipid metabolism, with disturbances in taurine, glycerophospholipid, purine, pyrimidine, amino acid, glucose, and oxaloacetate metabolic pathways.
Low levels of adrenal androgens, particularly serum DHEAS, have been observed in both ME/CFS and fibromyalgia.

Fibromyalgia patients experienced age-related gray matter reduction at a rate 3.3 times faster than healthy individuals, equivalent to 9.5 times the normal aging loss per year of disease, linked to pain sensitivity.
ME/CFS and fibromyalgia show approximately three-fold and six-fold higher prevalence, respectively, in females compared to males.
Substance P has been found to be increased in the cerebrospinal fluid of fibromyalgia patients, possibly linked to mast cell activation and women's overrepresentation in FM/ME-CFS.
miR-183-5p was the only miRNA identified as being involved in TRP ion channel disorder in ME/CFS and/or fibromyalgia.
Untargeted plasma metabolomics identified quinolinic acid as significantly downregulated in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, consistently across both ME cohorts.
Indoleacetic acid, a tryptophan metabolic product, was found significantly downregulated in ME/CFS patient plasma versus healthy controls in the untargeted analysis.
Untargeted pathway analysis (Mummichog) found the vitamin B3 metabolic pathway commonly disrupted in both ME/CFS subcohorts compared to healthy controls.
The arginine-proline metabolic pathway was found commonly dysregulated in both ME/CFS subcohorts versus healthy controls, consistent with prior findings in ME/CFS and Long COVID.
The aspartate-asparagine metabolic pathway was found commonly dysregulated in both ME/CFS subcohorts compared to healthy controls.

Pathway analysis linked L-adrenaline and S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH) in both ME/CFS subcohort comparisons, suggesting adrenaline-mediated inhibition of SAH hydrolase may halt the methylation cycle in ME/CFS.
The paper notes that postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is a common comorbidity of ME/CFS in which adrenaline plays an integral role.
Targeted quantitative analysis showed 3-hydroxykynurenine levels were significantly lower in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, an immune-regulatory kynurenine pathway metabolite, was significantly lower in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
The kynurenine/3-hydroxykynurenine (Kyn/3HK) ratio was elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, consistent with reduced 3HK levels.

The tryptophan/serotonin (Trp/5-HT) ratio was elevated specifically in male ME/CFS patients, approximately seven-fold higher than in female patients, suggesting reduced conversion of tryptophan to serotonin in males.
Hypoxanthine, a purine derivative and marker of cellular hypoxia, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Phenylalanine levels were significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, contrasting with some prior studies that reported decreased levels.
Kynurenine concentrations showed significant correlations with both sex and age across the combined ME/CFS and control cohort.
Quinolinic acid concentrations showed significant correlations with both sex and age in the combined cohort analysis.
Kynurenic acid concentration was significantly associated with sex in the combined cohort analysis.
Hydroxyanthranilic acid concentration correlated significantly with age.
Hydroxykynurenine concentration correlated significantly with age.

Wilcoxon testing found significant differences in nicotinamide and riboflavin (along with hypoxanthine, phenylalanine, and serotonin) between healthy controls and each ME/CFS subcohort, and between the two ME/CFS subcohorts themselves.

The two ME/CFS subcohorts (Gothenburg and Stockholm) showed markedly different metabolic profiles on PCA, with the Stockholm cohort showing the highest degree of discrimination from other samples, likely reflecting disease heterogeneity and differing comorbidities.
A weighted 1.67% of the eligible adult KPNC population met IOM-based criteria for ME/CFS-like illness.
Among those with ME/CFS-like illness, an estimated 14.12% developed the illness after a COVID-19 episode, representing 0.24% of the total population.
Persons with ME/CFS-like illness after COVID-19 were on average younger (mean age 36 years) than persons with ME/CFS-like illness without prior COVID-19 (mean age 45 years).
Persons with ME/CFS-like illness after COVID-19 were more likely to identify as Latino/Hispanic (41%) compared to those with ME/CFS-like illness without prior COVID-19 (27%).
Persons with ME/CFS-like illness after COVID-19 were less likely to be female (60%) compared to persons with ME/CFS-like illness without prior COVID-19 (75%).
Persons with ME/CFS-like illness after COVID-19 were more likely to have no common comorbidities (91%) than those with ME/CFS-like illness without prior COVID-19 (56%).

Persons with ME/CFS-like illness after COVID-19 were far more likely to be unvaccinated at time of first COVID-19 infection (96%) compared to those with ME/CFS-like illness without prior COVID-19 (22%).
Persons with ME/CFS-like illness after COVID-19 had experienced fatigue for a shorter average duration (2 years) than those with ME/CFS-like illness without prior COVID-19 (9 years).
Symptom prevalence, intensity, and frequency were generally lower in persons with ME/CFS-like illness after COVID-19 compared to those with ME/CFS-like illness without prior COVID-19.

Both ME/CFS-like illness groups (after COVID-19 and without prior COVID-19) had higher prevalence of 11 of 25 assessed symptoms — including joint pain, light sensitivity, bloating, weight gain, headaches, noise sensitivity, nasal congestion, night sweats, constipation, chemical/food sensitivity, and swollen glands — compared to those without ME/CFS-like illness.

Among persons with any history of COVID-19, older age (≥65 years and 50-64 years vs. 18-34 years) was associated with significantly lower likelihood of ME/CFS-like illness after COVID-19, as was Asian race/ethnicity.
COVID-19 vaccination at the time of first infection was associated with a markedly reduced likelihood of developing ME/CFS-like illness after COVID-19.

Among all participants, older age (≥65 years) was associated with lower likelihood of ME/CFS-like illness without prior COVID-19, while higher Charlson Comorbidity Index scores were associated with increased likelihood.

Persons with ME/CFS-like illness after COVID-19 had significantly better SF-36 scores for role limitations due to physical health and bodily pain than persons with ME/CFS-like illness without prior COVID-19, but significantly worse vitality (energy) scores.

Persons with ME/CFS-like illness after COVID-19 had significantly better cognitive function and less severe orthostatic symptoms, but significantly higher anxiety scores, than persons with ME/CFS-like illness without prior COVID-19.

Both ME/CFS-like illness groups (after COVID-19 and without prior COVID-19) had significantly lower SF-36 functional scores across all domains, lower cognitive function, higher orthostatic symptom scores, and higher depression and anxiety scores than persons without ME/CFS-like illness.
A much smaller proportion of persons with ME/CFS-like illness after COVID-19 (2.6%) were unable to work due to disability compared to those with ME/CFS-like illness without prior COVID-19 (26%).
Blood adrenaline levels were elevated in ME/CFS patients at rest compared to healthy controls.
β1 adrenergic receptor expression in blood was elevated in ME/CFS patients at rest compared to healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients showed a greater post-exercise increase in α2A adrenergic receptor expression in blood compared to healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients showed a greater post-exercise increase in β2 adrenergic receptor expression in blood compared to healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients showed a greater post-exercise increase in COMT expression in blood compared to healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients showed an increased noradrenaline response to an orthostatic (postural) challenge test in blood, compared to healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients showed no significant differences in baseline peripheral adrenergic biomarkers compared to healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients exhibited a diminished adrenaline response to exercise compared to healthy controls.
Knowledge of ME/CFS scores among medical students and primary care health professionals significantly increased after engaging with an immersive VR educational experience compared to before.
Empathy for people living with ME/CFS significantly increased among participants after the VR experience compared to before.

Baseline (pre-VR) knowledge of ME/CFS did not significantly differ between medical students and primary care health professionals, suggesting a persistent knowledge gap even among experienced practitioners.

Fatigue, difficulty concentrating, trouble sleeping, and unrefreshing sleep were the most centrally connected 'bridge symptoms' linking internalizing disorder (MDD/GAD) and functional disorder (ME/CFS/FM/IBS) symptom domains.
The internalizing disorder (MDD/GAD) symptom domain was more densely interconnected than the functional disorder (ME/CFS/FM/IBS) symptom domain.
ME/CFS symptoms joint pain and post-exertional malaise were strongly connected with the core FM symptom of musculoskeletal pain.
Sore throat and tender lymph nodes, two ME/CFS-specific symptoms, were strongly connected to each other but only weakly connected to the rest of the ME/CFS symptom set.
IBS abdominal pain showed no strong relationships with other symptoms in the network besides FM abdominal pain, indicating a distinct comorbidity pattern for IBS.
Symptom prevalence was significantly higher in females than males for the majority of the internalizing and functional disorder symptoms studied.

The female symptom network was slightly more connected than the male network, but the difference in overall global strength was not statistically significant; a difference in network structure seen in initial analysis became inconsistent after balancing subgroup sizes, suggesting it was driven by unequal power rather than true sex differences.

Older adults (>50 years) reported fewer MDD and GAD symptoms but more functional disorder pain symptoms (e.g., muscle pain, WPI items) than younger adults, who reported IBS symptoms more often; overall symptom connectivity was comparable between age groups despite structural differences.

Post-exertional malaise showed high connectivity with core symptoms of both ME/CFS and FM while remaining weakly connected to widespread pain, supporting it as a distinguishing diagnostic feature of ME/CFS.

Difficulty thinking (a CIS-measured FM/functional cognitive symptom) was the only non-overlapping functional disorder symptom that showed connections within the internalizing disorder domain of the network, likely due to conceptual overlap with concentration difficulty.
Weight loss and suicidality (MDD symptoms) and upper arm pain (FM/WPI symptom) were the least connected symptoms in the overall network.

Combining the widespread pain index (WPI) body-site items into a single pain measure increased overall network density, indicating these items may dominate/overshadow other, non-pain-related symptom relationships.

Removing participants with comorbid rheumatoid arthritis, heart failure, ulcerative colitis, celiac disease, Crohn's disease, or cancer did not meaningfully change the overall symptom network structure, suggesting the reported bodily symptoms were not attributable to these other medical conditions.

Individuals with functional disorders, particularly ME/CFS, have a substantially higher prevalence of comorbid mood and anxiety disorders than those without functional disorders, as reported in prior literature cited by the authors.
Patients with bleeding disorder of unknown cause (BDUC) had significantly lower plasma vitamin C levels than healthy controls.
A significantly higher proportion of BDUC patients had suboptimal or severely deficient vitamin C status compared to healthy controls.
Nearly half of BDUC patients had generalized joint hypermobility (positive Beighton score), far more frequent than in healthy controls.
BDUC patients with joint hypermobility had significantly higher bleeding assessment tool scores than those without hypermobility.
Skin hyperextensibility was significantly more common in BDUC patients than in healthy controls.
Ten patients (nine with Beighton ≥5 and one with Beighton 4 who was over 50 years old) met the 2017 diagnostic criteria for hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS).
There was no significant association between low vitamin C levels and either a positive Beighton score or an above-median BAT score within the patient group.
A pathogenic PTPN11 variant causing Noonan syndrome was identified in a 67-year-old woman with BDUC, whose syndrome had gone undiagnosed until her seventh decade of life.
A variant of unknown significance in COL1A1 was identified in a patient fulfilling hEDS criteria, potentially associated with an osteogenesis imperfecta/EDS overlap disorder or arthrochalasia EDS.
No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were identified in genes for vascular, classical, or classical-like EDS, excluding these subtypes in all screened BDUC patients.
Patients with a hypermobility-associated diagnosis (hEDS or Noonan syndrome) had higher bleeding scores than those without such a diagnosis.
Menorrhagia was the most common bleeding symptom, affecting nearly all women in the BDUC cohort, and heavy menstrual bleeding led to hysterectomy in a substantial subset.
A substantial majority (77%) of patients referred for suspected inherited bleeding disorders had no laboratory explanation for their bleeding phenotype, i.e., were classified as BDUC.

hEDS is commonly associated with a range of comorbidities including migraine, chronic fatigue, gut dysmotility, small fiber neuropathy, POTS, and anxiety, which contribute to significant impacts on quality of life and daily functioning.
Patients with hEDS experience an average diagnostic delay of 14 years between symptom onset and diagnosis.
A 2021 study found that patients with self-reported joint hypermobility or hEDS saw an average of 6 different providers over multiple years while seeking an accurate diagnosis.
hEDS is estimated to affect approximately 255 million people worldwide, making it the most common connective tissue disorder and the most common EDS subtype.
All 15 focus group participants with a clinical diagnosis of hEDS reported experiencing difficulty being diagnosed.
60% of study participants (9/15) reported being diagnosed with hEDS specifically by a medical geneticist.
Consistent with prior literature, the study sample was predominantly female (80%, 12/15), reflecting the reported excess of affected females in hEDS.

Focus group participants described extreme financial and time burdens of the hEDS diagnostic odyssey, including one participant who spent US $10,000 in a year and another who spent approximately US $100,000 and saw 200 or more physicians over 20 years before diagnosis.
Only 23% of US physicians surveyed felt very or mostly confident in making a rare disease diagnosis, contributing to diagnostic delays for conditions like hEDS.

A retrospective cohort study at the Toronto GoodHope EDS Clinic found that many highly symptomatic hEDS patients did not meet the 2017 hEDS diagnostic criteria and were left undiagnosed, suggesting a need to refine the criteria.
Focus group participants strongly endorsed including differential diagnosis information in the tool to avoid misattributing symptoms of vascular EDS (a life-threatening subtype) to hEDS.

MARS scoring of the hEDS diagnostic tool prototype by 3 participants showed moderately high to high ratings, indicating the tool was easy to navigate, functioned well, and was moderately to highly visually appealing.
Engagement subscale scores on the MARS were moderate, which was expected since the diagnostic tool was not designed to be entertaining or highly interactive.

MARS subjective quality scores indicated high satisfaction with the tool, with respondents indicating they would recommend it to others, although 67% said they would not pay for the app and most felt it was not intended for repeated use.

Most respondents on the app-specific rating scale felt the diagnostic tool would increase knowledge of the hEDS diagnostic process, encourage continued help-seeking, and increase the likelihood of receiving an accurate diagnosis and awareness of the importance of proper hEDS assessment.

A systematic review of 70 patient-facing digital health tools found that 84% of corresponding studies demonstrated one or more positive outcomes (e.g., knowledge, psychosocial well-being, behavior change, engagement), supporting the rationale for a patient-facing hEDS diagnostic tool.
Surgical management of joint instability in patients with non-vascular EDS is more likely to succeed when the diagnosis of EDS is established preoperatively.
Postoperatively, a high proportion of operated shoulders (72.7%) redislocated over time regardless of whether the dominant or non-dominant side was operated on.
Despite a high dislocation rate, the majority of patients (>70%) reported being satisfied or very satisfied with their joint surgery overall.
Nine of 22 operated shoulders (40.9%) required more than one surgical intervention.
Four of 9 operated elbows (44.4%) underwent more than one surgical intervention.
Nine of 18 operated wrists (50%) underwent more than one surgical intervention, mainly for scapholunate instability.
The knee was the joint most frequently requiring reoperation, with 30 of 50 operated knees (60%) undergoing more than one surgery, primarily for patellar instability.
Ten of 28 operated ankles (35.7%) required reoperation, most commonly for ligamentoplasty failure.
Approximately one-fifth (20.8%) of all surgical operations across joints were carried out arthroscopically.
Primary knee surgery was performed arthroscopically in 36% of cases.
Local or regional anaesthesia was ineffective in over a third of shoulder surgeries and over a quarter of wrist surgeries, consistent with reported resistance to local anaesthetics in EDS.
Across the cohort, 42% of patients experienced problems with general anaesthesia and 47% were insensitive to local/regional anaesthesia, consistent with known anaesthetic resistance in EDS.
Despite knee surgery, 58% of patients continued to need a mobility aid, and 62% had persistent lameness.
Despite ankle surgery, 64.3% of patients continued to need a mobility aid, and most had difficulty walking on uneven ground and could not run.
The reintervention rate for dislocation after primary Latarjet (coracoid bone block) procedure in this EDS cohort (2.7%, 3/11) was comparable to the rate reported in the general literature (1.6%).
Preoperative EDS diagnosis awareness varied greatly by joint operated, being known in only 22% of knee/elbow surgeries but 59% of shoulder surgeries.

Surgical intervention was uncommon among EDS patients, with only 17.3% of those followed in the reference centre undergoing joint surgery, and only 31.8% of surgical patients had a confirmed 2017-criteria EDS diagnosis.
Knee functional outcome (Lysholm-Tegner score) was better in patients who underwent a single surgery compared to those requiring multiple operations.
Dominant-side shoulders and wrists had worse functional scores and more frequent postoperative pain than their non-dominant counterparts.
Postoperative complications across joints included complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), deep vein thrombosis, sepsis/surgical site infection, and dysesthesia around scars.

The patient was diagnosed with classical-type EDS based on clinical criteria (2 major: skin hyperextensibility and general joint hypermobility; 3 minor: soft doughy skin, skin fragility, and complications of joint hypermobility) rather than genetic testing.
This case represents the first reported instance of coexisting chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis (CNO), sacroiliac arthritis, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in the same patient.
Intravenous disodium pamidronate (bisphosphonate) therapy for CNO resulted in disease remission after 2 years, allowing discontinuation of pharmacotherapy.

Addition of methotrexate plus later risedronate for CNO relapse with active inflammatory spinal lesions led to pain resolution and improved general condition, though later relapse occurred and prompted addition of sacroiliitis-directed therapy.
Addition of meloxicam and sulfasalazine for active sacroiliac arthritis resulted in resolution of symptoms.
The patient tested negative for HLA-B27 and HLA-Cw6, markers commonly associated with spondyloarthropathies.
The patient developed gastritis and colitis following oral antibiotic and diclofenac treatment, possibly reflecting a known predisposition to gastrointestinal disease in patients with EDS and CNO.

The patient's family history included a father with ankylosing spondylitis and Crohn's disease and a mother with sarcoidosis, suggesting a familial predisposition to autoimmune/inflammatory conditions.

Per cited literature, EDS diagnosis is typically made an average of 14 years after the first clinical manifestations appear, consistent with the delayed recognition of hypermobility and skin findings in this patient (not noted until age 17.5 despite prior hospitalizations).

MRI of the sacroiliac joints revealed active inflammatory lesions despite the absence of significant elevation in inflammatory laboratory markers (CRP normal), underscoring MRI's superior sensitivity for detecting sacroiliac arthritis.

The patient had mild anemia (reduced erythrocyte count, hemoglobin, and hematocrit) at the time of active sacroiliac arthritis/CNO diagnosis, which improved somewhat at follow-up after treatment modification.
The patient's height (182 cm) was above the 100th percentile for age, noted as part of her physical exam findings alongside joint hypermobility and skin rash.
Prior literature indicates EDS may increase risk of multiple rheumatological conditions including psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis, rheumatoid arthritis, and fibromyalgia.

A 22-year-old male with autism and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome presented with cerebral air embolism and diffuse bilateral cerebral infarction, found on imaging to originate from a large cavitary lung lesion in the left upper lobe.
The patient had significant ectasia of the main pulmonary artery (5.0 cm diameter), a finding considered most consistent with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS).

The authors note that cavitary nodule formation has been previously reported as a pulmonary manifestation of vascular EDS, thought to arise as a sequela of spontaneous pulmonary hemorrhage and hematoma formation.
The reported patient had co-occurring autism and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Genetic testing identified a pathogenic COL1A2 c.279G>A variant in the patient, confirming the diagnosis of arthrochalasia EDS.
The patient presented with a 43.6° lumbar dextroscoliosis with apex at L3, diagnosed before age 2 in the context of arthrochalasia EDS.
After 3.5 years of treatment with the Wood-Rigo-Cheneau (WRC) derotational brace plus weekly physical therapy, the patient's Cobb angle decreased to 8°.
The patient's Cobb angle stayed stable under 15° while on the WRC brace for 12 months, and measured 14° after being brace-free for 6 months at age 6.
The patient experienced no major complications from wearing the WRC brace and was able to participate fully in physical therapy without physical limitations.
Serial casting before age 2 years was reported in a landmark 2005 study (Mehta) to resolve scoliotic curves in 100% of treated patients.

In nine infants with infantile idiopathic scoliosis treated with an elongation bending derotation brace, four were fully corrected to curves under 10° and the remaining five improved from a mean of 57° to 21°.
Compared with the Boston brace, patients with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis treated with the WRC brace had significantly lower rates of spinal surgery and lower major curve progression.

Among 51 female AIS patients treated with the WRC TLSO brace, compliant patients (brace ≥20 hours/day, exercise ≥3x/week) improved on average 10.19°±5.5°, whereas non-compliant patients deteriorated on average 5.52°±4.3°.

In 93 AIS patients treated with the WRC brace, 83.8% (n=79) who wore it as prescribed showed no progression and slight improvement in Cobb angle from 31.97° to 28.97°, while the treatment failure group (n=14) worsened to a mean of 55.93°.
Bracing with a TLSO or Milwaukee brace was successful in preventing spinal surgery before age 10 in more than two-thirds of patients with infantile idiopathic scoliosis.
A rib vertebral angle difference greater than 20° and a Cobb angle greater than 30° are cited as specific findings associated with scoliosis curve progression risk.
Current literature on arthrochalasia EDS reports scoliosis as a less common clinical manifestation alongside congenital hip dislocation, severe joint hypermobility, and skin hyperextensibility.
The patient's family reported that a rib hump present with a curve over 50° resolved entirely with WRC brace treatment, with the curve reduced to between 11° and 20°.
Serial casting requires repeated general anesthesia exposure for cast changes in young children, raising concern for potential negative neurodevelopmental effects, an issue avoided by bracing.

Scoliotic deformity is theorized to initiate from anterior vertebral overgrowth creating a wedging effect that replaces normal thoracic kyphosis with lordosis, triggering compensatory spinal rotation.
Arthroscopic outside-in suture stabilization of a hypermobile anterior horn of the lateral meniscus significantly improved Lysholm Knee Scoring Scale scores from before surgery to final follow-up.

MRI findings correlated poorly with arthroscopic findings: MRI suggested an anterior horn meniscal tear in three knees, but arthroscopy found no true anterior horn tears in any of the 17 knees, instead revealing a parameniscal tear in all cases.

All patients presented preoperatively with anterior lateral knee pain, and most had lateral joint line tenderness, with a minority reporting locking sensation, hyperextension, or loss of full extension.

Unlike prior reports linking lateral meniscus hypermobility mainly to younger patients (often via discoid meniscus), this cohort included no discoid menisci and over half the patients were older than 50 years, suggesting the condition should also be considered in older patients with anterior lateral knee pain.

Whole exome sequencing identified a de novo heterozygous splicing variant in COL3A1 (c.1662+1G>A) that disrupts a conserved donor splice site and is classified as pathogenic, confirming the diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in the patient.
Targeted parental Sanger sequencing showed neither parent nor the unaffected sibling carried the COL3A1 variant, confirming it arose de novo in the proband.

Over a 6-year period, the patient experienced recurrent gastrointestinal perforations (sigmoid colon, descending colon, transverse colon, and multiple small bowel segments) requiring repeated emergency laparotomies, resections, and colostomies.

Pathology of resected bowel showed marked transmural inflammatory infiltrate, fibrinopurulent exudate with giant cells, focal thinning of the muscularis propria, and dilated congested submucosal and serosal blood vessels, unusual findings that prompted genetic testing for vEDS.

Follow-up imaging revealed a saccular hepatic artery aneurysm (18x17mm) with a dilated left hepatic artery branch communicating with a dilated distal left portal vein, suggestive of an arteriovenous fistula causing portosystemic shunting.

During a subsequent hospitalization the patient developed additional rapidly growing aneurysms: a 4.2 cm right paraspinal (T3-T4) false aneurysm and a 2x1 cm left wrist (Guyon's canal/hypothenar) aneurysm causing mass effect on the ulnar nerve with hand pain.

The high-risk paraspinal (T3-T4) aneurysm was successfully treated via endovascular coiling embolization due to its bleeding risk, while the wrist aneurysm was managed conservatively with physiotherapy and pain management.

The discussion notes that celiprolol, a beta-blocker, has shown promise in reducing arterial events in vEDS, but overall efficacy and safety of medical therapies for vEDS remain inconclusive due to limited studies with small sample sizes.

The discussion states that elective surgical treatment (open and endovascular) of vascular disorders in EDS patients has been associated with good outcomes and vascular interventions can be safely performed rather than withheld until rupture or acute symptoms.
Living with vEDS was associated with substantial psychological burden, including anxiety related to the constant threat of life-threatening complications, affecting both the patient and her family.

A 14-year-old female with hEDS and recurrent left posterior shoulder instability, who had failed two prior arthroscopic capsulorrhaphy/plication procedures, underwent arthroscopic-assisted latissimus dorsi (LD) tendon transfer with pectoralis minor (PM) release to dynamically rebalance the shoulder.
Postoperatively, pain scores decreased and functional scores markedly improved over 24-29 months of follow-up, with no subsequent dislocation or subluxation events on the operated shoulder.

Dynamic electromyography of the latissimus dorsi muscle demonstrated abnormal rapid firing patterns at rest and with humerothoracic abduction on the affected side compared to the contralateral side, indicating LD overactivity/spasm contributing to posterior shoulder instability.
Botulinum toxin injection into the latissimus dorsi muscle significantly improved the patient's shoulder pain and subluxations for approximately 6 weeks before symptoms recurred.

The patient had marked scapular dyskinesia with a resting protracted scapular posture attributed to pectoralis minor overactivity, and was tender at the PM insertion with a positive Tinel's sign, contributing to posterior shoulder instability.

Arthroscopic capsulorrhaphy and posterior labral repair procedures, while having <10% failure rate in patients without hEDS, are less effective in hEDS patients due to poor tissue structural integrity.
In a prior study, 5 cases of anterior shoulder instability secondary to EDS treated with Achilles tendon allograft capsulorrhaphy resulted in improved stability and pain in 4 of 5 shoulders.
The patient's percent and absolute NK cell (CD16+/CD56+) counts were below the reference range, suggesting innate cell-mediated immune dysfunction potentially related to his EDS.

16S rDNA sequencing and MALDI-TOF MS identified Priestia endophytica (formerly Bacillus endophyticus), an organism previously known only as a plant endophyte, in surgical wound cultures from this EDS patient, representing the first reported instance of this organism causing a human infection.

Acid-fast bacilli cultures from multiple debridements (first, fourth, and eleventh) were identified as Mycobacterium goodii, a rapidly growing nontuberculous mycobacterium associated with posttraumatic wound and hardware infections.

Combination antimicrobial therapy with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and doxycycline, guided by susceptibility testing, resulted in prompt wound healing in this EDS patient with dual mycobacterial/bacterial hardware infection.

EDS is stated to increase risk of infections and allergic disorders and is potentially associated with immune deficiencies, which the authors propose as a contributing factor to this patient's atypical infections.

The FDA recommends avoiding fluoroquinolone antibiotics in patients with EDS due to an association between this drug class and aortic/arterial aneurysm risk, which the authors cite as relevant to antibiotic selection in this case.
Men with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome had a significantly higher prevalence of penile fracture compared to disease-free controls.
Men with Marfan syndrome had a significantly higher prevalence of penile fracture compared to disease-free controls.

Adult Chiari revision patients requiring occipitocervical fusion (OCF) or ventral decompression (VD) had significantly higher preoperative rates of diagnosed Ehlers-Danlos syndrome than those undergoing posterior fossa decompression with/without duraplasty (PFD/D) revision alone.
Adult Chiari revision patients requiring OCF or VD had significantly higher preoperative rates of diagnosed dysautonomia than those undergoing PFD/D revision alone.
Adult Chiari revision patients requiring OCF or VD had significantly higher preoperative rates of diagnosed craniocervical instability (CCI) than those undergoing PFD/D revision alone.
A retroflexed odontoid was significantly more common among adult Chiari revision patients who underwent ventral decompression than in those undergoing PFD/D or OCF revision.
A retroflexed odontoid was significantly more common in the ventral decompression (VD) group compared with the PFD/D and OCF groups.
Rates of postoperative improvement did not differ significantly between the PFD/D, OCF, and VD revision surgery groups.

The authors identified residual dorsal compression, persistent syrinx, craniocervical instability, and ventral brainstem compression from a significant retroflexed odontoid as possible etiologies warranting revision surgery.

A novel mutation in the PRDM5 gene was identified in a patient with brittle cornea syndrome type 2 who presented with congenital glaucoma and keratoglobus, an association not previously well described.

Gene ontology and KEGG enrichment of MT-induced differentially expressed transcripts implicated responses to stress and infectious processes, including cytokine, chemokine, MAPK, and NFkB signaling pathways.
After filtering out non-coding RNAs, pseudogenes, and novel transcripts, 161 protein-coding RNAs remained differentially expressed with MT (22 upregulated, 139 downregulated).

GO/KEGG reanalysis of the top 24 individually consistent DE genes showed responses to bacteria and chemokine signaling as the top affected cell functions.

RT-qPCR validation in the RNAseq subcohort (n=6) confirmed that HBEGF expression was significantly downregulated following manual therapy.

In the real touch task, women with fibromyalgia showed a significant preference for slow (affective) over fast (non-affective) touch, similar to healthy controls, with no significant overall group difference in pleasantness ratings.

In the imagery task, participants with fibromyalgia rated imagined slow touch as more pleasant than imagined fast touch, comparably to controls, with no significant overall main effect of Group on pleasantness.
A significant Tool*Group interaction emerged in the imagery task, though post hoc comparisons showed no significant between-group differences in pleasantness for any specific tool.
Women with fibromyalgia reported significantly less experience of affective touch during childhood and adolescence compared to healthy controls, as measured by the TBIO questionnaire.
Adult experience of affective touch, and overall comfort with and fondness for interpersonal touch, did not differ between women with fibromyalgia and healthy controls.

In women with fibromyalgia, higher self-reported pain intensity (whole-body and forearm) before testing was significantly associated with lower expected pleasantness of imagined touch, particularly imagined hand touch.

In women with fibromyalgia, pleasantness ratings of the fast (non-affective) touch of the brush in the imagery task were significantly positively correlated with pleasantness ratings of the same touch in the real task, a relationship not seen in healthy controls.
Within the fibromyalgia group, self-reported whole-body pain intensity was significantly higher than pain intensity localized to the forearm at the time of testing.

Women with fibromyalgia reported moderate levels of kinesiophobia and pain catastrophizing.
The fibromyalgia sample had a markedly higher BMI than healthy controls, consistent with prior evidence linking obesity to fibromyalgia symptomatology.
Patients with fibromyalgia were found to have a higher prevalence of pruritus compared with individuals without fibromyalgia in a large population-based database.
The study also examined and reported an association between fibromyalgia and pruritus-related skin conditions.

Genetic polymorphisms in the serotonin transporter gene (5-HTTLPR) alter serotonin signaling and are associated with increased susceptibility to fibromyalgia and depression.
Fibromyalgia is characterized by reduced serotonin (5-HT) levels and a notable decrease in the serotonin transporter (5-HTT) in the cerebrospinal fluid of affected individuals.

Genetic variations in the 5-HT2A receptor are associated with fibromyalgia, with certain genotypes correlated with heightened pain sensitivity.
Decreased serum levels of 5-HIAA, a serotonin metabolite, have been linked to improved self-reported pain perception among FM patients.
Downregulation of the 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C receptors may contribute to the onset of chronic hyperalgesia in fibromyalgia.

Intermittent cold stress (ICS) induced mechanical allodynia in wild-type mice, lowering the mechanical withdrawal threshold compared to controls.
ICS induced thermal hyperalgesia in wild-type mice, shortening thermal withdrawal latency compared to controls.
Electroacupuncture (EA) at ST36 significantly reversed ICS-induced mechanical allodynia and thermal hyperalgesia compared to the untreated FM group.
Sham electroacupuncture (needle retention without electrical stimulation) did not reduce ICS-induced mechanical allodynia or thermal hyperalgesia.
Genetic deletion of TRPV1 (Trpv1-/-) abolished ICS-induced mechanical allodynia and thermal hyperalgesia, restoring pain thresholds compared to the FM group.
ICS markedly increased plasma pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-17, TNFα, and IFNγ in both the FM and Sham groups compared to controls.
Electroacupuncture markedly lowered the ICS-elevated plasma levels of IL-6, IL-17, TNFα, and IFNγ compared to the FM group.
TRPV1 knockout reduced ICS-elevated plasma IL-6, IL-17, TNFα, and IFNγ to levels comparable to the EA group.
In the somatosensory cortex (SSC), phosphorylated IL-17, PI3K, AKT, JNK, ERK, p38, and NF-κB were all significantly upregulated in FM and Sham groups compared to control mice.
EA and TRPV1 knockout, but not sham EA, considerably attenuated the ICS-induced upregulation of IL-17 and its downstream signaling (PI3K, AKT, JNK, ERK, p38, NF-κB) in the somatosensory cortex.
In cerebellar lobule V (CB5), phosphorylated TRPV1, IL-17, PI3K, AKT, JNK, ERK, p38, and NF-κB were significantly increased in FM and Sham groups compared to controls.
EA and TRPV1 knockout markedly suppressed the elevated TRPV1, IL-17, PI3K, AKT, JNK, ERK, p38, and NF-κB in CB5 compared to the FM group.

In cerebellar lobule VI (CB6), phosphorylated TRPV1, IL-17, PI3K, AKT, JNK, ERK, p38, and NF-κB were significantly increased in FM and Sham groups compared to controls, and this was abolished by EA and TRPV1 knockout.

In cerebellar lobule VII (CB7), phosphorylated TRPV1, IL-17, PI3K, AKT, JNK, ERK, p38, and NF-κB were significantly increased in FM and Sham groups compared to controls, and this was reversed by EA and TRPV1 knockout.

Immunofluorescence staining showed IL-17 and phosphorylated ERK signals were low in normal mice but markedly increased in the somatosensory cortex, CB5, CB6, and CB7 of FM mice, and this augmentation was reversed by EA (but not sham EA) and by TRPV1 knockout.

The authors conclude that TRPV1 is required upstream of IL-17A/IL-17RA activation, since TRPV1 knockout abolished the IL-17A, IL-17RA and downstream PI3K/Akt, MAPK, and NF-κB pathway activation seen in the FM model, whereas EA also reduced these pathways without deleting TRPV1.
The alternative MCAS criteria include far more accepted symptoms (153) than the consortium MCAS criteria (18), invoking a broader range of clinical systems.

Using California ICD-10 inpatient admission data, the diagnosis rate of idiopathic MCAS increased 12.6-fold since its ICD code was created in 2016, while the rate of systemic mastocytosis remained constant.
In a cited study of MCAS referrals, only 3% of patients demonstrated elevated tryptase levels during acute episodes, suggesting most referred patients lack objective evidence of mast cell activation.

In the same cited referral study, only 21% of patients achieved symptom control with mast cell-directed therapies, arguing against mast cell activation as the underlying mechanism in most referred patients.
In the cited referral study, 56% of MCAS referrals were based on patient self-evaluation and internet research rather than clinical/laboratory evidence.

Word-embedding analysis showed that semantic similarity between consortium and alternative MCAS criteria was much lower than between two independent SLE criteria sets, indicating the two MCAS definitions describe dissimilar symptom concepts.

LLM-simulated differential diagnosis using consortium MCAS criteria symptoms yielded anaphylaxis as the top diagnosis, with systemic mastocytosis and IgE-mediated food allergy also in the top 10, reflecting appropriate mast cell-related specificity.

LLM-simulated differential diagnosis for alternative MCAS criteria did not include any allergic or histamine-mediated conditions in the top 10, instead spanning rheumatologic, endocrine, hematologic, and infectious disease categories.

Mast cell-related conditions (e.g. mastocytosis, allergic disorders) were ranked notably lower among the differential diagnoses generated by alternative MCAS criteria compared to consortium MCAS criteria.

The top 50 differential diagnoses captured 75.6-89.4% of all diagnoses generated for control criteria and consortium MCAS criteria, but only 48.4% of diagnoses generated for alternative MCAS criteria, indicating much broader, less concentrated diagnostic spread for the latter.

Shannon diversity of diagnoses generated from alternative MCAS criteria was significantly higher than from consortium MCAS criteria and all control criteria, reflecting greater diagnostic non-specificity.

Bootstrap consistency (Bray-Curtis similarity) across 10,000 differential diagnosis iterations was significantly lower for alternative MCAS criteria than for consortium MCAS criteria and all control criteria, indicating less reproducible diagnostic outputs.

Diagnosis co-occurrence network analysis showed lower edge density for the alternative MCAS diagnosis network than for the consortium MCAS network, indicating a more diffuse, less interconnected set of associated diagnoses.

Based on diagnosis centrality in co-occurrence networks, the cosine similarity between consortium and alternative MCAS criteria networks was significantly lower than between two SLE criteria networks, confirming substantial divergence in associated diagnoses.
Serum beta-tryptase (TPSB2) levels did not differ significantly between long-COVID patients and matched controls.

Activated mast cells within the lung immune microenvironment promote lung inflammation and injury in antibody-mediated TRALI, shown both in vitro and in vivo.

Activation of the TLR3/MAPK signaling pathway in mast cells drives enhanced production of proinflammatory factors that contribute to lung inflammation and injury in antibody-mediated TRALI.

Pharmacologically targeting the TLR3/MAPK pathway to inhibit mast cell activation normalized the proinflammatory microenvironment and alleviated lung inflammation and injury in the preclinical TRALI mouse model.
Co-culturing lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-pretreated mast cell line with anti-MHC I antibody activates mast cells in vitro, modeling the TRALI 'two-hit' mechanism.
Mature Hoxb8 mast cells sensitized with sera from peanut allergic patients showed significantly higher activation (CD107a+) upon peanut extract stimulation compared to sera from nonallergic controls.
ROC analysis showed the Hoxb8 MAT achieved a peak diagnostic accuracy (AUROC 0.97) at 100 ng/mL peanut allergen, which was maintained at 1000 ng/mL.
BAT diagnostic accuracy reached its maximum (AUROC 0.99) at 10 ng/mL peanut allergen but declined at higher concentrations (100 and 1000 ng/mL) due to a hook effect.
sIgE against Ara h2 showed the highest diagnostic accuracy among serological markers (AUROC 0.91), outperforming sIgE against whole peanut extract and SPT (both AUROC 0.89).
SPT wheal size was significantly larger in peanut allergic patients compared to nonallergic controls.

At optimal cutoffs, the Hoxb8 MAT correctly classified 64/69 peanut allergic and 26/27 nonallergic samples, while the BAT correctly classified 65/69 allergic and 26/27 nonallergic samples, showing comparable performance.
Only a weak, though statistically significant, correlation (r=0.3) was found between Hoxb8 MC maximal activation and SPT wheal size results.
A strong but imperfect correlation was found between Hoxb8 MC maximal activation and sIgE against whole peanut extract (r=0.91) and Ara h2 (r=0.81).

In seven serum samples from previously identified BAT nonresponders, the Hoxb8 MAT correctly showed dose-dependent activation in all four confirmed peanut allergic samples and no activation in the three nonallergic samples.
Among 12 sensitized but tolerant (nonallergic, sIgE-positive) individuals, 11 remained correctly negative in the Hoxb8 MAT, while one showed a false positive result.

Both the Hoxb8 MAT and BAT results showed significant correlations with clinical disease severity graded by Astier classification, with the Hoxb8 MAT correlation strengthening with increasing allergen concentration while the BAT showed a hook-effect with optimal correlation at 10 ng/mL.

Logistic regression models incorporating all peanut allergen concentrations showed the Hoxb8 MAT and BAT achieved similarly high diagnostic accuracy (AUROC 0.95 and 0.96 respectively), outperforming SPT and sIgE measurements.

BAT requires roughly 100-fold lower allergen concentrations than the Hoxb8 MAT to induce comparable activation, potentially explained by higher FcεRI receptor density on primary basophils (~250,000 receptors/cell) compared to passively sensitized Hoxb8 MCs (~90,000 receptors/cell).

Basophils from so-called nonresponders (impaired FcεRI-dependent activation) have been reported to feature low tyrosine kinase Syk levels, posing a diagnostic challenge for BAT that the Hoxb8 MAT may overcome.
