IFNγ production by mast cells and CD8+ T cell infiltration were both markedly reduced in MrgB2−/− mice compared with wild-type mice after Tyrp-2 180 challenge.
siRNA-mediated knockdown of MrgX2 in human LAD2 mast cells reduced IFNγ production in response to Tyrp-2 180 stimulation.
Calcium flux upon Tyrp-2 180 stimulation was significantly reduced in MrgX2-silenced LAD2 mast cells compared with scrambled controls.
Treatment with the calcineurin inhibitor FK506 mitigated IFNγ production by LAD2 mast cells stimulated with Tyrp-2 180, and blocked NFAT1 nuclear translocation.

Tyrp-2 180 stimulation decreased cytoplasmic phosphorylated NFAT1 and increased nuclear dephosphorylated NFAT1 in mast cells; this translocation was abolished by FK506 co-treatment or by MrgX2 silencing.
The authors cite a prior study (Katayama et al.) reporting higher mast cell numbers in lesional than unaffected skin of active vitiligo patients, supporting the current study's conclusions.

The discussion notes that simvastatin and lenalidomide are clinically used vitiligo treatments whose mechanisms may involve mast cell apoptosis (via SCF signaling) and MMP-9 inhibition, respectively, though this was not directly tested in this study.
HBD2 promotes mast cell activation and degranulation, thereby indirectly contributing to allergic reactions.
Serum levels of HBD2 are elevated in patients with atopic dermatitis and psoriasis compared to presumed non-affected states.
Patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria and associated angioedema have higher serum HBD2 levels than those without angioedema.
HBD2 is proposed as a potential marker of inflammation and may have therapeutic applications, though data on its role in allergic skin disease remain limited.
Hematologic staining showed a significant increase in average positive mast cells per field in post-NACT compared to pre-NACT matched HGSOC tumors.
Both intraepithelial and stromal mast cells were significantly increased post-NACT compared to pre-NACT tumors, indicating mast cells infiltrate both tumor compartments.
Post-NACT mast cell counts (hematologic stain) stratified by upper/lower quartile showed no significant association with progression-free survival or overall survival.
Patients with lower levels of pre-NACT total mast cells experienced significantly longer progression-free survival.
Patients with lower levels of pre-NACT intraepithelial mast cells experienced significantly longer progression-free survival.
No significant associations were detected between total or intraepithelial pre-NACT mast cells and overall survival.
Intratumoral histamine expression was significantly upregulated following NACT, measured both by mean fluorescence intensity and integrated optical density.
Tryptase+/CPA3+ double-positive mast cells were significantly upregulated in post-NACT compared to pre-NACT HGSOC tumors.
Tryptase+/CPA3+ mast cells were significantly increased following NACT in both intraepithelial and stromal tumor regions.
Total and stromal Tryptase+ mast cells were significantly upregulated post-NACT, while intraepithelial Tryptase+ cells showed a non-significant trend toward increase.
Lower total Tryptase+/CPA3+ mast cell levels post-NACT (median stratification) were associated with improved overall survival.
Patients with progression-free survival of 12 months or less had significantly higher mean total Tryptase+/CPA3+ mast cells compared to patients with PFS over 12 months.

Higher levels of total Tryptase+ mast cells post-NACT (quartile stratification) were significantly associated with improved overall survival, contrasting the Tryptase+/CPA3+ subset's association with worse survival.
In LUVA human mast cells, chemotherapy (carboplatin+paclitaxel) treatment induced a significant over 7-fold increase in AREG mRNA expression.
Chemotherapy treatment of LUVA mast cells significantly increased CCL2 mRNA expression by 7.5-fold.
Chemotherapy treatment significantly decreased TGFB1 mRNA expression in LUVA mast cells, a known inhibitor of mast cell activation.
Chemotherapy treatment significantly decreased VEGFA mRNA expression in LUVA mast cells despite the known pro-angiogenic role of mast cells.
Chemotherapy treatment produced a 1.76-fold increase in TNF mRNA in LUVA mast cells, but this did not reach statistical significance.
No significant differences were observed in IL-2, CCL7, IL-10, or TGFB2 mRNA expression in LUVA mast cells after chemotherapy treatment.
LPS-challenged HepG2 cells secreted more IL-6 protein into the culture medium than negative controls, and this was prevented by botanical blend (BOT) treatment.
At day 1 of the LPS challenge, mRNA expression of TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8, and IL-1β was increased in LPS-only HepG2 cells, while BOT treatment kept expression at or below negative-control levels.
BOT treatment decreased TLR-4 mRNA expression compared to LPS-only HepG2 cells at day 1, though this difference disappeared by day 8.
By day 8 of LPS challenge, antioxidant enzyme genes GPX-2, SOD, and CAT were more highly expressed in BOT-treated HepG2 cells than in LPS-only cells.
BOT pretreatment reduced ROS production in HepG2 cells challenged with either H2O2 or LPS, achieving levels comparable to Vitamin C treatment and negative controls.

Intraperitoneal LPS challenge significantly reduced average daily gain and body weight and increased feed conversion ratio in weaning piglets during the week following challenge, with BOT-supplemented piglets showing intermediate performance.
Over the entire post-challenge period, BOT supplementation improved growth performance relative to LPS-only pigs, with a trend toward better ADG compared to both other groups.
Hepatic mRNA expression of TLR-4 and TNF-α was increased at days 21 and 28 post-challenge, IL-6 and IFN-γ mainly at day 21, and IL-8 at day 28 in LPS-challenged piglets versus negative controls.
BOT supplementation lowered hepatic expression of TLR-4, TNF-α, IL-6, and IFN-γ at day 21, and TNF-α and IL-8 at day 28, compared to LPS-only piglets.
Hepatic BD-2 expression was higher in LPS-challenged piglets, and BOT supplementation reduced BD-2 levels closer to negative controls.

Hepatic BD-3 expression was reduced by LPS challenge at day 21 but normalized by day 28, and BOT supplementation significantly enhanced BD-3 expression at both timepoints via an NF-kB-independent mechanism.
BOT+ piglets had higher hepatic ZO-1 expression than LPS-only piglets at day 28, indicating improved tight-junction gene expression in liver.

Hepatic antioxidant gene expression (GPX-2 at days 21/28, SOD-1 and SOD-2 at day 21) was decreased by LPS challenge, and BOT supplementation improved expression of all these antioxidant enzymes, with CAT also increased by BOT at day 28.
Jejunal mucosa mRNA of TNF-α, IL-6, and IFN-γ was increased with LPS challenge at day 28, with BOT treatment yielding levels closer to negative controls.
In jejunal mucosa, LPS reduced ZO-1 expression at day 21 while BOT increased it, and a similar protective pattern was observed for claudin-1 at day 28.

LPS-challenged piglets tended to have increased jejunal crypt depth and had a significantly lower villi-height-to-crypt-depth ratio at day 21, with BOT restoring these morphology parameters toward negative-control levels; a similar improvement with BOT was seen at day 28.

Although total mast cell numbers in jejunal mucosa did not differ between groups, the percentage of activated/degranulated mast cells at day 21 was significantly reduced in BOT-supplemented piglets compared to LPS-only piglets.
Liver TNF-α protein concentration showed only a trend toward being increased in LPS-challenged piglets compared to controls, with BOT-supplemented piglets showing an intermediate value.

Two piglets in the LPS-only (CTR+) group died from severe endotoxemia following the LPS challenge, while all pigs in the challenge groups showed transient signs of mild endotoxemia (lethargy, salivation, vomiting, panting) resolving within about 6 hours.
Sarcoidosis-associated small fiber neuropathy (SSFN) is a common complication estimated to occur in 40-86% of sarcoidosis patients based on prior literature.
Of 74 sarcoidosis patients with SFN symptoms, 48 (65%) were diagnosed with probable SFN per Besta criteria after excluding large fiber neuropathy and confounding conditions.
Among 48 probable SSFN patients, 35% reported a length-dependent and 44% a non-length-dependent pain phenotype, with no significant difference between the two (OR=1.4, P=0.4).
Continuous non-length-dependent pain was significantly less commonly reported than the other three pain phenotypes among probable SSFN patients.
Intermittent pain was reported with similar frequency in length-dependent and non-length-dependent presentations, with no significant difference between them.
Continuous length-dependent pain correlated positively with the number of abnormal thermal threshold testing parameters (TTT NOAs).
Continuous length-dependent pain correlated positively with SFNSL questionnaire scores.
TTT NOAs correlated positively with the SFNSL questionnaire score.
Patients with continuous length-dependent pain had significantly higher numbers of abnormal TTT parameters than those without this phenotype.
Corneal nerve fiber density measured by corneal confocal microscopy did not differ between SSFN patients with length-dependent versus non-length-dependent phenotypes.
Sudoscan (electrochemical skin conductance) and water immersion skin wrinkling also failed to distinguish length-dependent from non-length-dependent phenotypes.
No association was found between IENFD and length-dependent phenotype in this cohort, possibly due to use of 10 µm rather than 50 µm sections.
Pain, burning sensations, and paresthesia were the most frequently reported SFN-related symptoms among sarcoidosis patients, present in 50%, 44%, and 42% respectively.
The patient had repeatedly elevated anti-recoverin IgG antibodies in serum (titer 1:32) and in cerebrospinal fluid, indicating an autoimmune process following vaccination.

Quantitative sensory testing showed impaired A-delta fiber function in the upper extremities (with normal A-beta/A-gamma function and normal lower-extremity function), confirming small fiber neuropathy.
Skin biopsy showed presumably reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) in the neck, while thigh IENFD (12.54 fibers/mm) remained within normal range.
Corneal confocal microscopy revealed reduced corneal nerve fiber density, branch density, and fiber length, consistent with small fiber neuropathy involving corneal nerves.
Repeated CSF examinations showed elevated protein levels (563 mg/l, reference 200-400 mg/l) consistent with blood-brain barrier dysfunction.
Anti-SARS-CoV-2 spike antibodies were elevated in both CSF (11 E/ml) and serum (40 E/ml), while anti-capsid antibodies were negative.
Interleukin-4 and interleukin-1 were elevated with an accompanying Th1/Th2 shift, suggesting an exaggerated immune response to the vaccine.

Lower-limb weakness, gait disturbance, reduced fine motor skills, myoclonus, and cytoalbuminologic dissociation occurring five weeks after vaccination were interpreted as suggestive of mild Guillain-Barré syndrome as a manifestation of PACVS.

Nailfold capillary microscopy showed microbleeds, dilatation, and increased capillary branching, and laser perfusion measurement revealed marked endothelial dysfunction, consistent with endothelialitis.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy reduced the patient's overall symptom burden by approximately 90%.
A five-day course of intravenous methylprednisolone reduced pain and improved motor function but worsened brain fog.
Duloxetine and pregabalin, administered for presumed psychosomatic symptoms, did not improve the patient's condition.

A multi-agent regimen including ozone therapy, low-dose naltrexone, nattokinase, serrapeptase, fexofenadine, quercetin, clonidine, valacyclovir, alpha-lipoic acid, and N-acetylcysteine produced no significant symptomatic effect.
Quantitative sudomotor axon reflex testing showed increased latencies bilaterally, indicating autonomic small fiber involvement.
Small fiber neuropathy has been repeatedly reported in the literature as a side effect of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination with the BNT162b2 or Moderna vaccines.
OCT angiography revealed microcirculatory dysfunction with poor visualization of capillary blood flow bilaterally, despite a normal standard OCT.

A method using heat-induced epitope retrieval on formalin-fixed paraffin embedded skin punch biopsies enabled satisfactory PGP 9.5 immunohistochemical labeling of epidermal nerve fibers for epidermal nerve fiber density assessment in patients suspected of small fiber neuropathy.

Fifteen serum metabolic proteins, related to immune response, insulin resistance, and lipid metabolism, were significantly different between diabetic patients without DSPN and those with mixed small- and large-fiber neuropathy (MSLFN).

Seven serum metabolic proteins, particularly related to extracellular structure organization, were significantly different between patients with small-fiber neuropathy (SFN) and those with mixed small- and large-fiber neuropathy (MSLFN).
Three serum metabolic proteins related to immune response altered significantly between diabetic patients without DSPN and those with small-fiber neuropathy (SFN).

Temperature quantitative sensory testing (QST) and electromyography (EMG) were used to classify patients into no-DSPN, small-fiber neuropathy (SFN), and mixed small- and large-fiber neuropathy (MSLFN) groups for proteomic comparison.
In women, inflammatory bowel disease is commonly misdiagnosed as irritable bowel syndrome, leading to delayed diagnosis, increased disease burden, and poorer prognosis.
In women, spondyloarthritis is commonly misdiagnosed as fibromyalgia, leading to delayed diagnoses, increased disease burden, and poorer prognoses.

Joint manifestations are the most commonly observed extraintestinal manifestation of IBD and can precede or follow the diagnosis of IBD, linking IBD and spondyloarthritis as frequently co-occurring conditions.
Meta-analysis of 28 studies found significantly reduced NK cell cytotoxicity against K562 target cells in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, with a large overall effect size.
Effect sizes for ME/CFS vs HC differences in NK cytotoxicity varied by assay method, being largest for the whole blood 51Cr assay and smallest for PBMC-based assays.
After adjusting for potential publication bias using trim-and-fill correction, the combined effect size for reduced NK cytotoxicity in ME/CFS remained significant though somewhat attenuated.
Across E:T ratios, ME/CFS patients' NK cell cytotoxicity was approximately half that of healthy controls.
A diagnostic threshold of 17.1% cytotoxicity at an E:T ratio of approximately 25:1 discriminated ME/CFS from healthy controls with moderate sensitivity and specificity.
The estimated number of K562 target cells killed per individual NK cell was markedly lower in ME/CFS than in healthy controls, suggesting reduced per-cell killing efficiency.
Freezing and overnight shipping of blood/PBMC samples substantially reduces measured NK cell cytotoxicity and abolishes the deficit otherwise seen in ME/CFS compared to controls.
Statistical tests indicated evidence of publication bias in the NK cell cytotoxicity literature, suggesting under-representation of null/negative studies.
High statistical heterogeneity was observed across included studies, attributed to low cytotoxicity at low E:T ratios and several outlier studies.

Hospitalization for acute severe depression has been associated with reduced NK cell cytotoxicity that resolved after 6 months of successful treatment, suggesting neuroendocrine modulation of NK function relevant as a confounder for ME/CFS diagnosis.
The combination of male sex and major depression may be associated with greater NK cell function deficits compared to women, a potential confounder for ME/CFS differential diagnosis.
Obesity is reported to reduce NK cell cytotoxicity, representing a potential unaddressed confounder in ME/CFS studies since few reported BMI or excluded obese subjects.
One included study (Mawle et al.) found NK cell cytotoxicity equivalent between ME/CFS and healthy controls, appearing as a heterogeneity-driving outlier in the meta-analysis.

NK cell dysfunction has also been reported in long COVID and Gulf War Illness, conditions with symptom profiles overlapping ME/CFS, suggesting shared immune mechanisms warranting further investigation.

Univariate general linear modeling confirmed that estimated marginal effect sizes for reduced NK cytotoxicity in ME/CFS were significantly larger for whole blood and purified NK cell methods than for PBMC-based assays.

Patients with ME/CFS were significantly more likely to report a family history of ME/CFS (18%) compared to a non-ME/CFS chronic illness control group of multiple sclerosis and post-polio syndrome patients (3.9%).
Among ME/CFS patients, those with a family history of ME/CFS were more likely to report gastrointestinal symptoms than those without such a family history.
Long COVID and ME/CFS patients had significantly longer average Stroop task response times than healthy controls, with Long COVID slowest, then ME/CFS, then healthy controls.
Response times were slowest following an incongruent prestimulus, then congruent, then neutral (congruency sequence/Gratton effect), and this hierarchy held across all three groups.
Overall Stimulus reaction times were ranked Congruent > Incongruent = Neutral, with Incongruent and Neutral not significantly different from each other.

Power-function modelling of practice effects showed Long COVID had the highest initial reaction time (y-intercept) and fastest rate of learning compared with ME/CFS and healthy controls, which were similar to each other.

At the extrapolated end of the task (900s), reaction times were equivalent between Long COVID and ME/CFS and both remained significantly higher than healthy controls, indicating a persistent cognitive deficit not corrected by practice.
The incremental improvement in reaction time between task start and end (ΔRt) was larger in Long COVID than in ME/CFS, possibly reflecting shorter disease duration in LC.
Long COVID showed significant power-law practice effects (R²>0.5) in 7 of 9 prestimulus-stimulus pairings compared with 5 in healthy controls and only 4 in ME/CFS.

The prolonging effect of an incongruent prestimulus on the following stimulus response time (congruency sequence/Gratton effect) was present similarly in all three groups, suggesting this specific cognitive mechanism is not altered by ME/CFS or long COVID pathology.

Stroop, facilitation and interference effects derived from the prestimulus were significantly larger in Long COVID and ME/CFS than healthy controls during the first half of the task but became equivalent between groups in the second half.

Reaction time variance decreased as reaction times shortened across the task (heteroskedasticity), consistent with a practice/automaticity effect; elapsed time had the largest impact on this variance, with smaller contributions from disease group and prestimulus.

The authors propose that reduced TRPM3 ion channel activity in natural killer cells, previously reported in ME/CFS and long COVID, is a plausible molecular mechanism underlying defective neurotransmission contributing to the prolonged reaction times observed.

The authors suggest that loss of white matter integrity with increased axial diffusivity, potentially slowing axonal conduction along tracts connecting relevant brain regions, may also contribute to the prolonged Stroop task reaction times in ME/CFS and long COVID.

Prior studies found Long COVID patients had slower Stroop task response times, potentially related to dysfunctional attention with hypoarousal and increased brainstem-midbrain functional connectivity on fMRI.

Prior neuropsychological meta-analyses found impairment in ME/CFS for visuospatial immediate memory and reading speed, along with impaired episodic verbal memory processes and reduced attentional efficiency, while executive functioning did not appear to be affected.

Prior literature reviews/meta-analyses found the cognitive interference of word reading on colour identification impacts ME/CFS more than controls, and Stroop colour/word processing speed was compromised in ME/CFS.
Prior meta-analyses found reaction times were impaired in ME/CFS for both simple stimulus-response tests and more complex choice reaction time tests, though heterogeneity across studies was high.

Long COVID had significantly longer reaction times than ME/CFS for the incongruent-then-congruent (iC) and neutral-then-congruent (nC) pairings, suggesting particular difficulty processing the congruent stimulus after a different prestimulus.

Reaction time outcomes did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients diagnosed by Fukuda versus International Consensus Criteria, so these subgroups were pooled for comparisons with Long COVID.
The 2015 IOM report estimated that between 836,000 and 2.5 million Americans have CFS/ME.
Fewer than 20% of individuals meeting case criteria for CFS/ME had actually received a diagnosis from a healthcare provider, indicating substantial underdiagnosis.
Among diagnosed CFS/ME patients, the female-to-male ratio can be as high as four to one.
CFS/ME has a severe functional impact, with 48% of patients unable to engage in any constructive activity at their worst and 87% unable to work.
Post-exertional malaise typically emerges approximately 24 hours after physical, orthostatic, or cognitive overexertion and produces at least a 50% drop in energy and activity level.
Individuals with CFS/ME have an elevated risk of suicide compared to the general population.

Up to 10-30% of individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2 experience long-term symptoms consistent with CFS/ME regardless of initial illness severity, suggesting COVID-19 as a potential trigger for CFS/ME similar to other viral infections like EBV.
CFS/ME involves dysfunctional immune mechanisms, including altered CD8+ T-cells, reduced T regulatory cells, and altered NK cell activity.

EBV may drive an abnormal persistent immune response with pro-inflammatory cytokine overproduction, altered CD8+ T-cell function, and reduced T regulatory cell activity, contributing to chronic inflammation in CFS/ME, though its exact causal role remains unclear.
CFS/ME patients often exhibit gut dysbiosis with reduced beneficial bacteria (Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus) and overgrowth of pro-inflammatory bacteria, contributing to systemic inflammation.
Gut dysbiosis may cause 'leaky gut,' allowing lipopolysaccharides (LPS) to enter the bloodstream and trigger immune activation and inflammation in CFS/ME.
Reduced short-chain fatty acid (e.g., butyrate) production in CFS/ME patients may contribute to mitochondrial dysfunction and the condition's hallmark fatigue.
Higher estrogen levels in women are thought to promote a more robust immune response, potentially contributing to heightened immune dysregulation and autoimmune-like risk observed in CFS/ME.
Studies have found higher lactate levels, reactive oxygen species, and oxidative stress markers in CFS/ME patients, consistent with reduced mitochondrial function.

MRI research found reduced connectivity in the brainstem and hippocampus, particularly in the reticular activating system, with severity correlating with symptoms and disease progression, suggesting CNS involvement in CFS/ME fatigue.
The SNPs PTPN22 rs2476601 and CTLA4 rs3087243 are associated with infection-triggered CFS/ME, potentially contributing to impaired mucosal immunity and increased susceptibility following infection.
The SNPs IRF5 rs3807306 and TNF rs1799724 show decreased allele frequencies in CFS/ME patients whose illness was not infection-triggered.
CFS/ME appears to have a genetic component, supported by higher concordance rates in identical twins and increased prevalence of autoimmunity-related gene variants in post-infectious CFS/ME patients.

Graded exercise therapy (GET) for CFS/ME is controversial, as many patients report worsening of symptoms, particularly post-exertional malaise, following the structured gradual increase in physical activity.

A 2018 study showed that structural MRI-based morphological classification helps screen chronic fatigue patients, while self-reporting/questionnaires combined with machine learning algorithms show promise for early prediction and intervention.
History of other complex medical conditions, such as fibromyalgia or postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), is noted as a risk factor for developing CFS/ME.

Abnormal immune function, neuroinflammation, and dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which regulates stress responses via cortisol secretion, suggest potential mechanisms underlying CFS/ME.
IgG antibodies against tubulin were significantly and positively associated with a Long COVID diagnosis.
IgM antibodies against blood-brain-barrier/brain-damage proteins (claudin-5, S100B) were significantly and positively associated with Long COVID diagnosis.
IgA and IgM antibodies against cerebellar protein-2 were significantly and positively associated with Long COVID diagnosis.
IgG and IgM antibodies against myelin basic protein were significantly and positively associated with Long COVID diagnosis and were among the strongest single predictors.
IgG and IgM antibodies against MOG were significantly and positively associated with Long COVID diagnosis.
IgA, IgM and IgG antibodies against synapsin were significantly elevated and positively associated with Long COVID diagnosis.
An overall index of IgG-directed brain reactive autoantibodies (sum across neuronal antigens) was significantly and positively associated with Long COVID diagnosis.
A multivariate model combining IgG-MBP and IgM-MBP was the best single-domain predictor of Long COVID diagnosis.

Combining IgG-MBP, IgM-MBP, IgG-SARS-CoV-2, IgG-HHV6 and IgA-Activin A (all positively associated) with an IgA anti-viral protection index (negatively associated) produced the most robust predictive model for Long COVID diagnosis.

Peak body temperature during the acute COVID-19 phase correlated positively with multiple IgA-class neuronal autoantibodies and IgG-MBP/IgG-MOG, linking acute-phase inflammation severity to later brain-reactive autoimmunity.
IgG-MBP and IgG-MOG levels correlated positively with total BDI, HAMD, HAMA and Fibro-Fatigue scale scores, linking anti-myelin autoimmunity to depressive, anxiety and fatigue symptom severity.
IgA-MBP levels correlated positively with BDI, HAMD, and HAMA scores.
IgA-CP2 correlated positively with BDI and HAMA scores.
IgG-BRA correlated positively with HAMA and Fibro-Fatigue scores, while IgG-synapsin correlated positively with HAMA score.

IgM antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 and HHV-6 correlated significantly with a broad range of neuronal autoantibodies (tubulin, BBD, CP2, MOG, NFP, synapsin, BRA), linking viral persistence/reactivation to neuro-autoimmunity.
CRP, IgG-MOG and AOPP together positively predicted a large proportion (41.7%) of the variance in Fibro-Fatigue (chronic fatigue) scores.
CRP, IgA-MBP, education level, and IgG-MOG together positively predicted 37.4% of the variance in Beck Depression Inventory scores.
CRP and IgG-MOG together positively predicted 36.6% of the variance in Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores.
IgA-MBP, CRP and education level together predicted 30.4% of the variance in Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale scores.

A neural network model using neuronal autoantibodies plus inflammatory/oxidative markers predicted Fibro-Fatigue (CFS) severity with cross-validated precision of 0.721, with IgG-MBP, CRP, AOPP, IgA-synapsin, IgM-synapsin, and IgG-BRA as the strongest predictors.

A neural network model predicted the composite affective symptom score (depression+anxiety) with cross-validated precision of 0.801, with CRP, IgM-synapsin, education, IgA-MBP, IgG-MOG, IgA-synapsin, IgA-CP2, and IgG-MBP as the strongest predictors.
Long COVID patients showed significantly increased CRP, AOPP, and HOMA2-IR (insulin resistance) concentrations compared to healthy controls.
Long COVID patients had significantly higher Fibro-Fatigue, Hamilton Anxiety, Beck Depression Inventory, and Hamilton Depression scores than healthy controls.
During the acute COVID-19 phase, patients who later developed Long COVID had significantly higher peak body temperature and lower oxygen saturation (SpO2) than controls.
Age, sex, and research site were not significant predictors in any of the logistic regression models predicting Long COVID diagnosis from neuronal autoantibodies.
Across three included RCTs, Qigong produced consistent, significant group-by-time improvements in fatigue as measured by the Chalder's Fatigue Scale relative to control conditions.

Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory-20 subscales (general, physical, reduced activity, reduced motivation, mental fatigue) showed significant Qigong benefit in one RCT but were not significant in another RCT using the same measure.
Telomerase activity increased significantly in the Qigong group compared to the control arm in one RCT.
Qigong significantly affected peripheral blood neuropeptide Y levels relative to control, though the review did not specify the direction of change.
Sleep quality outcomes (PSQI) showed inconsistent Qigong effects across RCTs, with the total score significant in one study but not in others.
Anxiety symptoms (HADS) improved significantly with Qigong in one RCT but not in two others.
Depression symptoms (HADS) significantly improved with Qigong in two RCTs but not in a third.
Physical function (SF-36) significantly improved with Qigong in one RCT but not in another.
One RCT found Qigong significantly improved additional SF-36 subscales including bodily pain, general health, and vitality.
Mental health outcomes (SF-36/SF-12) showed a non-significant trend in one RCT and a significant effect in another.
A nonrandomized Tai Chi Chuan trial (excluded from this systematic review for lacking randomization) reported improved functional brain plasticity in ME/CFS patients.

Another nonrandomized Tai Chi trial (also excluded from this review) identified 60 functional brain connections associated with Tai Chi practice, linked to decreased fatigue and sleep complaints via enhanced left frontoparietal and default mode network connectivity.
At 6 months, adolescents randomised to the FITNET-NHS web-based CBT programme had greater improvement in physical function than those randomised to remotely-delivered Activity Management.
FITNET-NHS participants attended, on average, half a day more school per week than Activity Management participants at 6 months, and this benefit persisted at 12 months.
By 12 months, physical function improvement was similar between the FITNET-NHS and Activity Management groups, indicating the early advantage was not sustained.
Comorbid mood disorder did not significantly modify the relative effectiveness of FITNET-NHS versus Activity Management.
Pain and Clinical Global Impression outcomes improved similarly in both treatment groups, while fatigue results were mixed.
Rates of pre-defined markers of a worsening condition during treatment were similar between the FITNET-NHS and Activity Management groups.
A small quality-adjusted life-year gain was observed for FITNET-NHS compared to Activity Management, though the confidence interval crossed zero.
Similar proportions of participants in each arm met pre-defined criteria for a worsening condition during treatment, based on combined therapist and patient reports.
FITNET-NHS produced a very small gain in quality-adjusted life-years compared with Activity Management over the study horizon.
From an NHS perspective, delivering FITNET-NHS cost substantially more than Activity Management.
Cost-effectiveness analysis indicated FITNET-NHS is unlikely to be cost-effective compared with Activity Management at a standard willingness-to-pay threshold.
80% of Long COVID patients met criteria for post-exertional malaise based on the modified DePaul Symptom Questionnaire over the prior six months.
Day 1 CPET responses were consistent with aerobic deconditioning (VO2peak <80% predicted, without cardiovascular or pulmonary limitation) in 40% of the Long COVID patients.

There were no significant differences between day-1 and day-2 CPET responses (including VO2peak, peak work rate, and gas exchange threshold) in Long COVID patients, indicating PEM is not explained by impaired recovery of exercise capacity between days.
Pulmonary function testing was normal in the Long COVID cohort, ruling out a pulmonary basis for exercise intolerance.
The paper reports that CFS patients abroad lose nearly $20,000 per year due to the disease, reflecting a substantial personal economic burden.
The incidence of chronic fatigue syndrome is reported to range from 0.1% to 0.7%.
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is identified as a relatively more cost-effective intervention for CFS patients when measured in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs).

CBT is reported to have significant clinical effects in CFS patients, reducing fatigue symptoms and improving daily function, with greater treatment effects than other psychological treatments in reducing medical resource use and improving quality of life.
CBT-treated CFS patients show significant improvements in social functioning and occupational productivity, reducing indirect costs such as unemployment insurance expenditures and lost productivity.
Up to two-thirds of chronic fatigue syndrome patients also suffer from depression or anxiety, and this comorbidity increases medical visits, drug treatment needs, and overall socioeconomic burden.

Primary care management of CFS, including early intervention with psychoeducation and CBT, is reported to control costs and prevent symptom worsening, reducing the need for later specialist or hospitalization care.

A multidisciplinary primary care program combining nutrition, chronobiology, and exercise interventions improved fatigue and pain symptoms in CFS patients and reduced healthcare expenditures and indirect costs such as unemployment or reduced work capacity.
At its peak in late 2022, an estimated 181,000-682,000 Australians may have experienced long COVID symptoms, with 40,000-145,000 severely affected.
Severe long COVID cases decreased to an estimated 10,000-38,000 people by June 2023, down from the late 2022 peak.
The estimated economic burden of long COVID in Australia during 2022 was between $1.7 billion and $6.3 billion, representing 0.07% to 0.26% of GDP.
Labour market data showed 25,000 (February 2023) to 103,000 (June 2023) more working-age Australians reported being unable to work due to long-term sickness than predicted from pre-COVID-19 trends.
The rise in long-term sickness reports did not appear to translate into increased claims for Disability Support Pensions.
Numbers of working-age Carer Allowance recipients have grown markedly since 2022, potentially reflecting increased caregiving burden linked to long COVID.
Blood transcriptomic analyses in patients with post-COVID-19 condition and chronic fatigue syndrome did not show evidence supporting persistence of SARS-CoV-2.
Over half (54%) of patients undergoing lactulose breath testing for suspected SIBO reported brain fog symptoms.
Brain Fog Questionnaire scores were significantly higher in patients who reported brain fog compared with those who did not.
Patients reporting brain fog were more likely to be taking probiotics and proton pump inhibitors than those without brain fog.
There was no significant difference in the use of narcotics, prokinetics, or prebiotics between patients with and without brain fog.
Gastroparesis was more common among patients who reported brain fog than those who did not.
IBS was more common among patients who reported brain fog than those who did not.
SIBO and intestinal methanogen overgrowth (IMO), as determined by breath testing, were not associated with brain fog.

The proportion of SARS-CoV-2 infections leading to post-COVID-19 condition was approximately 6–10% during initial pandemic waves but has since decreased with changes in population immunity and less pathogenic variants.
Patients at the authors' post-COVID-19 outpatient clinic presented with a markedly reduced physical quality of life, with a mean SF36-PCS of 36.3 points at first visit.
Initiation of supportive therapy (pacing strategies, cognitive training, and physiotherapy) was associated with a 2.6-point increase in SF36-PCS at follow-up in the prior outpatient clinic cohort.

The NeuroNation MED® computerized adaptive cognitive training app has previously been shown to improve cognitive performance in healthy older adults and in patients with cognitive deficits due to Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease.
Post-COVID-19 condition and ME/CFS have overlapping symptoms, which creates diagnostic challenges in distinguishing between the two conditions.
The latency between a triggering exertion and the onset of post-exertional malaise (PEM) can vary from hours to several days, complicating patients' ability to identify triggers.
More than 200 distinct symptoms have been reported as a consequence of post-COVID-19 condition.
Treatment with dimethyl sulfoxide and exonuclease V significantly increased the efficiency of HHV-6A BAC transfection into JJHan T cells.
Combined stimulation with mitogens and glucocorticoids improved HHV-6A lytic replication compared to untreated conditions.
The interferon-mediated antiviral response was found to impair HHV-6A virus reconstitution.

Stabilization of HIF-1α using the compound IOX2 drastically accelerated HHV-6A reconstitution, implicating the hypoxic response as a key regulator of viral replication.
HHV-6A reactivation has been implicated in chronic fatigue syndrome, among other diseases, although its pathogenetic role remains unclear.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome overall has an estimated frequency of 1 in 5000, with hypermobile EDS accounting for about 90% of reported EDS cases.
Later in the discussion, hEDS prevalence is cited as approximately 1 in 3200, alongside its characterization as the mildest EDS subtype with less severe skin manifestations.

hEDS is commonly accompanied by chronic fatigue, functional bowel disorders, dysautonomia, gastroesophageal reflux, migraine, peripheral neuropathies, mast cell activation disorders, anxiety, urogynecologic disorders, and bleeding complications.
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is commonly present in hEDS patients, and preoperative crystalloid infusion with early vasopressor use may help manage it perioperatively.
Patients with hEDS undergoing neuraxial anesthesia are expected to have a greater rate of postdural puncture headache due to underlying tissue fragility.
Local anesthetic resistance has been reported in patients with hEDS.
Isolated or multiple Tarlov cysts, cerebrospinal-fluid filled perineurial cysts usually located in the S1-S4 spinal region, are a feature of hEDS reflecting meningeal involvement.

Unlike other EDS types, no pathogenic gene variant or structural collagen abnormality has been identified for hEDS, and its pathophysiology remains unknown, though dominant inheritance with variable penetrance is suspected.

Pregnant hEDS patients may experience higher rates of complications including ligament laxity, malposition injuries, abdominal wall herniation, pelvic floor weakness, rapid labor progression, wound healing deficiency, local anesthetic resistance, fatigue, POTS, GERD, and peripheral venous insufficiency.
Despite potential complications, pregnancy and delivery are relatively safe in hEDS patients compared to patients with other, more severe forms of EDS.
Endotracheal intubation can be challenging in hEDS patients due to tracheal cartilage collapse, cervical spine instability, and temporomandibular joint dysfunction.
Postpartum hemorrhage and complicated perineal lacerations occur more often in hEDS patients than in the general population, so postoperative care should focus on monitoring bleeding and hematoma.

In this case, a 24-year-old hEDS patient underwent successful cesarean delivery under general anesthesia (rapid sequence induction, videolaryngoscope-guided intubation, invasive blood pressure monitoring, careful positioning/padding, TIVA-style maintenance with sevoflurane/N2O) with stable vital signs and no adverse events in the intraoperative or postoperative period.

SOD3 is generally downregulated in cancer cells, which increases the likelihood of correctly identifying correlated, functionally related genes for enrichment analysis.

Pearson correlation analysis against SOD3 expression identified 100 correlated genes at |ρ|≥0.34 (32 positively, 68 negatively correlated), which were used for downstream disorder enrichment analysis.

In Classical-like Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome type 1 (caused by TNXB), gene ontology enrichment linked CDC42EP2 and CNN1 to Supramolecular Fiber Organisation, leading the authors to propose CNN1 as a novel candidate gene potentially involved via TGF-β-mediated matrix stiffness.

EMILIN1-related Connective Tissue Disease presents with joint hypermobility, skin hyper-elasticity, tendon ruptures and motor neuropathy; ontology analysis proposed MYH11 and SYNPO2 as novel candidate genes shared with Lethal Arteriopathy Syndrome due to Fibulin-4 Deficiency.

Lethal Arteriopathy Syndrome due to Fibulin-4 Deficiency (EFEMP2 mutation) presents with joint hypermobility and connective tissue dysfunction among other features; MYH11 and SYNPO2 were proposed as novel genes contributing to the phenotype.

In Autosomal Dominant Cutis Laxa (caused by ELN, FBLN5, or ALDH18A1), AOC3 and MYH11 were proposed as novel genes potentially contributing to vascular and connective tissue phenotypes, with ALDH18A1-linked type 3 uniquely presenting with impaired cognition possibly related to MYH11 dysfunction.

Renal Tubular Dysgenesis of Genetic Origin (caused by ACE, AGT, AGTR1 or REN mutations, disrupting the renin-angiotensin system) was linked via gene ontology to AOC3 and TAGLN, proposed as novel genes, with TAGLN implicated in arterial hypertension alongside all four causal genes.

Holt-Oram Syndrome (caused by TBX5) was ontologically linked to FOXF1, MYH11, and TAGLN, proposed as novel genes, with FOXF1-TBX5 ontology implicating cardiac left ventricle morphogenesis and multiple cardiac malformation phenotypes.

Multisystemic Smooth Muscle Dysfunction Syndrome (caused by ACTA2) was linked to FOXF1, KCNMB1, MYH11, and PLN, proposed as novel genes, with MYH11-ACTA2 ontology implicating aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection phenotypes.

Distal Hereditary Motor Neuropathy type 2 (caused by HSPB8, HSPB1, HSPB3 or FBXO38) was linked to KCNMB1, MYH11, TAGLN, and PNPLA2, proposed as novel genes, with PNPLA2 ontology implicating difficulty walking and running phenotypes.
Congenital Glaucoma (caused by CYP1B1, LTBP2, or TEK) was linked to CNN1 and DES, proposed as novel genes potentially affecting trabecular meshwork cytoskeletal integrity and outflow.

Megacystis-Microcolon-Intestinal Hypoperistalsis Syndrome (five genetic types) was linked to CDC42EP2, FOXF1, SGCA, and SORBS1, proposed as novel genes contributing to smooth muscle contraction dysfunction and oxidative stress in this disorder.

Retinoblastoma (caused by RB1) was linked to CHTOP, FXR1, and REST, proposed as novel genes, with REST and RB1 both reportedly downregulated by Interleukin-6 in cancer cells and REST implicated in H2O2 oxidative balance restoration.

Lynch Syndrome (caused by mismatch repair genes EPCAM, MLH1, MLH3, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, or TGFBR2) was linked to ADNP, CHTOP, HLTF, MTF2, WAPL, and ZMYM4, proposed as novel genes; notably ADNP with at least one causal gene was associated with the joint hypermobility phenotype.
TGF-β signaling was implicated in 10 of the 12 rare disorders analyzed (83%), despite TGF-β genes themselves falling below the Pearson correlation threshold used for gene list inclusion.

Oxidative stress (superoxide and hydrogen peroxide dysregulation) was found to plausibly play a mechanistic role in 10 of the 12 rare disorders examined (83%), with Classical-like EDS type 1 and Lynch Syndrome being exceptions.

Overall, of the 100 SOD3-correlated genes analyzed, 40 (22 unique) were ontologically associated with 12 significantly overlapping rare disorders, and 35 of those (21 unique) are proposed as novel disease genes.

SOD supplements have been reported to have some efficacy in treating chronic kidney disease patients by reducing TGF-β levels, suggesting possible therapeutic relevance to SOD3-related renal pathways.
SOD3 is under-expressed in aortic aneurysms, which the authors propose diminishes extracellular superoxide scavenging and contributes to vascular smooth muscle weakness and matrix instability.
SOD3 is also noted to be upregulated in the placenta of preeclampsia patients, discussed in the context of renin-angiotensin system dysfunction and Renal Tubular Dysgenesis.

A 38-year-old woman with refractory CSU and angioedema unresponsive to antihistamines and omalizumab achieved complete symptom resolution (UAS7 from 34 to 0) on abrocitinib 100mg/day, with no relapse at 1-year follow-up.

A 41-year-old man with CSU refractory to antihistamines, omalizumab, prednisolone, cyclosporine and methotrexate achieved complete resolution (UAS7 from 40 to 0) after 3 months of abrocitinib, with concurrent improvement of comorbid alopecia areata and allergic rhinitis.

A 26-year-old woman with refractory CSU achieved remission on abrocitinib (UAS7 30 to 0), relapsed 6 months after withdrawal, and achieved remission again on retreatment, during which she developed mild transaminase elevation that resolved with symptomatic treatment.

A 45-year-old woman with CSU and comorbid hypertension, asthma and hyperthyroidism, refractory to antihistamines, hydroxychloroquine, omalizumab and complicated by cyclosporine-induced metabolic adverse effects, showed continuous remission on abrocitinib (UAS7 36 to 7) with no metabolic abnormalities.

A 36-year-old man with CSU that worsened after each omalizumab injection (with chest discomfort) showed marked symptom improvement on abrocitinib (UAS7 25 to 5) without adverse reactions, chosen due to a birth plan precluding other immunosuppressants.

A 56-year-old woman with 5-year history of CSU refractory to antihistamines, corticosteroids, methotrexate and cyclosporine achieved symptom resolution on abrocitinib (UAS7 28 to 7) over 3 months, after which treatment was discontinued.

Across the six-patient case series, abrocitinib was generally well tolerated, with only mild dizziness in one patient and mild transaminase elevation in another, both resolving with symptomatic management.

The authors cite prior work indicating that upregulation of IL-9 and IL-10, acting through the JAK/STAT signaling pathway, contributes to CSU pathogenesis, and that JAK/STAT inhibition can suppress disease activity, consistent with the clinical responses observed in this case series.

The paper describes that type I and type IIb autoimmune reactions activate mast cells and basophils in CSU, causing degranulation, release of inflammatory mediators, increased vascular permeability, and activation of skin nerve fibers producing wheal and pruritus, with poor response to anti-IgE therapy in some patients suggesting mechanisms beyond IgE receptor stimulation.
Six of eight biopsy studies found significantly reduced intraepithelial nerve fiber density in BMS patients compared to controls, supporting SFN involvement in BMS pathophysiology.
Lauria et al. observed a 40% decrease in nerve fiber density in BMS patients along with morphological changes suggestive of trigeminal small fiber neuropathy.
Yilmaz et al. found reduced intraepithelial nerve fibers combined with increased TRPV1-positive and nerve growth factor (NGF) positive fibers in BMS patients, correlating with pain severity.
Beneng et al. identified increased P2X3-positive fibers and reduced neurofilament-staining fibers in tongue mucosa of BMS patients, supporting SFN involvement.
In a subsequent study, Beneng et al. observed only a non-significant trend toward increased Nav1.7 immunoreactive fibers in BMS patients.
Domaneschi et al. found no statistically significant differences in Nav1.7 or Nav1.9 channel expression in BMS patients versus controls, though dysregulation was suggested.
Penza et al., Borsani et al., and Puhakka et al. each documented significantly lower intraepithelial nerve fiber density in BMS patients compared to controls, consistent with small fiber damage.

Most QST studies (7 of 9) found evidence supporting SFN involvement in BMS, characterized by altered thermal thresholds, decreased heat pain tolerance, and signs of peripheral nerve fiber degeneration.
Grushka et al. and Svensson et al. reported significantly lower heat pain tolerance in BMS patients versus controls despite similar thermal detection thresholds, suggesting Aδ fiber dysfunction.
Ito et al. observed elevated thermal pain thresholds in various regions of the tongue in BMS patients, indicating peripheral nerve dysfunction.
Mo et al. showed significantly lower cold detection and cold pain thresholds and higher heat pain thresholds in BMS patients, consistent with thermal sensory loss typical of SFN.
Yilmaz et al. found significantly lower CDT, WDT, and CPT in BMS patients, suggesting ion channel impairments in Aδ and C fiber nerve endings.
Hartmann et al. found higher CDT/WDT and lower CPT, while Kolkka et al. found elevated WDT and CDT in BMS patients relative to controls.
Kaplan et al. found no significant differences in WDT, CDT, HPT, or CPT between BMS patients and controls, contrasting with other QST studies.
Puhakka et al. reported mixed QST results, with significantly higher CDT but no corresponding changes in WDT or HPT in BMS patients.
All three blink reflex studies consistently revealed evidence of SFN in BMS, either as a focal peripheral issue or part of a broader neuropathic process with possible central involvement.
Mendak et al. reported prolonged blink reflex latencies and frequent irregularities indicating mild sensory and autonomic small fiber neuropathy with possible CNS involvement.
Puhakka et al. observed longer blink reflex latencies in BMS patients versus healthy controls but the difference was not statistically significant.

Kolkka et al. found increased stimulation thresholds and decreased neurophysiological function of Aδ fibers in BMS patients, supporting focal SFN, with no influence from CNS-active drugs on thresholds.

Just et al. found that BMS patients exhibited higher pain thresholds and elevated sensation-related thresholds to capsaicin application on the tongue, indicating impaired small fiber (TRPV1-mediated) function.

Shinoda et al. found significantly increased artemin mRNA expression in tongue mucosa epithelial cells of BMS patients, suggesting enhanced activity of heat-sensitive nerve fibers via GFRα3 signaling and TRPV1 sensitization.

O'Neill et al. used corneal confocal microscopy and found significantly lower corneal nerve fiber density and length, plus an increased number of Langerhans cells in BMS patients, indicating systemic small fiber and possible inflammatory involvement.

The review notes that emerging pharmacotherapies such as sodium channel blockers are being explored to alleviate neuropathic pain by targeting hyperexcitability of damaged peripheral nerves, extrapolated from other neuropathic conditions rather than BMS-specific trial data.
Topical clonazepam is highlighted as a potential therapy aiming to desensitize TRPV1 receptors implicated in burning sensations in BMS, given reported elevated TRPV1 expression in patients.
Across included studies, functional sensibility in pathologic scars appears disturbed, with increased allodynia and altered thermosensory thresholds pointing to small fiber neuropathy involvement.
Nerve fiber density findings in pathologic scars varied depending on the skin layer examined and the staining technique used, limiting cross-study comparability.
The review identifies evidence implicating neuropeptides and neurogenic inflammation of the cutaneous nervous system in the formation and symptomatology of pathologic scars.

Peripheral neuropathy was diagnosed in 60.3% of patients with alcohol use disorder, with pure large fiber neuropathy and pure small fiber neuropathy each accounting for 28.6% of cases and combined large-and-small fiber neuropathy accounting for 42.8%.
All five clinical neuropathy scales (NSS, NDS, NIS, NIS-LL, mTCNS) had significantly higher mean scores in AUD patients compared with age- and gender-matched healthy controls.
ROC analysis showed that the NIS and mTCNS scales had the greatest sensitivity and specificity among all tested clinical scales for distinguishing AUD patients with neuropathy from those without.
The NIS scale performed best for detecting patients with large fiber neuropathy among AUD patients.
The NSS symptom questionnaire performed best for detecting patients with small fiber neuropathy among AUD patients.
All clinical scales except NSS showed a stronger correlation with measures of large fiber neuropathy than with measures of small fiber neuropathy.
Scores of all tested clinical neuropathy scales were negatively correlated with sural sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) amplitudes using linear regression.
NIS scale scores were positively correlated with cold detection threshold (CDT) results, a quantitative sensory testing measure of small fiber function.
NSS scores were positively correlated with heat detection threshold (HDT) results, a quantitative sensory testing measure of small fiber function.
NIS and NSS scores were negatively correlated with intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD), a skin biopsy-based measure of small fiber integrity.
In a prior study by the same laboratory, the NDS scale (used instead of NIS) showed a significant association with large fiber neuropathy in chronic alcohol-dependent subjects.

Diagnostic criteria for small fiber neuropathy in this AUD cohort required either two abnormal laboratory tests (SSR, QST, or IENFD) or the presence of at least one characteristic symptom (pain, postural hypotension, impotence, night diarrhea, or sphincter loss) plus at least one abnormal laboratory test.
Yeast two-hybrid, immunoprecipitation, and solid-phase binding assays showed that Ecm1 physically binds to Ctgf via the C-terminal cysteine knot (CT) domain of Ctgf.

Ecm1 expression significantly reduced αvβ6 integrin-mediated and Ctgf-potentiated TGFβ1 activation, as measured by PAI-1-driven luciferase reporter activity and active/total TGFβ1 ratio in conditioned media, in WB-F344 hepatic progenitor cells and human bile ductular epithelial cells (BDEC).

Presence of Ecm1:FLAG in conditioned media significantly reduced the induction of CTGF, αSMA, and procollagen type I gene expression in human hepatic stellate cell line LX-2 exposed to conditioned media containing β6:HA and Ctgf:V5.

Negative correlations between ECM1 and CTGF mRNA/protein were found in human livers with alcohol-associated hepatitis (AH), primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), and primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), based on public datasets and western blotting of patient liver homogenates.

Immunohistochemistry showed CTGF was co-expressed with CK19 in normal bile ducts and became highly upregulated in reactive ducts of human alcohol-associated cirrhosis (AC) livers compared to normal livers.

Untreated 7-week-old Ecm1 knockout mice showed elevated mRNA and protein levels of Ctgf, EpCAM, αSMA, and procollagen type I compared to age-matched wild-type littermates, consistent with spontaneous liver fibrosis in this model.

DDC-induced ductular reaction and liver fibrosis were enhanced in Ecm1 knockout mice compared to wild-type controls, with concomitant increases in hepatic hydroxyproline content and liver injury markers (ALT, AST, total bilirubin).

AAV8-mediated ectopic Ecm1 expression reduced Ctgf protein to 48.32%, αSMA to 61.21%, and procollagen type I to 50.82% of AAV8-GFP control levels, and reduced biliary epithelial cell proliferation (CK19+Ki67+) from 50.21% to 30.58% at 14 days after DDC feeding.

Ectopic Ecm1 expression decreased fibrosis area in DDC-treated livers, with αSMA+ staining at 4.27±0.49% vs 6.12±1.05% in controls, and Sirius red collagen staining at 5.00±0.42% vs 8.70±1.29% in controls (p<0.05).

Co-immunoprecipitation and proximity ligation assays confirmed direct interaction between Ecm1:FLAG and Ctgf proteins in DDC-damaged livers of AAV8-Ecm1:FLAG-infected mice but not in AAV8-GFP controls.

A higher satiety symptom sub-score was initially associated with longer gastric emptying time, but this association lost statistical significance after excluding two gastric emptying time outliers.
Each 1-point increase in the diarrhea symptom sub-score was associated with an approximately 7% reduction in small bowel transit time (i.e., faster transit).

Six of 15 individuals (46%) had multiple GI perforations.
Tracheal rupture, caused by medical intervention in all cases, occurred in 3 of 15 individuals (5.1% of the combined 59-individual clEDS1 cohort with literature).
Combining this cohort with the literature, 16.9% (10/59) of known clEDS1 individuals had a spontaneous GI perforation.
Overall, 22.0% (13/59) of known clEDS1 individuals had a GI perforation (spontaneous or nonspontaneous).

Diverticulosis was highly prevalent, seen in 12 of 15 individuals (80%) in this cohort, and in at least 22.0% of the total known clEDS1 population, suggesting higher prevalence than in the general population.
Most individuals (85%, 11/13 with molecular data) had at least one truncating or null TNXB variant.
The TNXB Cys4060Trp variant was identified 5 times across 3 unrelated individuals from different countries with no known familial connection.
Beighton hypermobility score (median 4/9) showed no association with occurrence of GI complications in descriptive analysis.
Skin hyperextensibility was observed in 13 of 15 individuals (87%) with clEDS1 and GI/tracheal complications.

Only 53% of individuals reported generalized joint hypermobility or a Beighton score ≥5, contrasting with a prior report of 100% joint hypermobility in clEDS1, suggesting that clEDS1 symptom severity may not predict GI fragility.

Age of GI perforation did not significantly differ between individuals diagnosed with clEDS1 before versus after their first perforation (median 47 vs 57 years for diagnosis, P=0.170; 49 vs 41 years for perforation, P=0.094).
Perforation occurred slightly earlier in individuals with biallelic truncating TNXB variants (46 vs 49 years), but this difference was not statistically significant (P=0.617).
Presence of hypertension was not significantly associated with earlier age of GI perforation (46 years with hypertension vs 49 years without, P=0.286).
The proportion of truncating variants in this cohort (79%) was similar to the proportion reported among pathogenic/likely pathogenic TNXB variants in ClinVar (85%).

The authors recommend avoidance of invasive GI procedures unless necessary, minimizing tension on the gut wall during endoscopy, having a surgical team on standby, and using a flexible scope during intubation to reduce iatrogenic tracheal/GI damage in clEDS1 patients.
Label-free proteomics of vEDS patient dermal fibroblasts versus controls identified 181 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs), of which 164 were downregulated and 17 upregulated.

Integration of proteomic DEPs with prior transcriptomic DEGs identified 67 shared genes/proteins, of which 54 were concordantly downregulated at both RNA and protein levels while 13 showed discordant (opposite) expression.
The 114 DEPs identified only at the protein level were enriched for apoptosis/autophagy regulation and ECM organization/collagen fibril assembly and GAG metabolism.
The only high-confidence STRING network formed by the 17 upregulated DEPs in vEDS fibroblasts was primarily composed of calcium-signaling proteins.

ClueGO network analysis of all DEPs showed the most interconnected biological network centers on ECM homeostasis, including collagen biosynthesis/fibril assembly/degradation, integrin- and proteoglycan-mediated ECM interactions, VEGFA-VEGFR2 signaling, platelet activation, and elastic fiber formation.
COL5A1 (collagen type V α1 chain), a predicted miR-29b-3p target, was downregulated at both mRNA and protein levels in vEDS fibroblasts.

NNMT (nicotinamide N-methyltransferase), a predicted miR-29b-3p target involved in nicotinamide metabolism, proliferation, and differentiation, was downregulated at both mRNA and protein levels in vEDS fibroblasts.
USP6NL, a predicted miR-29b-3p target regulating autophagy, cell cycle, and apoptosis, was downregulated at both mRNA and protein levels in vEDS fibroblasts.

COL1A1, COL1A2, and ELN, predicted miR-29b-3p targets encoding key ECM structural components, were downregulated at the protein level only (without corresponding mRNA changes) in vEDS fibroblasts, suggesting translational repression by miR-29b-3p.

Transfection of vEDS fibroblasts with a specific miR-29b-3p LNA inhibitor significantly increased mRNA expression of nearly all tested downregulated target DEGs (COL5A1, USP6NL, NNMT, TFEB, ATG9A, PTEN, NLRX1, ATP6V1A, DNAJB7, P3H1) except TP53INP2, with stronger effect at 72h vs 48h.
Western blot confirmed that COLLV(α1) and COLLI protein levels were significantly lower in untransfected vEDS patient fibroblasts compared to healthy control fibroblasts.

In vEDS fibroblasts transfected with the miR-29b-3p inhibitor, COLLI protein levels rose to match untransfected control levels, and COLLV(α1) levels exceeded control levels, compared to negative-control-transfected cells.
Blood miR-29b-3p levels were significantly higher in vEDS patients compared to healthy donors, confirming the in vitro fibroblast finding in a peripheral, minimally invasive sample type.
Prior miRNome analysis of vEDS fibroblasts (referenced from the authors' earlier study) identified 137 differentially expressed miRNAs (66 upregulated, 71 downregulated) compared to controls.

Immunofluorescence in all analyzed patient fibroblast strains confirmed disorganization of ECM components (collagens I/III/V, elastin, fibrillins, fibronectin, GAGs, proteoglycans) and altered integrin expression, with absence of α2β1 and α5β1 integrins and presence of αvβ3 integrin.

GO/KEGG enrichment of the 54 concordantly downregulated genes/proteins highlighted impaired protein transport/binding, RNA processing/splicing, autophagy regulation, and mitochondrial respiratory chain assembly (e.g., COA3, SCO1, TIMM21, TTC19).

PANTHER functional classification of the 181 DEPs showed the largest affected protein classes were metabolite interconversion enzymes (24%) and RNA metabolism proteins (16%), followed by protein binding-activity modulators, protein-modifying enzymes, scaffold/adaptor proteins, transporters, cytoskeletal proteins, translational proteins, and ECM proteins.
All enrolled vEDS patients carried a molecularly confirmed pathogenic dominant-negative COL3A1 variant, consistent with the disease-causing basis of vascular EDS.

Patients with EDS had significantly greater odds of being diagnosed with a patellar dislocation at 1 year after initial diagnosis compared with matched controls, the greatest odds among all cohorts studied.
Patients with MFS had significantly greater odds of patellar dislocation at both 1- and 2-year marks compared with matched controls, though to a lesser extent than EDS or all-JHS cohorts.

The all-JHS cohort (combined EDS and MFS diagnoses) had significantly greater odds of patellar dislocation at 1 year (aOR 11.40) and 2 years (aOR 8.73) after JHS diagnosis compared with matched controls.

Among patients who experienced a patellar dislocation, the all-JHS cohort had significantly greater odds of undergoing primary surgical stabilization at 1 year and 2 years compared with matched controls.
Among patients who experienced a patellar dislocation, the EDS cohort had significantly greater odds of undergoing surgical stabilization at 1 and 2 years compared with matched controls.

Unlike EDS, patients with MFS did not have significantly greater odds of undergoing surgical stabilization for patellar dislocation compared with matched controls, at either 1 or 2 years, despite having greater odds of the instability event itself.

There was no significant difference in rates of revision surgery to address recurrent patellofemoral instability between the JHS cohorts (EDS, MFS, all-JHS) and matched controls after primary surgical stabilization.
Survey respondents with EDS reported a median total out-of-pocket healthcare cost of $13,450 in 2022, indicating substantial financial burden.
EDS respondents reported a median functional status score of 6 out of 27 items with significant or complete limitations, indicating notable functional impairment.
Among respondents who changed work status, 82% said EDS played a major role in their decision to reduce hours or stop working.
More than half of respondents reported individual income under $25,000 and over 30% reported household income under $50,000 in 2022.
Nearly one-third (32.3%) of respondents received financial assistance from family/friends, and additional respondents relied on disability benefits (SSDI 16.0%, SSI 6.6%).
Respondents with at least one primary care visit had a median of 5 primary care visits in 2022.
Specialty physician visits were considerably more frequent than primary care visits, with a median of 12 visits in 2022.
19% of respondents reported not receiving the healthcare they needed, and 51% received it only sometimes.
The highest out-of-pocket costs among EDS patients were for alternative/nontraditional treatments, mental health treatments, and oral operations/related care.
The most frequently used out-of-pocket expense categories among EDS patients were over-the-counter drugs, prescription medications, and supplements.
95% of study respondents with EDS were female, consistent with prior reports of a female (and White) demographic skew in EDS.

EDS is described as commonly co-occurring with sleep disturbance, fatigue, postural orthostatic tachycardia, functional gastrointestinal disorders, dysautonomia, anxiety, and depression, which can be more debilitating than joint symptoms.
84% of respondents reported having hypermobile EDS, and 30% reported being diagnosed in 2021-2022.
More than 80% of respondents had some type of commercial insurance, while 29% reported receiving Medicaid in 2022.
Post-mortem genetic testing identified a novel COL3A1 gene mutation in a young, thinly built male who died of spontaneous pneumothorax, suggesting the variant contributed to the fatal event.

The authors note that COL3A1 mutations are primarily associated with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome but can also cause structural lung changes such as bullae, which may predispose to spontaneous pneumothorax.
The authors recommend implementing genetic testing of correlative or causative genes (such as COL3A1) in the workup of spontaneous pneumothorax cases, including forensic/post-mortem settings.
sHTAD (MFS, LDS, vEDS) is commonly associated with skeletal manifestations including hypermobile joints, chest deformities, and scoliosis.
Pain and fatigue were described by most patients with sHTAD as having a substantial negative impact on their daily functioning.

Patients described a substantial risk of social isolation and withdrawal, particularly during periods of severe surgery or acute pain/fatigue, while relatives reported exhaustion and uncertainty from managing an unpredictable illness.
Self-sufficiency in daily living was identified as a key QoL determinant, closely tied to dignity, autonomy, and social integration, even though some required help with strenuous tasks.

Many participants adjusted their education and career choices due to advice to avoid physically demanding work, transitioning to more sedentary or theoretical occupations, which was described as important for identity and QoL.

Fear related to potential life-threatening aortic complications was reported as a central, ongoing psychological burden for both patients and relatives, with coping strategies (avoidance, hypervigilance, or social support) varying between individuals.
Maintaining active engagement with family and friends was emphasized as vital for coping, sense of normality, and mutual support for both patients and relatives.
Despite receiving advice on physical activity restrictions, many patients and relatives found it difficult to translate this guidance into practical, safe exercise routines, causing frustration.
Feeling safe and receiving coordinated, multidisciplinary care was described as a fundamental need that significantly impacted the psychological and physical wellbeing of patients and relatives.
Being recognized, seen, and accepted by healthcare providers was emphasized as improving emotional support and mental well-being and reducing isolation.
Clear, factual, and practical information from healthcare providers was described as reducing unnecessary worry and anxiety, and enabling better coping and treatment adherence.

A cited 10-year longitudinal study of adults with Marfan syndrome found that older age predicted decline in physical health-related quality of life (physical function and bodily pain), while the mental HRQoL domain remained unchanged.

Prior Japanese studies (Shimizu et al.) found that accessible medical consultation did not affect subjective well-being in people with Marfan syndrome, contrasting with the present study's emphasis on the importance of healthcare interaction for QoL.

Cited literature indicates optimism and positive beliefs, along with societal participation, are positively correlated with QoL and play a role in preventing depression and fostering hope in this patient population.
The overall prevalence of generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton score ≥4) in this Portuguese university sample of young adults was 41.9%.
Females were significantly more likely to have GJH (48.2%) than males (20.4%), a large effect size.
No association was found between GJH and ethnicity in this predominantly Caucasian sample.
The overall prevalence of any TMD was 38.4%, with 27.2% having chronic painful TMDs and 11.2% having other (non-painful/mechanical) TMDs.
Females were significantly more likely than males to have chronic painful TMDs (29.6% vs 19.0%).
GJH was significantly associated with self-reported TMJ clicking symptoms in univariate analysis, though with a very small effect size.
GJH was significantly associated with perceived (self-reported) mouth opening limitation, though the effect size was small.
GJH was significantly associated with clinically examined TMJ clicking (OR=1.28), though not with clinically measured mouth opening limitation.
In multivariable analysis adjusting for ethnicity, age, and sex, GJH was not independently associated with chronic painful TMDs overall; only age and sex remained significant predictors.
Single diagnoses of myalgia and arthralgia were numerically more prevalent among young adults with GJH than without, but these differences were not statistically significant.
Univariate analysis showed the combined chronic diagnosis of myalgia and arthralgia was significantly more prevalent in young adults with GJH (16.1%) than without (10.4%).
After adjusting for age and sex, GJH remained independently associated with the combined chronic myalgia and arthralgia TMD subtype, though the effect size was modest.
A meta-analysis of eight studies found the prevalence of small fibre pathology in FMS patients to be approximately 49%.
First-degree relatives of people with FMS are 8.5 times more likely to have the condition, indicating strong familial aggregation.
Twin studies estimate the heritability of FMS at 48-54%, supported by a genome-wide linkage scan in 116 families.
A large-scale comparative genomic study found significant differences in GABRB3, TAAR1 and GBP1 genes in people with FMS, potentially influencing nociception, inflammation and mood.
The preponderance of neuroimaging data indicates global grey matter volume is unchanged in FMS compared to controls.
Decreased grey matter volume in the anterior cingulate cortex, prefrontal cortex and insula is associated with central sensitisation in FMS.
Currently pain-free FMS patients showed DMN resting-state connectivity similar to healthy controls.
FMS patients experiencing current clinical pain during scanning showed significantly increased DMN connectivity to the bilateral anterior insula, positively correlated with pain level.
Lower resting-state functional connectivity has been demonstrated in the medial hypothalamus, thalamus and amygdala in FMS compared to healthy people.
Decreased dopamine availability in pain-related brain regions is associated with pain in FMS.
Increased glutamate levels in the anterior cingulate cortex, amygdala and hippocampus are associated with pain in FMS.
During a temporal summation of pain paradigm, people with FMS showed higher brainstem BOLD activity than healthy participants despite similar spinal activity patterns.

In a case-control study of 43 FMS women and 40 healthy controls, the FMS subgroup with reduced skin innervation showed hyperconnectivity between the inferior frontal gyrus, angular gyrus and posterior parietal gyrus.

Microneurography studies (Serra and Evdokimov et al.) identified abnormal spontaneous activity and increased mechanical sensitisation in silent and mechanosensitive c nociceptors in a large proportion of people with FMS, similar to idiopathic small fibre neuropathy.

Electron microscopy of skin biopsies (Doppler et al.) showed reduced diameter of unmyelinated dermal axons at all sampled sites in FMS compared to healthy participants, and reduced further compared to idiopathic small fibre neuropathy at the proximal leg and index finger.
Jänsch et al. found SFP prevalence to be comparable between 158 women with FMS (69.7%) and 53 with small fibre neuropathy (73.6%).

Compared with SFN, FMS patients had reduced proximal skin innervation and higher corneal nerve branch densities, while SFN patients had reduced cold detection and prolonged A-delta conduction latencies.
SCN9A-encoded Nav1.7 dorsal root ganglion sodium channel variants have been proposed to play a role in severe FMS phenotypes.
In a retrospective study of 1139 patients with pure small fibre neuropathy, 11.6% (132 patients) had pathogenic voltage-gated sodium channel variants (SCN9A, SCN10A, SCN11A).
Microdialysis of muscle tissue in women with fibromyalgia revealed increased concentrations of glutamate, pyruvate and lactate, indicating peripheral metabolic and algesic alterations.

A 15-week exercise intervention in women with fibromyalgia produced significant reductions in pain intensity and peripheral metabolic markers (glutamate, pyruvate, lactate), suggesting exercise partially normalises peripheral pain-contributing factors.
Supervised regular physical activity significantly improved Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire scores and intraepidermal nerve fibre density at proximal and distal sites.

In a longitudinal skin biopsy study of 62 patients with FMS followed over 18 months, overall IENFD remained largely unchanged, but those who did show reduced proximal and distal IENFD, together with fatigue and BPI-motor/work sub-scores, predicted more severe disability on the FIQ.

Corneal confocal microscopy studies have shown reduced sub-basal plexus nerve density in people with FMS, with corneal nerve fibre loss associated with neuropathic pain descriptors selected by patients.

Sub-basal corneal nerve morphometry shows a negative correlation with the widespread pain index (WPI), and reductions in sub-basal plexus nerve density and length correlated with ocular and visual symptoms in FMS.

No significant correlation has been observed between corneal morphometry and screening instruments (painDETECT, Small Fibre Neuropathy Screening List) or functional measures such as quantitative sensory testing in FMS.

Quantitative sensory testing (QST) studies in FMS using the DFNS standardised protocol have produced inconsistent findings for thermal detection thresholds, with some studies showing thermal hypoesthesia, others hyperesthesia, and others no difference from healthy volunteers.
Most QST studies report cold hyperalgesia and consistently increased pressure pain sensitivity (pressure hyperalgesia) in FMS compared to healthy participants or other pain conditions.

Kaziyama et al. found that IENFD did not differ between sides of the body in patients with asymmetrical FMS pain symptoms, or between asymmetrical and symmetrical symptom cohorts, though pressure pain threshold was significantly reduced on the painful side.

Fasolino et al. assessed 57 patients with FMS and found no significant difference in QST sensory profiles between those with and without confirmed small fibre pathology, though both groups showed gain of function in mechanical pain sensitivity.
Heart rate variability studies in FMS have demonstrated cardiac autonomic alterations consistent with sympathetic hyperactivity and associated sympathetic hypo-reactivity to orthostatic stress.

A more recent study found reduced skin conductance and reduced reactivity to physiological manipulations such as anxiety and body temperature in FMS, suggesting reduced (rather than increased) sympathetic activity to the skin, contradicting the earlier hyperactivity model.

Ramírez et al. found that in women with FMS without severe anxiety or depression, there was a significant negative correlation between corneal innervation and symptoms of dysautonomia and neuropathy, but this correlation was absent in those with severe anxiety or depression, suggesting distorted symptom perception in that subgroup.
A recent study in men with FMS found a high prevalence of small fibre pathology (83%), with more than half of men showing generalised reduction in IENFD compared to only 15% of women.

A subset of people with FMS exhibited non-length-dependent small fibre pathology which correlated with the presence of trisulfate heparin disaccharide antibodies detected in participants' skin biopsies.
Skin biopsies have demonstrated increased expression of NMDA receptors in patients with FMS compared to healthy controls.
Increased inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction have been identified in skin biopsies of people with FMS.

In a proportion of people with FMS, symptoms compatible with small fibre neuropathy were present in the absence of structural small fibre pathology, with these individuals showing greater mechanical pain sensitivity, depression and anxiety.
Female patients reported significantly higher average, least, and worst daily pain scores than male patients.
Female patients reported significantly higher sleep interference scores (DSIS and WSIS) than male patients, by approximately one point.
Female patients had significantly higher revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (rFIQ) total and domain scores than male patients.
Widespread Pain Index (WPI) and symptom severity score (SSS), the diagnostic criteria components, were similar between male and female patients.
There was no statistically significant difference in BMI or obesity rates between male and female fibromyalgia patients, although females had a slightly higher mean BMI.
