Incidence of depression was not significantly different between male (57.9%) and female (65.8%) fibromyalgia patients.
Onset age of widespread pain was marginally earlier in male than female patients but did not reach statistical significance.
Male patients showed significantly greater loss of sensory function in thermal sensory limen (TSL) and mechanical detection threshold (MDT) than female patients on QST.

Female patients showed significantly greater gain of function (hyperalgesia) in cold pain threshold, heat pain threshold, and mechanical pain threshold than male patients, indicating more prominent central sensitization.
Loss of function in mechanical detection threshold (large fibre function) was significantly more common in male (39.4%) than female (15.8%) fibromyalgia patients.
Loss of function of small fibres (increased CDT/WDT) was more prevalent in male (34.2%) than female (26.3%) patients according to the LOGA classification.
Abnormal sensory gain (central sensitization, LOGA G1+G2+G3) was found in approximately two-thirds of both male (63.2%) and female (68.4%) patients.

The most prevalent LOGA subtype in both sexes was mechanical hyperalgesia without sensory loss (L0G2), seen in 28.9% of male and 26.3% of female patients, and gain of function in MPS was the dominant sensory abnormality overall.

Cold detection threshold was negatively correlated with weekly pain severity and functional impairment (rFIQ function domain) in both male and female patients, suggesting small fibre pathology contributes to pain and disability.
Mechanical pain sensitivity positively correlated with pain severity, symptom scores, and rFIQ in female patients but showed no such correlation in male patients.
A completely normal QST profile (L0G0, no sensory loss or gain) was more common in female (15.8%) than male (7.9%) patients.
At baseline, women with fibromyalgia reported significantly more pain and higher consumption of analgesics/relaxants than healthy controls.
No significant baseline differences were found between FM and HC groups in theta, alpha, or beta EEG power spectra, nor in baseline HRV variables.
In healthy controls, 1 mA anodal tDCS over the left dlPFC significantly increased beta spectral power at the central (Cz) electrode after stimulation.
In HC, 1 mA tDCS produced significantly greater increases in beta power at Cz than 2 mA when the two intensities were compared directly.
Comparing tDCS intensities between groups, the FM group showed significantly higher theta spectral power at Fp1 with 2 mA versus 1 mA, differing from the HC pattern.
In the FM group, 1 mA anodal dlPFC-tDCS significantly increased sympathetically-linked HRV markers including LF power, LF/HF ratio, and mean heart rate.
In the FM group, 1 mA anodal dlPFC-tDCS significantly decreased HF power, a marker of parasympathetic activity.
2 mA dlPFC-tDCS in the FM group significantly increased SDNN, RMSSD, PNN50, total power, SD1, SD2, and SampEn, indicating overall improvement in HRV/parasympathetic activity.

In the FM group, the Friedman test showed significant differences between tDCS intensities for SampEn, with 2 mA producing a greater increase compared to sham and 1 mA (LF and HF approached significance at p=0.05).
In the HC group, sham stimulation produced a significantly greater increase in DFA1 compared to 1 mA, suggesting a possible placebo-related autonomic response.

Mann-Whitney U tests showed no significant differences between FM and HC groups for any tDCS intensity after correction; however, uncorrected analysis showed a p<0.05 difference for SD2 after 2 mA with a medium effect size, with SD2 increasing more in the FM group.
Plasma BDNF levels were significantly higher in chronic widespread pain (fibromyalgia) patients compared to asymptomatic controls.
Plasma BDNF levels were significantly higher in chronic widespread pain (fibromyalgia) patients than in chronic primary musculoskeletal pain patients.
Plasma BDNF levels were significantly lower in chronic primary musculoskeletal pain patients compared to asymptomatic controls.
No significant correlations were found between plasma BDNF levels and clinical variables (e.g., pain intensity) in the study population.
Oral administration of PFOS reduced IgE/antigen-stimulated passive cutaneous anaphylaxis responses in a mouse model.
In bone marrow-derived mast cells, PFOS reduced IgE/Ag-stimulated degranulation.
PFOS reduced IgE/Ag-stimulated intracellular Ca2+ levels in mast cells.
PFOS reduced IgE/Ag-stimulated eicosanoid synthesis in mast cells.
PFOS reduced mRNA expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines in IgE/Ag-stimulated mast cells.
PFOS decreased phosphorylation of the tyrosine kinase Syk, central to IgE/Ag-stimulated mast cell activation.
PFOS decreased phosphorylation of the tyrosine kinase Lck, central to IgE/Ag-stimulated mast cell activation.
PFOS decreased phosphorylation of downstream signaling molecules PLCγ1, AKT, and MAPKs in mast cells.
PFOS activates the tyrosine phosphatase SHP-1, which mediates its inhibitory effect on FcεRI signaling in mast cells.
PFOS reduced phosphorylation of the FcεRI-associated tyrosine kinase Fyn in IgE/Ag-stimulated mast cells.
PFOS reduced phosphorylation of the FcεRI-associated tyrosine kinase Lyn in IgE/Ag-stimulated mast cells.

Fluorine-19 NMR spectroscopy showed reduced fluorine signals of PFOS upon interaction with the plasma membrane, indicating PFOS accumulates in the plasma membrane and interferes with FcεRI signaling close to the membrane.
PFOS attenuated lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated mRNA expression of TNFα, indicating modulation of innate immune (TLR) responses in mast cells.
PFOS attenuated lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated mRNA expression of IL-6, indicating modulation of innate immune (TLR) responses in mast cells.
When the TCCS correction angle was 30 degrees or less, peak systolic velocity measurements from TCCS and TCD were comparable.
TCCS-measured peak systolic velocity was significantly higher than TCD when the correction angle exceeded 30 degrees in type I MCA morphology, and at all correction angles in type II morphology.
The mean rank of middle cerebral artery stenosis grading by TCCS was higher than that determined by TCD or CTA, while TCD and CTA did not differ significantly from each other.
Optimal cut-off values for diagnosing MCA stenosis using TCCS increased with increasing correction angle, indicating that angle-specific cut-offs improve diagnostic accuracy.
RAL treatment reduced IgE-induced increases in mast cell volume and degranulation, and this protective effect was reversed by co-treatment with a RAR antagonist.

Histamine secretion from BMMCs was increased in the IgE-stimulated group compared with control, and decreased by 31.33% after RAL intervention, an effect that was counteracted when RAR was antagonized.
IL-6 gene expression in BMMCs was elevated with IgE stimulation and was reduced by 80.55% with RAL treatment, an effect counteracted by RAR antagonism.
IL-13 gene expression in BMMCs was elevated with IgE stimulation and reduced by 76.44% with RAL treatment, counteracted by RAR antagonism.
GM-CSF gene expression in BMMCs was elevated with IgE stimulation and reduced by 60.84% with RAL treatment, counteracted by RAR antagonism.
TNF-α gene expression in BMMCs was elevated with IgE stimulation and reduced by 26.68% with RAL treatment, counteracted by RAR antagonism.
IL-4 gene expression in BMMCs was elevated with IgE stimulation and reduced by 60.00% with RAL treatment, counteracted by RAR antagonism.
IL-1β gene expression in BMMCs was elevated with IgE stimulation and reduced by 54.75% with RAL treatment, counteracted by RAR antagonism.
Transcriptome sequencing identified 73 differentially expressed genes between the IR and IRR groups, with 25 upregulated and 48 downregulated after RAR antagonism.
RARβ gene expression was significantly down-regulated in the IRR group, confirming that the RAR antagonist effectively blocked retinoic acid receptor signaling.
KEGG enrichment analysis showed the NF-κB signaling pathway was enriched with five differential genes between IR and IRR groups.
GSEA showed the PPAR signaling pathway (vitamin A metabolism-related) was inhibited in the IRR group compared to IR, confirming RAR antagonist activity.

GSEA showed that inflammation-related pathways including PI3K/AKT, Toll-like receptor, TNF, IL-17, MAPK, and ErbB signaling, plus cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, were all significantly enhanced in the IRR group compared with IR.
Despite qRT-PCR and western blot confirmation, GSEA did not show a statistically significant enrichment of the NF-κB signaling pathway between IR and IRR groups.

qRT-PCR showed increased gene expression of NF-κB, MyD88, PI3K, AKT, mTOR, and S6K1 in IgE-stimulated BMMCs versus control, with RAL treatment decreasing these markers by 18.26%, 33.74%, 37.56%, 36.87%, 10.60%, and 81.13% respectively, an effect partially reversed by RAR antagonism.

Western blot showed significantly increased expression of p-PI3K, p-mTOR, p-AKT, p-P65, IKK-β, MyD88, IKBα, and p-ERK proteins in IgE-stimulated BMMCs versus control; these were significantly lower after RAL treatment and the effect was reversed by RAR antagonism.

The overall study concludes that antagonizing the RAR (mimicking vitamin A deficiency) exacerbates IgE-mediated mast cell activation via upregulation of MyD88-IKK-NF-κB and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling pathways, linking vitamin A status to allergic inflammation.
Tamoxifen citrate (TAM) was shown to specifically bind MRGPRX2, an interaction driven mainly by hydrophobic forces.
TAM formed hydrogen bonds with the TRP243, TRP248, and GLU164 residues of MRGPRX2, suggesting a specific molecular binding mode.
TAM induced calcium mobilization and degranulation of mast cells through the MRGPRX2 receptor.
TAM induced passive cutaneous anaphylaxis and active systemic anaphylaxis in C57BL/6 mice, indicating in vivo allergic/mast-cell-mediated reactions.
TAM increased the release of β-hexosaminidase, histamine, TNF-α, MCP-1, and IL-8 from mast cells both in vitro and in vivo.
MCF-7 and T-47D breast cancer cells were able to recruit mast cells to adjacent cancerous tissue.
Mast cell activation induced by TAM via MRGPRX2 significantly promoted the proliferation and migration of MCF-7 and T-47D breast cancer cells.
Clarithromycin, a mast cell membrane stabilizer, effectively reversed the TAM/MRGPRX2-induced mast cell activation-driven proliferation and migration of breast cancer cells.
Silencing MRGPRX2 effectively reversed the TAM-induced, mast cell activation-driven proliferation and migration of breast cancer cells.
The authors propose an anti-allergic therapeutic strategy for breast cancer treatment with TAM, positioning MRGPRX2 as a potential adjunctive therapeutic target.
Casticin treatment reduced the LL37-induced inflammatory skin phenotype in a mouse model of rosacea-like dermatitis.
RNA-seq analysis of mouse skin lesions showed that casticin inhibited mast cell activation in the rosacea model.
Casticin significantly reduced CD4+ T-cell infiltration in the rosacea-like dermatitis mouse model.
Casticin inhibited MRGPRX2-mediated mast cell degranulation both in vitro and in vivo, acting as an MRGPRX2 antagonist and influencing NF-κB signaling.
Molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and surface plasmon resonance demonstrated direct binding between casticin and MRGPRX2.
Salivary HBD2 levels differed significantly across the three study groups (isolated angioedema, angioedema with chronic urticaria, and healthy controls), with a small effect size.
Salivary HBD2 was significantly higher in patients with angioedema accompanied by chronic urticaria than in healthy controls.
Serum HBD2 levels did not differ between the angioedema patient groups and healthy controls.
No correlation was found between salivary and serum HBD2 levels in study participants, indicating salivary HBD2 does not reliably reflect serum HBD2 concentrations.
No correlation was observed between serum or salivary HBD2 levels and other serum biomarkers measured in participants.
Salivary HBD2 values were positively correlated with age among participants.
In a prior study by Cao et al., serum HBD2 levels were significantly higher in CSU patients with associated angioedema than in CSU patients without angioedema and in healthy controls.
In CSU patients (Cao et al.), there was a negative correlation between the percentage of peripheral basophils and serum HBD2 levels.

Multiple logistic regression in Cao et al. showed that elevated HBD2 (>72 pg/mL) and higher disease severity (UAS ≥ 28) were significantly associated with angioedema occurrence in CSU patients, while age, sex, and vitamin deficiency were not.
No significant association was found between HBD2 levels and CSU disease severity as measured by UAS7 in Cao et al.'s study.
Cao et al. found that serum HBD2 levels significantly correlated with translationally controlled tumor protein (TCTP) and vitamin D levels in CSU patients compared to healthy controls.
HBD2 induces mast cell degranulation through interaction with the G-protein-coupled receptor MRGPRX2.
In patients with skin diseases, HBD2 interacts with Toll-like receptor 4 via MRGPRX2 activation, inducing histamine-independent itching, and acts as a pro-inflammatory pruritogen.
Serum HBD2 levels are significantly elevated in patients with atopic dermatitis and psoriasis compared to healthy individuals, per cited prior literature.
Salivary HBD2 levels are significantly higher in patients with periodontal diseases compared to healthy individuals, suggesting HBD2 as a potential biomarker for periodontal disease detection.

Histamine synergistically increases HBD2 production in human keratinocytes when combined with TNF-α or IFN-γ, suggesting a paracrine loop between HBD2 and histamine that could amplify keratinocyte-mast cell interactions in CSU skin.
Aged rats formed tumors at a significantly higher rate than young rats after ovarian cancer cell implantation.
Tumor volumes were significantly larger in aged rats compared to young rats.

RNA-seq identified thousands of differentially expressed genes in gonadal adipose tissue when comparing aged vs young pre-tumor adipose, aged vs young tumor-surrounding adipose, and aged pre-tumor vs aged tumor-surrounding adipose.
A heatmap of consistently differentially expressed genes across the three comparisons identified 25 upregulated and 8 downregulated genes in aged rats, of which seven were adipokine-related genes.

Pathway enrichment analysis revealed differential enrichment of cytokine/cytokine-receptor signaling, IL-17 signaling, and glycerolipid metabolism KEGG pathways, as well as GO terms for fatty acid metabolism, immune response, and T cell regulation, across all three aged-vs-young comparisons.

TIMER analysis showed significantly higher infiltration of neutrophils, non-regulatory CD4+ T cells, and myeloid dendritic cells in aged rats compared with young rats in both pre-tumor and tumor-surrounding adipose tissue.
Activated mast cell infiltration was higher in aged rats than young rats both before tumor formation (pre-tumor adipose) and after primary tumor formation (tumor-surrounding adipose).

In aged rats, activated mast cell infiltration was lower in tumor-surrounding adipose (after tumor formation) than in pre-tumor adipose (before tumor formation), suggesting a temporal shift in mast cell activity during tumor development.

Metabolomic profiling of tumor-surrounding adipose tissue identified 905 metabolites and 37 differentially expressed metabolites between aged and young rats, comprising 17 upregulated and 20 downregulated lipids in aged rats.

The top 10 significantly differential lipid metabolites between aged and young rats included Coenzyme Q8, Coenzyme Q9, taurocholic acid, and several specific triglyceride and phosphatidylethanolamine species.

Punicic acid (FFA 18:3) and phosphatidylserine species were the strongest explanatory metabolites correlating with Pnpla3 gene expression in fatty acid metabolic process and glycerolipid metabolism pathways in aged tumor-surrounding adipose tissue.

LysoPE(0:0/22:5), a lysophosphatidylethanolamine/lysophospholipid, was the best explanatory metabolite correlating with cytokine receptor gene expression (Il1rl1) in aged tumor-surrounding adipose tissue.
Free fatty acids and triglycerides were the best explanatory variables in the IL-17 signaling pathway, correlating with S100a8 and S100a9 gene expression in aged tumor-surrounding adipose tissue.

Neutrophil infiltration levels correlated with expression of S100a8, S100a9, C3, Fcna, and Pnpla3 genes and with multiple lipids including 13-oxoODE, ceramide, Coenzyme Q8/Q9, PE(19:0_18:2), taurocholic acid, triglycerides, 9,10-DiHOME, and FFA(18:3) in aged tumor-surrounding adipose tissue.
Mast cell activation infiltration levels correlated with S100a8 and S100a9 gene expression and with Coenzyme Q8/Q9 and specific triglyceride lipids in tumor-surrounding adipose tissue.
A2780 ovarian cancer cells proliferated faster when cultured in conditioned medium from senescent (aged) 3T3-L1 preadipocytes compared with conditioned medium from young 3T3-L1 cells.

RT-qPCR validation confirmed that S100a8, S100a9, C3, Il1rl1, Lcn2, Hba-a1, and Fcna were increased, while Pnpla3 was decreased, in adipose tissue from aged rats compared with young rats, consistent with RNA-seq results.

Adding FFA (18:3) (punicic acid) to culture medium reduced ovarian cancer cell proliferation in A2780, HEYA8, and CAOV2 cell lines, consistent with its reduced level in vivo in aged rats' more aggressive tumors.

Five LLPS-related genes (PLA2G2A, GZMK, CD69, HSP90B1, and S100A11) were identified by LASSO and SVM-RFE as diagnostic biomarkers for ulcerative colitis, with the combined model achieving an AUC of 1.

qPCR on colon tissue from 10 UC patients and 5 healthy donors confirmed significantly higher expression of PLA2G2A, CD69, HSP90B1, and S100A11 in UC tissue, consistent with external dataset validation, while GZMK showed an upward but non-significant trend.
CIBERSORT immune infiltration analysis showed higher activated mast cell infiltration in UC tissue compared to normal controls, while resting mast cells were higher in normal controls than in UC.
The proportion of regulatory T cells (Tregs) was lower in UC patients compared to normal controls, suggesting an imbalance in Treg/Th17 immune regulation may contribute to intestinal inflammation.
The proportion of pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages was higher and anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages was lower in UC patients relative to controls, indicating disrupted macrophage polarity in disease.

Single-cell ssGSEA analysis showed that LLPS-related scores in epithelial cells, NK cells, B cells, T cells, and macrophages were significantly different between UC and control samples, identifying these as key cell types for LLPS involvement in UC.

GO and KEGG enrichment of the 44 intersecting LLPS-related differential genes showed involvement in immune system processes, MHC protein complexes, ER-to-Golgi transport vesicles, and disease pathways including rheumatoid arthritis, autoimmune thyroid disease, and intestinal immune network for IgA production.

CTD database analysis identified five candidate small-molecule compounds (decitabine, tetrachlorodibenzodioxin, tetradecanoylphorbol acetate, thapsigargin, and cisplatin) interacting with the five hub genes as potential UC treatment agents, though the authors note TPA and thapsigargin are likely unsuitable.
Dorsal and palmar hand skin temperatures were significantly higher in women with FMS than in healthy women.
Women with FMS had significantly higher tympanic (core) temperatures than healthy controls.

No significant differences were found between FMS and control groups in age, height, weight, BMI, menarche/menopause age, axillary temperature, or serum serine, citrulline, carnosine, GABA, and lysine concentrations.
Only the essential amino acid group (EAAs) showed a statistically significant correlation with dorsal dominant-hand temperature in FMS patients.
Serum tryptophan showed 15 positive correlations with hand thermographic variables, exclusively in FMS patients.
Serum methionine showed 11 positive correlations with hand temperature variables in FMS patients.
Serum lysine showed one significant positive correlation with hand temperature in FMS patients.
3-methylhistidine concentration correlated with nine hand thermographic variables only in FMS patients.
Histidine was significantly associated with the average temperature of the dorsal center of the dominant hand in FMS patients.
Glutamic acid showed 14 positive correlations with hand thermographic variables in FMS patients.
Asparagine showed 2 positive correlations with dorsal hand thermographic variables in FMS patients, differing in localization from controls.
Tyrosine showed 3 positive correlations with hand thermographic variables exclusively in FMS patients.
No statistically significant correlations were found between hand thermographic variables and a broad panel of other amino acids in FMS patients.
In healthy controls, only asparagine showed statistically significant positive correlations with hand thermographic variables (localized to the palm rather than dorsum as in FMS).
Aminoadipic acid, lysine, and serine concentrations were inversely correlated with several hand temperatures exclusively in healthy controls, not in FMS patients.
Leucine concentration showed significant positive associations with tympanic and axillary (core) temperatures in FMS patients only.
In the control group, tryptophan showed a positive correlation with axillary temperature and with the tympanic-axillary temperature difference.
A negative correlation was observed between aminoadipic acid and axillary temperature in the control group.
In multivariate regression, lysine significantly predicted dorsal-center hand temperature, explaining about 21.5% of variance in healthy women.

Multivariate regression showed serine and lysine were significantly associated with palmar middle fingertip and palmar center temperatures in healthy women, explaining 12.4% and 19% of variance respectively.
Multivariate regression showed citrulline significantly predicted axillary temperature, explaining about 20.2% of variance in healthy controls.
The authors' own prior work found elevated blood lysine levels in FMS patients compared to healthy controls (cited from a separate earlier study).
A cited machine-learning study identified blood tyrosine concentration as a key biomarker for diagnosing FMS.
TGM2 protein expression was higher in cultured scleroderma dermal fibroblasts than in healthy control fibroblasts by Western blot.
Immunohistochemistry showed elevated TGM2 expression in dermal fibroblasts of lesional diffuse cutaneous SSc skin compared with unchanged levels in limited cutaneous and nonlesional dcSSc skin.
Treatment of healthy control dermal fibroblasts with TGF-β1 for 24 hours induced TGM2 expression to levels resembling those in SSc dermal cells.

TGM2-neutralizing antibody BB7 dose-dependently reduced Col-1, αSMA, and CCN2 protein expression in both HC and SSc fibroblasts, with a more pronounced effect in SSc cells (70-90% reduction at 1000 nM).

SSc dermal fibroblasts deposited significantly higher levels of fibronectin and collagens I, III, and IV than HC fibroblasts, and TGM2 antibody BB7 reduced this ECM deposition, particularly in SSc cells.
BB7 blocked TGF-β1-induced expression of Col-1, Tenascin C, CCN2, and αSMA to a similar degree as a pan-TGF-β blocking antibody and an ALK5 inhibitor.
BB7, a pan-TGF-β blocking antibody, or the ALK5 inhibitor SB431542 each significantly reduced Smad2/3 phosphorylation, with a 60-80% decrease in Col-1 and αSMA, in scleroderma fibroblasts.
BB7 treatment reduced levels of active TGF-β1 secreted by scleroderma fibroblasts by more than 80% as measured by the mink lung cell bioassay.
TGM2 knockout mice were protected from bleomycin-induced increases in dermal thickness, whereas wild-type mice showed significantly increased dermal thickness after bleomycin.
Sircol assay showed a significant increase in dermal collagen content in wild-type mice after bleomycin, but no significant change in TGM2 null mice treated with bleomycin versus saline.

Polarized light microscopy and scanning electron microscopy revealed that TGM2 knockout mouse skin had thinner, less crosslinked collagen fibers compared with predominantly thick fibers in wild-type skin.
TGM2 null dermal fibroblasts showed markedly impaired wound closure compared with wild-type fibroblasts at 48 hours post-injury in a scratch assay.
TGM2 null fibroblasts had a reduced ability to contract 3D collagen-I matrices compared with wild-type fibroblasts, and TGF-β1 partially rescued contraction in TGM2 null cells.
Among eight SSc skin samples, three showed elevated extracellular TGM2 expression in the dermis, and these showed reduced TG activity after zampilimab treatment, indicating TGM2-specific activity.
TGM2 staining in inflammatory infiltrates was elevated in nonlesional and lesional dcSSc skin but unaltered in lcSSc skin.
TGM2 staining in the vascular/perivascular compartment was decreased in limited cutaneous SSc samples compared with other groups.
Patients with Sjögren disease had a 70% increased overall mortality risk compared to an age- and sex-matched general population, with a standardized mortality ratio of 1.7.
The most common causes of death among SjD patients were infections (35.7%), malignancies (23.8%), and cardiovascular disease (7.1%).
Older age was an independent predictor of mortality in SjD patients, with each additional year of age increasing mortality hazard by 11%.
C4 hypocomplementemia (low complement C4 levels) was an independent predictor of mortality, associated with an almost 4-fold increased mortality hazard.
Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was an independent predictor of mortality in SjD patients.
History of heart failure was an independent predictor of mortality in SjD patients, more than quadrupling risk.
Pulmonary involvement was an independent predictor of mortality in SjD patients.
A history of heart failure was an independent predictor of increased mortality risk in patients with Sjögren disease.
Pulmonary involvement was an independent predictor of increased mortality risk in patients with Sjögren disease.
Most PASC patients in both the Stanford clinic cohort and the multinational survey cohort reported no subjective change in PASC symptoms after receiving COVID-19 vaccination post-PASC onset.

In the multinational survey cohort, receiving more booster doses (none, monovalent only, or both monovalent and bivalent) was significantly associated with a greater proportion reporting improved PASC symptoms and a lower proportion reporting worsened symptoms.
In the Stanford clinic cohort, median BMI differed significantly between patients whose PASC symptoms improved, stayed the same, or worsened after vaccination.
In the Stanford clinic cohort, age, sex, and race/ethnicity were not significantly associated with post-vaccination PASC symptom change.
In the multinational survey cohort, sex, race, BMI, and vaccine brand were not significantly associated with post-vaccination PASC symptom change.
Acute post-vaccination adverse events were reported much more frequently among clinic patients whose PASC symptoms subsequently worsened than among those whose symptoms improved or stayed the same.
The number of vaccination doses received prior to the initial clinic visit was not significantly associated with PASC symptom outcome group.

The most common PASC symptoms reported at initial clinic visit (fatigue, brain fog, post-exertional malaise, lethargy, unrefreshing sleep) were similar in prevalence across patients regardless of whether they later reported improvement, no change, or worsening after vaccination.

Autoimmune disease history was reported by 15.2% of the multinational survey cohort participants prior to their first SARS-CoV-2 infection, a comorbidity the authors link to the female predominance of PASC and its overlap with sex-based vaccine reactogenicity differences.
Among participants with echocardiograms reviewed by the core lab, 42.3% had reduced LVEF (<55%) during hospitalization for MIS-C, with nearly all cases normalizing by 6 months.
Black race, higher C-reactive protein level, and abnormal troponin level were each associated with lower LVEF during MIS-C hospitalization.
Fifteen participants developed coronary artery z scores of 2.5 or greater (including one large/giant aneurysm), with 92.3% of those affected during hospitalization normalizing by 6 months.
The proportion of participants reporting return to greater than 90% of pre-MIS-C health status increased from 86.3% at 2 weeks to 95.1% at 6 months.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported symptom at 2 weeks post-MIS-C but declined markedly by 6 months.

The proportion of participants reporting return to greater than 90% of pre-MIS-C health status (energy, sleep, appetite, cognition, mood) increased from 86.3% at 2 weeks to 95.1% at 6 months post-discharge.
Fatigue, the most common symptom reported at 2 weeks after MIS-C, declined markedly by 6 months.
Parent/guardian-reported PROMIS Global Health fatigue T scores improved significantly from 2 weeks to 6 months after MIS-C.
Parent/guardian-reported PROMIS Global Health overall score improved significantly from 2 weeks to 6 months after MIS-C.
Parent/guardian-reported PROMIS pain interference T scores improved significantly from 2 weeks to 6 months after MIS-C.
During acute hospitalization for MIS-C, nearly half of participants required vasoactive support, a small fraction required ECMO, and mortality was low.
GI symptoms overlap substantially with IBS, affecting 38–92% of ME/CFS patients.
In a small study (N=48), over 70% of ME/CFS patients reported GI complaints and more than 35% used medication for these issues.
At least 25% of ME/CFS patients are confined to home or bed, reflecting moderate-to-severe disease.
Nearly half of ME/CFS patients cannot maintain employment, with one study reporting an 87% unemployment rate.
During severe episodes, 48% of ME/CFS patients are completely unproductive.
A meta-analysis found ME/CFS prevalence up to 0.89% using CDC-1994 criteria, and 1.14% based on clinical interviews.
ME/CFS is diagnosed more frequently in women than men, with a female:male ratio of 1.5 to 2.
Only about 4% of ME/CFS patients experience complete recovery over time.
The lack of universal consensus diagnostic criteria may cause diagnostic inaccuracy in up to 80% of ME/CFS cases.
Rectal bacterial infusion was reported to alleviate ME/CFS symptoms in a study population that largely also had IBS, supporting gut-brain communication in ME/CFS.
A pilot FMT study found the procedure safe but ineffective at improving fatigue severity or health-related quality of life in ME/CFS.
Metagenomic clustering showed that ME/CFS patients with comorbid IBS had increased unclassified Alistipes and reduced Faecalibacterium.
In ME/CFS patients without IBS, unclassified Bacteroides increased while Bacteroides vulgatus decreased.
Metabolic pathway analysis identified alterations in unsaturated fatty acid synthesis, atrazine degradation, vitamin B6 production, and pyrimidine ribonucleoside breakdown in ME/CFS gut microbiota.
A study examining viral taxa in feces, blood, and saliva found no significant differences between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
A systematic review by Newberry et al. noted 8 concordant and 7 discordant microbiome findings across studies but still supported the presence of dysbiosis in ME/CFS.
A small study accurately classified 83% of subjects as ME/CFS patients or healthy controls using gut dysbiosis metrics combined with elevated blood inflammatory markers from microbial translocation.
16S rRNA stool analysis showed decreased bacterial diversity/richness, reduced anti-inflammatory species, and increased pro-inflammatory Enterobacteriaceae in ME/CFS.
Cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2 peak) accounted for approximately 20% of variance in gut microbial diversity, linking reduced fitness in ME/CFS to lower diversity.

Elevated Enterococcus and Streptococcus species along with increased Enterobacteriaceae were documented, alongside lower beneficial Bifidobacteria and decreased anti-inflammatory Firmicutes in ME/CFS.

Nagy-Szakal and colleagues identified increased Alistipes and decreased butyrate-producing Faecalibacterium as candidate ME/CFS biomarkers; their higher Clostridium finding contrasted with Giloteaux's results.
In ME/CFS-discordant monozygotic twins, the affected twin showed reduced Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and lower gut alpha diversity.
Reduced Faecalibacterium has also been observed in fatigue associated with inflammatory bowel disease, cancer, multiple sclerosis, and type 1 diabetes, suggesting a shared cross-condition pattern.

A case study of ME/CFS-discordant monozygotic twins found the affected twin had reduced Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and lower gut alpha diversity compared to the unaffected co-twin.

In a comparison of ME/CFS with acute Q-fever fatigue, both patient groups shared similar microbial and proinflammatory patterns distinct from healthy controls, with increased Firmicutes and Actinobacteria and lower Bacteroidetes in 50 ME/CFS patients versus 72 controls.

A study of 35 ME/CFS patients and 70 controls found a unique microbial composition with reduced anti-inflammatory Firmicutes, and commonalities were seen between patients and their relatives but not external controls, highlighting confounding by lifestyle/genetics.

A study of 48 patients and 52 controls identified 26 bacterial markers distinguishing ME/CFS, with the largest differences seen in Coprobacillus, Eggerthella, and Blautia levels, alongside reduced Faecalibacterium and increased Coprobacillus.

Microbiome alterations identified as candidate biomarkers were substantially more common in ME/CFS patients with shorter disease duration (≤3 years) than in those with longer disease spans (>3 years), suggesting transient shifts early in illness.
An examination of viral taxa in feces, blood, and saliva found no significant differences in viral populations between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
A systematic review by Newberry and colleagues found eight concordant and seven discordant microbiome findings across studies, but still concluded that dysbiosis is present in ME/CFS.
Gut microbiome dysbiosis combined with elevated blood inflammatory markers from microbial translocation correctly classified 83% of subjects as ME/CFS patients or healthy controls in a small study.

Cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2 peak) accounts for approximately 20% of variation in gut microbial diversity, suggesting reduced diversity in ME/CFS patients may relate to lower physical fitness rather than disease per se.

Increased colonization by Gram-positive D-lactic-acid-producing bacteria such as Enterococci and Streptococci is hypothesized to lower intestinal pH and raise gut permeability, systemic inflammation, immune activation, and oxidative stress in ME/CFS.
Trials targeting bacterial overgrowth with antibiotics and probiotics did not improve fatigue symptoms, casting doubt on the D-lactate hypothesis as a driver of fatigue in ME/CFS.

Under the 'metabolic trap hypothesis,' researchers found numerous gene mutations in IDO-2 among ME/CFS patients that correlated with symptom severity, potentially impairing tryptophan-to-kynurenine conversion.
Elevated tryptophan and reduced kynurenine levels were confirmed in ME/CFS patients, consistent with the metabolic trap hypothesis of impaired IDO-2 activity.
Elevated KYN/TRP ratios and neuroactive metabolites such as quinolinic acid parallel ME/CFS symptoms including heightened sensitivity and central sensitization.
Viral infections such as Epstein-Barr virus can activate IDO to convert tryptophan to kynurenine, supporting the hypothesis of increased kynurenine production in ME/CFS.
Recent clinical investigations suggest that altered immunity and kynurenine metabolism likely initiate fatigue in ME/CFS rather than sustaining it chronically.
The higher rate of ME/CFS diagnosis in women may be linked to their greater lifetime antibiotic exposure compared to men, potentially through effects on the gut microbiome.
Antibiotics may contribute to oxidative stress via ROS production, consistent with reports of elevated ROS levels in ME/CFS patients.
Nagy-Szakal and colleagues observed raised plasma ceramide levels in ME/CFS, hypothesized to result from lipopolysaccharide hydrolysis and to further impair gut epithelial barrier integrity.
Thiamine, partially produced by gut bacteria like Bacteroides and required by Faecalibacterium for growth, is reduced in ME/CFS patients.

A recent RCT of acupuncture and moxibustion in China suggested improvements in fatigue linked to intestinal microbiome changes, though risk of bias existed due to lack of blinding and subjective fatigue assessment.
Ginseng administration has been shown to reduce fatigue in ME/CFS and other conditions, possibly via gut microbiome-mediated pharmacokinetics.

A systematic review found no evidence supporting benefits of elimination or modified diets for ME/CFS patients, a conclusion also extending to nutritional supplements overall, though supplements might help specific symptoms.
Metabolites glutamic acid and argininosuccinic acid are elevated in ME/CFS patients, raising concerns about contributions to neuroinflammation and cognitive dysfunction.

Rectal bacterial infusion alleviated ME/CFS symptoms in a study where a significant proportion of participants also had IBS, suggesting the IBS-targeted treatment also engaged gut-brain communication relevant to ME/CFS.
ImmunoVita supplementation significantly improved cognitive fatigue over 36 weeks but did not significantly affect overall fatigue.
A combination supplement of vitamins, minerals, and coenzymes showed no significant change in overall fatigue, functional impairment, or physical activity levels.

Supradyn® did not significantly improve overall fatigue or quality of life but significantly reduced sleep disorders, autonomic symptoms, headaches, and feelings of infection, and improved superoxide dismutase activity.

Multi-supplementation with coenzymes, amino acids, and vitamins significantly reduced fatigue scores and produced minor improvements in sleep quality and clinical global impression, but did not change health-related quality of life or depression.

Probiotic supplementation (Enterelle, Bifiselle, Rotanelle, Citogenex, Ramnoselle) was reported to significantly reduce fatigue scores and enhance mental/physical health in the results summary, though the discussion section characterized the same pilot study as showing only non-significant improvements in symptoms and inflammatory markers.

Combined CoQ10 and selenium supplementation significantly reduced fatigue, improved emotional role functioning and mental health subscores of quality of life, and improved lipid/thyroid/antioxidant biomarkers, while CRP, FGF21 and NT-proBNP were unchanged.

Combined CoQ10 and NADH supplementation significantly reduced cognitive fatigue, improved SF-36 physical functioning, sleep efficiency/quality/duration, and bodily pain, increased NAD+/NADH, CoQ10, ATP and citrate synthase levels, decreased lipoperoxides, and reduced nighttime awakenings compared to placebo.

ENADA (NADH) supplementation showed subjective improvement in 31% of patients but no significant abnormalities in immunologic markers or oxidoreductase activity and no significant correlation with immune function or clinical status.

GAA supplementation reduced activity, motivation, and mental fatigue but not general or physical fatigue, improved quadriceps strength and maximal oxygen uptake, increased muscular creatine, but did not affect daily energy expenditure or physical activity duration/intensity.
Acetyl-L-carnitine, propionyl-L-carnitine, and their combination improved general and mental fatigue, though many patients experienced symptom worsening during follow-up.
Acclydine (an alkaloid supplement) showed no significant changes in fatigue or functional impairment compared to controls, and no differences in IGF status.

Anhydrous enol-oxaloacetate (AEO) supplementation led to significant fatigue reduction in 22-33% of participants, with more pronounced improvement at higher doses; plasma oxaloacetate deficiency has been documented in ME/CFS patients.
CoQ10, an antioxidant that enhances ATP production, is found at reduced levels in ME/CFS patients and is linked to increased fatigue, autonomic dysfunction, and cognitive issues.

Mitochondrial dysfunction in ME/CFS is linked to impaired glucose and amino acid metabolism, reduced TCA cycle substrates, inefficient ATP production, and a shift toward lipid metabolism, though this appears to be a spectrum of abnormalities rather than a single pathology.
Genome studies revealed altered gastrointestinal microbiome structures in ME/CFS, including reduced species diversity and greater inter-patient variability.
The prevalence of irritable bowel syndrome, a functional gastrointestinal disorder, is much higher in ME/CFS patients than in the general population.
Psychiatric and gastrointestinal comorbidities (depression, anxiety, IBS) were highly prevalent among ME/CFS study participants, with rates ranging from 24% to 80% across included trials.

Six of fourteen included studies reported adverse effects related to treatment (nausea, dyspepsia, insomnia, epigastralgia, dizziness, tremors, muscle spasms, anxiety, diarrhea, and overstimulation), with two also noting adverse effects in the placebo arm.

All 14 included studies used the outdated 1994 CDC Fukuda diagnostic criteria, which do not require post-exertional malaise (PEM) for diagnosis and only require 4 of 8 possible symptoms, complicating cross-study comparability and generalizability to patients diagnosed with newer criteria (CCC, IOM, ICC).
In an initial uncorrected t-test comparison, CSF serine was significantly higher in ME/CFS than sedentary controls, leading a group of 16 elevated metabolites.
Multivariate general linear modeling identified 42 metabolites and 33 lipids in CSF that significantly differed between ME/CFS and sedentary controls, mapped to KEGG metabolic modules.
Before exercise, both female and male ME/CFS subjects had 25 metabolites and 26 lipids at higher CSF levels than sedentary controls.
In the post-exercise cohort, sedentary controls (especially females) had higher CSF levels than ME/CFS for 11 metabolites and 5 lipids.
Both frequentist and Bayesian analyses found 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5MTHF) was significantly lower in ME/CFS than SC, and lower in the non-exercise vs post-exercise state.
Elevated sarcosine, creatine, and creatinine alongside reduced dimethylglycine and choline in ME/CFS CSF indicated disrupted methylation downstream of the serine/glycine pathway.
ME/CFS CSF had a significantly greater number of elevated phosphatidylglycerol species compared with controls.
ME/CFS CSF had a significantly greater number of elevated phosphatidylethanolamine species compared with controls.
ME/CFS CSF had significantly more elevated sphingomyelin species than controls, and these sphingomyelins had significantly longer acyl chains.
Trans-aconitate, citrate, and glucose-phosphates were elevated in ME/CFS CSF, indicating disrupted energy (TCA cycle) metabolism, with trans-aconitate potentially short-circuiting the TCA cycle.
Dopamine was unexpectedly elevated in ME/CFS CSF at baseline (non-exercise).

Bayesian linear regression identified a set of metabolites (sarcosine, trans-aconitate, glucuronate, 7-methylguanosine, serine, L-acetylcarnitine, among others) that significantly predicted ME/CFS status.
Gender strongly influenced CSF metabolomic profiles: males (across ME/CFS and SC) had 49 metabolites and 8 lipids higher than females, while females had 2 metabolites and 9 lipids higher than males.
Males had significantly more elevated hexylceramide species than females in CSF, while females showed a non-significant trend toward higher phosphatidylglycerides.
In ME/CFS, exercise led to a marked reduction (consumption) of 29 metabolites and 37 lipids from non-exercise to post-exercise CSF levels.

In sedentary controls, exercise produced the opposite pattern from ME/CFS, with many more metabolites elevated after exercise than before, indicating active production/excretion rather than consumption.

Post-exercise, far fewer CSF metabolites differed between ME/CFS and controls than at baseline; only cysteamine was elevated in ME/CFS, while controls had higher phenylalanine, tyrosine, 1-methylhistidine, and riboflavin.
The ME/CFS cohort had higher CFS Symptom Severity Questionnaire scores and higher rates of comorbid fibromyalgia by both 1990 and 2010 diagnostic criteria compared with controls.

Pathway enrichment of the pooled significant disease-associated metabolites highlighted pyrimidine metabolism, methionine metabolism, ammonia recycling, arginine/proline metabolism, spermidine/spermine biosynthesis, and glycine/serine metabolism as disrupted in ME/CFS.
Contrary to prediction, CSF lactate did not change significantly with exercise in ME/CFS, whereas it rose in sedentary controls after exercise.

The overall CSF metabolomic/lipidomic profile in this ME/CFS cohort was hypermetabolic (elevated levels), contrasting with the hypometabolic CSF profiles reported by two prior independent studies (Walitt et al.; Lipkin and Fiehn).

Citing a study in twins discordant for ME/CFS, the paper notes that overexpression of WASF3 causes endoplasmic reticulum stress and disrupts mitochondrial respiratory supercomplex formation, reducing complex IV levels.
Citing prior work, the paper notes proliferating B cells from ME/CFS subjects have lower mitochondrial mass than controls, and preferentially utilize essential amino acids when stimulated in vitro.

Cited literature indicates that in Long COVID, CSF/plasma sarcosine and serine concentrations are significantly reduced and inversely correlate with depression, anxiety, and cognitive dysfunction scores.

Cited literature indicates fibromyalgia patients show altered gut microbiome, higher plasma serine and tyrosine, and lower choline, glutamine, 2-hydroxyisocaproate, and pyruvate compared with controls.
Homocysteic acid, a potent NMDA receptor agonist found in astrocytes, was elevated in ME/CFS CSF and was also depleted after exercise.

Most, but not all, of the 12 disaggregated DSM-5 MDD symptoms were associated with diagnoses of fibromyalgia, ME/CFS, and IBS, suggesting specific MDD features drive comorbidity with functional disorders.
A five-class Latent Class Analysis solution based on MDD symptom profiles provided the best balance of model fit and entropy among MDD cases.
MDD cases classified into the 'severe typical' latent symptom class had increased prevalence of fibromyalgia, ME/CFS, and IBS compared to other MDD symptom classes.

MDD cases classified into the 'anhedonia/weight gain' latent symptom class also showed increased prevalence of all functional disorders, but with differential association strength across specific FD pairs.
The severe typical MDD symptom class was equally associated with fibromyalgia and ME/CFS, indicating no differential relationship between this MDD subtype and these two functional disorders.
The overall pattern of results indicates that MDD-FD comorbidity does not arise from a single shared mechanism but likely reflects multiple distinct symptom-driven pathways.
Proton MRS studies show elevated glutamate levels with increased glutamatergic activity in the insula and posterior cingulate cortex of patients with FM.
Reduced GABA levels in the insula were found, indicating decreased GABAergic activity in this pain-processing brain region in FM.
fMRI studies show that individuals with FM display intensified neuronal activation in pain-processing brain regions compared to healthy controls when exposed to identical pressure stimuli.
Patients with FM express markedly increased levels of miRNA-320a compared to controls, correlating with symptom severity but not with cerebral pain processing.
Bjersing et al. identified nine microRNAs differentially expressed in cerebrospinal fluid between FM patients and healthy individuals, suggesting a disease-specific CSF miRNA pattern.

Metabolomic and proteomic profiling of urine and serum from 30 FM patients versus 25 healthy controls identified significant differences in three urine metabolites, five serum metabolites, and eight serum proteins that distinguish pain/soreness phenotypes.
S100B levels were significantly increased in the serum of women with chronic pain conditions including FM compared to healthy women.
S100A7 levels were significantly decreased in the serum of women with chronic pain conditions including FM compared to healthy women.
Low-dose naltrexone (4.5 mg oral daily for 12 weeks) reduced FM symptoms by more than 30% compared to placebo and improved thermal and mechanical pain thresholds.
A randomized placebo-controlled study in healthy volunteers showed PEA reduces peripheral and central sensitization while increasing pain modulation, supporting its rationale for use in FM.

Dietary Coenzyme Q10 supplementation improved muscle metabolic parameters and reduced pain, asthenia, and depressive symptoms in patients with FM, the latter linked to normalization of serotonin levels.
Alpha-Lipoic Acid supplementation has proven effective in reducing musculoskeletal pain in patients with FM.
Randomized clinical studies showed dietary carnitine supplementation reduces skeletal muscle pain and depressive symptoms in FM, with effects comparable to the antidepressant duloxetine.
A daily oral dose of 1000 mcg vitamin B12 improved disease severity and anxiety in FM patients with no reported side effects.
Meta-analysis studies showed vitamin D serum levels of patients with FM were significantly lower than in controls, especially in postmenopausal women.
Clinical studies of vitamin D supplementation showed it significantly reduces pain in FM patients but does not show beneficial effects on associated psychopathological symptoms.
Low magnesium levels are commonly found in patients with FM, which can reduce exercise capacity, increase inflammation, and contribute to muscle spasms.
A nationwide population-based cohort study demonstrated that iron deficiency anemia is associated with an increased risk of FM, with higher FM incidence compared to non-iron-deficient controls.
Ferric carboxymaltose was well tolerated and improved FM severity compared to placebo in iron-deficient patients with coexisting FM.
In a reserpine-induced FM rat model, two weeks of cationic liposomal carotenoid (beta-carotene and lutein) treatment normalized monoamine levels and oxidative stress markers to control values.

In a comparison of intravenous diosmin versus mannitol/dexamethasone in 150 patients per group with radicular pain, only the diosmin-treated group experienced significant pain relief without adverse effects.

In a double-blind trial, FM patients randomized to saffron extract or duloxetine showed no significant difference in FM evaluation scale scores, indicating comparable efficacy between the two treatments.
Quercetin exhibits analgesic activity by attenuating pain hypersensitivity through inhibition of the mTOR/p70S6K pathway affecting synaptic morphology in spinal dorsal horn neurons of db/db mice.

In reserpine-induced FM-type pain in rats, Tilia americana extract and its flavonoid fraction produced significant, dose-dependent antihyperalgesic and antiallodynic effects equivalent to tramadol or pramipexole.
Hesperidin decreased mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia in rats via D2 and opioid receptor binding, and reduced levels of TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and IL-6.
Naringenin suppressed mechanical allodynia and reduced pro-inflammatory prostaglandin E2 levels in in vivo nociception models, with analgesic activity mediated via TRPV1 receptor binding.
Gut microbiota studies in FM patients found lower abundance of Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae, Eubacterium, and Bifidobacterium, and overrepresentation of Rikenellaceae and Clostridia species.

A randomized active-controlled trial showed diosmin, a citrus flavone glycoside, bound opioid and D2 dopaminergic receptors and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines, alleviating hyperalgesia in an experimental pain model.

In a double-blind randomized trial, saffron extract (15 mg) showed comparable efficacy to duloxetine (30 mg) in treating FM symptoms, with no significant difference between groups on FM evaluation scales.

Quercetin exhibited analgesic activity by attenuating pain hypersensitivity through inhibition of the mTOR/p70S6K pathway, altering synaptic morphology and protein levels in spinal dorsal horn neurons of diabetic (db/db) mice.

Tilia americana aqueous extract and its flavonoid fraction produced significant, dose-dependent antihyperalgesic and antiallodynic effects comparable to tramadol or pramipexole in a reserpine-induced FM-type pain rat model.

Various flavonoids (kaempferol glycosides, baicalin, hyperin, luteolin, fisetin) demonstrated analgesic, antioxidant, and neuroprotective activities in preclinical pain models, with hyperin reported to have analgesic potency approximately twenty times that of morphine.
Chlorogenic acid was shown to alleviate streptozotocin-induced neuropathic pain through an antioxidative mechanism and downregulation of COX-2 expression.

Hesperidin alone or combined with diosmin decreased mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia in rats via D2 and opioid receptor binding, and separately reduced hyperalgesia through decreased TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 levels.

Naringenin's analgesic and antioxidant activities were mediated by TRPV1 receptor binding, and naringenin suppressed mechanical allodynia and reduced prostaglandin E2 levels in in vivo nociception models.
Piperine, a black pepper extract component, shows analgesic and neuroprotective efficacy with potential additive benefit for FM, and also enhances the bioavailability of curcumin formulations.

In the reserpine-induced FM model in female rats, two weeks of cationic liposomal beta-carotene and lutein treatment normalized monoamine levels, oxidative stress markers, ECoG spectral parameters, and behavioral measures to control values.

Studies of gut microbiota in FM patients found lower abundance of Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae, Eubacterium, and Bifidobacterium, while Rikenellaceae and many Clostridia class species were overrepresented.

Reduced abundance of GABA-producing Bifidobacteria in FM patients may cause an imbalance favoring glutamate over GABA, potentially contributing to heightened pain sensitivity via gut-brain axis mechanisms.

An ongoing 2024 randomized sham-controlled clinical trial (NCT06424041) is testing fecal microbiome transplantation from healthy donors in 80 women with severe FM, assessing effects on pain, fatigue, and sleep.

FM patients treated with milnacipran, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, showed reduced pain sensitivity and increased activity in brain regions of descending pain inhibitory pathways compared to those treated with placebo.

Red blood cell membrane-mimicking liposomes containing curcumin (RC-Lip) were successfully fabricated and showed potential for efficiently mediating inflammatory response in diabetic wound treatment, with high entrapment efficiency maintained across sonication conditions.

FM and IBS frequently co-occur, particularly in women, sharing sympathetic nervous system dysfunction, central sensitization, and overlapping symptoms such as headaches, migraines, sleep disturbances, and reduced quality of life linked to gut-brain axis disruption.

Clinical studies evaluating vitamin D supplementation for musculoskeletal pain found it significantly reduces pain in FM patients but showed no beneficial effect on associated psychopathological symptoms.

Meta-analysis studies showed vitamin D serum levels were significantly lower in FM patients than in controls, especially in postmenopausal women, suggesting a role in FM and a potential preventive strategy via supplementation.

In the PACE trial's graded exercise therapy (GET) arm, 160 participants exercised five days a week for up to 30 minutes over 24 weeks, yet their objective fitness failed to improve, contradicting the deconditioning hypothesis.
The CBT with graded activity (CBTplus) arm of the PACE trial also showed no improvement in objective fitness.

Three Dutch trials of CBTplus (8 months in adults, 5 months in adolescents) and guided self-instructions (≥16 weeks) based on CBTplus found no objective improvement in activity as measured by actometer.

A 12-week GET programme, an 18-week combined CBTplus/GET programme for more severely affected patients, and the Belgian reference centre evaluation all showed no objective improvement in fitness measured by VO2peak/VO2max or a timed step test.
A systematic review found that 51% of long COVID patients fulfill ME/CFS diagnostic criteria.

In a 2-day cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) study comparing 84 ME/CFS patients to 71 healthy sedentary controls, only ME/CFS patients showed significant declines in peak exertion measures on the second-day test, failing to reproduce day-1 results, unlike controls.
The ReCOVer study found that 16 weeks of CBTplus did not produce an objective improvement of activity (actometer) in long COVID patients.

The PACE trial reported high treatment acceptance and adherence: 87% of CBTplus and 85% of GET participants were adequately treated, adherence to the treatment manual was very good to excellent, and dropout was low (11% CBTplus, 6% GET), indicating adherence was not the cause of poor objective outcomes.

The Belgian reference centre evaluation (n=655) found patients received on average 41-62 hours of CBTplus/GET over 6-8 months with a very low dropout rate (2.8%), reflecting high patient motivation to engage with treatment.
CBTplus and GET did not lead to a reduction in CFS symptom count in the PACE trial.
Sunnquist and Jason (2018) re-examined the cognitive behavioral model and found their empirical findings inconsistent with it.

A systematic review (Kuut et al., 2024) labeled CBTplus effective despite its own results showing patients remained severely disabled after treatment, and failed to disclose that at least one author was involved in all eight reviewed studies.

Post-exertional malaise (PEM), the cardinal symptom of ME/CFS, is a disproportionate increase in symptoms following exertion with delayed onset (up to 72 hours), loss of strength/function, and abnormally delayed recovery, distinguishing it from normal post-exercise fatigue.
Severely ill, home- or bed-bound patients make up an estimated 25% of the ME/CFS population, and are highlighted as a priority group for biomarker research.

When reaction times were standardized to account for baseline processing speed differences, CFS patients showed no difference from healthy controls in Stroop interference (attentional selectivity), with strong Bayesian evidence supporting the null hypothesis.

Raw (non-standardized) reaction time analyses showed differences in the magnitude of Stroop interference between CFS patients and healthy controls, but this was entirely explained by generally slower processing speed in CFS patients rather than a specific attentional selectivity deficit.
Prior research cited in this protocol found that patients with chronic fatigue syndrome have abnormalities in the function of certain brain regions.
Previous studies cited in this protocol reported that Tuina massage therapy relieves fatigue and improves daytime functioning in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome.
Cited prior research found that Qigong practice can enhance muscle strength and physical performance.
Prior research cited in this protocol reported that Qigong can effectively enhance quality of life and decrease pain in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome.

A prior fMRI study cited in this protocol found abnormal structure and connectivity in specific brain regions of CFS patients, including the right superior frontal gyrus, left median cingulate gyrus, left middle occipital gyrus, and left middle temporal gyrus.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is described as a common intervention for CFS that identifies and adjusts maladaptive behaviors and beliefs, decreasing symptom severity and improving functional capacity, but mainly targets mental rather than somatic symptoms.

A gel electrophoresis shift assay showed that PTIC binds proteins in M1 macrophage lysates in a dose-dependent manner, with decreases in 100, 75, 55, 25, and 22 kDa bands and increases in 40 and 78 kDa bands.
Addition of 10% PTIC to THP-1-derived M1 macrophage cultures decreased the percentage of CD16+/CD36+/CD86+/IL-1β-expressing (M1) cells.
PTIC increased the percentage of CD14+/CD16+/CD163+/IL-10-expressing (M2) cells in THP-1-derived M1 cultures, favoring M2 polarization.
Surface plasmon resonance (Biacore) binding assays showed that the type I collagen in PTIC binds recombinant human LAIR1 with similar affinity to native porcine type I collagen (CI).
Blocking/agonizing LAIR1 with an anti-LAIR1 antibody reproduced the PTIC effect, decreasing M1 markers and increasing M2 markers, confirming LAIR1 as a functional receptor mediating the response.
PTIC decreased IFN-γ gene expression in M1 macrophages despite constant IFN-γ stimulation, while it increased IL-10 gene expression regardless of IFN-γ stimulation status.

PTIC produced a dose-dependent decrease in STAT1 phosphorylation at tyrosine701 in M1 macrophages without altering NF-κB (p65) or p38 expression, identifying STAT1 as the PTIC/LAIR1-regulated signaling node.
Anti-LAIR1 antibody reduced STAT1 phosphorylation more efficiently than PTIC alone or the anti-LAIR1+PTIC combination, further supporting LAIR1 as the receptor upstream of STAT1 dephosphorylation.

In a placebo-controlled trial of intramuscular PTIC in COVID-19 outpatients, an unadjusted accelerated failure time model showed the PTIC group achieved oxygen saturation/symptom recovery outcomes 2.70-fold faster than placebo.
PTIC treatment shortened COVID-19 symptom duration by a mean of 6.1 ± 3.2 days compared with placebo.
PTIC was safe and well tolerated with no serious adverse events; the most common adverse event was transient (15-20 min) injection-site pain, similar in frequency to placebo.

In a nested cohort of the trial, the percentage of IP-10-producing classical monocytes (Mo1) decreased significantly from day 8 to day 90 post-treatment with PTIC but not with placebo, with significant differences in circulating Mo1 numbers at days 15 and 90.

The percentage of IDO-producing non-classical monocytes (Mo2) increased significantly from day 8 to day 90 post-treatment with PTIC versus placebo, with significant differences in circulating Mo2 numbers.
The percentage of circulating LAIR1-expressing classical monocytes (Mo1), elevated during early COVID-19, decreased significantly over time in patients treated with PTIC compared with placebo.
The percentage of LAIR1-expressing non-classical monocytes (Mo2) increased to statistically significant levels from day 8 to 15 post-treatment with PTIC versus placebo.

At day 8 post-treatment, PTIC decreased serum IP-10, IL-8, M-CSF, HGF, and IL-1RA while increasing stem cell factor (SCF) and TRAIL, a cytokine/chemokine pattern indicating reduced pathogen-induced hyperinflammation.
Migration inhibitory factor (MIF) decreased on day 8 and eotaxin decreased on day 90 post-treatment with PTIC.
A higher proportion of PTIC-treated patients retained oxygen saturation ≥92% at days 8, 15, and 90 post-treatment compared with placebo.
Serum IP-10 (CXCL10) levels were significantly decreased following PTIC treatment compared to placebo.
Serum IL-8 levels decreased significantly with PTIC treatment relative to placebo.
Human M-CSF serum levels decreased on day 8 post-treatment with PTIC compared to placebo.
Serum HGF levels decreased on day 8 post-treatment with PTIC compared to placebo.
Serum IL-1RA levels decreased on day 8 post-treatment with PTIC compared to placebo.
Stem cell factor (SCF) serum levels increased on day 8 post-treatment with PTIC compared to placebo.
TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL) serum levels increased on day 8 post-treatment with PTIC compared to placebo.
Migration inhibitory factor (MIF) levels decreased on day 8 post-treatment with PTIC.
Eotaxin levels decreased on day 90 post-treatment with PTIC compared to placebo.
A higher proportion of PTIC-treated patients maintained oxygen saturation ≥92% at days 8, 15, and 90 post-treatment compared to placebo, reaching significance at day 15.
Mean oxygen saturation was significantly higher in the PTIC group than placebo at days 8 and 15 post-treatment, but not at day 90.
PTIC treatment produced significant improvements in dyspnea, cough, headache, and chronic fatigue syndrome intensity compared to placebo during treatment and follow-up.
Patients treated with PTIC did not present chronic fatigue syndrome symptoms at follow-up, in contrast to patients treated with placebo, suggesting a preventive effect against long-COVID fatigue.
All PTIC-treated patients had normal spirometry at 90 days post-treatment, whereas nearly a quarter of placebo patients had a mild restrictive pattern.
High-sensitivity CRP serum levels were significantly lower in PTIC-treated patients compared to placebo at days 8, 15, and 90 post-treatment.
Serum lactate dehydrogenase levels decreased on day 8 after PTIC treatment compared to placebo, consistent with reduced cell damage.
Serum albumin levels increased at days 15 and 90 post-treatment with PTIC compared to placebo, indicating an improved prognosis.
The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) decreased on day 8 after PTIC treatment compared to placebo.
In an external multivariate analysis cited by the authors, the percentage of macrophages in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) correlated with poor outcome in COVID-19 patients.

The authors note that the urokinase plasminogen activator receptor-associated protein (uPARAP/Endo180), a mannose receptor family member, is a plausible alternative or additional receptor for type I collagen not addressed in this study.

A cited LAIR1 knockout mouse study found upregulation of PI3K/AKT, p38, STAT-3, iNOS, and TLR signaling, along with NF-κB pathway genes (Myd88, Cd40, Rel) and cytokine storm genes (Il1b, Ccl2, Cxcl1, Cxcl10, Il12b) compared to wild-type.

A cited study reported that LAIR1 ligation on purified monocytes inhibited LPS-induced mRNA expression of il-6, tnf, il8, ccl2, cxcl10, tlr7, il10, and stat1, and reduced IL-8, TNF-α, IL-6, and IP-10 protein expression.
GSLS treatment prolonged swim time-to-exhaustion in a forced exhaustion swimming test in CFS model mice, indicating an anti-fatigue effect.
GSLS reduced escape latency in the Morris water maze test in CFS mice, indicating improved spatial memory/learning.
Pathological examination showed GSLS protected both peripheral (liver) and central (hippocampus) tissues from CFS-induced damage.
Biochemical index testing indicated that GSLS mitigate peripheral fatigue by reducing energy expenditure and oxidative damage and by inhibiting production of harmful metabolites.
GSLS altered abnormal brain levels of 14 neurotransmitters in CFS mice, with seven upregulated and seven downregulated, implicating neurotransmitter regulation in mitigating central fatigue.
Serum metabolomics analysis identified alterations in 19 metabolites across 11 metabolic pathways associated with GSLS treatment of CFS.
Bone mineral density did not differ significantly between women with hypermobile EDS and those with classical EDS across all assessed femoral and lumbar spine sites.
Multivariate logistic regression showed no evidence that the hypermobile EDS subtype increases the risk of a Z-score below -2.0 (low bone mass) compared to classical EDS.
Over half (56.7%) of EDS patients in the cohort reported a history of fractures, predominantly of the upper limb.
Vitamin D deficiency was common in the cohort, and mean vitamin D concentration was significantly lower in patients with classical EDS compared to those with hypermobile EDS.

No significant differences were found between hypermobile and classical EDS groups in markers of calcium-phosphate metabolism and bone turnover, including total calcium, inorganic phosphate, parathormone, bone-specific alkaline phosphatase, beta-CrossLaps, and osteocalcin.
Age-matched BMD Z-scores at the femoral Ward's triangle and trochanter were lower than the age-matched BMD Z-score of the lumbar spine (L1-L4) in both EDS groups.

Among 43,801 unique patients in the Swedish quality registry for pain rehabilitation, 2.8% carried an HSD/hEDS diagnosis, a higher proportion than the 1.9% previously reported for 1998-2016 in the same registry.
The HSD/hEDS group was on average nearly a decade younger than the reference group of mixed chronic pain patients.
The HSD/hEDS group had a substantially higher proportion of women than the reference group.

More people in the HSD/hEDS group were engaged in work, work training, or studies compared to the reference group, and fewer received social insurance compensation or reported physician visits due to pain in the past year.
People with HSD/hEDS reported an earlier onset of pain, on average 4 years earlier than the reference group.
Despite more pain locations and higher persistence, the HSD/hEDS group reported lower pain intensity during the last week compared to the reference group.
The HSD/hEDS group reported significantly more distinct pain locations than the reference group, with pain most commonly located in the lower back, shoulders, and hip/seat in both groups.
A higher percentage of the HSD/hEDS group reported persistent pain compared with the reference group, while intermittent pain rates were similar.

The HSD/hEDS and reference groups showed similar overall patterns of activity interference from pain, but the HSD/hEDS group had significantly less interference in 5 of 11 MPI-S subscales, including participation in activities, activity restriction, enjoyment with family/friends, changed relationships, and job satisfaction impact.
Change in work ability since pain onset was the most affected MPI-S item in both groups, while changed relationships showed the lowest impact score in both groups.
In multivariable regression, the number of pain locations significantly predicted pain intensity in the HSD/hEDS group, whereas whether pain was persistent or intermittent did not.
In the reference group, unlike HSD/hEDS, both the number of pain locations and whether pain was persistent or intermittent significantly predicted pain intensity.
Both pain intensity and the number of pain locations significantly explained interference in daily activities for both the HSD/hEDS and reference groups.

Onset of pain (i.e., age or duration since onset) was not a significant predictor of interference in daily activities for the HSD/hEDS group, and was only marginally significant for the reference group.
Individuals with joint hypermobility frequently experience joint pain and have a high incidence of comorbid fibromyalgia.
Prevalence of joint hypermobility as measured by the Beighton scale varies widely (2-57%) depending on the population assessed, including ethnic variation.
Estrogen inhibits lysyl oxidase activity in engineered ligaments and decreases their mechanical function in a dose-dependent manner, though some doses used exceeded physiological levels.

Serum relaxin levels peak during the menstrual cycle at a time corresponding to highest risk for ACL injury, and the ACL expresses relaxin receptors, though this remains mainly a correlational finding in humans.
Serum relaxin levels have been reported to be higher in females with benign hypermobility syndrome compared to those without, though menstrual cycle timing was not accounted for.
Antisense gene therapy targeting decorin increased large collagen fibril formation and partially improved mechanical function in healing rabbit MCL scar tissue, but the response was inconsistent.
Fibromodulin knockout mice show a fourfold increase in lumican expression and deposition in tendons, indicating a compensatory relationship between small leucine-rich proteoglycans.
The biglycan gene is located on the X chromosome and is subject to X-inactivation in females, proposed as a possible contributor to sex differences in joint hypermobility.
Muscle integrity and physical fitness are reported to be compromised in children with heritable connective tissue syndromes involving joint hypermobility, as well as bone integrity.
Dysregulated TGF-beta signaling associated with fibrillin gene mutations in Marfan syndrome may underlie compromised muscle integrity in affected individuals.
Wound healing is compromised in individuals with various forms of EDS, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, and Marfan syndrome, primarily documented in skin injuries.
ACL reconstructions using autologous graft tissue in EDS patients have resulted in good functional repair and maintenance of joint stability for several years.
Reports on pregnancy in individuals with hypermobility-type EDS or hypermobility spectrum disorders indicate a high rate of successful pregnancies with no obvious increase in joint injuries.
A subset of individuals with hEDS have a reported higher incidence of dysregulated menstrual cycles, which may complicate assessment of menstrual joint laxity changes in this population.

Collagen fibril diameters in tissues from individuals with joint hypermobility disorders are variable depending on the specific mutation involved, indicating hypermobility is not consistently correlated with uniformly small collagen fibrils.
Neuromuscular training programs such as FIFA-11+ can lower the elevated female ACL injury rate to levels observed in males, but the benefit reverts once the program is stopped.

The review proposes that disruption of mechanotransduction (via integrins, piezo-1/2, TRPV4) rather than the specific mutated molecule itself may underlie the common phenotype of joint hypermobility across genetically diverse syndromes.

The overall estimated frequency of joint hypermobility syndromes is approximately 1 in fewer than 1000 individuals, involving a broad range of mutated molecule classes including collagens, proteoglycans, glycoproteins, enzymes, growth factors, and receptors.
A novel heterozygous missense mutation in COL5A1 (c.386G>T) was identified in an infant with severe classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
A variant in COL1A2 was also identified in the infant but did not segregate with the disease phenotype in the family.
The infant's clinical presentation of classical EDS was more severe than that of his mother and grandmother despite carrying the same familial genetic background, illustrating variable expressivity.

Management of the infant's severe cEDS included vitamin D and iron supplementation, physiotherapy, and avoidance of excessive stretching, with later surgical intervention required for cervical dislocation.
Four studies using CBT-based psychosocial interventions (some combined with physiotherapy) all found statistically significant improvements in QoL-related outcome measures in people with EDS/JHMS.

Two studies using mindfulness-based psychosocial interventions (one face-to-face, one online) both found statistically significant improvements in QoL-related outcome measures in people with EDS/JHMS.

A 12-week cognitive behavioural and physiotherapy intervention delivered by a multi-disciplinary team was associated with a statistically significant change in pain-related outcome measures pre- to post-intervention.

In a 6-week CBT-based outpatient rehabilitation programme, pain self-efficacy, disability, and DAPOS anxiety/depression scores improved significantly at 5-month follow-up, but average pain intensity did not significantly change.

Overall, the six included studies were judged methodologically weak (five 'weak', one 'moderate' on EPHPP quality assessment), limiting confidence in the reported benefits of psychosocial interventions for EDS/JHMS.
None of the included studies reported effect sizes, which the authors note limits interpretation of the clinical meaningfulness of the statistically significant results.
The systematic review identified only six eligible studies across multiple databases, indicating a substantial evidence gap regarding psychosocial interventions for QoL in EDS/JHMS.
Hypermobile patients with neck pain had a significantly lower C0-2 Cobb angle than non-hypermobile neck pain patients.
Hypermobile neck pain patients showed a decreased C2-7 angle as measured by Jackson physiological stress lines compared to non-hypermobile neck pain patients.
Hypermobile neck pain patients had increased cranial tilt compared to non-hypermobile neck pain patients.
Hypermobile neck pain patients had a greater C2-7 sagittal vertical axis compared to non-hypermobile neck pain patients.
No significant differences in neck disability were observed between hypermobile and non-hypermobile neck pain patients.
No significant differences in health-related quality of life were observed between hypermobile and non-hypermobile neck pain patients.
Among hypermobile patients with neck pain, a more physiologic cervical lordosis was weakly associated with lower neck disability scores.
87.5% of patients assessed at the GoodHope EDS Clinic self-reported a lifetime history of anxiety or depression on the intake screening questionnaire.

Individuals diagnosed with G-HSD had significantly greater odds of self-reporting a history of anxiety or depression than those not diagnosed with EDS/G-HSD or those with non-hypermobile EDS subtypes.
Self-reported disordered eating, PTSD, self-harm, and suicidal behavior were all reported at rates well above general population lifetime prevalence.

On clinician history-taking, the majority of patients across diagnostic groups reported a history of anxiety (62%) and depression (53%), while PTSD, personality disorder, OCD, suicide attempts, current suicidal ideation and self-harm were reported less frequently but still above population norms.
G-HSD patients had significantly greater odds of a clinician-recorded history of depression and anxiety compared to those with non-hypermobile EDS subtypes.
There were no significant differences by diagnostic category in patient-reported history of PTSD, personality disorder, or obsessive-compulsive disorder.
Dysphoria scores on the IDAS-D did not differ significantly across diagnostic categories (non-hypermobile EDS, hEDS, G-HSD, not-EDS/G-HSD).
43.4% of patients across all diagnostic groups screened positive for likely internalizing disorder based on the validated IDAS-D cutoff, with no significant difference between diagnostic categories.

Borderline personality symptom severity (BSL-23) did not differ significantly by diagnostic category, and 20.1% of the total sample screened positive for likely borderline personality disorder with no significant group differences in this rate.

Pain intensity, fatigue, and self-reported autonomic dysfunction (COMPASS-31) differed significantly by diagnostic category, with individuals with hEDS, G-HSD, and not-EDS/G-HSD reporting greater pain, fatigue, and autonomic dysfunction than those with non-hypermobile EDS subtypes.
