Mental health concern rates largely did not differ between individuals diagnosed with EDS/G-HSD and those referred but ruled out for EDS/G-HSD who nonetheless presented with complex chronic pain, suggesting that a non-diagnosed comparison group with similar symptom burden may not represent a well-matched 'healthy' control as used in prior case-control studies.
The Spider pain domain showed a strong positive correlation with the CALI-9 activity limitation measure among adolescents with symptomatic hypermobility.
The Spider fatigue domain showed a strong negative correlation with the Peds-QL Multidimensional Fatigue Scale, consistent with the MFS's reverse scoring.
The Spider depression domain was strongly correlated with the RCADS-25 depression subscale.
The Spider anxiety domain showed a moderate correlation with the RCADS-25 anxiety subscale.
The Spider cardiac dysautonomia domain showed a strong correlation with the orthostatic subscale of the COMPASS-31.
The Spider neuromusculoskeletal domain showed a strong correlation with selected sections of the Bristol Impact of Hypermobility (BIoH) questionnaire.
The Spider urogenital domain showed a moderate correlation with the Dysfunctional Voiding Scoring System (DVSS).
The Spider gastrointestinal domain showed a strong negative correlation with the Peds-QL Gastrointestinal Symptoms scale, consistent with reverse scoring of the comparator.
Adolescents with symptomatic hypermobility had significantly higher Spider pain domain scores than non-hypermobile controls.
Adolescents with symptomatic hypermobility had significantly higher Spider fatigue domain scores than non-hypermobile controls.
Adolescents with symptomatic hypermobility had significantly higher Spider anxiety domain scores than non-hypermobile controls.
Adolescents with symptomatic hypermobility had significantly higher Spider depression domain scores than non-hypermobile controls.
Adolescents with symptomatic hypermobility had significantly higher Spider cardiac dysautonomia domain scores than non-hypermobile controls.
Adolescents with symptomatic hypermobility had significantly higher Spider neuromusculoskeletal domain scores than non-hypermobile controls.
The Spider urogenital domain did not significantly differentiate between the symptomatic hypermobility group and non-hypermobile controls, likely due to low symptom reporting.
Adolescents with symptomatic hypermobility had significantly higher Spider gastrointestinal domain scores than non-hypermobile controls.

A scoping review of 54 studies found that musculoskeletal characteristics were reported in 85% of studies of adolescents with HSD/hEDS, cardiovascular (including orthostatic intolerance) in 37%, fatigue in 24%, gastrointestinal in 22%, urogenital in 15%, and psychosocial features in 11%.
A survey of American clinicians found only 24% regarded HSD/hEDS as multisystemic, and only 4.4%-18.9% recognized associated comorbidities such as fatigue, anxiety, and bowel disorders.
A prior study reported that 99% of participants with HSD/hEDS had unmet medical needs.
A UK-based study reported the prevalence of HSD/hEDS as 194.2 per 100,000, approximately 1000 times more common than rheumatoid arthritis and nearly as prevalent as fibromyalgia.

Addition of irbesartan to celiprolol reduced the composite risk of fatal/nonfatal arterial events or new/worsening arterial lesions in patients with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome compared with placebo.
Irbesartan lowered the risk of recurrent symptomatic or nonsymptomatic arterial events compared with placebo.
A reduction of progression of arterial lesions was observed at all vascular sites assessed with irbesartan treatment.
Irbesartan significantly reduced systolic blood pressure compared with placebo, but this reduction was not related to the reduction in the primary composite arterial event outcome.
Irbesartan treatment was associated with episodes of hypotension, requiring downtitration in some patients.
24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring identified hypertension in 40% of patients with vascular EDS.
A quarter of patients classified as hypertensive by ABPM had normal office BP readings, indicating masked hypertension in vEDS.

Baseline pulse pressure coefficient of variation strongly correlated with its reduction following celiprolol therapy, suggesting celiprolol reduces short-term PP variability proportionally to its initial magnitude.
Two of four patients who experienced vascular events during the study period had the highest short-term pulse pressure variability values in the entire cohort, suggesting a possible prognostic link.
Hypermobility assessed by the Bulbena score was significantly more frequent in malignant hyperthermia (MH) susceptible patients than in healthy controls.
Hypermobility was also significantly more frequent in MH patients than in non-MH-susceptible relatives of MH patients.

Goniometric assessment in a subset of 11 MH patients versus 11 matched controls showed significantly larger range of motion (ROM) in mostly proximal joints (elbow and knee hyperextension, hip abduction, shoulder external rotation, knee flexion) in the MH group.
Among 7 unrelated MH families with identified RYR1 gene variants, five (71%) presented hypermobility, suggesting hypermobility may be associated with certain RYR1 variants causing MH.

Four of the identified RYR1 variants were already listed as diagnostic variants by the European Malignant Hyperthermia Group, three previously reported with MH and associated myopathy and one with MH but no associated myopathy.
A novel RYR1 variant (p.Phe41Ser) was identified that had not previously been reported in association with MH, only with associated myopathy.

A probably pathogenic CACNA1S variant previously reported in association with MH was identified in one family; the patient did not present hypokalemic periodic paralysis, a phenotype otherwise linked to CACNA1S variants.

Within the MH group, there was no significant difference between patients with and without hypermobility regarding age, sex, clinical complaints, osteoarticular dysmorphisms, CK levels, IVCT result, or contracture intensity.
No difference in hypermobility frequency was found between the MHSh and MHShc functional subgroups, despite prior proposals that they differ in resting cytosolic calcium.
Unlike the general population, presence of hypermobility in MH patients was not associated with age or sex.

The authors hypothesize that hypermobility in MH patients may arise from RYR1-related calcium dysregulation affecting fibroblasts of tendons/ligaments and collagen production, rather than from muscle weakness, since MH patients with hypermobility had no muscle weakness.
Of 796 patients referred for suspected connective tissue disorders, 53.6% were referred with suspicion of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and molecular confirmation was achieved in 60 cases.
28.1% of registry patients were referred with suspicion of osteogenesis imperfecta, and molecular confirmation was achieved in 98 cases via genetic testing.
In-depth analysis of 173 OI patients found that the majority of cases were caused by mutations in COL1A1.
In-depth analysis of 173 OI patients found that the majority of cases were caused by mutations in COL1A2.
Rarer causative variants were identified in additional genes involved in collagen synthesis and bone regulation among OI patients.
Genotype-phenotype correlation analysis showed that glycine substitutions in COL1A1 and COL1A2 were more prevalent among patients with severe OI phenotypes.

A Japanese population-based cohort study of 126 million individuals over 10 years found an incidence of angioid streaks of 0.52 per 100,000 person-years and pseudoxanthoma elasticum of 0.08 per 100,000 person-years, with overlap observed in 363 patients.
A retrospective cross-sectional study of 1852 angioid streak cases found PXE as the identified systemic association in 12.3% of patients.
In the same cross-sectional study, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome was identified as the underlying systemic association in 1% of angioid streak cases.
After a diagnosis of angioid streaks, an underlying systemic disease association is identified in up to 50% of patients.

The ABCC6 gene encodes a 165 kDa ATP-binding cassette transporter localized primarily in hepatocytes that promotes ATP efflux; reduced activity of this transporter leads to low plasma pyrophosphate (PPi), a critical anti-mineralization factor, underlying PXE pathogenesis.
ENPP1 gene variants are associated with generalized arterial calcification of infancy overlapping with the PXE phenotype.
GGCX gene variants are associated with vitamin K-dependent coagulation defects in PXE-related genetic subtypes.
Pseudoxanthoma elasticum is distinguished by lower levels of inorganic plasma pyrophosphate (PPi), a calcification inhibitor.

The 46-year-old female case patient with a 20-year history of angioid streaks presented with progressive vision loss and metamorphopsia due to bilateral angioid streaks with active choroidal neovascularization in the left eye; diagnosis of PXE was confirmed by angioid streaks larger than an optic disc diameter, characteristic skin findings, and histopathology showing short, fragmented, basophilic elastic fibers.
Three intravitreal aflibercept injections improved best-corrected visual acuity from 0.3 to 0.9 in the affected left eye and reduced subretinal fluid, while the right eye remained stable.

Cardiology evaluation of the case patient revealed grade II hypertension, extrasystolic arrhythmia (Lown class II), and calcareous plaques of the abdominal aorta on CT angiography, consistent with PXE-related vascular mineralization.

In a study of 23 eyes of 20 PXE patients treated with aflibercept for active CNV over 48 weeks, central retinal thickness was significantly reduced and 81.8% of eyes remained stable within 15 letters of visual acuity.

A 12-month prospective clinical trial of 15 PXE patients with active CNV treated with aflibercept using a pro-re-nata regimen found BCVA improvement (not statistically significant) and a significant decrease in central retinal thickness.

In 14 eyes of 13 patients switched from ranibizumab to aflibercept for refractory/recurrent CNV, central retinal thickness decreased significantly and 71% of patients had no intraretinal/subretinal fluid after 12 months.

A study of 33 eyes of 23 PXE patients found a relatively poor long-term visual prognosis, with best-corrected visual acuity decreasing over a mean follow-up of 109 ± 42 months despite anti-VEGF treatment.
Classic choroidal neovascularization has a worse visual prognosis than other CNV subtypes because it may progress to fibrotic scarring with consequent worsening of visual acuity.

Biallelic pathogenic COL12A1 variants cause a myopathic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (COL12A1-related disease) characterized by congenital hypotonia, joint hyperlaxity with contractures, variable muscle weakness, and MRI-evident muscle involvement.

Patients with biallelic loss-of-function variants affecting both COL12A1 long and short isoforms had a severe congenital phenotype with profound weakness, respiratory insufficiency, and minimal motor milestone attainment, whereas variants sparing the short isoform were associated with milder disease.

Fibroblasts from patient F1P1, homozygous/compound heterozygous for LoF variants affecting both isoforms, showed no detectable intracellular or extracellular Collagen XII immunoreactivity compared to control.

Patient F4P4, homozygous for a variant affecting the long isoform only, showed reduced intracellular/extracellular Collagen XII immunoreactivity and barely detectable secreted Collagen XII in conditioned medium.

Patient F5P5, compound heterozygous for a LoF allele and a novel missense variant (p.A1110D) affecting only the long isoform, showed no significant Collagen XII abnormality by immunofluorescence compared to control, though secreted protein in conditioned medium was reduced.

A novel missense variant p.A1110D in COL12A1, absent from gnomAD and highly conserved with inconsistent in silico predictions, was identified as a paternally inherited allele in two affected siblings and had not previously been reported to cause disease.
COL12A1 is highly constrained for loss-of-function variation in the general population, with only 102 of 320.4 expected predicted LoF variants observed in gnomAD v4.0.0.

Gingival hypertrophy was a common dysmorphic feature seen in six of eight patients with biallelic COL12A1 variants, along with micrognathia, dental abnormalities, bluish sclerae, and myopathic facies.
All patients exhibited distal joint hyperlaxity typically affecting wrists and ankles, with concurrent joint contractures (present in six patients) commonly affecting long finger flexors and knees.
Creatine kinase levels were normal in four patients but mildly elevated (approximately 500 U/L range) in two patients (F2P2 and F6P7).

Muscle MRI in the three milder patients (F4P4, F5P5, F7P8) showed a distinctive pattern with predominant posterior thigh/hamstring involvement and relative sparing of medial and anterior compartments, distinct from the 'central cloud' rectus femoris/vastus lateralis rimmed pattern typical of COL6-related dystrophy.

Cardiac involvement was found in four patients, including one with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome and others with mild valvular anomalies (thickened mitral valve leaflets, mitral regurgitation, dysplastic mitral/tricuspid valves).

Three patients (F4P4, F5P5, F5P6) with biallelic COL12A1 variants presented with a milder disease course, achieving independent ambulation at ages 3 years, 15 months, and 16 months respectively, expanding the phenotypic spectrum beyond the originally described severe congenital phenotype.

Muscle biopsies in four patients showed subtle variation in fiber size consistent with a mild myopathic process without dystrophic features, supporting a concomitant myopathic process alongside the connective tissue disorder.

COL12A1-related disease (myopathic EDS) is clinically distinguishable from Collagen VI-related dystrophy (COL6-RD) by more widespread joint laxity affecting larger joints, less prominent contractures, nonprogressive muscle weakness allowing functional improvement, and distinct oral phenotypic features (gingival/dental abnormalities) atypical for COL6-RD.
Progressive scoliosis requiring spinal surgery occurred in three patients (F2P2, F6P7, F7P8), with progressive thoracic kyphoscoliosis noted in two others (F1P1, F3P3).
Generalized joint hypermobility, assessed via a per-leg Beighton score, was not associated with risk of non-contact ACL injury in female team sport athletes.

Side-to-side difference in AP knee laxity measured by KT-1000 arthrometer was not significantly associated with non-contact ACL injury risk, though prevalence of SSD >2 mm was somewhat higher in the injury group.
Baseline knee hyperextension (genu recurvatum), measured with a goniometer, was not associated with non-contact ACL injury risk.
Femoral anteversion angle measured by Craig's test was not significantly associated with non-contact ACL injury risk, consistent with a recent systematic review.
Hamstring extensibility, measured as static knee range of motion, was not associated with non-contact ACL injury risk in this cohort.
Navicular drop, a measure of foot pronation, was not associated with non-contact ACL injury risk, consistent with other prospective cohort studies.
Anieto et al. found no direct correlation between generalized joint hypermobility (GJH) and fitness or motor performance.
de Boer et al. found no significant association between GJH and total motor performance.

de Boer et al. found a positive relationship between manual dexterity and motor performance specifically in girls with higher Beighton scores, though the effect appeared to decrease with increasing body mass index.
Engelbert et al. found no significant correlation between the number of hypermobile joints and delayed motor development.
Yardımcı and Mutlu found no significant differences in cognitive, language, proprioception, and motor domains between toddlers with and without GJH.
Fatoye et al. found children with GJH showed higher levels of passive range of motion compared to children without GJH.
Fatoye et al. found no significant difference in gait speed between children with and without GJH.

Nikolajsen et al. observed differences in walking kinetics in children with GJH, indicating a different underlying biomechanical strategy even though overall gait pattern appeared similar to healthy children.
Hanewinkel et al. found no significant association between GJH and 6-Minute Walk Test performance, suggesting GJH might not impact aerobic capacity or endurance.
Both Juul et al. and Moore et al. found no significant difference in physical activity levels between children with and without GJH.

Wright et al. found that typically developing children scored significantly higher on the RTSBc coordination test than children at risk of low motor coordination or already classified with low motor coordination.
Sobhani et al. reported a cumulative GJH prevalence of 34.1%, with variation based on gender and age.
Blajwajs et al. assessed GJH broadly and noted variation in prevalence across ethnic groups, age, gender, and measurement parameters used.
This review, consistent with Romeo et al., identified overlap in symptoms and motor difficulties between children with developmental coordination disorder and those with joint hypermobility.
Anieto et al. and Juul et al. together demonstrated both beneficial and detrimental effects of GJH on motor performance, reflecting a broader dichotomy seen across the included studies.
Serum miR-217 fold-change expression was significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum miR-532 fold-change expression was significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
There was a statistically significant difference in serum AST levels between fibromyalgia patients and controls, though clinical significance is uncertain.
Serum miR-217 levels showed a significant negative correlation with AST levels in fibromyalgia patients.
Serum miR-532 levels showed a significant negative correlation with AST levels in fibromyalgia patients.
Nearly all participants across the three groups showed clinically significant fatigue impairment on the MFIS, though the proportion differed significantly by group (highest in PCC, lowest in MS).

PCC and fibromyalgia patients reported significantly higher fatigue intensity than MS patients across multiple domains including tiredness/lack of energy, need for more sleep, muscular weakness, pain, concentration difficulties, and impact on physical activity.
PCC patients alone scored significantly higher than MS patients in the perceived impact of fatigue on life and feeling bad about being tired.
Fibromyalgia patients alone scored significantly higher than MS patients on apathy, persistent tiredness regardless of physical activity, and fatigue interfering with sexual desire.
No statistically significant differences were found between PCC and fibromyalgia patients on any item of the Fatigue Intensity Scale.
The FICS Intensity Scale showed strong concurrent validity, correlating significantly with the established MFIS total score.

MS patients scored higher than PCC and fibromyalgia patients in the negative impact of mood on fatigue, fatigue worsening with heat, greater improvement of fatigue after rest, and reduced fatigue from motivational activities.
Fibromyalgia patients scored significantly higher than both MS and PCC patients in fatigue accompanied by muscle pain, supporting a pain-fatigue interplay specific to fibromyalgia.

PCC and fibromyalgia patients scored higher than MS patients in delayed fatigue after exertion (post-exertional malaise), fatigue accompanied by headaches and joint pain, and episodes of worsening fatigue, though these effects lost significance after controlling for fatigue severity, suggesting they mark severity rather than disease specificity.

PCC patients reported greater fatigue worsening with cold exposure than MS patients, a novel finding possibly linked to dysautonomia, while MS patients needed more breaks during physical exercise than PCC; the cold-sensitivity finding lost significance after adjusting for fatigue severity.

No significant differences were found across the three groups in cognitive fatigue-related items, motivation, breaks needed after activity, energy depletion, meal-related fatigue changes, physical vs mental fatigue predominance, or difficulty predicting fatigue onset.

Autoimmune disease diagnosis prevalence differed significantly among groups, with PCC patients showing the lowest percentage and fibromyalgia patients showing a significantly higher percentage than MS patients.

Women with multiple nociplastic pain conditions in comorbidity (MIX group) reported significantly higher total traumatic experience scores than healthy controls, vulvodynia, and chronic headache groups.
MIX group scored significantly higher on emotional neglect than other groups, indicating greater childhood emotional neglect among women with comorbid nociplastic pain conditions.
The MIX group differed significantly from the chronic headache group on emotional abuse scores, showing higher levels of reported emotional abuse.
Both MIX and fibromyalgia groups reported higher bodily threat trauma scores than healthy controls and vulvodynia patients, with no difference between MIX and FM.
Although the overall model for physical abuse trauma scores was significant across groups, no specific pairwise group differences reached significance in post-hoc tests.
The overall model for sexual approach trauma was significant across groups, but no pairwise group differences were significant in post-hoc testing.
The overall model for sexual abuse trauma was significant across groups, but no pairwise group differences were significant in post-hoc testing.
Healthy controls showed significantly better (higher) overall defensive functioning scores than the MIX group.
Healthy controls scored significantly higher on mature defense mechanisms than both the MIX and fibromyalgia groups.

Fibromyalgia and MIX groups scored highest on neurotic defense mechanisms, differing significantly from vulvodynia and healthy controls, with FM also higher than chronic headache, which in turn was higher than vulvodynia.
Although the overall model for immature defense mechanisms was significant across groups, no specific pairwise differences were significant in post-hoc analysis.
Healthy controls scored significantly lower on total alexithymia than the chronic pain groups, indicating less alexithymic difficulty among controls compared to CH, FM, VU, and MIX patients.
Fibromyalgia and MIX groups scored significantly higher than healthy controls on the Externally Oriented Thinking subscale of alexithymia.
Healthy controls scored significantly lower than all chronic pain groups on Difficulty Identifying Feelings, and chronic headache patients scored lower than fibromyalgia and MIX groups.
Although the overall model for Difficulty Describing Feelings was significant across groups, no pairwise group differences reached significance in post-hoc tests.
In patient 1, acute serum tryptase rose 5.4-fold over baseline (12.5 to 72.4 ng/mL) during an anaphylactic reaction to yellow jacket stings.
In patient 1, urinary LTE4 increased 126-fold from baseline (53 to 6,700 pg/mg creatinine) during acute MCAS, the largest relative increase of any mediator measured.
Across all three patients, N-methylhistamine showed the smallest relative acute/baseline increase compared to LTE4 and (2,3-dinor)-11β-PGF2α.
Urinary PGD2 metabolite (2,3-dinor)-11β-PGF2α increased markedly in all three patients during acute MCAS episodes, exceeding N-MH increases but generally below LTE4 increases.
Patient 1 with cutaneous mastocytosis tested positive for the KIT Asp816Val mutation with a negative bone marrow biopsy, while subsequent TPSAB1 mutation testing was negative.

Following identification of markedly elevated acute LTE4 in patient 1, treatment was intensified (doubled fexofenadine, increased aspirin, added montelukast), and the patient subsequently had no reaction to 3 further yellow jacket stings.

Patient 2 was started on cetirizine, famotidine, montelukast, and increasing-dose aspirin after her acute mediator profile showed elevated LTE4 and PGD2 metabolite but minimal N-MH rise, and she subsequently had no further attacks.

Patient 3 developed postoperative anaphylaxis with hypotension, urticaria, and wheezing within 5 minutes of intravenous sugammadex infusion, with subsequent labs showing acute elevations in tryptase and all three urinary MC mediator metabolites.

In a prior series cited by the authors, LTE4 showed the greatest average acute/baseline increase (average ratio 35.98) among the three urinary MC mediator metabolites accompanying 20%+2 tryptase rises.

Per a 2024 review cited by the authors, acute/baseline threshold ratios of N-MH (>1.7), (2,3-dinor)-11β-PGF2α (>1.6), and LTE4 (>1.87) were associated with mast cell activation in perioperative anaphylaxis patients with inconclusive tryptase.

The authors note that in anaphylactic patients with elevated LTE4 excretion, no corresponding increase in urinary eosinophil-derived neurotoxin was detected in cited literature, arguing against eosinophils as the primary LTE4 source in MCAS/anaphylaxis.
Children born to women with IBD had a modestly increased risk of major congenital anomalies compared with matched children of women without IBD.
The elevated overall risk of congenital anomalies in children of women with IBD was partly driven by increased risks of heart defects and urinary system anomalies.
The risk of major congenital anomalies was similar between children of women with ulcerative colitis and those with Crohn's disease.
Periconceptional histological inflammation, compared with histological remission, did not significantly influence the risk of major congenital anomalies in the child.
Clinically active IBD, compared with quiescent disease around conception, was not associated with an increased risk of major congenital anomalies in the child.
The paper states that systemic mast cell activation disease has a prevalence of 17% in Germany, meaning gastroenterologists frequently encounter it in practice.

Gain-of-function STAT6 mutations cause a primary atopic disorder with severe early-onset atopy, GI involvement, and skeletal abnormalities including joint hyperextensibility and vascular abnormalities in about a third of patients.
STAT3 AD-HIES (Job syndrome) presents with eczema, infections, and skeletal/connective tissue abnormalities including bone fragility, scoliosis, and vascular abnormalities.

ERBIN protein deficiency presents with eczema, eosinophilic esophagitis, recurrent respiratory infections, high IgE, and skeletal/connective tissue abnormalities including joint hypermobility and vascular abnormalities.
Loeys–Dietz syndrome, caused by AD TGFBR deficiency, is a Marfan-like connective tissue disorder with a notable prevalence of allergic disease.

Abnormal mast cell activation is described as one of the core immunopathological mechanisms in inborn errors of immunity with atopic phenotypes, alongside Th2/eosinophil-driven inflammation and IgE overproduction.
DOCK8 deficiency carries a substantial risk of severe allergic reactions including anaphylaxis, attributed to the highest ratio of food-specific IgE to total IgE among the HIES conditions discussed.
Dupilumab treatment in STAT3-AD-HIES patients has been reported across multiple studies to substantially improve cutaneous lesions, pruritus, and IgE levels.
Omalizumab use in STAT3-AD-HIES patients has been associated with improved skin signs, decreased serum IgE, and improved pulmonary manifestations.

Harrison et al. reported HSCT in STAT3-AD-HIES achieved a 100% survival rate with minimal peri-transplant complications, improved infection rates, resolution of skin disease, and stabilization/improvement of lung function.

HSCT is described as the only recommended curative option for DOCK8 deficiency, with best outcomes when performed early, resulting in reduced IgE, improved T/B cell function, and faster resolution of infections/eczema than food allergies.
A single ZNF341-deficient adult with severe atopic dermatitis showed significant clinical improvement and reduced IgE level after dupilumab administration.
Constitutive STAT3 phosphorylation caused by IL6ST mutation makes JAK inhibition (ruxolitinib or tofacitinib) an effective treatment option.
In STAT6 GOF patients unresponsive to corticosteroids, topical tacrolimus, methotrexate, and mepolizumab, JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib, tofacitinib) and dupilumab achieved clinical improvement.
In Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, biological agents anakinra (for autoinflammation) and omalizumab (for eczema resistant to systemic immunosuppression) have shown effectiveness in some studies.
